On Ecclesiastical Writers

Johannes Trithemius

Book on Ecclesiastical Writers.

2
Docto ac praestanti uiro domino Iohanni de Amerbach in artibus liberalibus Parisiensi magistro: Frater Iohannes de Lapide monachus ordinis Carthusien̄. sacrarū litterarū humilis indignus eiusdē studij professor: plurimā in domino salutem optat. Exhibuisti mihi nuper amatissime frater in domino: librū quēdam a reuerēdo doctissimoqꝫ patre domino Iohanne de Trittenhem abbate in Spanhem editū de Ecclesiasticis scriptoribus praetitulatū: postulans ut eum legendo respicerem: si dignū tua imp̄ssione censerem: qua multiplicandus in noticiā usum plurimorum uenire posset: te operā daturū ut res citius ꝑficeret spōdebas. Ego dilectioni tuae (cui nihil me negare fas est) morē gerere cupiens: animoqꝫ uolūtario ac prompto illū in manus suscipiēs legi (quāq apud te iam definitū suspicarer quid esses facturus) Quo diligēter pspecto examinato: nō reperti ullū opus oportunius his nr̄is temporibus manus meas incidere potuisse: qđ mihi acceptius cūctis litteraꝝ acererit: spōdebas. Inuenitur etenim multa praeclara volumina: quorū cum tituli auctores uel incogniti uel incerti ha beant: fit ut inter apocrypha deputent: Et ea inde ĩ neglectū in cōtemptū penitus uenire: nemo q recte sapit ignorat. Reperiunt praeterea nūc praesertim int lectroribꝰ imp̄ssos plurimi: quos suis auctoribus iniuste detractos alienis falso ascriptos esse cognoscimus. Quod utrum librariorū ignorantia: an odio uel fauore aut utilitatis cuiusuis gratia factū sit: meū nō est dijudicare. Eo tñ fit: ut illi afficint iniuria: isti aliorū studijs uane laudent: lectoribus quoqꝫ uaria errandi praestet libros imꝑssos plurimi: quos suis auctoris iniuste detractos alienis falsascriptus esse cognoscimus. Quod utrum librariorū ignora¬ tus: an odio uel fauores aut utilitatis cuiesuis gratia factum sit: meũ non est judicare. Et ea inde in neglectum et in contemptum penitus uenire: nemo que recte sapit ignorat. Reperiuntur praeterea, et nunc praesertim int lectroribus impessos plurimi: quos suis auctoribus iniuste detractos et alienis falsa scriptus esse cognoscimus. Quod utrum librarius ignorans: an odio vel fauorem aut utilitatis cuiusvis gratia factum sit: meũ non est judicare. Ego diligitur de rebus honestis scripserùm: siue uita defuncti sint: siue adhuc ea fungant: quoad fieri posset: in unũ colligeret uolumẽ: singulis singula sua opera addictendo. Verũ cũ huiuscemodi officiũ ꝑdifficile sit et ĩmensi laboris: uirũ requirit̃ industrium: rerũ gestarũ cognitorẽ: lectionibꝰ ac librarorũ reuolutõs infatigabile: nō est quisq̃ inuentus usque ad hoc praefens tem¬pus qui hoc attēptare praesumpserit: praeter illũ ante memoratum uirtutem: diuino spiritu afflatus suscitatus: ausus est id aggredi pugi li suo studio: singulari admūeto modo ordine: narratiõe uera: elegantiqꝫ sermone: coepit ac foeliciter ꝑfecit. Cui reuera totus litteratorum praeteritorum: praefentiũ: futurorum qđ coetus minime condignas ac debitas reddere poterit gratias. Habes itaque iã uir optime quid de oblato mihi libro sentiam: quāti eum ego faciam. Quam ob causam meo non solum consilio sed hortatu atque rogam curare uelis: ut que totius fieri possit impessioni tuae illum subijcias ꝑficias. Sic enim omnes bonarum artium cultores una cum collectore tibi facies sempiterna laude ac memoria obnoxios. Condigna praetereia mercedẽ a remuneratore omnium pro gloria sua laborantium altissimo deo recepturus. Vale frater amatissime: Ex domo Carth. Basil̃. v. Calend. Septembris Anno domini Mill̃. CCCC.XCIII.

To the learned and excellent man Master Johannes de Amerbach, Parisian master in the liberal arts, Brother Johannes de Lapide, monk of the Carthusian order, humble and unworthy professor of sacred letters and of the same study, wishes abundant greeting in the Lord.

Recently, most beloved brother in the Lord, you showed me a certain book, composed by the reverend and most learned father, Master Johannes de Trittenheim, abbot in Spanheim, entitled On Ecclesiastical Writers, asking that I look it over by reading it; if I should judge it worthy of your printing, by which, multiplied, it could come into the knowledge and use of very many, you promised that you would take pains for the matter to be completed more quickly. Wishing to accommodate your affection, to which it is not right for me to deny anything, and taking it into my hands with a willing and ready spirit, I read it, although I suspected that you had already decided what you were going to do. When it had been carefully inspected and examined, I found that no work more opportune for these times of ours could have come into my hands, nor anything more acceptable to all men of letters.

For many splendid volumes are found, whose titles or authors, since they are either unknown or uncertain, come to be reckoned among apocrypha; and from this they fall utterly into neglect and contempt, as no one who thinks rightly is ignorant. Furthermore, especially now among readers, very many printed books are found which we know have been unjustly taken away from their own authors and falsely ascribed to others. Whether this has been done through the ignorance of copyists, or from hatred or favor, or for the sake of some advantage, it is not for me to judge. Yet the result is that wrong is done to the former, the latter are vainly praised for the studies of others, and it offers readers various occasions for error. [The source scan here carries a second, degraded OCR capture of the foregoing sentences on misattributed printed books; not re-rendered. See ERRATA, 2026-07-10.]

I [unclear] concerning honorable matters, whether they are dead or are still living, so far as it could be done, he gathered into one volume, assigning to each his several works. But since an office of this kind is very difficult and of immense labor, and requires an industrious man, a knower of deeds done, untiring in readings and in the turning over of books, no one has been found up to this present time who presumed to attempt it, except that virtue mentioned before, breathed upon and raised up by the divine Spirit, who dared to undertake it with his little study, in a singularly admirable manner and order, with true narration and elegant speech; he began it and happily completed it. To him, indeed, the whole company of learned men past, present, and future will by no means be able to render fitting and due thanks.

You have, therefore, excellent man, what I think of the book offered to me, and how highly I esteem it. For this reason, not only by my counsel but by my exhortation and request, may you wish to take care that, as soon as it can be done, you submit it to your press and complete it. For thus you will make all cultivators of the good arts, together with the compiler, indebted to you with everlasting praise and remembrance. Moreover, you will receive a fitting reward from the rewarder of all who labor for his glory, the Most High God. Farewell, most beloved brother. From the Carthusian house of Basel, the fifth day before the Kalends of September, in the year of the Lord 1493.

| LIBER DE SCRIPTORIBVS ECCLESIATICIS Fol. I | | Disertissimi uiri Reuerēdiqꝫ in christo patris: dn̄i Iohānis de Trittenhem abbatis Spanhemensis: ad Reuerendissimum in christo patrem: dominū Iohannem de Dalberg Episcopū Vuormaciensem: (Epistola. | | REuerendissimo in christo patri et domino:dño Iohāni de Dalberg diuina prouidentia Vuoꝛmaciesi Epifcopo: Frater Iohānes:uoca- tus abbas in Spanhem:ordinis sancti Benedicti:modicum id quod est.Consueuerunt olim ueteres(reuerēdissime pater)si quid ope/ ris noui cudissent:ut robur firmitatem acciperet perpetuam:id uiris dicare praestantibus:quatenꝰ aemulorum lingua uenenata lu/ mine maiestatis reuerberata : dentem praui morsus nusq̃ualuislet infigere. Nec eos fallebat opinio:quae ex humilitate processit:cum doctis semp praesulibus ami/ ca sit in subditos laudibus attollenda benignitas:quae bonorū studia remunerat: prauorum coercet. Hoc nostri quoqꝫuetustatis exemplum pro posse imitantes: opera quae scriptitant dicata ecclesiarū praelatis ac uiris doctioribꝰ solent submit/ tere:ut eorū auctoritate comprobata: secure ualeant in publicum prodire. In lu- cem em̄ sine timore prodeūt:quae testimonio pontificis fulciunt̉. Nemo quippe ni stolidꝰ facile accusat: qđ iudicio maioꝛ comprobari nō ignorat.Tuto quiescit innocentia ouium:quā pastoris boni miseratio contuetur.Cum igit̉ exempla ue- terum nobis sint incitamenta uirtutū:dignum est ut eoꝛ imitemur mores sacros: quorum canimus laudes: quatenus dum ex illis atqꝫ ex nobis alij proficiunt: ordo ecclesiasticae hierarchiae inuiolabilis p̃feueret.Et licet minor sim q̇ ut meis opusculis quempiā delectari cōfidam:id tamen qđ habeo in dn̄i gaçophylacium humiliter offerre institui:in quo Crcoesi diuitijs aera duo uiduae iure praeferūt̉. Cũ itaqꝫnuper ad instantiā amicorū:Librū de scriptoribꝰ ecclesiasticis multo labore comportassem(quenadmodū res ipsa testatur)ne uestiğijs ueterum oberrarē: huncipsum laborem meū alicui uiro doctissimo ecclesiastica dignitate praestāti submittere decreui:cuius auctoritate beniuolentia dentes inuidorū sine morsu transiret.Cũqꝫ hinc multa cogitatio mihi succreuisset : cui eandem lucubratiūcu- lam confiderem gratiorem: se multi obtulere uacillant:i de quorū doctrina be/ niuolentia spes non modica ꝓmissa uigebat:inter quos tu mihi pater reuerēdissi/ me:potior:eminentior:doctioꝛ occurrifti:qui om̄es doctrina uincis: eruditiōe superas uniueros. In te nobilitas generis alti relucet: epifcopalis auctoꝛitas emi/ net:bonestas morū conspicit̉:bonarū artium omnimoda scientia collaudat̉.Nū talem poterimus uitū praeter te usq̇ inuenire:in quo baec omnia simul concutrrātet Inter alemanos neminet tibi pater reuerēdissime noui aequalem:in quo genus: di/ gnitas eruditio tanta refulgeant.Non loquoꝛ ad aurem:testis affit omīpotens: nec blandus capto laudator:quoniā germania om̄is te uitū undecūqꝫ peritissimū nō ignorat.Te colunt docti:te nobiles ac principes obseruant:tu nobis qđ Pla- to narratur fuisse Antimacho:tuo comprobatꝰ eloquio:dooctus merito iudicatur. Publica fama quae non mentit̓ agnouimus:q̃ profūda scientia in sacris litteris tibi abūdet:q̃ ꝑspicax interpretatio iuris:quāta deniqꝫ suauitas:dulcedo:leporqꝫ dicē- di ac perorandi: ut doctiffimis uiris:quorū in catalogo mentionē fecimus: te con/ ferendū nō dubitemꝰ. Testant hoc lucidissimae orationes quas habuisse diceris: testantur epistolae:testantur epigrāmata plura.Siquidē clarissima nominis tui fa/ ma:nō solum nostris Germanis: led Italis Gallis cū laude inotuit.Hinc subijt animū ut tanto tibi pontifici subiectum opus de scriptoribus ecclesiasticis infcri/ berem:dicarēqꝫ tuo nomini:quatenus sub umbra pontificalis culminis quiescerē securus.Sed dum intueor corusci luminis in te splendorem:reuerberor:retrahor totufqꝫ formidine tantae maiestatis tuae concutior: ne forte tibi patri sublimi atqꝫ doctiffimo scientia: merito dignitate prorfus inferior:inde displiceā:unde pla/ a

Book on Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 1

The letter of the most eloquent man and reverend father in Christ, lord Johannes of Trittenheim, abbot of Sponheim, to the most reverend father in Christ, lord Johannes von Dalberg, Bishop of Worms.

To the most reverend father and lord in Christ, lord Johannes von Dalberg, by divine providence Bishop of Worms: Brother Johannes, called abbot in Sponheim, of the Order of Saint Benedict, [offers] the little that he is.

The ancients were formerly accustomed, most reverend father, if they had forged any new work, to dedicate it to distinguished men, so that it might receive perpetual strength and firmness, and so that the venomous tongue of rivals, beaten back by the light of majesty, should nowhere have power to fasten the tooth of a wicked bite. Nor did the opinion deceive them, which proceeded from humility, since kindness in learned prelates must always be praised toward their subjects: it rewards the pursuits of good men and restrains those of the wicked.

We too, imitating as far as we can this example of antiquity, are accustomed to submit the works that we write, dedicated, to prelates of churches and to more learned men, so that, approved by their authority, they may be able to go forth safely into public. For those things go forth into the light without fear which are supported by the testimony of a bishop. Indeed no one, unless foolish, readily accuses what he knows has been approved by the judgment of a superior. The innocence of the sheep rests safely when the compassion of the good shepherd watches over it.

Since, therefore, the examples of the ancients are incitements to virtues for us, it is fitting that we imitate the holy customs of those whose praises we sing, so that, while others profit both from them and from us, the order of the ecclesiastical hierarchy may remain inviolate. And although I am too insignificant to trust that anyone will take delight in my little works, nevertheless I have resolved humbly to offer what I have into the Lord’s treasury, in which the widow’s two small coins are rightly preferred to the riches of Croesus.

Accordingly, when recently, at the insistence of friends, I had brought together with much labor a Book on Ecclesiastical Writers, as the matter itself bears witness, lest I wander from the tracks of the ancients, I decided to submit this very labor of mine to some most learned man, outstanding in ecclesiastical dignity, through whose authority and goodwill it might pass by the teeth of the envious without a bite. And when much thought arose in me as to whom I might entrust this little night-work with greater favor, many presented themselves to me as I wavered, from whose learning and goodwill no small hope, once promised, was strong. Among them you, most reverend father, occurred to me as more powerful, more eminent, more learned: you surpass all in learning; you exceed everyone in erudition.

In you the lofty nobility of birth shines forth; episcopal authority stands out; probity of morals is seen; every kind of knowledge of the good arts is praised. Could we find such a man anywhere besides you, in whom all these things come together at once? Among the Germans I know no one equal to you, most reverend father, in whom lineage, dignity, and such great erudition shine. I do not speak in secret; let the Almighty be witness. Nor am I a flattering praiser: all Germany knows you to be a man most skilled in every respect.

The learned honor you; nobles and princes respect you. You are to us what Plato is said to have been to Antimachus: approved by your eloquence, a man is deservedly judged learned. We have learned by public report, which does not lie, how profound a knowledge in sacred letters abounds in you, how discerning an interpretation of law, and finally how great are the charm, sweetness, and grace of your speaking and delivering orations, so that we do not hesitate to compare you with the most learned men of whom we have made mention in the catalogue. The most brilliant orations which you are said to have delivered bear witness to this; your letters bear witness; many epigrams bear witness. Indeed the most illustrious fame of your name has become known with praise not only among our Germans, but among Italians and Frenchmen.

Hence it came into my mind that I should inscribe to you, so great a bishop, the work on ecclesiastical writers placed under your authority, and dedicate it to your name, so that under the shadow of the pontifical summit I might rest secure. But when I behold in you the splendor of a flashing light, I am beaten back, drawn away, and wholly shaken with fear of your great majesty, lest perhaps I, in knowledge, merit, and dignity altogether inferior to you, a lofty and most learned father, should displease you from the very point from which

cere praesumebā. Scio em̄ occupationes tuas plurimas: & sacrata studia nō igno- ro: quibus molestus esse meis nenij s nō debueram. QVtorum instantia saepe rogatus sum:ut librum quē de scriptoribꝰ ecclesiasticis olim inchaueram:iam pro noticia librorū habenda: quandoque nacta oportunitate pficiam.Diu fateor distuli:ne si tam ardua inconsulte aggredi praesumerē:aemulorum odia ex leuita- te mea prouocarem.Nunc autē quoniā ad petitionem amicorum doctorū accessit consilium: qui ad hanc subeundā prouinciam me rationibus suis animarunt:non potui diutijs eorum petitionibus resistere:maxime cum hoc no strum opusculum tantorū uirorum patroninio fulciatur. Non em singulorum diuersitates mihi licuit ubique exprimere.Nā ut iam dixi:uestigia patrum fecutus sum:&amp; ubi dissonabant illi:quod ueri credidi cōplexus.Tu autē si aliud quod solidiori ueritate constet inueneris:libenter cedam tuae sententiae.Placuit autē mihi nouo scribendi modo procedere:ut lector ipse noticiam librorum ex principijs facilius possit intenire.

[unclear] I was presuming. For I know that your occupations are very many, and I am not unaware of your sacred studies, with which I ought not to have troubled you by my trifles. But your learning encourages me, which your kindness and humanity render lovable to all, since it shrinks from no one’s letters and judges no one unworthy of its address. Therefore, weak though I am, I approach your highness; I humbly submit the present little work to you; I appoint you its judge and defender. Receive, I beg you, most reverend and most learned father, this lucubration of ours, such as it is; examine it, judge it, defend it, and, if you judge it worthy, pursue it with kindly favor. And you who turn over the writings of the ancients in continual reading, deign also, if ever there is leisure, to inspect their catalogue. But I have not yet communicated the present little work to anyone, until I may know it to have been approved by the testimony of your authority. Friends await it; the printers are waiting for it; but I judge the opinion of your paternity to be preferred to all. May your most clement paternity indulge me, I pray, because I have presumed to bring my foolishness to ears occupied with arduous matters; for I have such confidence in your humanity, gentleness, and kindness that I may in no way doubt the benevolent reception of our catalogue. And I shall count it among the greatest delights if I learn that you take pleasure in my little lucubrations. Farewell, most reverend father; hold me, your most devoted servant, together with the volume sent, commended to you. From Spanheim, the sixth day before the Kalends of May, in the year of the Lord 1492.

Prologue of the same reverend father, lord Johannes of Trittenheim, to the Book on Ecclesiastical Writers.

At the insistence of many I have often been asked that, when some opportunity should at last be found, I should complete the book which I once began on ecclesiastical writers, for the purpose of having knowledge of books. I confess that I put it off for a long time, lest, if I should presume thoughtlessly to undertake so arduous a matter, I might provoke the hatred of rivals through my own levity. But now, since the counsel of learned friends has been added to their request, who by their arguments have encouraged me to undertake this province, I could not resist their petitions any longer, especially since this little work of ours is supported by the patronage of such great men. For why should I fear the hatred of detractors, when I see that a refuge among the learned lies open to me? There will be, I do not doubt, those who judge this labor of ours worthy of praise; there will also be those who disparage it from a zeal of rivalry. What then? Shall we therefore abandon the exercises of good works, lest we provoke the hatred of rivals? Far be it. Whoever does not imitate the wicked offends them; but he who fears to offend the envious does injury to the good. And indeed to have displeased the wicked is praiseworthy, since they are accustomed to love nothing unless it accords with their morals. Therefore now, importunate friends and exactors, receive the book composed on ecclesiastical writers, which with diligent prayers you so greatly desired to be brought to completion. I have done what I could, and I have expended my ready powers on this work, although in many respects the capacity itself is less than the desire. For I, in the manner of those who are half-blind, entered the path of the preceding fathers under their guidance, and, gathering from their little works the several things suitable to my purpose, I have carried them together into this bundle. I have also inserted into our catalogue many writers found by long investigation, with great labors and expenses. Do not wonder, excellent reader, if in the notes and titles of books my opinion does not always agree with yours. Who could enumerate, much less reconcile, the opinions of individuals amid so manifold a variety of books? You will therefore grant pardon if you sometimes find a volume marked beforehand for another person, or in another way, than your opinion understands. For it was not possible for me everywhere to express the differences of individuals. For, as I have already said, I followed the footsteps of the fathers; and where they disagreed, I embraced what I believed to be true. But if you find something else established by more solid truth, I shall gladly yield to your opinion. It pleased me, however, to proceed by a new manner of writing, so that the reader himself may more easily be able to discover knowledge of the books from their beginnings.

On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 2.

Beginning, therefore, with the disciples of the apostles, down to the last year of the emperor Frederick III, namely the year of the Lord 1493, I have drawn up a catalogue of illustrious men. In it I have marked down the names, dignities, writings, and times, not of all, but only of those whom I found, adding opposite them the openings of the titles of their volumes; those I had not seen I passed over with a space. I could not readily find the times at which certain men flourished; nevertheless I placed them in what seemed to me a suitable place. And let the knowledge of one who knows supply this defect in both respects, namely that he may reckon the times of individuals and restore those misplaced to their own places. I confess also that I deliberately passed over many whose writings are not easily found, nor their times. I also know many very learned men still living who are said to be publishing various little works; concerning them, since I have no certain knowledge, I prefer to pass over in silence rather than to ponder uncertainties. And, to use Jerome’s words: if any who still write about the living have been omitted by me in this catalogue, let them impute it not to me but to themselves, since they have hidden their writings [unclear] to come into the light. But I believe that, content with their writings and talent, they will not care about the losses caused by my silence. For of those whom I found, I wished to depict not their praises but their books. This task, indeed, would demand a rather lengthy volume. Go now, therefore, into the world, work completed by our labor; go, offer to lovers of books the treasure which you contain. Why do you fear? Why do you delay? Do not fear to come forth in public; do not dread the hatred of rivals, supported as you are by the patronage of so many saints. Come then, book, go forth, slight indeed in talent, but a displayer of great matters. Why do you tremble as if slothful and useless? Go forth confidently: a thousand will praise you, while scarcely one will blame you. The love of God, by which you were written, may it, I pray, mercifully excuse you always and everywhere, together with your author.

The End.

The book of the most commendable man and reverend father in Christ, lord Johannes of Trittenheim, abbot of Sponheim, On Ecclesiastical Writers, happily begins.

To the church of the Corinthians: one epistle.

Also to James the apostle: two epistles.

Besides, of the itinerary of his life: books, “Clement to lord James.”

Likewise, of Peter’s disputation: ten.

But these last two volumes are counted among the apocrypha, as is clear in XV, dist. Sancta Romana. Other epistles of his are also reported, but apocryphal. One: “When in the city of Rome.”

Clement, fourth bishop of the holy Roman Church from blessed Peter, as some think, by nation a Roman, a holy man beloved of God, adorned also with the beauty of morals, whose life and passion are contained in ecclesiastical writings. He sat in the pontificate nine years and ten days. He was banished into exile for the faith of Christ by [unclear] Constans. He died in the third year of Caesar Trajan, and in the 103rd year of the Lord. This most blessed martyr is said to have written, in the person of the Roman Church, some epistles full of instruction in the faith, of which the principal one is extant:

Dionysius the Areopagite, an Athenian, an eminent philosopher, converted to the faith by the blessed apostle Paul, was ordained, as some think, the first bishop of Athens, a man of exceptional sanctity and incomparable learning. After the death of the apostles, blessed Clement, bishop of the city of Rome, sent him with Rusticus the priest and Eleutherius the deacon to preach God to the nations in France, another bishop having been ordained in his place.

He wrote many excellent little works in the Greek language:

On the Celestial Hierarchy: one book, “Every best gift.”

On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy: books [unclear], “Of our priesthood indeed.”

On the Divine Names: [unclear], “Now already the man of God after.”

Book

On mystical theology, one book: The super-substantial Trinity. On symbolic theology, one book: Holy indeed, Timo[thy?]. To Gaius, seven letters: Darkness hides [light?]. To Dorotheus the minister, one letter: The divine darkness is inaccessible. To Zosipater the priest, one letter: Do not think this a fault. To Polycarp, one letter: I indeed did not know [unclear]. To Demophilus, one letter: The Hebrew histories say. To Saint John the Evangelist, one letter: I greet you, holy soul. To Apollophanes the philosopher, one letter: To Apollophanes [unclear]. On the death of Paul, to Timothy, one letter: I greet you, divine disciple.

These are the writings of blessed Dionysius that I find among the Latins; if he gave anything more, it remained among the Greeks. But since the aforesaid little works were wrapped in great obscurity, they were made clear by the explanation of the following fathers. Of these, John Scotus, a monk of our order, first translated and polished them; then Hugh of Saint Victor, Robert of Lincoln, Albert the Great, and Dionysius the Carthusian, and many others, whose memory is not now ready to hand. Blessed Dionysius suffered in the Parisian field, together with the companions named above, under the emperor Domitian, in the year of the Lord 96, in the ninth indiction, and in the ninetieth year of his age. He was buried at Paris in the church consecrated in his name, shining with miracles.

Lucius Annaeus Seneca of Corduba, philosopher, disciple of the Stoic Photion, and uncle of the poet Lucan, was a man of most restrained life. By the testimony of blessed Jerome, I have placed him, celebrated in the catalogue of ecclesiastical writers, for this reason: because he was also the very close friend of the apostle Paul, and composed many elegant works for instruction in the moral life. Nero Caesar, ill-starred, killed him two years before Peter and Paul were crowned; Nero had once been his most unworthy pupil. Of his little works I have found the following:

On moral instruction, one book: Every sin is an action. On the four virtues, one book: Four kinds of virtues. On the remedies of fortune, one book: Although of all the poets. Declamations, ten books: You demand a matter more pleasant. On clemency, to Nero, two books: To write on clemency. On benefits, to Brutus, seven books: Among many [unclear]. On anger, to Novatus, three books: You have demanded of me, Novatus. On providence, one book: You have asked me, Lucilius, why. On the happy life, to Gallio, one book: To live, brother Gallio, all. On consolation, to Marcia, one book: Unless I knew you, Marcia. On consolation, to his mother, one book: Often now, best mother, [unclear]. On tranquility of life, one book: As I inquired into myself, certain things. That injury does not befall the wise man, one book: So great, almost among the Stoics. On the shortness of life, one book: The greater part of mortals. On liberal studies, one book: Concerning liberal studies, that. On natural questions, eight books: How much difference there is between philosophy [unclear]. Of suasory sentences, one book: But as of any thing whatever, great. Controversies, five books: Two brothers [unclear] between themselves. On poverty, one book: Honest, says Epicurus. To Polybius, of consolation, one book: For comparisons are firm. On the games of Seneca, one book: What was done in heaven. On abundance of words, one book. On marriage, one book. Tragedies, ten books. On the death of Claudius, one book.

On Ecclesiastical Writers Fol. 3

Letters to Paul: five books. “I believe you, Paul, [unclear].” Letters to Lucilius: twenty-two books. “Do therefore thus, my Lucilius.”

These are the writings of Seneca which at present I have been able to find. He is said, however, to have written some other little works, which have not yet come into our hands. He was indeed a most ardent lover of wisdom, and a zealous searcher after it, and of so tenacious a memory that, when two thousand names had been read before him, he immediately recited them from memory. Moreover, when a certain poet had produced two hundred verses and, after collecting them on paper, recited them in order before Nero, Seneca immediately, using his memory in place of the volume, repeated those same verses one by one, beginning from the last and proceeding in reverse order as far as the first. He is read to have retained in memory the names also of all his servants. He flourished at Rome in the times of the apostle Paul, under the emperor Nero, in the year of the Lord 50.

[Marcellus?], son of Marcus, prefect of the city of Rome, a certain disciple of Simon Magus, sufficiently instructed in secular letters, converted to the faith of Jesus Christ by the preaching of blessed Peter the apostle, composed many things for the usefulness of the church of God. For at the request of Christians he wrote:

On the Confounding of Peter and Simon: one book. To Saints Nereus and Achilleus: a book. On the Acts of Peter and Paul: a book. On the Arts of Simon: a book. On the Death of Saint Petronella: a book. On the Passion of Saint Felicula: a book. On the Passion of Saint Nicomedes: a book.

He also published other things concerning the deeds of the saints, which have not come to our knowledge. He flourished at Rome in the time of Saint Peter, in the year of the Lord 50.

Linus, the first bishop of the city of Rome after blessed Peter, a Tuscan by nation, a man of most holy life, shining with many miracles both in life and after death, sat in the pontificate for eleven years, three months, and twelve days. Since he was a very learned man and beloved of God, he wrote in the Greek language, concerning the holy apostles Peter and Paul, pastors on one day:

Their Martyrdom: one book. And certain letters.

At last, punished with capital sentence by the prefect Saturninus, whose daughter he had freed from a demon, he was made a martyr, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October. He flourished at Rome under the emperor Galba, in the year of the Lord 70.

Philo, a Jew by nation, an Alexandrian, of the race of priests, is placed by blessed Jerome among the ecclesiastical writers for this reason: because in his little works he is very often occupied with praise of Christians. When he had been sent to Rome as an envoy of his nation, he is recorded to have enjoyed the friendship of blessed Peter the apostle; and for this reason he also adorned with praises the followers of Saint Mark, his disciple, at Alexandria. He was, moreover, a man most learned in every respect, and was regarded as another Plato, so that it was commonly said: “Either Plato imitates Philo, or Philo imitates Plato.” For so great a similarity of thought and eloquence between them is reported. He wrote many and most elegant books, of which the following are given below:

On the Life of the Wise Man: one book. On the Conversion of Life: a book. On the Confusion of Tongues: a book. On the Nature of Quadrupeds: three books. On the Things Which We Attest by Sense: a book. On Learning: a book. On the Heir of Divine Things: a book. On the Unequal Division: a book.

On the Three Virtues: one book. On Nature and Invention: one book. On Agreements: one book. On the Succession of Generation: one book. On the Change of Names: one book. On Giants: one book. On the Five Books of Moses: one book. On Dreams: one book. On the Tabernacle: one book. On the Contemplative Life: one book. On Agriculture: one book. On Drunkenness: one book. On Victims and Promises: one book. On Prudence: one book. On Ideas: one book. On Alexander: one book. On the Reason of Animals: one book. Let Every Fool Be a Slave: one book. He is read to have written many other things also, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under the emperor Nero, in the year of the Lord 50.

Josephus, a Jew by nation, a Jerusalemite, a priest by religion, son of the priest Matthias, a philosopher, rhetorician, and distinguished writer of the times, whom I would not place in our catalogue unless the Church read his writings and blessed Jerome had done so before, after the destruction of Jerusalem was captured by the emperors Vespasian and Titus and brought to Rome. Because of the excellence of his talent he was splendidly honored by the Senate and people of Rome. Although he remained a Jew, nevertheless he often praised the race of Christians, and in the eighteenth book of the Antiquities set down a notable testimony concerning our Lord Jesus Christ. His volumes were held in such authority among the Romans while he was still alive that they were placed in the public libraries; and after his death he himself was granted a bronze statue by the Senate and people. Of his little works I have seen only the following.

On the Jewish War: seven books, "Since the war which ..." Antiquities of the World: twenty-four books, "To write a history ..." Against Apion: two books, "Sufficiently, as I think ..." On the Power of Speaking: one book.

He flourished at Rome under the emperors Vespasian and Titus, and remained among the living down to the times of the emperor Trajan, in the year of the Lord 100.

Ignatius, third bishop of the church of Antioch after the blessed [unclear], a man of outstanding holiness and a singular, most fervent lover of our Lord Jesus Christ, used to say, as Dionysius bears witness: "My love is crucified." Since this most blessed prelate was a learned and zealous preacher of the divine word, he wrote some elegant letters full of fervor, in which he showed himself to have been a lover of holy martyrdom. Of these, the following are said to be the more important:

To the Church of the Ephesians: one letter. To the Magnesians: one letter. To the Trojans: one letter. To the Romans: one letter. To Saint John: one letter. To the Blessed Virgin: one letter. To the Philadelphians: one letter. To Polycarp: one letter. To Saint John the Elder: his own. To Mary the Christ-bearer: his own.

Adam begot three sons. Adam begot three sons.

On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 4

He suffered at Rome under the emperor Trajan, in the year of the Lord 111.

Papias, hearer and disciple of Saint John, bishop of Hierapolis in Asia, a most steadfast propagator and defender of the Christian faith, and a disciple and zealous imitator of the holy apostles, wrote little works of no contemptible authority. Of these there survives an outstanding work, divided into five volumes, which he entitled thus:

Explanation of the Sayings of the Lord, five books.

Other things that he wrote we have not seen.

He first devised the novelty of the thousand years, after which he dreamed that Christ would reign again in the flesh with his elect upon the earth. Others later spread this error, and were called Chiliasts from the thousand.

He flourished in the times of Caesar Trajan, around the year of the Lord 100.

Hegesippus, a Jew by nation, converted to the faith of Christ, shone forth wonderfully in the church of God in learning and holiness; his feast, with those of the other saints, has obtained a place in the martyrology. He wrote several little works of excellent talent. Of them I have found only an outstanding work, from the time of the Lord’s Passion down to his own age:

A History of Ecclesiastical Acts, five books, “The Parthian war which between ...”

I have seen no other of his works.

He flourished near the apostolic times, under Antoninus Pius, in the year of the Lord 160.

Justin, converted from a philosopher to the catholic faith, an eminent lover and worshipper of Christ, when in the city of Rome he refuted Crescens the Cynic, who was blaspheming Christians, as gluttonous, afraid of death, and a follower of lust and debaucheries, was accused before the Senate through that man’s plots because he was a Christian, and was crowned with martyrdom for Christ. He wrote many distinguished little works in defense of our faith. Among them these are reported:

Against the Gentiles, to Antoninus, two books.

To Aurelius, Against the Gentiles, one book.

Likewise Against the Gentiles, one book.

Reproofs Against the Gentiles, one book.

On the Monarchy of God, one book.

On the Soul, one book.

[unclear], entitled [unclear], one book.

Against Trypho the Jew, one book.

Against Marcion, one book.

Against All Heresies, one book.

He also composed many other things which have not come to our knowledge.

He flourished under Antoninus Pius, in the year of the Lord 150.

Quadratus, an Athenian, bishop after the martyr Publius, formerly a hearer and disciple of the holy apostles, a steadfast man of incomparable learning, laboring much for the usefulness of the Christian faith, made great progress: he gathered back into the unity of faith the church dispersed by fear of persecution. Since he was an eminent teacher, he wrote, among other things, on behalf of the Christians to the emperor Hadrian, full of instruction:

An Apology, one book.

And other things unknown to us.

At last he suffered for the defense of the catholic faith on the seventh day before the Kalends of June.

He flourished under the emperor Hadrian, in the year of the Lord 120.

Aristides, an Athenian philosopher, a man most learned in secular letters and very zealous in the divine Scriptures, shone with such notable eloquence that he offered the nations a marvel of himself; under the garb of a philosopher, Christian ...

bearing faith and conduct: he shone forth, renowned not without a reputation for holiness. He wrote:

An Apologeticum for the Christians, To the emperor Hadrian, 1 book, and certain other works. He flourished under the emperor Hadrian, in the year of the Lord 120.

Melito the Asian, bishop of Sardis, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and no less venerable for holiness than for doctrine, shone forth renowned among the Catholic preachers. He wrote many excellent volumes for the benefit of the Church of the faithful, of which these are reported:

On Easter, 2 books On the Life of the Prophets, 1 book On the Fallen, 1 book On the Body and the Soul, 1 book On Baptism, 1 book On Truth, 1 book On the Generation of Christ, 1 book On Prophecy, 1 book Of Eclogues, 6 books On the Passing of Saint Mary, 1 book: “Melito, servant of Christ, bishop.” On the Church, 1 book On the Lord’s Day, 1 book On the Senses, 1 book On Faith, 1 book Philoxenia, 1 book That which is entitled Key, 1 book On the Devil, 1 book On the Apocalypse of John, 1 book

He also published other little works, which antiquity has not permitted to come down to our memory. Tertullian, commemorating in a certain passage his elegant and declamatory talent, states that he was regarded by our people as a prophet. It should certainly be noted that the book On the Passing of Saint Mary, ascribed to him, is reckoned among the apocrypha, 15, distinction, Sancta Romana. He flourished under the emperor Marcus Antonius Verus, in the year of the Lord 160.

[Unclear], very studious and learned, distinguished in talent and speech, and an excellent declaimer, wrote many volumes for the benefit of the faithful, and shone forth as an excellent expounder of the Lord’s discourses. Of his little works the following are reported:

Against Marcion, 1 book Against Hermogenes, 2 books To Autolycus, 4 books Commentaries on the Gospels, 3 books On the Proverbs of Solomon, 1 book

He also composed other short and numerous treatises pertaining to the edification of the Church, which among the Latins are rarely found together. He was ordained bishop in the year of the Lord 183, in the eleventh indiction.

Apollinaris of Hierapolis in Asia, bishop, a learned man and distinguished defender of the Christian faith, renowned in talent and eloquent in speech, wrote little works not of contemptible reading, in which he showed himself a man not so much learned as zealous. Of these, the following are reported:

An Apologeticum for the Christians, 2 books Against the Gentiles, 1 book On Truth, 3 books Against the Cataphrygians, 2 books

On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 5

But he also published some other works, knowledge of which antiquity has taken away from us. He flourished under Marcus Antoninus Verus, in the year of the Lord 165.

Dionysius, bishop of the church of the Corinthians, a most eloquent man, very learned in the divine Scriptures, and a most watchful shepherd of Christ’s flock, was of such painstaking diligence that he instructed not only the people of his own city with salutary teachings, but also summoned the congregations of foreign cities to steadfastness in the faith by letters. These letters are said to be so useful and extensive that they may not improperly be called books; of them the following are listed:

To the Lacedaemonians: one epistle. To the Athenians: one epistle. To the Nicomedians: one epistle. To the Cretans: one epistle. To the [Cnossians?]: one epistle. To the Roman pope: one epistle. To the [Amastrians?]: one epistle. To Chrysophora, a woman: one epistle.

He flourished under the rulers Marcus Antoninus Verus and Lucius Aurelius, in the year of the Lord 170. Not without a reputation for holiness, he wrote various works.

Tatian, a heresiarch, hearer and follower of Justin Martyr, did not for a long time depart from his side. But afterward, when Saint Justin had been crowned, swollen with pride in his eloquence, he founded a new heresy which is called that of the Encratites; later Severus increased it, from whom the heretics of the same faction were called Severians. They abominate meats; they do not drink wine; they do not accept the Old Testament; nor do they believe in the resurrection. Tatian wrote almost innumerable volumes, which nevertheless have not come to my knowledge. For because of the error of the teacher, even his volumes, despised, perished. There survives, as Jerome attests, a distinguished volume of his which he entitled:

Against the Nations: one book.

He flourished under Marcus Antoninus Verus, in the year of the Lord 170.

Philip, bishop of Crete, that is, of the city of Gortyna, whom Dionysius, bishop of the Corinthians, placed above, mentions in his epistle which he had written to the church of the same city, was a noble and learned man. He published for the benefit of believers volumes sufficiently furnished, as they say, which have by no means come into our hands. There survives his:

Against Marcion: one book.

He also wrote certain epistles to various persons and various treatises, which have still by no means come into our hands. He flourished in the year of the Lord 170, in the times of the emperor Marcus Antoninus Verus.

Modestus, a man of flourishing talent, though of what dignity or rank he was is unknown to us, wrote, as blessed Jerome attests, little works not to be despised in reading, in which the abundant vein of his talent is seen. Of these there survives a distinguished volume:

Against Marcion: one book.

The rest are unknown to us.

He flourished under the rulers Marcus Antoninus Verus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 185.

Irenaeus of Lyon in Gaul, bishop after the triumph of the blessed martyr Pothinus, formerly a hearer of the martyr Polycarp, a man very studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, was sent as legate to Rome under Pope Eleutherius and was approved as most renowned no less in holiness than in learning. He wrote many excellent volumes, of which these are reported:

Against the Nations: one book. On Discipline: one book. To Blastus, on schism: one book. Against Heresies: five books. “Inasmuch as [unclear] the truth,”

He also wrote many other works which have not yet come to my knowledge at all. At last, when persecution against the Christians was raging, he was crowned with martyrdom for the Catholic faith, along with almost the whole people of his city, on the fourth day before the Kalends of July.

He flourished under Marcus Antoninus, in the year of the Lord 175.

Theodotion, an Ephesian by birth, formerly a disciple of Tatian the philosopher while he was still a believer, a man certainly most learned in every respect and the third translator of the divine Scriptures: besides the translation of the Scriptures which he made from Hebrew into Latin, he also composed certain other little works, which nevertheless have not yet come into our hands at all. He flourished in the time of the emperor Commodus, in the year of the Lord 180.

Rhodon, Asian by race, once a hearer and disciple of Tatian, a man very learned both in the divine Scriptures and also in secular letters, is said to have written many things in Greek; examples of these are rarely found among our people. Of them, however, the following are reported as the more important, which we have set down below:

Against Marcion: three books Against the Cataphrygians: one book To Callistion: one book On the Hexaemeron: six books

He flourished under the princes Commodus and Severus, in the year of the Lord 200.

Clement, priest of the Alexandrian church, once a hearer and disciple of Pantaenus, the Stoic Christian philosopher, who after him held the ecclesiastical school at Alexandria for many years, was a devout, learned, and most eloquent man. He wrote many excellent volumes, among which these are reported:

Stromata, that is, Miscellanies: eight books Against the Gentiles: one book The Pedagogue: three books On Easter: one book On Fasting: one book On Disputation: one book On the Salvation of the Rich Man: one book On Detraction: one book Against the Judaizers: one book On Ecclesiastical Canons: one book

He also published many letters and various treatises, whose titles we do not know.

He flourished in the times of the princes Commodus and Severus, in the year of the Lord 300.

Melciades, whom Rhodon recalled in his work which he composed against the Cataphrygians, Montanus, Prisca, and Maximilla, insane prophets: a man very learned in secular letters and exercised with constant study in the divine Scriptures, wrote not a few little works for the edification of the faithful. Of these the following are reported: Apologeticus for our faith: one book.

He is also said to have written many other things, which have not come to my knowledge.

He flourished in the times of Marcus Antoninus Commodus, in the year of the Lord 170.

Against Montanus, one book. But he published several other works, which have not come to my knowledge.

He flourished under the emperors Commodus and Severus, in the year of the Lord 180.

Serapion, formerly an anchorite, eighth bishop of the church of Antioch, a man of keen intelligence, is said to have been very zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, venerable no less in life than in knowledge. He is reported to have composed several little works for the benefit of believers, in which he shows himself a learned man and a very vigorous defender of the Christian faith. Among these are counted:

To Domno, Judaizing, one book.

To Carinus, on Montanus, one book.

On the Gospel under the Name of Peter, one book.

Short Letters, but Many, one book.

He was ordained bishop of the aforesaid city under Commodus, emperor of the Romans, in the 193rd year of the Lord, in the first indiction.

Apollonius, senator of the city of Rome, a man most learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, venerable no less for holiness than for knowledge, when he had been denounced before the Senate because he was a Christian and would not deny Christ, received sentence of death; the old law among them prevailing, that Christians who had once been brought before their judgment should not be released without denial.

He wrote, among other things:

An Apology for Our Faith, one book.

After he had recited this in order before the Senate, he was beheaded.

He flourished at Rome under the emperors Commodus and Severus, in the year of the Lord 190.

Tertullian, priest, by homeland a Carthaginian of the province of Africa, the son of a centurion, a proconsular man, a man of sharp and vehement intelligence, most learned both in divine and in secular writings, inasmuch as he taught rhetoric gloriously for many years at Carthage, wrote in the Latin language almost innumerable little works, in which he powerfully crushed the errors of the heretics. The most blessed martyr Cyprian held this man’s writings in such veneration that he let no day pass without reading them. For he was accustomed to say to his secretary, “Give me the master,” meaning Tertullian. At last he is said to have slipped into the error of Montanus, on account of which his little works are counted among the apocrypha, Distinction 15, Sancta Romana. And although he erred in some matters, nevertheless he wrote well in many, as his volumes testify:

On the Patience of God, one book. “I confess [unclear] God [unclear].”

Against Praxeas, one book. “In various ways the devil has emulated.”

Against Marcion, one book. “If anything was done before.”

Against the Jews, one book. “A discussion recently occurred.”

Against All Heresies, one book. “Of two heretics, as [unclear].”

On the Prescriptions of Heretics, one book. “In the condition of the present times.”

Against Hermogenes, one book. “We are accustomed to [unclear] heretics.”

Against the Valentinians, one book. “The Valentinians very frequently.”

On the Flesh of Christ, one book. “The confidence of Christians [unclear] resurrection.”

On the Resurrection of the Flesh, one book. “For the proper faith of the resurrection.”

Aduersus Apolloniū: li. Quaesisti ꝓxime Fabi frat̉. Nos quidē neqꝫ expauesci. Nō dubito frate te post ux. Haeretici nuptias auferūt. Principes sep Africe uiri. Scripsit quoqꝫ et alia plura uariosque tractatus: qui ad manꝰ nostras adhuc minime uenerunt: uixitqꝫ usque ad senectam senium studiosus. Claruit Seueri imperatoris temporibus. Anno dn̄i. Ducentesimo. ORigenes qui Adamantius presbyter: natione alexandrinus: Leonidis martyris filius: Clemētis alexandrini quondā discipulꝰ: uir magni excel- lentis ingenij fuit: ita ut studio eruditione similem nūqͣ habuerit. Anno Seueri pertinacis decimo: aduersum christianos persecutione mota: ac Leonide patre ꝓ fide christi martyrio coronato: cum matre uidua sex fratribus pauper derelictus est: annos natus circiter decem septem. Substantiam aūt omnē pro- pter christi confessionem fiscus occupauerat: ita ut unde uiuerent amplius nil ha- berent. Et licet annoꝝ numerus minor supputaret̉ in iueuene: erat tamē iam mi- rabilis in eo doctrina: fidei christianae admiranda constatia. Proposuerat em̄ cū patre suo Leonide ꝓ fide chrisci fortiter occubere: si nō matris fraude ad eccl̓iae utilitatē magnus doctor futurus: eum contigisset praeseruari. Nam cum ad locū agonis patri mane pridie deliberasset occurrere: sublatis a matre noctu uestimē- tis obseratis tabernaculi ualuis domi cogitur remanere. Cum uero inuirū cre- uisset: agere uitam apostolicam instituit: annucians in circuitu suo uerbum dei nudis pedibus multis annis inessit. Super lectum denique plumis stratum nunquā dormivit: a uino carnibus: praeter infirmitate omīo se abstinuit: ieiunijs: uigilijs: orationibus continuis diuinarum scripturā studijs expositionibꝰ deo de- uote seruiens intentꝰ fuit. Christi quoqꝫ consilio unam tantum tunicā induere cō- fueuit: omniū mūdanoꝝ cōtemptor effectus: nihil de crastino cogitauit. Amo- re castitatis ut mulieribus secure auderet praedicare: se castrari fecit: licet in hoc facto çelus sine scientia manserit. Ob eius doctrinam: eloquētiam apostolicam uitam Māmea Alexandri imperatoris christianissima mater: eū audiendi deside- rio capta: ex Alexandria Antiochiā accessit: eius mellifluam doctrinam cum in- genti admiratiōe audiuit. Erat autē in studio diuinaꝝ scripturaꝝ adeo intētus: ut nec cibum unqͣ nec somnū caperet: nisi unus e fratribus lectionē scripturā cūctis audientibꝰ praemisisset. Nouū uetus testamentū uelut alter Esdras memoriter nouerat: iam senex contra suā aetatē linguā hebraicā didicit: oīm interpretū editiones praeter septuaginta in unā mirabili studio cōportauit. In editionibꝰ scri- pturaꝝ dictandis tam admirandae memoriae subtilitatis fuit: ut septe notarios totidēque in scribendo uelocissimas puellas: praeter alios iuuenes om̄es insimul ex eiꝰ ore diuersa scribetes: incredibili ꝓnūciādi agilitate fatigaret. Et cū tantꝰ habere- tur esset inter oēs ecclesiasticos doctor insignis: magnis tn̄ notat̉ erroribꝰ: quibꝰ uel ipse desipuit: uel alijs inferentibꝰ falla scriptis deprauatꝰ fuit. Semꝑ em̄ de Ori- gene uaria fuit doctoꝝ opinio: qbusdā haereticū asserētibꝰ: alijs sibi fraudē affirmā- tibꝰ impossitā. Mirandū nō est: si primꝰ sine exemplo errauerit: ꝗ tot uolumīa sine magistro praecedente explicuit. Nostrū tñ est: ne dū de Origene sed de qbuscūque scriptoribꝰ cū sancta eccl̓ia Romana sentire: supuacuas opiniōes contemnere. Edidit aūt pene infinita uolumina: De quibꝰ ego latinis infusa uiditantū subiecta.

BOOK On persecution, to Fabius: one book. To Scapula: one book. An exhortation to chastity: one book. On monogamy: one book. On the pallium: one book. On spectacles: one book. On ecstasy: one book. On modesty: one book. On fasts: one book. Against Apollonius: one book. “You asked recently, brother Fabius.” “We indeed are not frightened.” “I do not doubt, brother, that after [your] wife.” “Heretics take away marriages.” “The foremost men of Africa always.” He also wrote many other things and various treatises, which as yet have by no means come into our hands; and he lived on into old age, zealous in his declining years. He flourished in the times of the emperor Severus. In the year of the Lord two hundred.

Origen, who is Adamantius, a priest, an Alexandrian by nation, son of the martyr Leonides, once a disciple of Clement of Alexandria, was a man of great and excellent talent, so that in zeal and learning he never had his equal. In the tenth year of Severus Pertinax, when a persecution was set in motion against the Christians, and when his father Leonides was crowned with martyrdom for the faith of Christ, he was left poor with his widowed mother and six brothers, being about seventeen years old. But the treasury had seized all their substance because of the confession of Christ, so that they no longer had anything from which they might live. And although the number of his years was reckoned as smaller in the young man, nevertheless his learning was already marvelous, and the constancy of his Christian faith admirable. For he had resolved to die bravely with his father Leonides for the faith of Christ, had he not, by his mother’s stratagem, since he was to become a great teacher for the usefulness of the Church, happened to be preserved. For when he had determined, on the morning before, to run to his father at the place of contest, his garments were taken away by his mother during the night, the doors of the chamber were bolted, and he was compelled to remain at home.

But when he had grown into a man, he resolved to live an apostolic life, proclaiming the word of God in his circuit; for many years he went about with bare feet. Indeed he never slept on a bed stuffed with feathers; from wine and meats, except because of illness, he abstained entirely; he was intent on serving God devoutly with fasts, vigils, continual prayers, studies and expositions of the divine Scriptures. By Christ’s counsel he also accustomed himself to wear only one tunic; having become a despiser of all worldly things, he gave no thought for the morrow. From love of chastity, so that he might dare to preach safely to women, he caused himself to be castrated, although in this deed his zeal remained without knowledge.

Because of his doctrine, eloquence, and apostolic life, Mammaea, the most Christian mother of the emperor Alexander, seized by a desire to hear him, came from Alexandria to Antioch, and heard his honey-sweet teaching with great admiration. He was, moreover, so intent on the study of the divine Scriptures that he never took either food or sleep unless one of the brothers had first recited a reading of the Scriptures while all listened. Like another Ezra he knew the New and Old Testament by memory; already an old man, contrary to his age, he learned the Hebrew language; with wonderful zeal he gathered into one all the editions of the interpreters besides the Seventy.

In dictating editions of the Scriptures he was of such admirable memory and subtlety that he wore out seven notaries and just as many girls extremely swift in writing, besides other young men, all writing different things at the same time from his mouth, by the incredible agility of his utterance. And although he was held so great and was an outstanding teacher among all ecclesiastical men, nevertheless he is marked by great errors, in which either he himself was foolish, or, through others inserting false things, was corrupted in his writings. For there has always been varied opinion among the learned concerning Origen, some asserting that he was a heretic, others affirming that fraud was imposed upon him. It is not surprising if the first man, without precedent, erred, who explained so many volumes with no teacher preceding him. Yet it is our part, not only concerning Origen but concerning any writers whatsoever, to agree with the holy Roman Church and to despise superfluous opinions. He published almost infinite volumes. Of these, I have set down below those which seem to have been poured into Latin.

On Genesis: sixteen homilies. On Exodus: forty-two homilies. On Leviticus: sixteen homilies. On Numbers: twenty-eight homilies, “Not all are worthy in Numbers.” On Joshua: twenty-six homilies, “The Lord gave a name.” On Judges: nine homilies. On the beginning of [unclear]: two homilies. On Isaiah the prophet: nine homilies, “While King Uzziah lived.” On Jeremiah the prophet: thirteen homilies, “God, ready to do good.” On Ezekiel: fourteen homilies, “As in the last days.” On the Gospel of Matthew: thirty-nine homilies, “Not only from the beginning did God.” On Elkanah: one book, “As formerly among the people of the Jews.” On the beginning of Job: four books. On the Song of Songs: four books. Also on the Song of Songs: two books, “About to speak concerning the Song of Songs.” Against the heretics: five books, “Blessed is the man,” etc.; this psalm. Against the philosopher Celsus: eight books, “Adamantius said, who.” Periarchon: four books, “You exhort me, holy Ambrose.” On the Epistle to the Romans: fifteen books, “All who believe and are certain.” On the beginning of John: one book, “Because the other apostles of Paul.” On the martyrs: one book. He also composed many other things, which have not come into our hands.

There are those who write that they have read six thousand treatises of Origen, a great number unknown to the Latins. Nor is there any doubt that many little works of his have recently been translated which have by no means come to the notice of our reading. He died, however, an old man, poor, and was buried at Tyre, under the emperors Valerian and Gallienus, in the year of the Lord 261, in the ninth indiction, in the seventieth year of his age.

Ammonius of Alexandria, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, most learned in secular letters, a philosopher and rhetorician the most celebrated of all his time, subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech, wrote in the Greek language certain excellent volumes, by which he left his memory to posterity. Of their number the following are extant:

On the Harmony of Jesus and Moses: one book, “In the first canon four.” One out of Four: one book, “Since indeed many have undertaken.” And certain other things.

The most impious Porphyry, a very bitter enemy of the Christians, a pagan philosopher, falsely accuses him of having denied the faith and become a heathen; but it is agreed that he remained a devout Christian until death.

Book

He flourished under Alexander, son of Mamaea, in the year of the Lord 230.

Ambrose, a hearer of Origen, at first a Marcionite and afterward corrected by Origen himself, an outstanding confessor of the Christian faith, even deserved to be promoted to the office of deacon. He was certainly a most learned man and a devoted lover of books; when he supplied at his own expense notaries and scribes, our Adamantius composed almost infinite volumes. He was so devoted a cultivator of Origen’s labors that day and night he urged him, by spoken and written words, to write something new, so that in a certain familiar letter he is named by Origen as the taskmaster of the work. He was accustomed to say that he never went to bed while Origen was present, nor took food, unless first, from the brothers who were always at hand, he had made the sacred writings resound. He wrote to Origen giving thanks for his conversion.

Of letters: one book.

ON ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS. Fol. 8.

Alexander, bishop of Cappadocia: when out of desire for the holy places he was going to Jerusalem, there, by divine revelation, he was ordained bishop after Saint Narcissus; he shone forth illustrious for great sanctity and learning; and at last, for the faith of Christ, under the most impious tyrant Decius, he completed [his] martyrdom. He wrote many elegant letters to various [persons], of which the following are reported foremost: On the peace of the Church, to the [Antiochenes?]: a letter. To the Antiochenes: a letter. For Origen against Demetrius: a letter. To Origen: several letters. He suffered at Caesarea under Decius, in the year of the Lord 253, in the 1st indiction.

[Julius] Africanus, a most learned man, philosopher, distinguished historiographer and theologian, and a most ardent lover of the divine Scriptures and of books: by his own studies and at his own expense he founded a notable library at Caesarea in Palestine, in which he gathered many volumes, both of secular and of divine Scriptures. He composed, moreover, several little works of great usefulness, of which the following are reported: Of Chronicles: 5 books. On the Holy Trinity: 1 book. On circumcision: 1 book. On Attalus: 1 book. On the Pasch: 1 book. On the Sabbath: 1 book. To Origen, on Susanna: 1 book. To Aristides the philosopher: 1 book. And he is said to have composed many others, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under Marcus Aurelius, in the year of the Lord 220.

Gregory, bishop of Neocaesarea in Pontus, hearer and disciple of Origen, a learned and holy man, who also wrote much, and, living, shone with miracles. While still a youth, he—together with his brother Athenodorus, seeking the study of secular philosophy—submitted himself to the school of Origen, by whom, little by little and imperceptibly, he was converted, together with his brother, to the faith of Christ, and became equally a most learned and most holy man. Of his writings there is extant, [addressed] to Origen: A Panegyric: 1 book. Of Interpretations on Ecclesiastes: 1 book. And several letters. He flourished under the prince Gordian, in the year of the Lord 240.

Cornelius, after Peter the twenty-second bishop of the city of Rome, Roman by country, son of Castinus, was made pope after the glorious martyrdom of Fabian. He sat in the chair of Peter for two years, a learned and most holy man, until at last he too, crowned with martyrdom, passed, released from the flesh, to those above. He wrote several letters for ecclesiastical utility; of these I have found only the following.

To Fabius, bishop of Antioch: On synods: one epistle. To the same, on the Novatians: one book. On Novatian: one epistle. On the acts of synods: one epistle. He wrote several epistles to Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, and other ones to others. He flourished under Decius, the tyrant prince, in the year of the Lord two hundred and fifty-five.

Cyprian, bishop of the church of Carthage in Africa, a learned and most holy man, gloriously taught rhetoric for many years, and was a magnificent teacher in all secular literature. Then, persuaded by the presbyter Cecilius, from whom he obtained his surname, he was converted to the faith of Christ and distributed all his substance to the poor. And not long afterward, having been chosen presbyter, he was also ordained bishop. Since he was zealous in the divine scriptures, he usefully published many things for the edification of the faithful.

And he wrote the following volumes in the Latin tongue, namely: On the grace of God, to Donatus: one book. “You advise well, Donatus.” Against Demetrianus: one book. “While you bark against, and against.” On piety and almsgiving: one book. “Many great things there are, brothers.” On the praise of martyrdom: one book. “You have desired, Fortunatus.” On jealousy and envy: one book. “To be jealous, because it seems good.” On the good of patience: one book. “About to speak of patience, brothers.” On mortality: one book. “Although among very many of you.” On virginity: one book. “Discipline, guardian of hope.” On the fallen: one book. “Peace, behold, most beloved brothers.” On the sacrament of the chalice: one book. “Cyprian to his brother Cecilius, greeting.” On the unity of the Church: one book. “Since the Lord warns.” On the Lord’s Prayer: one book. “The evangelical precepts.” On the vanity of idols: one book. “That idols are not gods.” On the life of clerics: one book. “I had indeed promised you.” On the two mountains: one book. “The proof of the chapters which in.” To Antonianus, on Novatus: one book. “We have received your first letters.” On the Jews, to Quirinus: one book. “The Jews into offence against God.” To Pope Cornelius: eight epistles. “We have learned, dearest brother.” On dice-players: one book. To Julianus, his friend: one book. Epistles to various persons: one book.

But he is said to have composed many other things which have not come into our hands. The little book On the Twelve Abuses of the Age, ascribed by very many to Cyprian, does not have the flavor of his style. At last he suffered under Valerian on the same day as the Roman woman, but not in the same year, namely in the year of the Lord two hundred forty-nine, on the eighth day before the Kalends of October.

Pontius the presbyter, hearer and disciple of blessed Cyprian, a learned and holy man and an excellent declaimer, after the glorious triumph of his master came into Gaul and at the city of Cimella obtained the palm of martyrdom for the faith of Christ. This Pontius, by the diligence of his honey-flowing preaching, converted the two emperors Philips to Christianity; he persuaded them, the first of the Roman princes, to renounce idols. He also wrote in an elegant style a notable volume, which contains:

The Life of Saint Cyprian: one book.

He flourished under the emperor Philip, in the year of the Lord two hundred forty.

Dionysius, thirteenth bishop of the city of Alexandria, once hearer and disciple of Origen, while he was still a presbyter held the public school under Heraclas and acquired great glory for his learning. For he was a man most learned in every science, a philosopher, rhetorician, and notable theologian. Agreeing with the doctrine of Cyprian and of the African synod on rebaptizing heretics, he wrote very many epistles on that matter to various persons; of these the following are counted as one in number:

On penitence, to Fabius: one epistle. To the Romans: two epistles. To Saint Pope Sixtus: two epistles. To Philemon, presbyter of Dionysius: one epistle. To Dionysius after he had been made pope: one epistle. To Novatian the heretic: one epistle. To the Laodiceans, on penitence: one epistle. To Origen, on martyrdom: one epistle. “Dionysius to his brother Novatian.”

On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 9

On the order of offenses: a letter. To the Alexandrians, on exile: a letter. On Easter: a book. To Heraclas, bishop in Egypt: a book. On the Sabbath: a book. To [Hermammon?]: a book. On the persecution of Decius: a book. Against Nepos, the Chiliast: a book. Against Sabellius: a book. To Ammon, bishop of [Berenice?]: a letter. To Dionysius the pope: a book. To Telesphorus: a letter. To Euphranor: a letter. To the Armenians, on penitence: a book. A canon on penitence: a book. On nature, to Timothy: a book. On temptations: a book. Commentaries on Ecclesiastes: a book.

There are also said to be several letters of his to Basilides. There is extant his notable letter against Paul of Samosata, which he had written a few days before his death. He also composed many other works for ecclesiastical usefulness, which are unknown to us. He flourished under the rulers Gallus and Volusianus, in the year of the Lord 255.

Novatian, priest of the Roman church, tried to seize the episcopal chair against Cornelius; when he could not do so, he stirred up the first schism in the Roman church, established the heresy of the Novatians, refusing to receive apostates who repented, and rebaptizing those duly baptized. The author of this error was Novatus, Cyprian’s priest.

He wrote:

On Easter, one book. On the Sabbath: a book. On circumcision: a book. On prayer: a book. On Jewish foods: a book. On perseverance: a book. On the holy Trinity: a book. Several letters to various persons.

It is said besides that he wrote some other works, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished in the times of the emperor Philip, in the year of the Lord 250.

Malchion, priest of the church of Antioch, a learned and eloquent man, taught very [unclear], since he [unclear] rhetoric in that same city most flourishingly for many years. He published some excellent little works, which in their time seemed to contribute much to the defense of the Christian faith against heretics. Of these there is extant a notable work of dialogues:

Against Paul of Samosata: a book. To Dionysius the pope, from the synod: one letter.

He flourished under the rulers Claudius and Aurelian, in the year of the Lord 270.

Victorinus, bishop of Poitiers, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures, trained in Greek and Latin eloquence, wrote many excellent little works, in which he magnificently exercised his talent. He was, moreover, a distinguished preacher of the divine word, and at last was crowned with martyrdom for the faith of Christ [unclear]. Of his writings the following are reported:

Book

On Genesis: one book. On Exodus: one book. On Leviticus: one book. On Isaiah the prophet: one book. On Ezekiel: one book. On Habakkuk: one book. On Ecclesiastes: one book. On the Song of Songs: two books. On the Apocalypse: one book. Against all heresies: one book. And many other works. He flourished in the times of the emperors Valerian and Gallienus, in the year of the Lord 270.

[P] [unclear] gathered [books?] of the Scriptures; he was so distinguished at Caesarea for [his love?] of books [unclear]. Finally he copied out with his own hand a great part of Origen's books, and placed them in the same Caesarean library. From him Eusebius obtained the surname Pamphili. Moreover, before Eusebius began to write, he wrote some little works of no contemptible authority, of which I have found only:

Against the mathematicians: one book. An Apology for Origen: one book. He is also said to have written certain letters full of faith and learning. At last, after blessed studies and many labors for the church of God, he was crowned with martyrdom for the faith of Christ at Caesarea in Palestine, under the persecution of Maximian, who ruled around the year of the Lord 240.

Anatolius of Alexandria, bishop of Laodicea in Syria, a man skilled in the divine Scriptures and, in secular letters, second to none in his time, an outstanding rhetorician, astronomer, and geometer, left many distinguished little works of his genius; yet very few of them have come to our knowledge. There is extant his notable volume entitled:

On Easter: ten books. On instruction in arithmetic: one book. He flourished under the emperors Probus and Carus, in the year of the Lord 285.

Archelaus, bishop of Mesopotamia in Syria, a learned man and acute disputant, wrote some little works in the Syriac tongue, which are rarely found among the Latins. He disputed vigorously against Mani, the heresiarch, coming out of Persia, and confuted all his arguments, although he could not recall him from error. He wrote that same disputation:

Against Mani: one book. The other works are unknown to us. He flourished under the emperors Aurelian and Probus, in the year of the Lord 280.

Lucian, priest of the church of Antioch, afterward bishop of Nicomedia, a learned and eloquent man, was of excellent talent in delivering homilies to the people, and venerable no less for his life than for his knowledge of the Scriptures. Under the persecution of Maximian he was crowned with martyrdom for the faith of Christ, and was buried at Helenopolis in Bithynia. He wrote, among other things:

On Our Faith: three books. And various other treatises, sermons, homilies, and letters. He flourished under the emperor Maximian, in the year of the Lord 240.

Pierius, priest of the church of Alexandria, a man of such learning and eloquence that he was called the younger Origen, was most excellent in delivering homilies to the people. Under Theonas, bishop of Alexandria, in life and doctrine

Cūqꝫ ad epōs accedēs se baptiçari expeteret:nō credebant ueriti ne uir saeculari tumēs eloquentia sacramētis fidei conaret̉ illudere: & ideo sententiā dif/ ferebant.Arnobius uero cernens sibi fidem minime adhiberi:in argumentū sin ceritatis suae scripsit et obtulit episcopis insigne uolumen: Aduersum gentes: li.vij In psalteriū quoqꝫ: li.j De rhetorica institutione: li.j Alia quoqꝫ multa edidit quae ad noticiam meam non tenerunt. [unclear], shining forth: he was an outstanding cultivator of voluntary poverty for the love of Christ, and an admirable teacher of the people. He wrote countless treatises, which, however, have not come to our knowledge. There is extant his very long work delivered to the people on the vigil of Easter: On Hosea the Prophet, one book. He flourished under the emperor Diocletian, in the year of the Lord 290.

Phileas, bishop of the city of Thebaid in Egypt, a noble and most learned man, distinguished no less in character than in knowledge of the Scriptures, after many labors and various treatises published for the benefit of the faithful, at last under the emperor Maximian became a martyr for the faith of Christ and flew away to the heavenly ones. Of his writings there is extant a disputation held Against the Unjust Judge, one book; On the Praise of Martyrs, one book. Other things that he wrote are unknown to us, although many are reported by the fathers. He flourished under the prince Maximian, in the year of the Lord 240.

Arnobius the presbyter, an outstanding philosopher and rhetorician: while he was still a pagan and teaching rhetoric, he was called by divine mercy and began to profess himself a Christian. And when, going to the bishops, he sought to be baptized, they did not believe him, fearing that a man swollen with worldly eloquence was trying to mock the sacraments of the faith; and therefore they deferred their judgment. But Arnobius, seeing that no trust was being placed in him, as proof of his sincerity wrote and offered to the bishops an excellent volume, Against the Nations, seven books. Also On the Psalter, one book; On Rhetorical Instruction, one book. He also published many other things which have not come to my knowledge. He taught rhetoric in Africa under the prince Diocletian, and had many excellent and noble pupils who turned out to be most learned men. He therefore flourished around the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 300.

John Climacus, which in Latin means “of the ladder,” abbot of Mount Sinai, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, excellent in talent, gentle and humble, devout and most holy in life and conduct, most urgently sought and obtained that he be made [unclear]. Then, after nineteen years, when he had learned, according to the rule of monks, to fight and conquer as a solitary, with the permission of his abbot he sought the wilderness, in which he lived alone with God for many years in all holiness. Finally, when his most holy life had become known to everyone, by the unanimous consent of all he was elected abbot, and, though resisting, was recalled to the monastery. He wrote to John, abbot of Raythu, a very famous work, very suitable for the instruction of monks, containing thirty sermons, which is entitled On the Thirty Steps, one book, “From good and concerning good and” [unclear]. To the Shepherd, one sermon, one book. In the lower book, several letters to monks, one book. And certain other things.

[unclear] of the emperors who reigned in the year of the Lord 216. Ildephonsus, after Saint Eugenius bishop of the see of Toledo, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and an outstanding rhetorician, not ignorant also of literature, excellent in meter and prose, subtle in talent, eloquent in speech, and above all the bishops of his time fluent and eloquent; in life and conduct worthy of God and most holy. For he was endowed with constant fear of God, compunction—
