liberal, not extravagant; dignified in his gait; praiseworthy in integrity; singular in patience; renowned for his talent in discourse; supreme in wisdom. When he was still a boy, touched by the divine spirit, despising the things of the world and the affections of his parents, he sought the Agaliensian monastery, and for many years conducted himself fittingly there as a monk. He also built a convent of virgins in the little village of [unclear], which he endowed from his parents' resources. Then, made abbot of the Agaliensian monastery, he disciplined the monks' conduct, managed the property with discretion, and preserved his way of life. After this, by princely violence, he was brought back to Toledo, and there, after the death of his predecessor, was appointed bishop. He wrote many distinguished little works. Among them the following are reported: On the Holy Trinity, one book; On His Own Weakness, one book; On the Virginity of Saint Mary, one book; Notes on the Daily Office, one book; Notes on Sacred Matters, one book; Notes on the Sacraments, one book; On the Knowledge of Baptism, one book; On the Progress of the Spiritual Desert, one book; Hymns of Various Kinds, one book; Various Sermons, one book; Many Epigrams, one book; also On the Mass, one book; Letters to Various Persons, one book; and several others. When this most blessed prelate Hildefonsus had completed to the end the book on the virginity of Mary, the most pure Mother of God, whom he had always been accustomed to serve with all the zeal he could and with the greatest devotion, the most holy Lady of the world appeared to him, holding that book in her hands and thanking him for such service, which she affirmed was most pleasing to her. He, wishing to honor her more highly, established that her solemnity should be celebrated every year on the eighth day before the Lord's Nativity; and that solemnity has now prevailed, so that throughout the whole church of the faithful it is celebrated in honor of her most pure conception on the sixth day before the Ides of December, that is, 8 December. Hence the blessed Mother of God again appeared to him and brought him a priestly garment, which we call an alb, and a chair; concerning these many wondrous and glorious things are told. He flourished.

Firmianus Lactantius: formerly a hearer and disciple of the rhetorician Arnobius, a man abundantly learned in secular letters and nobly instructed in the divine scriptures, so that in the art of speaking he easily obtained the first place after Cicero. He taught rhetoric gloriously, first at Nicomedia, then at Rome under Diocletian, having been summoned by him. There, when through a scarcity of pupils he had fallen into poverty, he was at last made tutor of Caesar Crispus, the son of Constantine, already an old man, in Gaul. He wrote many distinguished volumes, of which these are reported: On the Divine Institutes, one book, beginning “Great and excellent”; On the Origin of Error, one book, beginning “Although in the first book”; On False Wisdom, one book, beginning “I would wish it to be declared to me”; On True Wisdom, one book, beginning “As I was thinking and with my mind”; On Justice, to Constantine, one book, beginning “There is no doubt with me”; On True Worship, one book, beginning “What was his duty”; [unclear], beginning “It is well”; To Asclepiades, one book, beginning “I have often observed, Donatus”; On Persecution, one book, beginning “[unclear] I am by no means at rest”; Letters to Probus, three books.

On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 2

Letters to Severus: two books. A Symposium in hexameter verse: one book. An Epitome against the Gentiles: one book. Entitled On Grammar: one book. On Paradise, in hexameter: one book. “There is a happy place in the beginning.” He is said to have written not a few other works besides, but they have not come into our hands. He flourished under the emperor Constantine, to whom he was a very close friend, in A.D. 320.

Eusebius, bishop of the church of Caesarea in Palestine, surnamed Pamphili, formerly a disciple of the very learned eunuch Dorotheus, a most zealous restorer in the divine Scriptures: although he was an Arian, when he came to the first council of the fathers held at Nicaea, he laid aside his error and, following the judgment of the fathers, at their command composed the creed which is called Nicene; as testimony to his own most pure faith he offered it to them to be read and confirmed. In it he powerfully crushed the errors of the Arians, and nothing was either added to or taken away from his composition, but to this present day it is publicly sung in the church of God. After this, persevering in the orthodox faith, he was most holily brought to his end. He wrote many excellent volumes in Greek. Of these the following are current among the Latins, namely:

Against Porphyry: thirty books. On the prophet Isaiah: ten books. Expositions of the Gospel: twenty books. On Evangelical Preparation: thirteen books. “When what Christianity is.” Ecclesiastical History: ten books. “The successions of the holy apostles.” An Epitome of the Chronicle: one book. “Moses, of the Hebrew nation.” Theophanies: five books. On the Disagreement of the Evangelists: one book. Topics: one book. Apology for Origen: six books. And On Pamphilus: three books. On the whole Psalter: one book. Martyrology: one book. He also composed many other works, which have not come to my notice. He flourished under the great emperor Constantine, to whom he was a very close friend because of his outstanding learning and the holiness of his life, in A.D. [320?].

Rheticius, of the Aedui, bishop of Autun, a man zealous in the divine Scriptures, in his time a teacher of renowned reputation, is said to have written not a few little works, especially commentaries on the divine books; but we recall that few have come to our notice, namely:

On the Song of Songs: one book. Against Novatian: one book. Saint Jerome censures his exposition on the Song of Songs as inept. He flourished in Gaul under Constantine the Great, in A.D. 320.

Jacob, surnamed the Wise, bishop of Nisibis, a city of the Persians, a man of great learning and incomparable holiness, one of the number of the confessors under Maximian [unclear], was present at the Council of Nicaea; by the addition of homoousion he condemned the most impious Arius. This man of most holy conduct often freed the flock committed to him from many dangers by his prayers. He wrote for the edification of the faithful, in the Syriac language, not a few little works. Of these there are current:

On Faith: one book. Against All Heresies: one book. On General Charity: one book.

HNtonius monachus et amp; abbas:natione aegyptius:uir sanctissimus:heremiqƺ cultor insignis:cuius praeconia laudum uniuersus personat orbis: multis religiosae ac beatae uitae normam praebuit: qui ꝺeisi litteras non didicerit: in diuinis tamen scripturis adeo eruditus fuit: ut nullus doctorum se ei praeferre praesumeret.Habebat memoriam pro libris:intellectũ et amp; sensum pro litteris:gra¬ tiam pro studio lectionis. Book

On love of neighbor: one book. On fasting: one book. On prayer: one book. On resurrection: one book. On life after death: one book. On humility: one book. On patience: one book. On penance: one book. On satisfaction: one book. On virginity: one book. On the sense of the soul: one book. On circumcision: one book. On the blessing of unleavened bread: one book. On Christ, that he is the Son of God: one book. On chastity: one book. Against the Gentiles: one book. On the construction of the tabernacle: one book. On the conversion of the Gentiles: one book. On the kingdom of the Persians: one book. On the persecution of Christians: one book. Chronicle of the times: one book. On the words of Isaiah: one book. Thus the whole work already indicated comprises twenty-five books. He flourished under the great emperor Constantine, in the year of the Lord 330.

Methodius, bishop of Olympus in Lycia and afterward of Tyre, learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, a confessor and distinguished defender of the Christian faith and a diligent emulator of evangelical perfection, after publishing many volumes, was crowned with martyrdom for the faith of Christ in the last persecution, or, as others affirm, under Decius and Valerian, at Chalcis in Greece. He wrote quite a few volumes in a polished and well-composed style, of which these are reported:

Against Porphyry: two books. Symposium on the ten virgins: one book. On the resurrection: one book. On the woman with a divining spirit: one book. On the departure of the soul: one book. On Genesis: one book. On the Song of Songs: one book. On the last times: one book. “For it must be known, brothers.” Also a Chronicle: one book.

He flourished under the great emperor Constantine, or, as others hold, under Decius and Valerian, in the year of the Lord 255.

Antonius, monk and abbot, Egyptian by birth, a most holy man and an outstanding dweller in the desert, whose praises the whole world resounds, provided many with a rule of religious and blessed life. Though he had not learned letters, nevertheless he was so learned in the divine Scriptures that none of the doctors would presume to prefer himself to him. He had memory in place of books, understanding and sense in place of letters, grace in place of the study of reading. In the Egyptian language he dictated various letters, of apostolic sense and speech, to different monasteries. Of these that distinguished one is extant:

To the Arsenoites: one letter. To other monasteries: six letters.

Blessed Athanasius the bishop [wrote] his life in a distinguished Greek volume

he described in discourse.

He flourished while Constantine the Great and his sons were reigning, in the year of the Lord 330, shining with many miracles.

Juvencus, a priest, Spanish by nation, a noble and most learned man, a philosopher, poet, rhetorician, and distinguished theologian, venerable to the Church no less for his way of life than for his knowledge of the Scriptures, published for the edification of readers many excellent volumes, both in meter and in prose; but few of them have come to my knowledge. I have read the distinguished work which he composed in hexameter and pentameter verses:

On the Four Gospels, 3 [4?] books. “Nothing immortal is held in the structure of the world.” On the Sacraments, 2 books.

The rest which he is said to have composed have not come into our hands.

He flourished under Constantine the Great and his sons, in the year of the Lord 330.

Eustachius, by birth a Pamphylian, first bishop of Beroea in Syria and then twenty-third bishop of Antioch after Peter, a learned and holy man, endured many hardships from the Arians for the Catholic faith. For, banished into exile to Trajanopolis of the Thracians, he died there; after the Arians invaded his church, they held it for many years. He wrote very many short works, chiefly against the Arians, and various other diverse treatises, namely:

Against the Arians, 3 books. Against Origen, 1 book. On the Soul, 1 book. Almost innumerable letters, 1 book.

He flourished in the times of Constantine and his sons, in the year of the Lord 330.

Athanasius, nineteenth bishop of the city of Alexandria, a holy man and most learned in the divine Scriptures, endured many persecutions from the Arians for the Catholic faith. Indeed, the whole world was narrow for him, with the Arians persecuting him everywhere, and nowhere did he seem safe, nowhere secure. For a man’s enemies were those of his own household. Fleeing, therefore, from the face of the emperor of the Arians, he came to Trier, a city of Gaul, where he was honorably received by Saint Maximinus the archbishop and hid with him for seven years in a cistern without water, which to this day is shown in the crypt at the monastery of Saint Maximinus in Trier. While lying hidden in this place for many years, as we have said, he did not see the sun; and there he composed the creed “Whoever wishes to be saved,” until at last, betrayed by a certain girl, he escaped again by flight. If anyone desires to know his deeds more fully, let him read the Tripartite History. He wrote almost countless short works in Greek. Among these I have found the following among the Latins:

You are one God: God the Father; God the Son. Now concerning the individual names of the persons. How in the one God. Here now concerning the several names. Here the person contradicting is. I ask of you concerning the unique deity. For which reason most earnestly. Without beginning of times, above all. When you have read this faith. To those who say that the Son of God was created. To the most blessed lord, and deservedly. Their first objection is. When at the city of Nicaea.

On the Unity of the Trinity, 1 book. On the Proper Persons of the Trinity, 1 book. On the Assumption of Man, 1 book. On the Names of the Trinity, 1 book. On the One Substance of the Trinity, 1 book. On the Blessedness of Faith, 1 book. On the Profession of the Catholic Rule, 1 book. On the Unity of Faith, 1 book. On the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, 1 book. On the Trinity of the Holy Spirit, 1 book. To Bishop Lucifer, 1 book. Against the Objections of the Arians, 1 book. A disputation against Arius [unclear], 1 book. Against Valens and Ursacius, 1 book. On Virginity, 1 book. On the Titles of the Psalms, 3 books.

He published several letters to various persons, and also various sermons and treatises, which either have not yet been translated into Latin or have not come to my notice. He died in the time of the emperors Valentinian and Valens, in the year of the Lord 379, the forty-sixth of his priesthood, on the sixth day before the Nones of May, in the seventh indiction.

Theodorus, bishop of Heraclea of the Thracians, diligent and learned in the divine Scriptures, and an outstanding declaimer, of elegant and well-composed speech, produced commentaries on the sacred volumes, not to be despised for reading. Of these the following are reported:

On the Psalter: one book. On the Gospel of Matthew: one book. On the Gospel of John: one book. On the epistles of Paul: fourteen books. He is also said to have written some other works, but they have not come to my notice. He flourished in the times of Constantine II, in the year of the Lord 340.

Eusebius, bishop of Emesa, a man most learned in the divine writings, second to none in his time in delivering homilies to the people, a rhetorician-theologian most celebrated in everyone’s opinion, is said to have written many, almost innumerable, little works; but we have been able to find only the titles and numbers of a few, namely:

Against the Gentiles: one book. Against the Jews: one book. To the Novatians: one book. On the Epistle to the Galatians: ten books. Of many homilies: one book. Sermons to the people. He flourished when Constantine and his brothers were reigning, in the year of the Lord 350.

Oriphilius, Cypriot, bishop of [Litensis?] or Leucontheon, a man most learned both in divine and in secular writings, and easily the most eloquent of all prelates in his age, is said to have written not a few volumes and to have expounded the divine Scriptures in many ways; but I do not recall that anything of his works has come into our hands. His exposition is reported:

On the Song of Songs: one book. He flourished in the times of the emperor Constantius, in the year of the Lord 301.

Serapion, formerly bishop of [Monuseos?] and a very close friend of the blessed abbot Antony, was a man of such learning and eloquence that, because of the excellence of his talent, he received the surname Scholasticus. He is said to have written many little works. Of these the following are extant:

Against the Manichaean: one book. On the titles of the Psalms: one book.

He flourished under the emperor Constantius, in the year of the Lord 341.

Acacius, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, a man indeed practiced in the divine Scriptures, but perverted by Arian impiety, was held in such great regard by the emperor Constantius that he obtained the appointment, in the place of Pope Liberius, of Felix, an Arian priest, as bishop. This Acacius, because he was one-eyed, was called Monoculus. He wrote many and various treatises, which truly would have been useful if they had had a Catholic author. Of these, the more important are said to be those which we have set down below:

On Ecclesiastes, 17 books.

[Sethematon], 1 book.

[Simmiton], 1 book.

He was distinguished under the emperor Constantius, in the year of the Lord 350.

Hilary, bishop of Poitiers in Aquitaine, a man highly venerable in character, life, and learning, suffered many wrongs from the Arians for the faith of Christ. For, through the faction of Saturninus, bishop of Arles, he was banished from the synod of Beziers to Phrygia; for four years he bore harsh exile with steadfast courage. There, by his prayers, he is read to have called a dead man back to life. Since he was a man most learned in every respect, he composed many little works. Concerning him, the following are reported as to their number:

Against Dioscorus, 1 book.

Against Valens and Ursatius, 1 book.

On the Holy Trinity against the Arians, 12 books. “As I consider.”

Defense of the Catholic Faith, 1 book. “God, who is everywhere, everywhere.”

Against the Arians, 1 book. “To the most beloved brothers.”

On the Gospel of Matthew, 1 book. “The step which Matthew.”

On the Synods, to the bishops of Gaul, etc., 1 book. “I had resolved with myself.”

On Certain Psalms, 22 treatises. “The time for speaking has now passed.”

On the Psalm “Blessed are the undefiled,” 42 treatises.

To the emperor Constantius, 3 books.

Hymns, 1 book.

Mysteries, 1 book.

On the Book of Job, 1 book. “To the most blessed, most glorious.”

Against Auxentius, 1 book.

On Heresies, 1 book.

On the Song of Songs, 1 book.

Chronicle, 1 book.

Letters to various persons, 1 book.

He also published some other works which have not come into our hands. At length, after returning from his exile to his own city, he died under the emperor Valentinian, in the year of the Lord 371, in the fourteenth indiction; his feast is celebrated on the Ides of January.

Victorinus Afer, a man of consular rank, the most celebrated rhetorician of all in his time, taught rhetoric in the city of Rome under the emperor Constantine, where, because of the excellence of his learning, he earned a bronze statue in the Forum of Trajan. Converted to the faith of Christ in his old age, he published many treatises on the holy Scriptures, in the dialectical manner, sufficiently obscure and scarcely accessible even to very learned men. Of these the following are extant:

Against the Arians, 1 book.

On the Holy Trinity, 1 book. “In the first discourse of this work.”

Against Heretics, 1 book. “Logos, or,” etc.

On the Homoousion also, 1 book. “Life lives, and life [is] one, not [unclear].”

On the Trinity, hymns, 1 book. “Be present, true light, Father.”

CCC.XCV Ptatus epilcopus mileuitanũ: natione Afer: vir in divinis scripturis studio fus et eruditus: ingenio praestans: uita deuotus et catholicus: feret p defensione fidei nostrae quaedam praeclara scripsisse opuscula: quibus abun dans ingenium magnifice exercitauit: Equibus extare dicitur grande et insigne uolumen quod scripsit: DE SCRIPTORIBVS ECCLESIASTICIS Fol. 14

On the Epistles of the apostle Paul: fourteen books. And certain other things. He flourished at Rome under the emperor Constantius II, in the year of the Lord 360.

Titus, bishop of Bostra, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and notably instructed in secular letters, keen and forceful in intellect, is said to have composed many little works, by which he transmitted the memory of his name with glory to posterity. Of these, the following are reported:

Against the Manichaeans: two books. Commentaries on the Gospel: one book. And many other things. He flourished in the year of the Lord 340. And he died under the emperor Valens.

Damasus, pope, a Spaniard by nation, sat after Liberius in the chair of Peter for eighteen years; a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and notably instructed in secular letters, a very celebrated rhetorician and poet, and highly skilled in composing verses; subtle in intellect, devout and most holy in life; greatly beloved of the priest Saint Jerome. He wrote various little works in both kinds. Of these the following are extant:

The Deeds of the Supreme Pontiffs: one book. “Blessed Peter, of the apostles...” On the Faith, against Heretics: one book. “After the Nicene council...” Letters to Various Persons: one book. “Damasus, bishop of the city...” Various poems. And other things. He flourished under Valentinian and Valens, in the year of the Lord 370.

Apollinaris of Laodicea, bishop in Syria, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, and by far most learned in grammatical instruction, keen and forceful in intellect, distinguished in speech, wrote in defense of the Catholic faith certain very excellent volumes, by which he commended his name to posterity. Of these there is extant a work Against the mad Porphyry: thirty books, very celebrated. And certain other things. He flourished under the emperor Gratian, in the year of the Lord 380.

Didymus of Alexandria, blind from early childhood, and for this reason entirely ignorant even of the elements, presented so great a marvel of himself that he learned dialectic and geometry, which especially requires sight, to perfection. In the divine Scriptures he was most learned, the teacher of blessed Jerome and the very close friend of Saint Antony; keen in intellect and distinguished in life. He wrote in the Greek language the following works:

Against the Arians: two books. On Doctrines also: one book. On the Canonical Epistles: eight books. “James, etc., just as mortal...” On the Holy Spirit: one book. “All things indeed which are divine...” On the book of Saint Job: one book. On Isaiah the prophet: ten books. On Hosea, to Jerome: four books. On Zechariah, to the same: five books. On the Gospel of Matthew: one book. On the Gospel of John: one book. On the Psalter also: one book. And certain other things. He flourished as an octogenarian under the emperor Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 395.

Optatus, bishop of Milevis, an African by nation, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, outstanding in intellect, devout and Catholic in life, is said to have written in defense of our faith certain excellent little works, in which he exercised his abundant intellect splendidly. Of these there is said to be extant a large and notable volume which he wrote:

Contra Eunomium. li. ii

Against the Donatists: six books. And several letters. And many other things. He flourished under the emperors Valentinian and Valens, in the year of the Lord 370.

Basil, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, a learned and most holy man, was of such authority among the Greeks that no one, however learned, ever dared to contradict him in any matter of doctrine or writings. He wrote many excellent little works in the Greek language, but few of them have come into our hands.

On the Holy Spirit: one book. Against Eunomius: one book. On the Hexaemeron: nine books. “In the beginning,” etc. [unclear]. The Rule of Monks: one book. “The human race.” An Exhortation of Monks: one book. “Hear, my son, the admonition.” On the Instruction of Boys: one book. On Faith: one book. “God indeed without inter-.” On Hidden Speech: one book. “God [gave] the use of speech.” On Several Psalms: one book. “All Scripture is divinely [inspired].” To a Fallen Virgin: one book. “It is time to cry out.” Several homilies. He also composed other treatises, sermons, and letters to various persons. He flourished under Valentinian and Valens, in the year of the Lord 380.

Ephrem, a monk and distinguished inhabitant of the desert, and deacon of the church of Edessa, was ordained priest by blessed Basil; because of his humility he now approached the divine mysteries to be performed, for he was held worthy before God and men. Nevertheless, so far as pertained to his office, in admonishing the people he delivered countless homilies. As is read in the Life of the Holy Fathers, he was seen to have received from an angel a book written in golden letters; from this, soon on the next day and thereafter, with the Holy Spirit speaking in him, he had such grace in declaiming that in his time he found no one like himself. He wrote, in the Syriac language for the instruction of readers, certain devout little works, of which the following are found among the Latins, namely:

On the Holy Spirit: one book. On Compunction of Heart: one book. “Grief compels me.” On Contrition of Heart: one book. “Come, my dearest ones, to me.” On Penance: one book. “Our Lord Jesus Christ, who.” On the Struggles of the World: one book. “In the struggles of this.” On the Day of Judgment: one book. “Come, most beloved brothers.” On the Resurrection: one book. “Glory to almighty God.” On the Blessedness of the Soul: one book. “Blessed is he who has hated.” On Thoughts: one book. “In the holy Scriptures.” On Hard Preaching: one book. “Whenever, brothers.” On the Celebration of the Mysteries: one book. “I ask you, brothers.” Lamentation over the City of Edessa: one book. He also published not a few other works, especially sermons and homilies to the people, which have not yet come to my knowledge. He flourished under Valentinian and Valens, a very close friend of blessed Basil, as you will be able to find in his legend, in the year of the Lord 380.

Gregory, bishop of [Nyssa?], brother of blessed Basil, prelate of Caesarea in Cappadocia, a man very studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, stirred by zeal for his brother, himself also wrote some little works in the Greek language. Of these I have found among our people only:

On the Image and Formation of Man: one book. “Man, from the rational soul.” Against Eunomius: two books.

Book

He flourished, the younger brother, under the emperors Valentinian and Valens; he composed various works. In the year of the Lord 480.

Gregory, formerly a monk, bishop of Nazianzus, a man of such great learning, integrity, and eloquence that not even his adversaries dared in any way to contradict the things said by him; so much so that, for confirming an authority, it was enough that Gregory had merely said something. He was a cultivator and lover of the monastic life; when, because of the excellence of his learning and the holiness of his life, he was called to the episcopate, he fled and hid himself, preferring to be abject in the house of the Lord rather than to be exalted among the crowd with perishable honors. But almighty God did not will so bright a light to be hidden under the bushel of the aforesaid way of life, since it could be extended to the salvation of many. Found, therefore, by divine indication, he was led by the people to the episcopal see, and immediately, in excuse for his flight, there was dictated the solemn homily in which the governance of souls is shown to be the art of arts. On account of his distinguished learning and holiness of life this Gregory was called Gregory the Great before the blessed pope of the same name. He wrote many small works in the Greek tongue. Of these the following are extant:

On the death of his brother Caesarius: one book. On the praise of Cyprian the martyr: one book. On the praise of Bishop Athanasius: one book. On the praise of Maximus the philosopher: one book. A denunciation against the same: one book. On virginity, in hexameter: one book. On the Holy Spirit: one book. Apologetic works, when he had fled: one book. On the Nativity of the Lord: one book. On the fruitful Epiphanies: one book. On the Holy Spirit on the day of Pentecost: one book. On himself, after returning from the country: one book. On Jeremiah, in the presence of the emperor: one book. On the reconciliation of a monk: one book. On the devastation by hail: one book. Against Eunomius: one book. Against Julian the Apostate: one book.

He published many sermons and homilies, and various treatises on diverse subjects, which have not come to my knowledge. At length, worn out by old age, when he saw that he could no longer be adequate for governing the people, he ordained another bishop in his place and returned to the pursuit of his beloved solitude.

He flourished under Valentinian and Theodosius. In the year of the Lord 490.

One book. I confess that I have been defeated. Christ is born; glorify him. Again my Jesus. I was longing for you, O. On the solemnity of this. I grieve for my belly. He loosed our tongue. What praiseworthy [unclear].

Eutropius, monk and priest, a man of most religious way of life, very devoted and learned in the divine Scriptures, and fully instructed in secular letters, is said to have composed some small works. Of these the following alone are known to us by title:

To two virgins, sisters: one book. Chronicle, and up to his own times: one book.

He flourished under the emperors Valentinian and Valens. In the year of the Lord three hundred seventieth. There are also those who write that he was a disciple of Augustine and flourished in the year of the Lord 430.

Es[y]tius, priest and monk, formerly hearer and disciple of the blessed Gregory, bishop of Nazianzus, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, admonished by the example of his teacher, is said to have written many small works of explanations on the divine books, and to have composed various volumes both on the New and on the Old Testament, which have not yet come into our hands. I have read only that distinguished work of great size which he wrote to Euthicianus, the venerable deacon:

On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. [unclear].

On Leviticus: one book. To the venerable deacon Eu[unclear]. Of the rest I have seen nothing. He flourished under the emperors Arcadius and Honorius, in the year of the Lord 400.

Ambrose, bishop of Milan, a Roman by birth, a man most celebrated for faith and holiness, easily the most learned of all in divine Scriptures and in secular letters, perfectly trained in Greek and Latin speech; his merit the whole world proclaims, and holy mother Church confirms his works and books with a great proclamation of authority. In expounding and explaining the divine Scriptures he surpassed all teachers; no earthly power could ever break his faith, so that, though many bishops had been banished into exile for the faith, no one ever dared to touch Ambrose. For he was like a hammer of heretics, a most steadfast assailant; no human authority could ever impose silence on his tongue when it spoke in the faith of Christ.

Always ready to undergo any dangers for the faith, with the Lord protecting him, he escaped everywhere free and unharmed. He wrote many excellent little works, of which I have found only the following:

On Duties: three books. Not wishing to seem arrogant. On the Calling of the Gentiles: two books. Among the defenders of free [will?]. Hexaemeron: six books. So much of opinion. On Human Dignity: one book. Let us make man according to. On Paradise: one book. Concerning Paradise [unclear]. On Cain and Abel: two books. Concerning Paradise in the preceding. On Noah’s Ark: one book. We undertake holy Noah. On Abraham the Patriarch: two books. Abraham, of this book. On Isaac and the Soul: one book. In the father, for us, of holy Isaac [unclear]. On the Good of Death: one book. Since concerning the soul in the preceding. On Flight from the World: one book. Often for us concerning escape [unclear]. On Naboth the Jezreelite: one book. Necessary for discipline. On Elijah and Fasting: one book. The life of the saints is a rule for others. On Tobit: one book. First of all, how much we learn. On Interpellations: four books. The story of Naboth, at the time. Apology of David: one book. A divine [unclear] for the present has resounded [unclear]. On Solomon: one book. When the prophetic book had been read, which. On the Mysteries for Those Being Initiated: five books. Many disturbances for us. On the Sacraments: one book. The apology of the prophet David. On Pastoral Care: one book. It is quite remarkable, dearly beloved. On the Faith, to Gratian: two books. Concerning moral matters, a daily. On the Mystery of Easter: one book. Brothers, I desire to discharge the debt. On the Death of His Brother: one book. The mystery of Easter concerning. On Faith in the Resurrection: one book. We have brought down, beloved brothers. On Repentance: one book. In the preceding book, something. Exhortation to Virgins: one book. If that is the end of virtues. To a Devoted Virgin: one book. I admonish you, brothers. To a Fallen Virgin: one book. If according to the heavenly sentence.

[Unclear] Ambrose, [unclear] doctor [unclear].

Against Symmachus: one book, “Ambrose, bishop, to the most blessed ...” A Consolation for Valentinian: one book, “Although the increase ...” Against Auxentius: one book, “Dalmatius the tribune ... me ...” On Handing Over the Basilicas: one book, “I see that you, beyond the usual ...” On the Instruction of a Virgin: one book, “You entrust to me a pledge ...” On the Death of Theodosius: one book, “This earthquake for us ...” On the Instruction of Priests: one book, “You have undertaken the office of priesthood ...” On Circumcision: one book, “No ordinary [matter] most people ...” On the Synagogue, to Theodosius: one book, “The army always with continual ...” The Revelation of Gervasius and Protasius: one book, “To my lady sister, of my life and eyes ...” On the Passion of Saint Agnes: one book, “Ambrose to the virgins of Christ ...” On Choosing a Bishop: one book. On Judgments: one book. On Saint Job: one book. On the Forty-Two Stations: one book. Of Hymns and Prefaces: one book. On the Epistles of Paul: fourteen books, “Although also with a mystical veil ...” Letters to Various Persons: ten books, “You admonish well, brother ...” On the Gospel of Luke: ten books, “As we are about to write on the book of the Gospel ...” Of Many Sermons: one book, “We gladly preach ...” On Certain Psalms: treatises, or eleven books; he wrote [unclear]. He also published some other works, which have not come to my knowledge. Finally, he is said to have made Hegesippus and certain others Latin from Greek. He flourished under the most merciful emperor Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 380.

Philastrius, bishop of Brescia, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, was known to and intimate with blessed Ambrose of Milan. Saint Augustine mentions him in a certain letter written to Quodvultdeus. For the common benefit he wrote certain excellent little works, none of which I remember to have come into our hands. With blessed Augustine as witness in the same place, an outstanding work of his is reported, which he wrote: On 156 Heresies: one book, “The Simonians from Simon ...” I have not seen the rest. He flourished under the most Christian emperor Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 380.

Evagrius, a monk, disciple of Saint Macarius the Egyptian, afterwards bishop of Antioch, a man most learned in every respect, educated in both secular and divine writings, skilled in Greek and Latin eloquence, and even in the episcopate preserving the austerity of his former life, was of such abstinence that he was regarded as a marvel. He was the first to commend the life of the holy fathers to writing; from his own vein he published many little works, of which, however, very few have come to my knowledge. The following are reported as his: To the Anchorites, very useful: one book, “The priest Evagrius to Innocent ...” Also To the Cenobites: one book. On the Eight Principal Vices: one book. Exhortatory Pieces to a Virgin: one book. He made the Life of Antony Latin: one book. On the Life of the Holy Fathers: one book. He also wrote many other things and translated from Greek into Latin works unknown to us. He flourished under the prince Gratian, in the year of the Lord 380.

Maximus, bishop of Constantinople, an Alexandrian by birth, a philosopher and distinguished theologian, in whose praise Gregory Nazianzen published a book, endured many injuries from the Arians and, finally driven from the episcopate, wrote many things against them. Of these there survives an outstanding work addressed to Gratian:

On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 16

Against the Arians: one book. The rest are unknown to me. He flourished in Greece under Emperor Gratian, in the year of the Lord 380.

Ambrosius, a priest, Alexandrian by nation, once a hearer and disciple of Didymus the Blind, learned the divine Scriptures magnificently as Didymus explained them, and composed various expositions on them, which among the Greeks at that time were held at a great price. Of these, the following are reported among us:

Commentaries on Job: [unclear] book. Against Apollinaris of Laodicea: [unclear] book. He flourished under the emperors Theodosius and Arcadius, in the year of the Lord 400.

Petronius, bishop of Bologna, a monk in his manner of life, very learned and eloquent in the divine Scriptures, revered no less for holiness than for knowledge, shone with many miracles in life and after death, as is read in his history. Among other things he wrote:

On the Life of the Holy Fathers: [unclear] book. On the Ordination of a Bishop: [unclear] book. And other works unknown to us. He died under Theodosius and Valentinian, in the year of the Lord 385, in the fourteenth indiction.

Pachomius, abbot, a most magnificent founder of the monks of his time, founder of many monasteries, and a man of most holy way of life, shining with many miracles in life and after death, since he was a learned man, instructed in the divine Scriptures, wrote many letters for the edification of the brethren. Of these, the following are reported:

To Abbot Cornelius: one letter. To Abbot Syrus: one letter. To the superiors of the monasteries: one letter. To the brothers working outside: one letter. Also a Rule for Monks: one book. He flourished under the emperors Valentinian and Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 390.

Aurelius Clemens Prudentius, a Christian poet, a man very learned in secular literature, sufficiently skilled in the divine Scriptures, excellent in verse and prose, was held for fifty-seven years by the loves of the world. He read and expounded many small works of the poets, and from his own vein wrote many profound poems. At last, however, in old age, after rejecting the vanity of the world, he betook himself to the sacred Scriptures; in verse and prose he expounded many hidden things of both Testaments. He wrote many excellent small works. Of these, after the measure of the meter had been made, I found the following:

Against Symmachus the Idolater: one book. “Paul, herald of God, who savage...” On Struggle: one book. “A faithful old man, first...” On the Divinity: one book. “God is three highest things.” Against the Patripassians: one book. “There are very many things, but few...” Against the Sabellians: one book. “Yield, profaner of Christ...” Against the Jews: one book. “These things, if Jewish; if in...” On the Hexaemeron: six books. “There are those who, akin to the Jewish...” Of Various Hymns: one book. “It is worthwhile, cloud...” Praises of Saint Vincent: one book. “The winged messenger of the day, the light...” Praises of Saint Lawrence: one book. “Blessed martyr, make the day prosperous...” Praises of Romanus against the Gentiles: one book. “The ancient parent of the shrines...” Histories: one book. “Romanus, brave man of Christ...” “Eve was a dove, then can...”

On the nature of the soul: one book. On the resurrection of the flesh: one book. On the martyrs: one book. On the state of the soul: one book. Hamartigenia: one book. On the hope of pardon, a prayer, or book. Against the Marcionites: one book. Peristephanon: one book. He also wrote not a few letters. He also published some other works, which have not come into our hands. He flourished under the emperor Gratian, in the year of the Lord 380.

John, monk and priest of Damascus, a learned and holy man, about whom wonderful things are related because of the excellence of his teaching and the sincerity of his life, held in great esteem at Constantinople and appointed prelate of the monks, turned many away from wickedness. He wrote in Greek some treatises of profound meaning, but few of them have come into our hands. I have read only that distinguished work:

On the tradition of the orthodox faith: three books. “No one has ever seen God.” The History of Barlaam and Josaphat: one book. Of the rest I have seen nothing. He flourished under Theodosius, the most devout prince, in the year of the Lord 490.

Iconius the African, whom blessed Augustine records in the third book On Christian Doctrine to have belonged to the Donatist party, although in certain matters he disagrees with them, was certainly an acute man and much practiced in the divine Scriptures. He wrote not a few treatises, of which these are reported, namely:

On internal war: three books. An expository work on various causes: one book. On the Apocalypse of John: one book. Rules of Sacred Scripture: one book. Several letters to various persons, and many other works. He flourished when Theodosius and his sons were ruling, in the year of the Lord 390.

Heraclides the monk, a man holy in conduct and distinguished in learning in the divine Scriptures, a most diligent [unclear] of the holy fathers, anchorites and monks, gathering the flowers of virtues into the little garden of his heart, produced the honey of spiritual sweetness. Among other things he wrote, for the edification of readers, a distinguished work on the life and conduct of the holy fathers living in the wilderness or in monasteries under a rule, whose title is:

Paradise: one book. He flourished in the times of the emperor Gratian, in the year of the Lord 380.

Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium, a man very studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, sufficiently imbued also with secular letters, and no less worthy of the priesthood by his manner of life than by his knowledge of the Scriptures, wrote among other things the useful work:

On the Holy Spirit: one book. Of the rest which he is said to have composed, nothing has come to my knowledge. He flourished in the times of the devout emperor Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 390.

Epiphanius, bishop of Salamis, a city of Cyprus, a man sufficiently learned in the divine Scriptures and of such holiness that he deserved to be illumined with the spirit of prophecy and to become a performer of many miracles. He was a very close friend of blessed Jerome and wrote several letters to him. If anyone desires to know his deeds, let him read the Tripartite History. He composed some treatises, of which these are reported:

On ninety heresies: one book. “The Simonians from Simon.” “Here he meets those who are in doubt; discuss.” “I ask for my body in Christ.” “Written in heaven of two.” “Whoever errs [unclear] of ours.” “Brothers Ephebus the gravedigger, etc.” “O goddess, all equal souls give.” “Whither does rage hurl you?” “The more faithful innocent [unclear].”

On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 2

Against all heresies: one book. On the errors of Origen: one book. To Theophilus of Alexandria: one book. Letters to various persons: one book. And certain other works. To the most beloved lord and son. He flourished under the most religious emperor Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 390.

Theophilus, the twenty-first bishop of the church of Alexandria, a man devoted to the Scriptures and a most vigorous assailant of the Origenists, who burned with great discord against Saint John Chrysostom and compelled him, driven from the episcopate by plots, to die in exile, as is contained more fully in the histories of the ancients. He is said to have written certain little works, of which few have come to my knowledge. There is extant by him, to various persons on various matters: Letters: one book. To Epiphanius on heresies: one book. On Easter: one book. To the most beloved lord, a[unclear]. He also published many other things, as may be gathered from the letter of blessed Jerome addressed to him, in which he asks that they be sent to him to be translated. He flourished under the emperors Theodosius and Valentinian, in the year of the Lord 390.

Antiochus, bishop of a certain city, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, and nobly instructed in secular letters; his character and learning commended him to his people. He wrote for the edification of readers certain excellent volumes, of which these are reported the more important: Against avarice: two books. On the illumination of the man born blind: one book. Several homilies to the people: one book. And other works unknown to us. He flourished under the emperors Theodosius and Arcadius, in the year of the Lord 390.

Macarius, an Egyptian monk, formerly a disciple of the blessed father Antony, a devout man of most holy life, of whom many miracles are told, and how he even obtained voices of the dead from their tombs for the confirmation of the faith. He sent a letter useful to all religious persons: To monks: one book. It begins: Certainly at first, if he shall have begun. And others to other persons. He flourished in great holiness under the emperors Constantine and Constantius, in the year of the Lord 450. His deeds are extant.

Faustinus, a priest, very learned in the sacred Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, of the party of Lucifer, and for that reason deservedly blameworthy. He wrote many excellent volumes, which are judged useful for the confutation of heretics. Of these I have found only the titles of a few: Against the Arians and Macedonians: seven books. An Apology to Valentinian: one book. He flourished under Valentinian and Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 370.

Jerome, priest and monk, born of his father Eusebius from the town of Stridon, a man very learned in secular letters, and among all the doctors most learned in the divine Scriptures; distinguished by knowledge of many languages; interpreter of the sacred law; a prudent hammer of heretics; bringing forth from his treasury new things and old, and giving to his fellow servants at the proper time the measure of spiritual wheat, he stripped the proud Hebrews and enriched the humble Latins. This is the true evangelical steward, faithful and prudent, who, bringing forth from his treasury new things and old, and giving to his fellow servants at the proper time the measure of spiritual wheat, stripped the proud Hebrews and enriched the humble Latins. This is the distinguished doctor of the Church of Christ, who, with his pious mother Rebecca, that is, the grace of God, brought forth the hidden things of Esau, wandering through the byways of errors, [unclear], and [unclear] the meek Jacob, faithful and serving Christ [unclear].

[unclear]. This is Jerome, sincere lover of Jesus Christ, who, letting no time pass idly, meditated day and night on the law of the Lord, and, scarcely granting his body the sleep necessary for it, always, by day and by night, wrote, read, taught, or prayed; this is attested by the almost countless books which he published. This defender of truth, cultivator of virtue, most bitter enemy of vices, when he was a priest of the Roman Church and steadfastly rebuked the crimes of the clergy, withdrew from the city because of their envy; and coming to Judea he visited the glorious sepulchre of the Lord, and, establishing for himself a place of habitation beside the Bethlehemite manger, became known as famous to the whole world, divine providence surely arranging this: that he who was to be a light of the world should rest there where the true Sun of justice had made himself known to men by being born. A holy and fitting inhabitant of the most holy place, firm in faith, kindled with charity, mature in his way of life, who could not be seduced by prosperity, whom no adversity ever cast down from his holy purpose. But why, a foul praiser, do I touch the holy head of the man with impure lips? It would have been more fitting for me humbly to keep silent than shamelessly to speak of so holy a man. Now therefore let us record in order what we have found concerning his writings and minor works:

These are the works from the writings of the most blessed teacher Jerome which at present have occurred to us as needing to be recorded. Nor do we doubt that he wrote more things which are not contained in this catalogue, especially because they either are unknown to us, or remain scattered among many things. For among all the doctors of the Church none was of more benefit than Jerome: besides innumerable little works, he translated the Old Testament from Hebrew into Latin, corrected the New according to the Greek truth, and faithfully offered it to the Church to be read. He also made many volumes of the Greeks Latin, namely those of Origen, Josephus the Jew, Eusebius of Caesarea, Didymus of Alexandria, Victorinus the martyr, and others.

On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. j9

At length he died after many labors, full of days, under the emperors Honorius and Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 422, in the fifth indiction, on the last day of the month of September, at the hour of compline, in the ninety-ninth year of his age. He was buried at Bethlehem, shining with many miracles; Eusebius, his disciple, wrote his life.

Audentius, a Spanish bishop, a man whose talent was exercised in the divine Scriptures, wrote against the Manichaeans, Sabellians, and Arians, but with special intention against the Photinians, who afterward were called Bonosiacs, a notable work, which is said to have been entitled:

On the Faith, Against Heretics, one book.

He also published some other works, which have by no means come to my knowledge.

Rufinus, monk and priest of the church of Aquileia, an eloquent man and very learned in the divine Scriptures, skilled in Greek and Latin speech, was of no small reputation among the ecclesiastical doctors. Although his writings are many, nevertheless they are counted among the apocrypha, distinction 15, Sancta romana, because he wrote invective letters against the most holy man Jerome, as can be understood from reading them. But afterward, when they returned to the harmony of brotherly love, the works of Rufinus were made authentic insofar as they were not said to be contrary to Jerome. Concerning the writings of Rufinus, therefore, the following are reported:

On the Prophet Hosea, one book.

On the Prophet Amos, one book.

On the Prophet Joel, one book.

On His Faith, to Bishop Laurentius, one book. “To me indeed, most faithful father.”

Invectives Against Jerome, three books. “I have read your writings, [unclear].”

On His Faith, to Anastasius, one book. “I have heard that certain men, when among.”

On the Blessings of the Patriarchs, one book.

On the Sacraments, one book.

Exhortation to Proba, one book.

Additions to the Ecclesiastical History, three books. He flourished in the times of the emperors Arcadius and Honorius, and wrote many and various works, in the year of the Lord 400.

John, bishop of Constantinople, [unclear] of the eloquence of Eusebius, bishop of Emesa, is named Chrysostom, that is, “golden mouth.” He was a man very learned in the divine Scriptures, of outstanding talent in declaiming homilies to the people, and no less distinguished for holiness than for learning; he was held by the people in great reverence and love. This most blessed prelate suffered many injuries from Theophilus of Alexandria, and by his fraudulent and deceitful machinations was driven from the episcopate into exile, as is found in his life and in the Tripartite History. He wrote many volumes in Greek; of these I, among the Latins, have seen only the following:

“When I behold you, blessed [unclear].”

That No One Is Harmed Except by Himself, one book. “I know that to the coarser.”

On the Restoration of the Fallen, one book. “Who will give water to my head.”

On the Gospel of Matthew, three books. “As they report Matthew.”

On the Gospel of John, 87 homilies, one book. “They who [unclear] the contests.”

On Paul’s Epistle to the Hebrews, six books. “In many ways and in many.”

To Stagirius the Monk, Possessed by a Spirit, three books. “There is certainly nothing.”

“It had indeed been fitting for a man.” c. 5

On giving alms: one homily. “What, when someone asks for alms.” On blessing those who curse: one homily. “A desire comes to me to groan.” On restraining concupiscence: one homily. “Having been roused from sleep itself.” On mercy toward the poor: one homily. “How, then, are they worthy?” On avoiding scandal: one homily. “Observe how greatly Paul.” On loving persecutors: one homily. “Let us join ourselves to one another.” On consolations: one homily. “As by food life.” On distributing riches: one homily. “If craftsmen who [work] with their hands.” On praising God with formed faith: one homily. “Let us also imitate the patriarch.” On the love of God: one homily. “Let us also pursue heavenly things.” On the rewards of the saints and Gehenna: one homily. “By no means the same equally for all the blessed.” On concealing good works: one homily. “The management of your affairs.” On hope and presumption: one homily. “Let no one despair if through.” On contempt of the world: one homily. “As [unclear] in the days.” On charity: one homily. “I love charity best.” An exhortation to a good life: one homily. “This very thing most nearly to perdition.” To Theodore the monk: one book. “If I could [send] tears with letters.” To Cyriacus the bishop, on exile: one book. “Again I shall exhaust the field.”

He also wrote many homilies, sermons, and almost innumerable letters, which have not come into our hands. At length, after many labors and holy exercises, by the treachery of Theophilus of Alexandria and of the empress Eudoxia, he died in exile in Pontus, on the sixth day before the Kalends of February, in the year of the Lord 411, in the ninth indiction.

Severianus, bishop of Gabala, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and an admirable teacher in delivering homilies to the people, was of incredible eloquence. Hence he was frequently summoned to Constantinople by the blessed John, the above-mentioned bishop, and by the emperor Arcadius to deliver a sermon. To this man Saint John commended his people when he was compelled into exile, venerating not only his teaching but also the merit of his life. But Severianus, commending himself to the people more than was fitting, supplied kindling matter for discord between himself and John. But when the patriarch returned from exile, they returned to the bonds of brotherly love, as the homily given afterward in the church of Constantinople testifies. Of the writings of Severianus, a most learned man, few are held among the Latins, and still fewer have come into our hands:

On the Epistle to the Galatians: one book. On baptism and Epiphany: one book. In the church of Constantinople: one homily. “At the coming of the Lord and [unclear].” On the death of the innocents: one homily. “Whither zeal tends, whither [unclear].”

There also survive among us certain other homilies of his, brief indeed but very useful. Concerning his other little works, although many are reported, I have so far found nothing. He flourished under Arcadius and Honorius, at the same time as John Chrysostom, in the year of the Lord 400.

Tychonius the African, defending the Donatist schism, a man who was quite practiced in the divine Scriptures, would have composed teaching sufficiently useful if he had remained in ecclesiastical unity. But because he charged true Catholics as though they were traditors and persecutors, he rightly fell into contempt together with his volumes. Of his writings the following volumes survive:

Against the nations: one book. That the servants of God are hated by the world: one book. Against the complaints of all: one book.

They say that he composed many other volumes besides, which have not come to my notice. He flourished under Constans, son of Constantine the Great, emperor, in the year of the Lord 360.

Concerning the rest I have seen nothing.

He wrote this revelation itself in the Greek language; Avitus, a presbyter, Spanish by birth, translated it into Latin speech, and, adding his own letter, sent it through Orosius to the Easterners to be read. He flourished under the emperors Honorius and Theodosius, around the year of the Lord 410.

Severus, a presbyter, surnamed Sulpicius, born from the province of Aquitaine, a man noble in birth and letters, and conspicuous for his love of poverty and humility. Dear also to the holy men Martin of Tours and Paulinus of Nola, bishops, in his old age he was deceived by the Pelagians; and, recognizing the fault of loquacity, he kept silence until death, so that the sin which he had contracted by speaking he might healthfully amend by keeping silent. He wrote little works not to be despised in reading, of which the following are reported:

On the Life of Saint Martin, Bishop, three books: “Most mortals.”

The Conference of Postumianus and Gallus, three books: “When I, into one place.”

Letters to His Sister, one book.

Letters to Various Persons, one book.

To Paulinus, Bishop of Nola, two books.

He is also said to have written some other things, which have not come to my knowledge.

He flourished with Saint Martin, archbishop of Tours, under the emperors Arcadius and Honorius, in the year of the Lord 420.

Ausonius, bishop of Bordeaux, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, and in secular letters second to none in his time, excelling in verse and prose, shone forth no less illustrious for holiness than for learning. While at Trier, in the council under the emperor Maximus, together with the holy men Martin, Ambrose of Milan, and Jerome the presbyter, he did many splendid things. While staying there he wrote, among other things, in meter, a notable little work entitled:

Mosella, one book.

On the Latin [unclear] of the Same Country, one book.

But he is also said to have written many other little works, which have by no means come down to us.

He flourished under Maximus, in the year of the Lord 220.

Augustine, bishop of Hippo, by nation a Carthaginian in Africa, a man most learned among all the doctors both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, eloquent in speech, renowned in expression, profound in understanding, so that I should believe no one able either to read or to possess all his works. Hence without doubt he is proved to lie who admits that he has found Augustine entire. For he surpasses all writers both in the number of his books and in usefulness, having composed more than a thousand distinguished treatises. No one expounded sacred Scripture so profoundly as Augustine; no one established Christian morals so usefully; nor did anyone defend the catholic faith more ardently than he. The king brought him into the wine-cellar, and clothed him with such great strength that he powerfully laid low all the adversaries of the faith with the sword of his mouth.

If you have him as your teacher, even if the rest are lacking, he alone is sufficient for you. Now therefore, from the many books which he published, let us record at least a few:

On the Holy Trinity, fifteen books: “The reader about to read these things which concerning the Trinity.”

On the City of God, twenty-two books: “The most glorious city of God.”

On the Predestination of the Saints, two books: “Indeed, to have said, I know the Apostle.”

On Genesis According to the Letter, twelve books: “All divine Scripture.”

On Genesis, Unfinished, one book: “Concerning the obscure things of natural matters.”

On Genesis against the Manichaeans, two books: “If the Manichaeans would choose.”

On the Academics, three books: “Would that, Romanianus, men.”

On the Happy Life, one book: “If to the harbor of philosophy.”

Also On Order, three books: “On the order of things.”

On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 24

On the vigils of Easter: 23 treatises. On the Creed: 3 treatises. Of exhortation to the candidates: 1 treatise. On the Ascension of the Lord: 2 treatises. On Saints Perpetua and Felicity: 4 treatises. On Saint Vincent: 2 treatises. On spiritual almsgiving: 1 treatise. On bodily alms: 1 treatise. On Samson: 1 treatise. On Susanna and Joseph: 1 treatise. On the dedication of the temple: 2 treatises. Sermons on various subjects: 251. Letters: more than 251.

He also published many other works; if anyone desires to know them more fully, let him read the list of his books edited by Possidius, from which we too have taken many items. Jacobus de Voragine, bishop of Genoa, writes in his treatise which he composed on the books of Augustine that the number of his books, treatises, sermons, and letters rises above one thousand and thirty. And he concludes thus: And therefore no one has ever been found who could discover all the books of Augustine. And Possidius says: He lies who professes that he has read you entire, Augustine. But in this work I have deliberately omitted certain treatises which are ascribed by very many to blessed Augustine. Among these is the book On Spirit and Soul, in whose thirty-seventh chapter Boethius is cited, who was born a long time after Augustine. Moreover, the style itself does not smell of Augustine. Likewise the book On True and False Penitence, which has now been printed under Augustine’s name, is falsely ascribed to him, since in the seventeenth chapter, near the end, Augustine himself is cited. The book On the Conflict of Virtues and Vices, which begins “The apostolic voice,” both echoes the style of Pope Gregory and agrees with the older copies. Likewise the book On the Ladder of Paradise, whose beginning is “When one day,” is inscribed in ancient copies to blessed Bernard, and seems to display his spirit and manner of speech. Why should I strive after many details? So many are the treatises and sermons falsely inscribed to blessed Augustine that a review of them would require its own volume. Nor is it for me, as I think, to sit in judgment and deprive of their titles works that are another’s. Let the prudent reader carefully consider what he should do or hold in these matters.

The holy doctor Augustine died in the city of Hippo, while it was being besieged by the Vandals, in the year of the Lord 430, in the fourteenth indiction, in the seventy-sixth year of his age and the fortieth of his priesthood, according to Marianus Scotus, on the fifth day before the Kalends of September, in the third month of the city’s siege; amid the assaults of the besieging Vandals, at the very end of his days, he was answering the books of Julian the Manichaean and gloriously persevering in defense of the Christian faith. He made no will, because he had nothing from which to make one, except the church’s library, which even at his death he most diligently commended to the brothers to be preserved. Poor in possessions, rich in merits and knowledge, Augustine the bishop rested in the Lord; Possidius, bishop of Calama, wrote his life.

Atticus, bishop of the city of Constantinople after blessed John Chrysostom: a man learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters; yet in this [unclear], from which matter many scandals arose in the church of God. He wrote for us works not to be despised. Of these there is extant an outstanding work addressed to the queens, daughters of the emperors of Constantinople:

On Faith and Virginity, 2 books. And certain letters. And not a few other works.

He flourished under the rulers Honorius and Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 420, [unclear].

Claruit sub Theodosio et Honorio principibus: Anno dn̄i.CCCC.xx. Sidorus senior: episcopus Cordubensis: uit in diuinis scituris ualde peri tus: & foecularium litterarum nō ignarus: ingenio promptus: & satis diser tus eloquio: non minus conuersatiõe morum q̃ scientia scripturarum infi- gnis: cuius eruditio apud ueteres in magno precio existebat: scripsit non pauca in diuinis uoluminibus opuscula. De quib⁹ ego tamẽ reperi: opus egregium qđ̓ edidit ad sanctum Orosium presbyterum Hispanum.

Paulinus, priest, a disciple of Saint Augustine of Hippo and afterward bishop of Nola in Campania, to whom many letters of Augustine and Jerome, and various treatises, are said to be addressed, was very learned in the holy Scriptures and, in secular letters, second to none in his time. He shone forth, no less distinguished for holiness than for learning. Concerning him the blessed Pope Gregory writes in the third book of the Dialogues that he was of such great piety and compassion that, after he had spent all his possessions for the use of the poor and the freeing of captives, he even handed himself over into servitude for the son of a certain widow; from that servitude he was at last released, together with many captives, because of the merit of his life. He wrote many volumes both in meter and in prose, of which these are reported. First, at the request of Saint Augustine, he wrote:

The Life of Blessed Ambrose of Milan, one book.

The Life of Saint Felix, bishop of Nola, one book.

On the Sacraments also, one book.

On the Death of a Baptized Infant, one book.

A Panegyric of Theodosius, one book.

Hymns in Diverse Meter, one book.

On Contempt of the World, one book.

On Penitence, one book.

On the Blessings of the Patriarchs, one book.

On the Praise of the Martyrs, one book.

To Sulpicius Severus, four letters.

Letters to Various Persons, one book.

He also published some other works, which have not come to my knowledge.

He flourished under the emperors Honorius and Valentinian, in the year of the Lord 420.

Nicetas, bishop of the city of Romaciana, was devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, acute in intellect, clear and polished in speech. For the edification of readers he wrote little works not contemptible in their reading. Of these, the following are reported:

To the Competentes, who are being prepared for baptism: A Preparatory Work, one book.

On the Errors of Paganism, one book.

On the Faith of the One Majesty, one book.

Against Genealogy, one book.

On the Creed also, one book.

On the Victim of the Paschal Lamb, one book.

To a Fallen Virgin, one book.

And certain other works.

He flourished in the time of the emperors Theodosius and Honorius, in the year of the Lord 420.

Simplicianus of Milan, bishop after Saint Ambrose, was devoted to the divine Scriptures and a lover of poverty. By many letters he urged Augustine, still a priest, to exercise his intellect and devote himself to expositions of the Scriptures, so that he might be seen as, as it were, another Ambrose, one who compelled the work of Origen. Hence Augustine also resolved many questions and letters addressed to his person. But he himself too wrote useful letters to Augustine and various others, which are found here and there in part.

He flourished under the emperors Theodosius and Honorius, in the year of the Lord 420.

Isidore the Elder, bishop of Corduba, was very skilled in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, ready in intellect and sufficiently eloquent in speech, distinguished no less for the conduct of his morals than for knowledge of the Scriptures. His learning was held in great esteem among the ancients. He wrote not a few little works on the divine volumes. Of these, however, I have found an excellent work which he published to Saint Orosius, the Spanish priest.

58
DE SCRIPTORIBVS ECCLESIATICIS Fol. 25 In quattuor libros Regum: li. iiij De caeteris nil reperi. Claruit sub Theodosio et Honorio principibus: Anno dn̄i.CCCC.XX. O Rosius presbyter: natione Hispanus: beati Augustini quondam auditor: uir in diuinis scripturis eruditus: & in saecularibus litteris peritissimus: ui- ta et conuersatione clarissimus fuit. On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 25

On the four books of Kings: four books.

Of the rest I have found nothing.

He flourished under the rulers Theodosius and Honorius, in the year of the Lord 420.

Orosius the priest, a Spaniard by nation, formerly a hearer of blessed Augustine, was a man learned in the divine Scriptures and most skilled in secular letters, and very distinguished in life and conduct. Blessed Augustine, when he came to him from Spain to learn the question concerning the nature of the soul, sent him to Saint Jerome in Bethlehem of Judea; after staying there a little while, he learned clearly the question for which he had come, and, returning to Hippo, brought with him relics of the protomartyr Stephen. To this most studious man there are extant several little works of blessed Augustine and solutions of various questions of the Scriptures. He himself also wrote the following volumes:

An Apologetic work.

Against the Pelagians: one book. “I have obeyed your commands, blessed...”

On the honorable chronicle of the world: seven books. “Since among you, heavenly...”

On the nature of the soul: one book.

Several letters to Augustine: one book.

Also letters to various persons: one book.

On the Song of Songs: one book.

He flourished, illustrious in life and doctrine, together with Saint Augustine, in the year of the Lord 420.

John, bishop and patriarch of Jerusalem, studious and learned in the holy Scriptures, but too much devoted to the doctrines of Origen, stirred up writings of the fathers against himself, namely of the most holy priest Jerome and of Bishop Epiphanius, as is found in the letters sent by them to him. But John himself, giving an account of his study, says that he imitated not the faith of Origen but his genius. For on this account especially he wrote a work worthy of note:

Against the detractors of his study: one book.

And certain letters to various persons.

And certain other things.

He flourished in the times of the emperors Arcadius and Honorius, in the year of the Lord 400.

Maximus, bishop of Turin, most learned in the holy Scriptures and second to none in his time in delivering homilies to the people, was not only distinguished in doctrine, but also shone most brightly in holiness of life. He wrote many excellent little works, which holy mother Church has accepted with great authority to be read. Of these the following are reported:

On the chapters of the Gospels: one book. “Most glorious of the Christian...”

On the Acts of the Apostles: one book. “The solemnities for us...”

In praise of the apostles: one book. “The memory of the holy fathers...”

In praise of John the Baptist: one book. “The feast of Saint Cyprian...”

On the life of Eusebius of Vercelli: one book.

On Saint Cyprian the martyr: one book.

On the grace of baptism: one book.

On avarice: one book.

On hospitality: one book.

On the waning of the moon: one book.

On alms: one book.

On the words of Isaiah: one book.

On the passion of the Lord: one book.

On the fast of Lent: one book.

On the general fast of the servants of God: one book.

On the betrayal by Judas: one book.

On the cross of the Lord: one book.

59

De Epiphania dn̄i: bo. De Pascha: bo. De pentecoste: bo. De poenitentia Niniuitarū: bo. De nõ timēdis hostibꝰ carnalibꝰ: bo. De gratias post cibũ agend̓. bo. Aduersus eundē alij li. Altercationis ptiū dialogus: li. Et alia plura: quae omīa ꝓpter auctoris errores ab ecclesiastica bibliotheca merito abiecta sūt. Hic tꝑe famis angustiae omīa sua in elemosynis pauperibus distribu it: multos nobiles religiolos: sub pietatis specie deceptos suae haeresi sociauit. Claruit sub Archadio honorio principibus: Anno dn̄i.CCCC.XX. Nnocentius papa primus:uir doctus atqƺ sanctussimus natione Albanus post beatū Petrum quadragesimus secūdus: untuersali ecclesiae annis xv.praefuit: multa pro eius utilitate gloriose ordinauit.Ad hunc cū ad huc eēt p̄sbyter:btūs Hieronymꝰ historiā mulieris septies ꝑcussae cōposuit:qd̓ ꝓ logus eiudē oꝑis ostēdit.Qui cū in diuinis scripturis eēt eruditiffimꝰ:scripsit no- nulla ꝓ aedificatiōe fideliū praeclara opuscula:De ꝗbus ego dumtaxat ista reperi: Decretum cōtra Pelagianos: li. j Diu mirati sumus. Contra Bonosiacos: li. j In requirendis de his. Epistolarū multarū ad diuerfos: li. j Reuerendissimo Dama. De caeteris nihil uidi. Moritur Anno dn̄i.CCCC XVII.Indictione.xv.quarto Calend Augusti. Vsebius Cremonensis: monachus discipulus beati Hieronymi presby¬ teri:uir studiosus eruditus: uita cōuersatione uenerabilis: orationibꝰ sanctis diuinis lectionibus magistri sui reuerēdissimi exemplo iugiter in tentus:magnā sanctitatis opinionē cōsecutus est.Scripsit ad Damasum Portuen- sem ep̄m: Theodosiū senatorē Romanae urbis: satis elegās prolixū uolumē: De transitu sancti Hieronymi: li. j Contra paganos de. Ossidoniꝰ Afer:eptus Calamēsis:bti Augustini quondā auditor atqƺ discipu¬ lus: uir in diuinis scripturisdiosus: saeculariū litteraꝝ nõ ignarꝰ:ml̓tis annis cū sctō Augustino familiariter conuersatus:uita doctrina inter ec¬ clesiasticos praesules clarꝰ effulsit.Scripsit aut inter caetera ad aedificationē fideliū: Vita sancti Augustini: li. j Inspirante rerum omniū. Indiculū librorū eius: li. j

Book

On the Lord’s tomb: one book. On the office of the Mass: one book. On the accusation of the Lord: one homily. On the resurrection of the Lord: one homily. On Saint Lawrence: one homily. On Saint Stephen: one homily. On the Kalends of January: one homily. On the Nativity of the Lord: one homily. On the Epiphany of the Lord: one homily. On Easter: one homily. On Pentecost: one homily. On the repentance of the Ninevites: one homily. On not fearing carnal enemies: one homily. On giving thanks after food: one homily.

He wrote many other things: sermons, treatises, letters, homilies, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under the emperors Arcadius and Honorius, in the year of the Lord 420. And he died under Theodosius the Younger.

Julian, bishop of Campania, a man of sharp and vehement talent, learned in the holy Scriptures, schooled in Greek and Latin discourse, before he openly revealed in himself the impiety of Pelagius, was distinguished among the doctors of the Church. But afterwards, wishing to defend his heresy, he wrote against the holy doctors little works agreeing with his own opinion, of which there are extant:

Against Saint Augustine: one book. Other books against the same: [unclear]. A dialogue of an altercation of the parties: one book.

And several others, all of which, because of the author’s errors, have deservedly been rejected from the ecclesiastical library. In a time of famine’s distress he distributed all his possessions in alms to the poor; he associated with his heresy many noble religious men, deceived under the appearance of piety. He flourished under the emperors Arcadius and Honorius, in the year of the Lord 420.

Innocent, the first pope, a very learned and holy man, Alban by nation, the forty-second after blessed Peter, presided over the universal Church for fifteen years; he gloriously ordained many things for its benefit. To him, when he was still a priest, blessed Jerome composed the history of the woman struck seven times, as the prologue of that same work shows. Since he was most learned in the divine Scriptures, he wrote certain excellent little works for the edification of the faithful. Of these I have found only the following:

A decree against the Pelagians: one book. “We have long wondered.” Against the Bonosiacs: one book. “In inquiring about these things.” Many letters to various persons: one book. “To the most reverend Dama.”

Of the rest I have seen nothing.

He died in the year of the Lord 417, in the fifteenth indiction, on the fourth day before the Kalends of August.

Eusebius of Cremona, monk and disciple of blessed Jerome the priest, a studious and learned man, venerable in life and conduct, continually intent upon holy prayers and divine readings after the example of his most reverend master, achieved a great reputation for holiness. He wrote to Damasus, bishop of Portus, and Theodosius, senator of the city of Rome, a sufficiently elegant and lengthy volume:

On the passing of Saint Jerome: one book. “Against the pagans, concerning.”

Possidius the African, bishop of Calama, formerly a hearer and disciple of blessed Augustine, a man zealous in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, having lived familiarly for many years with Saint Augustine, shone brightly among ecclesiastical prelates in life and doctrine. Among other things, moreover, he wrote for the edification of the faithful:

The Life of Saint Augustine: one book. “By the inspiration of the maker of all things.” A short catalogue of his books: one book.

60
