Cur9 frater Richardus mox ut defuũto pre regnu sulcepit: insta, te et praedicate Leandro: haeresi renunciavit: & totã gentem Vuelogothoru libi subdita: ad fide catholica couertit. Ad hũc Leandru btũ Gregori9 uolumina co métarioru in lob edidit. Scriptit aũt et ipse nónulla opuscula. De quibus feruntur LIBER

Gregory, the first pope, from being a monk of the order of Saint Benedict, Roman by homeland: after the pontificate of Pelagius he sat in the chair of Peter for thirteen years and six months. He was most learned in the divine Scriptures, and indeed very learned in secular letters; prince of theologians, splendor of philosophers, and light of rhetoricians; upright and most holy in life and conduct. While he was explaining the divine Scriptures, the Holy Spirit several times appeared to him in visible form, and by invisible teaching disclosed to him the hidden mysteries of those same Scriptures. At Rome, at Saint Peter’s, he held a synod of twenty-four bishops, established many things for the utility of the Church, and promulgated a decree on the immunity of monasteries. He wrote several necessary volumes. Of these the following are reported: To Leander, bishop of Seville.

Moralia on the Book of Job, thirty-five books: “Among many it is often asked.” On Pastoral Care, two books: “The weight of pastoral care.” Dialogues on the Miracles of the Saints, four books: “On a certain day, too much [unclear].” On the Song of Songs, four books: “After [unclear] from the joys of paradise.” On Ezekiel the Prophet, two books: “By the inspiration of almighty God.” Homilies on the Gospels, forty, in two books: “Our Lord and Redeemer.” A Brief Explanation of the Four Gospels, four books: “Matthew, as in the order.” On the Seven Penitential Psalms, two books. Letters to Various Persons, ten books: “Gregory, bishop, servant.” Rationale of Divine Things. [unclear]. On the Sacraments.

While he was still a deacon, on behalf of Pope Pelagius he wrote a very distinguished letter to Elias, bishop of Aquileia, who was unwilling to accept the three chapters of the Council of Chalcedon; this letter is not found among his letters. He is also said to have written very many other works: namely, on the Prophets, on the Books of Kings, also on the books of Moses, and on other sacred Scriptures. After his death, before they had yet been copied, his most wicked rivals, envying his glory and holiness, burned them with fire, as John the Deacon laments in the book of his life. The most blessed Pope Gregory died in the second year of the emperor Phocas, which was the year of the Lord six hundred and nine, in the eighth indiction, on the fourth Ides of March, shining with many miracles.

Leander, bishop of Seville, from being a monk, Carthaginian by homeland, from the province of Spain, born of his father Severianus: a most studious man, nobly learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, sweet in speech, most excellent in talent, and also holy in life and conduct and beloved of God. By his preaching and effort Hermingild, son of Leuvigild, the Arian king of the Goths, was brought back to the confession of the orthodox faith, and on the vigil of Easter, slain by his heretical father, received the crown of martyrs. His brother Richard, as soon as after his father’s death he had taken up the kingdom, at Leander’s urging and preaching, renounced heresy and converted the whole people of the Visigoths subject to him to the Catholic faith. To this blessed Leander, blessed Gregory dedicated the volumes of his commentaries on Job. Leander himself also wrote some little works, of which there are reported

the following. When, on account of the Catholic faith, he had been banished into exile by the Arians, he wrote:

Against heretics, two books. Against the ordinances of the Arians, one book. On virginity, to Florentina, one book. Prayers in a twofold edition on the psalm[s], one book. On contempt for death, to his brother, one book. On the praise of sacrifices, one book. Letters to various persons, one book.

But he also published some other works, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished in the year of the Lord 590, under the emperor Maurice. He died under Reccared, the most devout prince of the Goths, renowned for miracles.

Priscian the grammarian, by homeland a Caesarean, a man most learned in secular letters, skilled in Greek and Latin eloquence, held in great esteem with Chosroes, king of the Persians, wrote certain distinguished volumes on the grammatical art, which among the ancients were held in great authority. Of these the following are reported:

To Julian the patrician. On the parts of speech, two books. On construction, one book. On accents, one book. On cosmography, one book. On natural questions, to [unclear], one book.

He is also said to have written some other works, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished, as some think, in the times of Chosroes, king of the Persians, and of the emperor Heraclius, in the year of the Lord 620.

Marcus, a monk and disciple of our holy father Benedict, and most dearly loved by him, a man learned in the divine scriptures and very skilled in secular letters, an orator and distinguished poet, renowned in morals and manner of life, wrote, after the blessed Pope Gregory, adding some things, running most elegantly in heroic verse:

The Life of Saint Benedict, one book. And certain other things.

He flourished down to the reign of Heraclius Augustus, in the year of the Lord 610.

Fortunatus, bishop of Poitiers, an Italian by nation, a man learned in the divine scriptures and most learned in secular letters, subtle in intellect, eloquent and polished in speech, excelling all the doctors of his age in verse and prose, having been freed from pain in the eyes by [Saint Martin?], came to Tours to his tomb to give thanks; and, having gone on to Poitiers, he was first ordained priest and then bishop there, and was renowned for great learning and religion. He wrote many useful and devout little works in elegant verse. Of these I have seen only the following. To Saint Radegund, daughter of the last king of the Thuringians and captive of the king of the Franks, afterwards abbess of the monastery of Poitiers, in hexameter verse:

The Destruction of the Kingdom of the Thuringians, one book. “[The condition?] of war, a sorrowful lot.” To [Jovinus?] on Radegund, one book. “You who eagerly lick the Aonian [unclear].” To Justin the Younger, one book. “Glory of the highest [Father?] and of the Son, and [unclear].” To Sophia Augusta, one book. “To whom, marrying one equal in merits [unclear].” On Radegund’s psalm, one book. “After the ashes of the fatherland and [unclear].” In praise of Bishop Martin, one book. “When he was spreading apostolic light.” On the venerable Bishop Leontius, one book. “Among whom [unclear] begot [a ray?].” On praise of the same, one book. “Let every age know [unclear].” Seventy-seven hymns, one book. “Let every age know [that] [unclear] has come.”

Cum adhuc iunior esset magnū studiū litteris sanctis impendit: adeo ut eleganti stilo scripferit: f

On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 37

On the miracles of Saint Martin: four books. The life of Saint Hilary of Poitiers: one book. To Oporicus on his own life: one book. The life of a holy bishop: one book. Letters to various persons: one book. Poems to friends: one book. “The king, the summit of the region,” etc. He also composed many other works, which, since they are short, I have not wished to mark under the name of books. For he wrote many epitaphs and brief verses, which I have seen. He flourished under Justin the Younger Augustus, in the year of the Lord 570.

Gregory, bishop of Tours, formerly a monk and once a disciple of Saint Avitus, bishop of the Auvergnats, a learned and noble man, and also gentle and humble, was of such great holiness and purity that even in life he shone with miracles. When he visited the thresholds of the apostles Peter and Paul, he was received by the blessed Pope Gregory with the greatest reverence and charity, as a truly holy man and a special friend, uniquely beloved by him. He wrote several volumes in a simple and plain style, of which there survive:

On the praise of the holy martyrs: one book. On the life of certain confessors: two books. On the miracles of Saint Julian the martyr: one book. On the miracles of Saint Martin: four books. History of the Franks: ten books. An epitome of the same: one book. Chronicle of ecclesiastical history: one book. The other works which he composed have not yet come to our knowledge through reading. He flourished in the times of the emperor Maurice, in the year of the Lord 600.

Martin, bishop, formerly ruler and abbot of the monastery of Dumio, a man learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, coming from the regions of the East into Gaul, converted the people of the Sueves by teaching and miracles from Arian impiety to the right faith; he established rules of orthodox faith, founded monasteries, and reformed churches. He wrote to Mito, king of Galicia, on the four virtues which are called cardinal, an instructive volume which he wished to entitle:

The Form of an Honorable Life: one book. A book of letters full of the cultivation of virtues: one book. And certain other works which I have not seen. He flourished under Theodemir, king of the Sueves, while Justinian Augustus governed the Constantinopolitan empire, in the year of the Lord 540.

Paterius, notary and secundicerius of the Roman Church, a man trained by constant study in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, gathered all the testimonies of divine Scripture by which the blessed Pope Gregory clarified the obscure points of his exposition, and published three books: two, namely, on testimonies of the Old Testament, and one on the Testament; and he entitled the codex itself:

Testimony: four books. “When of the most blessed and apostolic...” I have seen nothing concerning the rest. He flourished at Rome at the same time when Pope Gregory presided over the universal Church, and at his urging he compiled the aforesaid volume, while Maurice Augustus held the empire and after him Phocas, in the year of the Lord 600.

Columbanus, first founder and abbot of the monastery of Luxeuil, a Scot by nation, a man of outstanding holiness, merit, and learning, father of many thousands of monks and founder of several monasteries, an excellent sower of the divine word, coming from Ireland into Gaul and Germany, increased divine worship, monasteries, and servants, as once the chief of the Druids had done. While he was still rather young he devoted great study to sacred letters, so that he wrote in an elegant style:

Book

Commentaries on the whole Psalter, one book. And certain letters to the brothers. He died under the emperor Maurice, in the year of the Lord 598, in the first indiction, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of December.

John, bishop of Constantinople, a Cappadocian by nation, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, of inestimable holiness, so intent upon alms and works of piety that the emperor Maurice, moved against him by a zeal of avarice, ordered all the poor and beggars to be expelled from the city of Constantinople. He wrote in Greek to Saint Leander, bishop of Seville, and certain other things. He flourished under the emperor Maurice, in the year of the Lord 600.

Licinianus, bishop of Cartagena, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, after many exercises of study, was killed at Constantinople by his rivals with a cup of poison under the emperor Maurice. Sudden death did not harm him, since Scripture says: “The just man, by whatever death he may have been overtaken, shall be in a place of refreshment.” For then he truly begins to live, when, adorned with good works, he goes through death to Christ, never to die. He wrote certain little works not to be despised in reading, of which I have not yet deserved to see any. The following are said to be his: On the sacrament of baptism, one book; Letters to various persons, one book; and certain other things. He flourished under the emperor Maurice, in the year of the Lord 590.

Severus, bishop of the city of Malaga, formerly the companion and colleague of the aforesaid bishop Licinianus, a man learned in the holy Scriptures, nobly instructed in the disciplines of secular letters, acute in intellect and distinguished in speech, wrote against Vincentius, bishop of the city of Zaragoza, who had passed from the Catholic faith into Arian depravity: A Correction, one book; On virginity, to his sister, one book; Letters to various persons, one book. He flourished in the year of the Lord 580, under the emperor Maurice, under whom he died.

Eutropius, bishop of the church of Valencia, formerly abbot of the monastery of Servitanum of the order of Saint Benedict, to whom Licinianus, while still living in the aforesaid monastery, wrote many letters, a man magnificently learned both in divine writings and in secular letters, and excellently imbued with monastic disciplines. While he was still abbot he wrote to Bishop Licinianus why, after infants have been baptized, the triple anointing with chrism follows afterwards, one book; On the correction of monks, one book; and several letters to various persons. He flourished in the times of the emperor Maurice, in the year of the Lord 600.

John, bishop of Gerona, formerly a monk of our order, a Goth by nation, from the province of Lusitania, a man studious and learned in the divine writings, also distinguished in morals and conduct, learned and famous in Greek and Latin speech: when, as a young man, he went to Constantinople out of love of learning, after seven years had passed he returned to Spain. When King Leovigild could not bring him over to Arian impiety, he condemned him to a fairly harsh exile for ten years. Recalled from there by the most Christian king [Reccaredus?], he founded a monastery, where by word and example he showed his brothers the path of regular discipline. He wrote: An Exhortation to monks, one book; Additions to the chronicle, one book; [unclear], of which we spoke above: a little work [unclear], one book.

ON ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS. Fol. 38.

He composed also many other [works], which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under [Richard / Reccared?], most Christian king of the Visigoths, in Spain, in the times of the emperors Maurice and Phocas, in the year of the Lord 600.

Maximus, bishop of the city of Saragossa, learned in the divine Scriptures and not moderately erudite in secular [letters], prompt in talent and polished in eloquence, excelling in verse [and] prose, published in either style quite illustrious volumes, which have as yet by no means come to the notice of our reading. But there is reported [as] his a notable volume, a pleasant work: On the deeds of the Goths in Spain: 1 book. He flourished in the times of the emperor Phocas, in the year of the Lord 610.

Jonas, a monk, disciple of Saint Columbanus the abbot, companion of his pilgrimage, a Scot by nation, a studious man, erudite, renowned for knowledge, no less venerable for religion than for learning, wrote in composed speech, at the request of the brothers, for the edification of many: The Life of Saint Columbanus: 1 book. The Life of Saint Attala the monk: 1 book. The Life of Saint Eustasius the abbot: 1 book. He flourished under the emperor Heraclius, in the year of the Lord 630.

Leontius, bishop of the city of Neapolis on the island of Cyprus, a man erudite in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, also most renowned in life and conversation, a prelate worthy of God. He wrote, among the other little works of his talent, a notable volume on the acts [and] admirable conversation of that patriarch of Alexandria who, on account of [his] incredible piety [and] compassion toward the poor, was surnamed John the Almsgiver: 1 book. Of the rest I have found nothing. He flourished in the times of the emperor Phocas, in the year of the Lord 610.

Isidore the Younger, bishop of Seville after Leander, a man most erudite in the divine Scriptures, second to none of his time in secular letters, subtle in talent, clear in sense, composed in eloquence, excelling in verse [and] prose, shone forth no less distinguished for sanctity than for learning. He is called "the Younger" to distinguish him from the elder, bishop of Cordoba, of whom we made mention above, or also from another, bishop of Seville, who preceded him. This Isidore the Younger wrote many illustrious little works, of which I have found only the following. To Braulio the bishop: Of Etymologies: 20 books. ["Discipline [is so called] from learning…"] On Genesis, allegorically: 1 book. ["The history of the sacred law…"] On Exodus: 1 book. ["Certain mysteries…"] On Numbers: 1 book. ["Therefore this one book…"] On Leviticus: 1 book. ["The following Leviticus book…"] On Deuteronomy: 1 book. ["The book of Deuteronomy [is] found…"] On Joshua: 1 book. ["After the death of Moses, the servant…"] On Judges: 1 book. ["The history of the Judges…"] On Kings: 3 books. ["After the book of Judges there follows…"] On Ruth: 1 book. On Paralipomenon [Chronicles]: 1 book. On Ezra [and] Nehemiah: 3 books. On Tobias: 1 book. On Judith: 1 book. On Esther: 1 book. On Job: 1 book. On the Psalter: 1 book. On the Proverbs of Solomon: 1 book. On Ecclesiastes: 1 book. On the Song of Songs: 1 book. On the book of Wisdom: 1 book. On Ecclesiasticus: 1 book. On Isaiah the prophet: 1 book. On Jeremiah: 1 book. On Ezekiel: 1 book. On Daniel the prophet: 1 book. On the twelve minor prophets: 12 books. On the Maccabees: 2 books. On the four Gospels: 4 books. The book of generation, etc.: 1 book. On the Epistles of Paul: 13 books. On the canonical epistles: 7 books.

On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 39

Sermons to monks, one book, “I fear in Christ, venera...” Decree of the three councils of Arles, three books, “Concerning the rest I have found nothing.”

In the third sermon, which is on the monk’s battle against vices, he acknowledges both himself and those to whom he speaks as professed monks of the order of the Rule of our most holy father Benedict. He flourished in the times of the emperor Constantine, son of Heraclius, and of his sons, in the year of the Lord 670; under them he presided gloriously over the synod of Arles.

Audoenus, who was also called Dado, bishop of Rouen, a Gaul by nation, brother of Saint Ado the monk, a learned and most holy man, founder of the monastery of Rebais, since he was learned both in the holy Scriptures and also in secular letters, wrote in a very elegant style to Rupertus, bishop of Paris:

The Life of Saint Eligius, bishop of Noyon, three books, and certain other things.

He flourished with great holiness, virtues, and signs in the times of the above-mentioned emperor Constantine, in the year of the Lord 660.

Theodorus, seventh archbishop of Canterbury, consecrated by Pope Vitalian, a Greek by nation, from Tarsus in Cilicia, a monk of our order in the city of Rome, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, second to none in his time in secular letters, highly skilled in Greek and Latin speech, excellent also in verse and prose, renowned no less for holiness than for knowledge: after holding a synod in England, he made many provisions for the English church. Among other monuments of his talent he wrote an outstanding work on the kind of penance to be imposed on those who had offended in many crimes. The title of this work is:

The Penitential of Theodore, one book; some letters to various persons.

He died, not without a reputation for holiness, under Justinian the Younger, in the year of the Lord 690, in the third indiction, in the seventy-eighth year of his age, and the twenty-second of his episcopate.

Leo, the second pope, a Sicilian by nation, sat in the chair of Peter after Agatho for only eleven months. A man most learned in divine and secular writings, sufficiently instructed in the Greek and Latin languages, subtle and eloquent, no less holy than learned, he translated from Greek into Latin the sixth synod, which had been celebrated in the city of Constantinople in the time of Pope Agatho, his predecessor; in it Macarius, bishop of Antioch, was condemned with his accomplices, Cyrus, Sergius, Honorius, Pyrrhus, and Peter, bishops, who taught that in our Lord Jesus Christ there was only one will and operation. He also wrote:

Many letters to various persons, one book, and certain similar things.

He died under the emperor Constantine, son of Constantine, in the year of the Lord 677, in the fifth indiction, on the fifth day before the Nones of July.

Adamnan, priest and abbot of the monastery of Iona, which Saint Columba once built on the island of Scotland, a man very studious and learned in divine writings, not ignorant of secular letters either, cautious in mind, sweet in speech, distinguished in life and conduct, not without a reputation for holiness, was the father of many monks. Among other things he wrote, in a sufficiently composed style, a volume:

On the Places of the Holy Land, one book, and certain letters.

He flourished under Justinian the Younger Augustus, in the year of the Lord 690.

Benedict, abbot in Britain, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and an outstanding preserver and promoter of regular discipline, wrote a notable little work for monks, in which all the rules of the holy fathers

Book

comparing [it with] the rule of our most blessed father Benedict, he shows that the rules of all the others harmonize with it, and that it by no means differs from any. For this reason he entitled his book The Concord of the Rules, one book.

He wrote other works.

He flourished under Emperor Constantine, in the year of the Lord 670.

Delmus, bishop of the West Saxons, formerly abbot of the monastery of Maildub in Scotia, of the Order of Saint Benedict, a devout man of outstanding holiness, zealous and learned in the Holy Scriptures, and in secular letters the most learned of all in England in his time, excellent in verse and prose, a most fervent preacher of the word of God. He wrote in both styles certain instructive volumes, of which I have found only the following. While he was still abbot, at the command of the synod of his people, he wrote against the error of the Britons a notable and useful work:

On the Celebration of Easter, one book.

On the Virginity of the Saints, in verse, one book.

On the Same Subject, in prose, one book.

Several letters to various persons, one book.

He is also read to have written many other works, which have not come to the notice of our reading.

He flourished under Justinian the Younger, in the year of the Lord 680.

Ceolfrid, after Benedict the second abbot of the monastery of the holy apostles Peter and Paul in England, of the Order of Saint Benedict, teacher and nurturer of Bede the priest, a devout and learned man, and a vigorous governor of regular discipline. He wrote to the king of the Picts, who requested it, a fairly lengthy letter in the form of a little book:

On the Observance of Easter, one book.

He flourished in England in the times of the emperor Justinian the Younger, namely in the year of the Lord 680. At last, when he was returning from visiting the thresholds of the apostles, he died in the city of Langres, in the seventy-fourth year of his age.

Egidius, a monk of the Order of Saint Benedict, Greek by nation, learned in the divine Scriptures, very skilled in secular letters, a physician, philosopher, and distinguished poet, venerable no less in his manner of life than in knowledge, wrote certain little works of no contemptible usefulness, of which I have found only the following. A notable work composed in meter:

On Pulses, one book.

On Veins also, one book.

Of the others I have seen nothing. It begins: “When a vein is made [unclear].” “The powers of talent with modest [unclear].”

He flourished under Emperor Tiberius, in the year of the Lord 700.

Bede, monk and priest of the monastery of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, which is in England, of the Order of Saint Benedict, a man most zealous and very learned in the divine Scriptures, and very skilled in secular letters, a philosopher, astronomer, calculator, and distinguished poet, not ignorant of the Greek language, excellent in talent, not elaborate in eloquence, yet sweet and well composed. He wrote many volumes, in which he proves the keenness of his intellect. When he was seven years old, he was given by the care of his relatives to be educated by Abbot Benedict, and then by Ceolfrid of the said monastery of Wearmouth; and from that time he spent the whole course of his life in residence in the same monastery, devoted all his effort to meditating on the Scriptures, and, amid the observance of regular discipline and the daily care of singing in church, always found it sweet either to learn, or to teach, or to write. In the nineteenth year of his age he received the diaconate, and in the thirtieth the rank of priesthood, both through the ministry of Bishop John, at the command of Abbot Ceolfrid. From the time he received the priesthood until the end of his life he composed the following little works:

On Genesis as far as Isaac, one book.

On Exodus, one book.

On Numbers, one book.

so that by ordinance of the prelates of England they were read publicly in the churches. And since, in the attribution of the homilies, according to custom they wrote the name of the author as the venerable priest Bede, being unable to proclaim him otherwise while he was alive, the title once assigned at the beginning has prevailed down to the present day, so that he is called Bede the Venerable rather than Saint Bede. For while he was living it was not permitted to name him otherwise, even if he was holy. There are those who invent other reasons for this title “venerable”: some from the inscription of the epitaph, others imagining that Bede was blind. But they are wrong, for Bede was not blind, nor do we know that such an epitaph was inscribed on his tomb. And indeed, were I not consulting brevity, I could very easily refute these ravings.

He died under the emperor Leo, in the year of the Lord 732, in the fifteenth indiction, in the seventy-second year of his age, on the day before the Kalends of June.

Gregory, the second pope, a Roman by birth, sat in the chair of Peter after the pontiff Constantine for sixteen years and nine months. He was certainly a learned and most holy man, who ordained Boniface, an English monk by nation, as bishop of Mainz. He wrote certain works full of learning, among which the following are reported:

To the Questions of Justinian, one book of responses. Against the emperor Leo, one book. To John, bishop of Constantinople, one book. Letters to various persons, one book.

He died under the emperor Leo, in the year of the Lord 731, in the fourteenth indiction, on the third day before the Ides of February. Gregory III succeeded him.

Boniface, the first archbishop of Mainz, a Scot by nation, a monk of the order of Saint Benedict, when he was a boy of five years was offered by his parents to a monastery in England called Mischele; there, devoting himself to letters and morals, he became a learned and most holy man. After he had been ordained priest, from love of pilgrimage for Christ he came into Germany, and there, preaching the word of God, he was ordained bishop of Mainz by Pope Gregory [II?]; by his successor Gregory III he was raised to be archbishop and primate of Germany. Since he was a learned man, he taught the people committed to him not only by word but by writings. Of his works I have found only:

Letters to various persons, one book. The Life of Certain Saints, one book.

He died while preaching in Frisia, crowned with martyrdom, in the times of the emperor Pippin, in the year of the Lord 755, in the eighth indiction, in the thirty-sixth year of his episcopate, on the Nones of June. Blessed Lullus, whom he had ordained archbishop after himself, caused his body to be brought back to the monastery of Fulda, situated in Buchonia, and honorably buried.

Verus, bishop of Seville in the province of Baetica, where Isidore had once held the episcopate, was a man learned in the divine scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, sharp in intellect, brilliant in speech, distinguished no less by life than by learning. For the edification of the faithful, especially of the church of Orange in Gaul, he wrote:

The Life of Bishop Eutropius, famous for miracles and virtues, one book.

And certain other things. He is said to have flourished in the times of the emperor Pippin, in the year of the Lord 760.

Walafrid, abbot of Saint Gall, as is said, a German by nation, was a man devoted to the divine scriptures, most learned in all secular letters in his time, distinguished in talent and eloquence, strong in verse and prose, a monarch of regular discipline, father of many monks. For the edification of all the faithful he wrote with devotion:

The Life of Saint Gall in prose, one book. The same afterward in verse, one book. On the Divine Offices, one book. Several letters to various persons.

And he is said to have written some other things, which have not come into our hands. He flourished in the times of Augustus Tiberius, around the years of the Lord 700.

On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 4j

Gregory, the third pope of that name, presided over the Roman and universal Church after Gregory II for eleven years: a pious, merciful, and most holy man, and very learned both in secular letters and in divine Scripture; distinguished for Greek and Latin eloquence. In a synod held at Rome he excommunicated the emperors Leo and Constantine, who despised the images of the saints, and deposed them from imperial rule. He also wrote, among other things, to the same emperors:

A Commonitorium, one book. To the Same, one book. Against the Same, one book. Letters to Various Persons, one book. And certain other works.

He died under the emperors Leo and Constantine, in the year of the Lord 742, in the tenth indiction, on the fourth day before the Kalends of December.

[unclear]

John, monk and priest, surnamed Chrysoras, by nation a Damascene from Syria: a man learned in divine Scripture and in secular letters, and no less renowned for his life than for his knowledge. Stirred and provoked by the writings of Pope Gregory III, with which he attacked the error of Emperor Leo, he too wrote in Greek, among his own people:

Against Emperor Leo, two books, in the Greek language. And certain other works.

He flourished under Emperor Leo, in the year of the Lord 730.

Willibald, first bishop of Eichstätt, by nation a Scot, brother of Saint Walpurga, virgin and abbess of Heidenheim; a monk and disciple of Saint Boniface the martyr, of the Order of Saint Benedict; a learned and most holy man, renowned in talent and speech. At the request of Saint Lullus, archbishop of Mainz, he wrote for the edification of the faithful, in a sufficiently distinguished style:

Life of Saint Boniface, Bishop, one book. “Illustrious, therefore, and truly blessed...”

I do not know whether he published anything more.

[unclear]

He flourished under Pippin, father of Charlemagne, in the year of the Lord 760.

Zacharias, pope, by nation a Greek, after Gregory III presided over the universal Church for ten years: a most learned man, who, because of his learning and holiness of life, is rightly judged worthy to be compared with the best pontiffs. He translated the four books of the dialogues of blessed Pope Gregory the Great from Latin into Greek, and enlightened many who were ignorant of the Latin language by the reading of them. He also wrote from his own talent, in the Latin language:

Letters to Various Persons, one book, very elegant and useful.

Among these there are extant several to Saint Boniface, archbishop of Mainz. He died under Pippin, two years before the martyrdom of the same Saint Boniface, in the year of the Lord 752, in the fifth indiction, on the Ides of March.

[unclear]

Alcuin, or Albinus, monk and deacon, abbot of the monastery of Saint Martin of Tours, by nation an Englishman, formerly a hearer of Saint Bede the priest: a man most learned in divine Scripture, and in the knowledge and skill of secular letters second to none in his time; excelling in verse and prose. Summoned from Britain by the emperor Charlemagne, he was held in such familiarity by him that he was called the emperor’s beloved master; under his instruction the emperor himself took pains to be initiated in all the disciplines of the liberal arts. He wrote many excellent volumes, among which are listed:

On the Holy Trinity and Faith, three books. “To the glorious lord Emperor Charles...” On the Questions of Fredegisus, one book. “To the most desired son Fredegisus...” To Eulalia, on the Nature of the Soul, one book. “Dearest in the love of Christ...” Sentences, one book. “To the most beloved son Guido...” On Genesis, one book. On the Song of Songs, one book. On Ecclesiastes, one book. On the Gospel of John, seven books.

DE SCRIPTORIBVS ECCLESIASTICIS Fol. 42

On the Epistles of Paul: thirteen books. On the Apocalypse of John: one book. On the adoption of the sons of God: one book. On ecclesiastical dogmas: one book. A Mirror for Little Children: one book. On the propriety of the names of God: one book. A dialogue addressed to his disciples: one book. The Life of Saint Vedast, bishop: one book. A handbook on certain psalms: one book. Letters to various persons: one book. On the liberal arts: one book. He is also said to have written many other works, which nevertheless have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under the rule of Charlemagne, in the year of the Lord 770.

Usuard, a monk of the order of Saint Benedict, a Gaul by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, ready in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, by order of the emperor Charlemagne after Eusebius, Jerome, and Bede gathered from the writings of the ancients the deeds and passions of the holy martyrs, confessors, and virgins into a single volume of no small size, which we call: A Martyrology: one book. And certain other works. He flourished under the same emperor Charles, in the year of the Lord 770.

Paul, a monk of the monastery of Cassino, of the order of Saint Benedict, an Italian by nation, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly taught in secular letters, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, was held in great esteem by the emperor Charles on account of his knowledge of letters. Formerly, before his conversion, he was a deacon of the church of Aquileia and the chancellor of Desiderius, the last king of the Lombards; and, captured with him by Charles, he was led into Gaul and at length became a monk. He wrote not a few volumes, both in verse and in prose; of these I have found only the following. At the request of [Adelperga?], daughter of King Desiderius, he added: To the chronicle of Eutropius: two books. The deeds of the bishops of Metz: one book. The Life of Pope Gregory the First: one book. The Life of Saint Arnulf, bishop: one book. The Life of Saint Benedict, in verse: one book. The deeds of the Lombards: six books. Many hymns in various metres: one book. Letters to various persons: one book. By order of Charles he arranged histories and readings for the whole year, suitable to the several feasts of the saints. And he digested and wrote many other works. He flourished in the times of the same Charlemagne, in the year of the Lord 780.

Hadrian, pope, the first of that name, a Roman by nation, sat in the pontificate after Stephen III for twenty-three years; a learned and most holy man, held in the highest honor by the emperor Charles. He established many things for the benefit of the Church, and at the command of the emperor Charles condemned the Felician heresy in a synod of 350 bishops at Frankfurt. Since he was studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, he abridged thirteen books of letters of Saint Gregory the pope into two, selecting the more useful portions. He also wrote from his own vein to Leo the Younger and Constantine his son, emperors: On the veneration of images: one book. To the emperor Charles: one book. Letters to various persons: one book. He died while Charlemagne was emperor, in the year of the Lord 795, in the fourth indiction.

On the day of the Nativity of the Lord, the eighth day before the Kalends of January.

Chrodegangus, bishop of Metz, nephew of King Pippin through his sister, ennobling the nobility of his birth by holy conduct and zeal for the Scriptures, an outstanding venerator of the bodies of the holy martyrs, wishing to instruct the clergy and people committed to him in justice by word and example, wrote for the clergy of the church of Metz a sufficiently instructive and useful Rule of Canons, 1 book, and certain other things.

He transferred the bodies of the holy martyrs Gorgonius, Nabor, and Nazarius from Rome into Francia; and the body of Saint Nazarius was laid up in the monastery of Lorsch, then of the order of Saint Benedict, in the diocese of Worms.

He flourished under King Pippin, father of the emperor Charles, in the year of the Lord 760.

Leo III, Roman by nation, sat as pope after the pontiff Adrian for twenty years: a man very learned in both divine and secular writings, and also most renowned for the holiness of his character and life. He anointed Charles, great in name and in deed, to the empire of the Romans, and transferred this dignity from the Greeks to the Franks. Among other things he wrote letters to various persons, 1 book.

He died under Charles on the Ides of June, in the year of the Lord 816, indiction 9.

Aimo, the third bishop of the church of Halberstadt in Saxony, formerly abbot of the monastery of Hersfeld, of the order of Saint Benedict, German by nation, once a hearer of Alcuin the monk, for whom Rabanus, then abbot of Fulda, composed twenty-two books On the Universe, was certainly a very learned man from every point of view, a most acute interpreter of the divine Scriptures, and of excellent talent in delivering homilies to the people.

He was first a monk of the monastery of Fulda with Rabanus; afterward he was made the third abbot of Hersfeld; finally he was consecrated third bishop of Halberstadt. He governed the same church vigorously by word and example for thirteen years. He wrote almost countless little works; of these, the following which we have placed below are reported:

On the five books of Moses, 5 books.

On Joshua, 1 book.

On Judges, 1 book.

On Ruth, 1 book.

On Kings, 1 book.

On Chronicles, 1 book.

On Tobit, 1 book.

On Ezra and Nehemiah, 1 book.

On Judith, 1 book.

On Esther, 1 book.

On Job, 1 book.

On the Song of Songs, 1 book.

On Isaiah the prophet, 4 books. Incipit: “The prophet Isaiah, of noble [unclear].”

On Jeremiah, 1 book.

On Ezekiel, 1 book. Incipit: “And it happened,” etc., says blessed Jerome.

On Daniel, 1 book.

On the twelve minor prophets, 14 books. Incipit: “The word which was made unto.”

Also on the Psalms, 1 book.

On the Gospels, homilies, 2 books. Incipit: “The Lord, consulting human [unclear].”

On all the epistles of Paul, 14 books. Incipit: “From Corinth, the metropolis.”

On the canonical epistles, 8 books.

On the Acts of the Apostles, 5 books.

On the Apocalypse, 1 book. Incipit: “We read in the ecclesiastical [history?].”

On the variety of books, 4 books. Incipit: “Since there is one and most holy [unclear].”

On the Holy Trinity, 1 book.

Book I, On the memory of Christian affairs

He is said also to have written many other things: letters, various sermons, treatises, which have not come to my knowledge. He died under the emperor Louis, son of Charlemagne, in the year of the Lord 824, in the twelfth indiction. He was buried in the church of Saint Stephen at Halberstadt.

Claudius, a monk of the order of Saint Benedict, formerly, as they report, Bede’s disciple in England, colleague of Albinus the Levite and abbot, a Scot by nation, a man very zealous and learned in the divine scriptures, not ignorant of secular learning, practiced in verse and prose, composed many small works on the sacred volumes:

On the five books of Moses: five books, of which they report [unclear]. Also on Judges: one book. On the book of Ruth: one book. On the Gospel of Matthew: one book. And many other things.

He flourished in Gaul under Charlemagne, in the year of the Lord 800.

Freculphus, bishop of Lisieux in the province of Rouen, a monk of the order of Saint Benedict, to whom Rabanus, while still an abbot, devoted his talent in many volumes, a man most zealous and very skilled in the divine scriptures, and quite fit for teaching the people, no less distinguished in manner of life than in knowledge, is reported to have written certain excellent small works. Of these I have read only a large and distinguished volume, containing from the beginning of the world down to the birth of our Lord Jesus Christ:

A history of deeds accomplished: seven books, through a certain sequence of time.

Of the others he has as yet seen nothing.

He wrote the aforesaid work to Helisachar, in which he also unraveled the more difficult questions of the scriptures; he set forth in a lucid style the deeds of both the Jews and also the gentiles from the beginning of the world down to the Virgin’s giving birth.

He flourished under Louis, in the year of the Lord 840.

Theodulfus, bishop of Orléans, formerly abbot of the monastery of Fleury of the order of Saint Benedict, a man learned in the divine scriptures, instructed from youth in secular letters, excellent in verse and prose, is reported to have composed some small works in both styles, but they have not yet come into our hands. When this man was innocently sent to prison by the emperor Louis, I do not know on what suspicion, he composed the hymn “Gloria laus”; and when on Palm Sunday, as the emperor was passing by the prison, he sang it in a loud voice, it so pleased the emperor that he immediately allowed him to go free. Among other things he wrote, in various meters:

Hymns: one book. Letters: one book.

He flourished under the empire of Louis, in the year of the Lord 840.

Einhard, chancellor of the emperor Charlemagne, a German by nation, afterwards a monk of the order of the holy father Benedict, a man most learned in secular letters and not ignorant of the divine scriptures, wrote small works of reading not to be despised. Of these they report the following. Imitating Bede, who abbreviated the Hebrew psalter by extracting from it all the verses having the words of a prayer, he himself abbreviated the Gallican psalter, extracting from it all the verses having the words of a prayer. He also wrote, both in his own person and in that of the emperor:

Letters to various persons: one book. The Life of the emperor Charles: one book. A history of the times: one book. And certain other things.

He flourished under Charles and under Louis his son, in the year of the Lord 820.

On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 43

from Britain into Gaul: with Charles the Great, the emperor, he was held in high esteem. Since he was a man most learned in all the Scriptures, he published, in a clear style, very distinguished little works. Among them the following are reported:

On the Gospel of Matthew, 2 books. On human duties, 1 book. On the division of nature, 1 book. He also composed many other works, which have not come to my knowledge.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Charlemagne, in the year of the Lord 800.

Hilduin, abbot of the monastery of Saint Denis at Paris, of the order of the divine father Benedict, archchaplain of the Sacred Palace, to whom Rabanus, abbot of Fulda, dedicated commentaries on the four books of Kings, was a man very learned in the divine Scriptures and very skilled in secular letters, excellent both in verse and in prose. He wrote to the emperor Louis, in both styles:

The Life of Saint Denis, 2 books. And certain other works.

He flourished under the emperor Louis, son of Charles, in the year of the Lord 840.

Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, formerly a monk of Saint Denis at Paris, was a man exceptionally learned in the divine Scriptures, second to none in his time in secular letters, distinguished for wisdom and honorable conduct, and most eloquent. He wrote several little works of considerable authority, of which I have found only the following. In the person of the emperor Charlemagne he wrote, with great learning:

To the Church of Ravenna, 1 book. The Life of Saint Remigius, bishop, 2 books. To Walo, bishop of Metz, 1 book. Of many letters, 1 book. Of the rest I have seen nothing.

He flourished under the emperors Charlemagne and Louis his son, in the year of the Lord’s nativity 800. And he wrote many doctrinal works.

Amalarius Fortunatus, archbishop of Trier, a German by nation, a monk of Luxeuil, and cardinal of the Roman Church, was a learned and most eloquent man, distinguished in Greek and Latin eloquence. Sent by the emperor Charlemagne to Constantinople to the emperor, he confirmed peace and friendship between them by his remarkable industry and eloquence, as is contained in the deeds of the Treveri. He wrote, among other things:

On Ecclesiastical Offices, 1 book. Enough, and indeed more than enough. To Louis on the same subject, 4 books. On the Mysteries of the Mass, 1 book. Letters to various persons, 1 book.

He died under the emperor Louis, in the year of the Lord 813, in the sixth indiction, around the sixteenth year of his episcopate.

Angelomus, monk of Luxeuil, of the order of Saint Benedict, was a man endowed with a noble talent for expounding the divine writings, so that the ancients, in comparison with him, seem not to have expounded what he expounded. He was also not ignorant of secular writings. At the command of Drogo, bishop of Metz, who was the son of Charlemagne and brother of the emperor Louis, he wrote a most excellent work, and one of such a kind that I do not remember having read its like elsewhere in the holy Scriptures:

On the Books of Kings, 4 books. Incipit: “Therefore, since by very many brothers.” To Lothar, on the Song of Songs, 1 book. Incipit: “Before the imperial glory.” On Divine Offices, 1 book. And certain other works.

He flourished under Louis and Lothar his son, in the year of the Lord 830.

Rabanus

Book

Rabanus Maurus, sixth archbishop of Mainz, formerly abbot of the monastery of Fulda of the Order of Saint Benedict, German by nation, from the city of Fulda in Buchonia, once a pupil of Albinus the Englishman, was a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in secular letters, a philosopher, rhetorician, astronomer, and most subtle poet; to whom, to speak without envy, neither Italy bore a like man nor Germany an equal. In the monastery of Fulda, while still a young man, he put on the monastic habit, and advanced wonderfully both in morals and in knowledge; whence also, consecrated fourth abbot of the same community, he presided for twenty-four years over the sheep entrusted to him, by word and example, and composed almost innumerable little works on the Scriptures. At length, offended by the wickedness of his monks, who said that, being too intent on the Scriptures, he neglected temporal affairs, the devil bringing this about in them, they conceived displeasure against him and were scandalized in him by that by which they ought most of all to have been edified. Therefore, giving place to anger, and not consenting to remain any longer with ungrateful sheep, he left the monastery and its inhabitants, and went over to Emperor Louis, son of Charles, with whom he remained for many days. But the monks, led by repentance, sent an embassy to him and asked that he return to the monastery; but they did not obtain it. He therefore remained with the emperor until the death of Otgarius, archbishop of Mainz; having been appointed in his place, he presided over the aforesaid church of Mainz for nine years. Having also held a synod, he established many things for the benefit of the faithful. While still settled in the monastery of Fulda, he wrote many volumes, both in verse and in prose, chiefly on the holy Scriptures, all of which he explained from beginning to end. Concerning his writings the following are reported. To Freculphus, bishop of Lisieux, of whom we made mention above, he wrote a distinguished work:

On Genesis, three books: “In the beginning,” etc.; many things on [unclear]. On Exodus, three books: “Exodus can be called a going out.” On Numbers, three books: “The book of Numbers [is] manifold.” On Leviticus, three books: “Of the following book, that is, Leviticus.” On Deuteronomy, three books: “The children of Israel moved camp.” On Joshua, two books: “To the most blessed lord and truly [unclear].” On Judges, one book: “After the death of Joshua.” On the book of Ruth, three books: “Therefore to those examining the history.” On Kings, to Hilduin, three books: “There was a man,” etc.; “Let us first say.” On Chronicles, three books: “Adam,” etc.; “the tenth from Adam.” On Ezra and Nehemiah, [three?] books: “Chosen lord and deservedly.” On Tobit, one book: “The book of Esther, which the Hebrews.” On

On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 44

On the Gospel of John: one book, “Among all the things of divine history …”

On all the epistles of Paul: twenty-four books, “To the venerable brother Lupus …”

On the canonical epistles: seven books.

On the Acts of the Apostles: one book.

On the Apocalypse of John: one book.

On the praise of the holy cross: one book, “The King of kings, the Lord … the world …”

To Bishop Haymo, On the Universe: twenty-two books, “First among the Hebrews of God …”

On universal nature: one book, “The discussion of the universe …”

On the instruction of clerics: three books, “To the lord, most reverend and religious Haistulf … Because you, venerable …”

On the divine offices: one book.

On computus, a dialogue: one book.

To King Louis: one book.

On questions of the canons: one book.

To Bishop Reginald: one book.

On the blessings of the patriarchs: one book.

Letters to various persons: one book.

Of almost innumerable sermons: one book. He also published many other works, which have not come to my knowledge. He died under the princes Louis and Lothar, in the year of the Lord 855, in the third indiction, in the ninth year of his episcopate. He was buried in the monastery of Saint Alban near Mainz, not without a reputation for sanctity; I have read his epitaph in nearly twenty verses.

Bellator, a priest of a certain church, zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, rich in the reading of the ancients, distinguished in talent and eloquence, and sufficiently instructed in secular letters, is said to have expounded many volumes on the holy Scriptures, in which he magnificently exercised his talent. There survives, among the rest, his notable volume, which he published at the request of friends:

On the Book of Wisdom: seven books.

I have found nothing about the others. He says that he flourished in the times of Emperor Louis, in the year of the Lord 841.

Strabus, a monk of Fulda, German by nation, formerly a hearer and scribe of Abbot Rabanus, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly taught in the studies of secular letters, subtle in talent and distinguished in eloquence, wrote no few small works in exposition of the sacred volumes; in these, showing himself a learned man, he transmitted his name with glory to posterity. Therefore, imitating his teacher Abbot Rabanus, he wrote:

On Genesis: one book.

On Exodus: one book.

A very brief treatment of the Book of Leviticus.

On Leviticus: one book.

And many other works. This Strabus, indeed, is remembered as the first to have brought together, from the sayings of the holy fathers, the gloss which is now called ordinary, on the whole Bible; others afterwards enlarged it with many added judgments of the fathers. He flourished under Emperor Louis, in the year of the Lord 840.

Lupus Servatus, priest, to whom Rabanus, abbot of Fulda, is read to have written eight books on the epistle of Paul the Apostle to the Romans, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures and, according to the age of his time, abundantly skilled in secular letters, wrote some small works of his talent, of which very few have been able to come to my knowledge. There survives his volume:

On Three Questions: one book.

And certain letters, as well as other works. He flourished under Lothar, son of Louis, in the year of the Lord 850.

John, called Erigena, a monk learned in the divine Scriptures, most learned in the discipline of secular letters, fully instructed in Greek and Latin eloquence, subtle in talent, composed in speech, at the command of Charles, son of Louis …

of Louis, brother of Emperor Lothar, translated into Latin: The Hierarchy of Dionysius, four books. He wrote on the same, four books. And certain other things. He flourished under Emperor Lothar, in the year of the Lord 850.

Ansegisus, abbot of the monastery of Lobbes, of the order of Saint Benedict, afterward archbishop of Sens, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, nobly instructed in secular letters, distinguished in speech and talent, arranged and brought together for the use of the catholic Church the laws of Emperor Charles the Great and of Louis, which I have seen, as follows, namely: The ecclesiastical statutes of Charles, two books: “While our Lord Jesus reigns.” The secular laws of the same, two books: “Concerning peace we admonish that.” The ecclesiastical statutes of Louis, two books: “To all of you either by sight.” The secular laws of the same, two books: “If slaves through contumacy.” He also published some other things besides, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under Emperor Lothar, son of Louis, in the year of the Lord 840.

Amulus, bishop of Lyons in Gaul, a man devoted to the divine Scriptures, learned by reading the ancients, and not moderately instructed in secular letters; distinguished in both the Hebrew and the Latin language, keen and forceful in talent, scholastic and composed in eloquence, wrote little works of reading not to be despised. Of these I have read only the distinguished work addressed to Charles: Against the Jews, one book: “The detestable perfidy of the Jews.” Of the rest I have as yet seen none. He flourished under Louis, son of Charles the Great, in the year of the Lord 830.

Bertramus, priest and monk, very skilled in the divine Scriptures, excellently instructed in the letters of secular disciplines, subtle in talent, distinguished in eloquence, and no less notable in life than in learning, wrote many excellent little works, of which few have come to my knowledge. To King Charles, brother of Emperor Lothar, he wrote a commendable work: On Predestination, one book. On the Body and Blood of the Lord, one book. He flourished in the times of Emperor Lothar, in the year of the Lord 840.

Turpinus, archbishop of Reims, friend and secretary of Emperor Charles the Great, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, nobly instructed in secular letters, having a talent exercised in verse and prose, advocate of the poor, beloved by God in life and conduct, who declares that he, together with Charles, often fought the Saracens with their own hands and weapons, wrote elegantly: The Deeds of Charles the Great, two books. Letters to various persons, one book. He flourished under the same Charles and Louis his son, in the year of the Lord 830.

Anastasius, keeper of the apostolic library, a most sagacious restorer, learned in the divine Scriptures, nobly instructed in secular letters, very skilled in Greek and Latin expression, is said to have composed some little works; but none of them has come into our hands. He translated many volumes of the Greeks into Latin. For, at the command of Pope Nicholas I, he translated: The Life of John the Almsgiver, one book. One Hierarchy of Dionysius, one book. The seventh universal synod, one book. The Lives of many fathers, one book. And many other things. He flourished under Louis, the second emperor, in the year of the Lord 860.

ON ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS. Fol. 45.

Nicholas, pope, the first, a Roman by country, sat in the pontificate after Benedict III for eight years, a man magnificently learned in the holy Scriptures, most holy in life and conversation, who established many things for the usefulness of the Catholic Church; by whose permission and authority the use of Sequences in the Gallican churches first began, Notker, abbot of Saint Gall, procuring [it]. He wrote, among other things, in the person of his pontificate: Of letters, to various [persons]: book. He dies under Lothair, or Louis II, emperor, in the year of the Lord 869, in the second indiction, the 8th [day before] the Ides of December.

John, deacon of the Roman church, a man erudite in the holy Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular letters, venerable in life and conversation no less than in learning. He wrote, for the edification of many, [addressed] to Pope John VII, in a quite illustrious style, a great volume which contains: The Life of Saint Gregory, pope, the first: 3 books. And certain others. He flourished under Charles the Bald, emperor, in the year of the Lord 870.

Otgerus [Notker], bishop of Liège, from [being] abbot of the monastery of Saint Gall, of the order of the Divine father Benedict, a Teuton by nation, a man most erudite in the divine Scriptures, and, in the disciplines of secular letters, the most learned philosopher of all his time, a distinguished poet and musician, and venerable no less for sanctity than for knowledge. He wrote, both in meter and in prose, many little works, of which few have come into our hands. I have read only the volume which he entitled "Of Sequences," which he had written while still a monk in the monastery of Saint Gall, [addressed] to Liutward, bishop of Vercelli and archchaplain of Charles the Great, emperor. This work begins thus: The Prologue or preface: a letter. ["By the merit of [his] supreme sanctity."] The Sequence-book, thus: book. ["Let all now render thanks."] On music and symphony: 1 book. ["When the prudent [son] and of the prudent."] On the expositors of sacred Scripture: 1 book. Of letters, to various [persons]: 1 book. Of the rest which he composed, nothing has come to the notice of our reading. Of this most learned man's Sequences, Pope Nicholas I approved [them] and commanded [them] to be sung at the masses. He, on account of the renown of [his] knowledge and life, [was] first abbot, then in his old age consecrated bishop, [and] presided, tenth in order, over the governance of the church of Liège, under Lothair the emperor, son of Louis, in the year of the Lord 850; under whom also he dies, not without an opinion of sanctity.

Christian, who [is] also [called] Druthmar, monk and priest of Corbie, of the order of holy memory Benedict of Cassino, an Aquitanian by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, imbued with the Greek and Latin tongue, who, coming from Aquitaine into Gaul, made his name known by writing. Of his little works I have hitherto deserved to see only a great and illustrious work, [addressed] to the monks of the monasteries of Stavelot and Malmedy—existing under one abbot in the diocese of the church of Liège—written in open speech: On the Gospel of Matthew: 1 book. ["He did not make this title…"] Of others I have seen nothing. In the prologue of his exposition of the Gospel according to Matthew, he promised to write also on the other evangelists, which he is said also to have done, but [it is] unknown to us.

Wandelbert, deacon and monk of the monastery of Prüm, of the order of Saint Benedict, of the diocese of Trier, a Teuton by nation, a man erudite in the divine Scriptures and magnificently learned in secular letters, prompt in talent and renowned in eloquence, wrote, both in meter and in prose, not a few volumes, of which I have seen only [those addressed] to a certain abbot Marward: The Life of Saint Goar the priest: 1 book. The Miracles of the same: 1 book. A Martyrology, in meter: 1 book. He flourished under Lothair the emperor, in the year of the Lord 850.

In totũ psalterium: li. In euangeliũ Matthaei: li. In Canonem missae: li. De officijs diuinis: li. Ad ep̄m Eduorũ: li. Sermones quoqꝫ plures. li. Book

[H]lmannus, a monk of the monastery of Altuvillare, of the Order of Saint Benedict, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and excellently instructed in secular letters, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, wrote various small works both in verse and in prose, by which he made his name known also to posterity. And because in his time Francia was being laid waste by the Northmen, after the example of the prophet Jeremiah he lamented the desolation of that land and of his monastery in a fourfold alphabet, composing:

On the lamentation: one book. The Life of Bishop Vinardus: one book. The Life of Saint Syndulphus: one book. The Life of Saint Helena Augusta: one book. The Translation of the same: one book.

He is said also to have written some other works, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under the emperor Charles III, in the year of the Lord 890.

Milo, a monk of the monastery of Saint Amand, of the Order of divine Benedict, a Gaul by nation, a man most learned in every respect, a distinguished orator, poet, and musician, and no less venerable for uprightness of morals than for knowledge of the Scriptures. He wrote not a few volumes both in verse and in prose. Of these the following especially are reported:

To Charles the Bald, On Sobriety, in verse: one book. The Life of Saint Amand, in verse: one book. Letters to various persons: one book.

He flourished in the times of the second emperor Charles, surnamed the Bald, in the year of the Lord 870, and composed many excellent works.

Hucbaldus, a monk of the monastery of Elnone, of the Order of Saint Benedict, a Gaul by nation, a man most highly learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters; in music, poetry, philosophy, and the other liberal arts second to none in his time, as the many small works written by him in both styles attest. Of these I have so far found only the following: to the emperor Charles the Bald, a remarkable work of 136 verses, in which all the words begin with one letter, c, as: “Carmina clarisonae calvis cantate Camenae”; it is entitled:

On the Praise of Bald Men: one book. On the Art of Music: one book. The Deeds of Saint Lebuinus: one book. Letters to various persons: one book.

He also described the lives of many saints in adorned eloquence, and composed chants in their honor with sweet and regular melody. He flourished in the times of the emperor Charles the Bald, in the year of the Lord 880.

Remigius, a monk of Auxerre, of the Order of Saint Benedict, and afterwards, as they report, bishop of that same city, a man most highly learned in divine and human writings, a distinguished writer in verse and prose, teacher of Saint Odo, the first abbot of Cluny, renowned in life and doctrine. He published many volumes in both styles, of which the following are reported:

On the Song of Songs: one book. On the whole Psalter: one book. On the Gospel of Matthew: one book. On the Canon of the Mass: one book. On the Divine Offices: one book. To the bishop of the Edui: one book. Also several sermons: one book.

In addition he composed many other works both in sacred letters and also in secular writings, expounding Donatus and the ancient authors, which are possessed by many. He flourished under the emperor Charles the Bald, in the year of the Lord 880.

On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 46

Constantinus, a monk of the monastery of Cassino, of the order of Saint Benedict, African by nation, a man very devoted to the divine Scriptures and, in secular letters, especially in philosophy and medicine, most learned, fully furnished with Greek, Latin, and Arabic eloquence, wrote many little works on medical matters, which are held in esteem among physicians. He also translated many volumes of the ancient physicians from Greek and Arabic into Latin, which he prefaced with his own prefaces and letters. Of his little works:

Universal Diets, five books: “What first compelled ...” Particular Diets, three books: “We have completed in the first book ...” On Medicinal Weights, one book: “Medicinal weights ...” On Urines also, one book: “I have seen that [unclear] ...”

As for the rest of his volumes, which he wrote and translated in great number, I do not recall that any have come into our hands. They are better known to physicians.

Ambrosius Ansbertus, monk and priest of the order of Saint Benedict, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, gentle in talent and sweet in speech, produced many commentaries on the sacred books, by which he transmitted the fame of his name to posterity. Yet few have come to my knowledge. For I have found only the following:

On the Song of Songs, one book: “The gift of wisdom with Solomon ...” On the Psalter also, one book. On the Apocalypse of John, ten books. On Cupidity, one book. Letters to various persons, one book.

He flourished under Emperor Arnulf, in the year of the Lord 890.

Paschasius Ratbertus, abbot of Corbie, of the order of Saint Benedict, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, nobly furnished with Greek and Latin eloquence, sharp in intellect and orderly in speech, wrote not a few little works in verse and prose. Of these I have found only the following: to Placidus, abbot of our order, a distinguished work:

On the Sacrament of the Altar, one book: “Whoever among Catholics rightly ...” Life of Saint Adalhard, bishop, one book. On the Lamentations of Jeremiah the prophet, one book.

He also translated some things from Greek into Latin and composed many others. He flourished in the times of Emperor Charles the Fat, in the year of the Lord 880.

Ericus, monk of the order of Saint Benedict, of the monastery of the city of Auxerre, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and very learned in the disciplines of secular letters, excellent in verse and prose, was an outstanding teacher in homilies delivered to the people. He wrote lucidly in meter:

Life of Germanus of Auxerre, six books. Homilies to the people, one book.

Several sermons and letters. He also composed many other things in both styles, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished around the times of Emperor Charles the Fat, in the year 880.

Otfridus, monk of the monastery of Weissenburg, of the order of the divine father Benedict, German by nation, formerly a hearer and disciple of Rabanus Maurus, abbot of Fulda, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and exceptionally learned in secular letters, a philosopher, rhetorician, and distinguished poet, excellent in talent and eloquent, transmitted [unclear]. Following the example of the emperor Charlemagne, he also endeavored to reduce the barbarism of the German language to grammatical rules, which he accomplished in part. Hence those things which he wrote in his native speech cannot easily in our age be read and understood, even by a man however skilled in the German language. Of his little works the following are extant. To Luitbert, the eighth archbishop of the church of Mainz, on the Gospel, a great and distinguished work, which he entitled:

The Grace of Theotista, five books: “The summit of dignity ...”

100
LIBER Ad Ludouicum regẽ: li. Ad Salomonẽ ep̃m: li. Ad monachos sancti Galli: li. In psalterio uolumna .iiij. li. De iudicio extremo: li. De gaudijs regni caelestis: li. Carmina diuersi generis: li. Dreualdus qui Albertus: monachus Floriacensis coenobij: ordinis san- cti Benedicti: uir undecũqƺ illustris atqƺ doctissimus: nomen suũ scribendo notificauit: dum ad aedificationẽ simpliciũ fratrũ alterno stilo multa uolu, mina in scripturis sanctis cõposuit. Hic erat insignis musicus: archican- tor ecclesiae Thuronen sis: qui audita fama Bernonis Gigniacensis sanctissimi abba- nis: ordinē sub eo ingressus est : abbas postea Cluniacensis cõstitutꝰ: magna san- ctitate ordine illustrauit. Qui cũ esset declamator homeliarũ praecipuis: multos ad frẽs sermões cõposuit. Scripsit etiã inter caetera ingenij sui opera: Vitam sancti Gerardi li. Laudes sancti Martini: li. Chronica succinctam: li. Hymnos etiã uarios cantus in honore sanctoꝝ dulci regulari melodia cõpo- fuit. Rogantibus quoqƺ fratrib⁹: libros beati Gregorij papae sup̃ lob abbreuiās: in unũ uolumen cõportauit. Claruit tꝑibus Arnoldi impato. Anno.DCCCC.XX. RAtbodus quartus decimꝰ epũs Traiectensis: natione teutonicus: uir in diui nis scripturis ualde eruditus: saecularium lrãꝝ non ignarus: ingenio subtī- lis: eloquio clarus: uita cõuersatione sanctissimꝰ: multis uiuus mor- tuus miraculis coruscavit. Hunc in oībus litteris humanitatis Nāno ph̄us doctissi- mus instruxerat: qui aduocatus in palatio regis Caroli grossi fuit : postea mona- steriu ingressus: tandem epũs ut diximus consecratus: ecclesiam Trajectensem in graui Danorũ psecutione decẽ septẽ annis strenue gubernauit. Scripsit aūt nō, nulla praeclara opuscula: De quibus ista ferunt: Laudes sancti Martini: li. Laudes sancti Bonifacij epĩ: li. De sancta Amalberga: li. Homeliarũ sermonũ: li. De sancto V uillebrordo flores: li. Integrum quoqƺ de sancti Martini translationem composuit. Et uarios can- tus in honore sanctorũ. Moritur sub Ludouico filio Arnoldi imperatoris: Anno domini:DCCCC.XVII. ¶Indictione quinta: iij. Calendꝰ. decembris: Episcopat⁹ fui anno.xviij.Sepultus apud Dauantriã: ubi residere in ep̃atu antea cõsueuerat. DE SCRIPTORIBUS ECCLESIASTICIS Fol. 47

Book

To King Louis, one book. To Bishop Salomon, one book. To the monks of Saint Gall, one book. On the Psalter, four volumes, books. On the Last Judgment, one book. On the joys of the heavenly kingdom, one book. Poems of various kinds, one book. Letters to various persons, one book. He also composed many other things besides, which, lost through the negligence of earlier men and erased and torn through the ignorance of monks, have not come down to me. He flourished under the emperors Louis, Lothar, and Charles, succeeding one another in turn, in the year of the Lord 870.

Drevaldus, also called Albertus, a monk of the monastery of Fleury, of the Order of Saint Benedict, a man distinguished on every side and very learned, made his name known by writing, since for the edification of simple brothers he composed many volumes on the Holy Scriptures in alternating style. Among the other little works of his talent, he wrote, in lucid speech, a history from the time of the translation of the body of Saint Benedict from the monastery of Monte Cassino to the monastery of Fleury down to the time of Odo, king of the Franks:

The Miracles of Saint Benedict, one book. And many other things which I have not seen. He flourished in the times of Emperor Arnold, in the year 990.

Odo, first abbot of Cluny, of the Order of Saint Benedict, formerly a hearer of Remigius, the monk of Auxerre, a man zealous and learned in the Holy Scriptures, an outstanding restorer of the fallen order of the divine father Benedict, shone forth clearly no less by holiness than by noble learning. He was an excellent musician, arch-chanter of the church of Tours, who, when he had heard the fame of Berno of Gigny, a most holy abbot, entered the order under him; later appointed abbot of Cluny, he adorned the order with great holiness. Since he was an outstanding declaimer of homilies, he composed many discourses to the brothers. Among the other works of his talent he also wrote:

The Life of Saint Gerard, one book. Praises of Saint Martin, one book. A Concise Chronicle, one book. He also composed various hymns and chants in honor of the saints, in sweet and regular melody. At the brothers' request also, he abridged the books of blessed Pope Gregory on Job and brought them together into one volume. He flourished in the times of Emperor Arnold, in the year 920.

Ratbod, the fourteenth bishop of Utrecht, a German by nation, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, subtle in talent, distinguished in speech, most holy in life and conduct, shone with many miracles while living and after death. Nanno, a most learned philosopher, had instructed him in all humane letters; he was an advocate in the palace of King Charles the Fat; afterwards he entered a monastery; finally, as we have said, consecrated bishop, he vigorously governed the church of Utrecht for seventeen years in the severe persecution of the Danes. He wrote some excellent little works:

Of which these are reported: Praises of Saint Martin, one book. Praises of Saint Boniface, bishop, one book. On Saint Amalberga, one book. Of homilies and sermons, one book. Flowers on Saint Willibrord, one book. He also composed a complete work on the translation of Saint Martin, and various chants in honor of the saints. He died under Louis, son of Emperor Arnold, in the year of the Lord 917, in the fifth indiction, on the third day before the Kalends of December, in the eighteenth year of his episcopate. He was buried at Deventer, where he had previously been accustomed to reside in his episcopate.

Egino abbas Prumiensis coenobii in diocesi Treverensi: ordinis sancti Benedicti: natione teutonica: vir in divinis scripturis eruditissimē: & in sacerdibus litteris nobiliter doctus: inter doctores Germaniae et Galliae suo tempore facile obtinuit principatū. Tandē ad ecclīam suā reuersus: denuo nescio an ob candē causā pullus: p̄ sui cōsolatione uaria utroq̄ biq̄ cōpoluit: quae legētiū intellectibq̄ nó minē placere poterūt q̄ pdesse: De quibq̄ De primo suo exilio: li. i (ista ferūt Altius de scdo praenotatē frenēf. li. i Alius qui uocat inefficax: li. i De corpore et sanguine dñi: li. i Contra Anthropomorphitas: li. i Agonisticon id est praeloquioq̄ li. vi Confessionū quōq̄ li. i Vita sancti Vrsmari Lobien. li. i Alia quōq̄ nōnulla scripsisse dicit: quae ad noticiā meā non uenerāt. Tephanus ex clerico Metēlis ecclīae: epūs Leodienēlis: post Franconē: vir in divinis scripturis doctus et in sacerdibus litteris magnēs peritū: & nó minē sanctitate q̄ scientia uenerabilēs. Scripsit nō spernēdae utilitatis plura LIBER

[Aurelianus?], cleric of the church of [Réôme?]: very zealous in Holy Scripture, and nobly learned in secular letters; in his time an excellent and distinguished musician. He wrote to Bernard the archchanter, afterwards bishop, on the rules of modulations, which they call tones or tenors, and on the matter itself and its terms, a notable volume: A Regular Tonary, one book. Its title is: [unclear]. He also wrote certain other things. He flourished about the times of the emperor Arnulf, in the year of the Lord 900.

Egino, abbot of the monastery of Prüm in the diocese of Trier, of the Order of Saint Benedict, German by nation, a man most learned in divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in secular letters, easily held the first place among the doctors of Germany and Gaul in his time. He wrote works of great authority, of which I have found the following. To Albero, first bishop of Metz, from the birth of Christ down to the nine hundred and eighth year of the same, chiefly containing the deeds of the Franks and Germans: A History or Chronicle, ten books. He wrote: On Ecclesiastical Discipline, two books, beginning, “In the first place one must inquire.” Of the rest I have not yet seen anything. He wrote the aforesaid work, as noted above, on ecclesiastical discipline and the Christian religion, at the command of Ratbod, archbishop of Trier; he compiled it from the decrees of the holier fathers and of general councils in two books, and lucidly divided it, in the customary manner, by rubrics into nearly nine hundred chapters. He flourished under the emperor Arnulf, in the year of the Lord 910.

Hildouin, from being abbot of the monastery of Lobbes, of the Order of Saint Benedict, first bishop of Liège, then, driven out, came to Hugh, king of Italy, to whom he was joined by a line of kinship; by him he was appointed bishop of Verona, and at last, after Lampert, was made archbishop of Milan. He ordained Ratherius, a monk, as bishop of the church of Verona; a man sufficiently learned in divine Scriptures. At the request of the brothers, while he was still abbot, he wrote: The Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes, one book; Sermons to the Brothers, one book; and certain other things. He flourished under Hugh, king of Italy, in the times of Conrad, emperor of the Romans and Germans, in the year of the Lord 920.

Ratherius, from being a monk of the monastery of Lobbes, after Hildouin bishop of Verona; a man learned in divine Scriptures and very skilled in the arts of humanity, which they call liberal; simple in character, gentle in disposition, and scholastic in speech. He came to Hugh the king in Italy with Bishop Hildouin, and after Hildouin’s translation to the archiepiscopal see of the church of Milan, he was appointed bishop of the city of Verona. Not long afterwards, driven out from there by Hugh because he had admitted Arnulf, duke of Bavaria and Hugh’s enemy, into Verona, he was relegated to exile at Pavia. At length, returned to his church, and again, I do not know whether for the same reason, driven out, he composed various works in each place for his own consolation, which could no less please the understanding of readers than profit it. Of these they report the following: On His First Exile, one book; Higher Concerning the Second, with the prefixed [unclear], one book; another, which he calls Inefficax, one book; On the Body and Blood of the Lord, one book; Against the Anthropomorphites, one book; Agonisticon, That Is, Pre-speeches, six books; also Confessions, one book; Life of Saint Ursmar of Lobbes, one book. He says that he also wrote some other works, which have not come to my knowledge. And finally, as the monk Sigebert writes, after being made bishop of Liège, he was also driven out from there. He flourished in the times of Henry, first emperor of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 920.

Stephen, from being a cleric of the church of Metz, bishop of Liège after Franco; a man learned in divine Scriptures and greatly skilled in secular letters, and no less venerable for holiness than for knowledge. He wrote many works of no contemptible usefulness

opuscula: quibnomelau posteris innotuit: Ad Hermánũ archiepẽm Colonienẽ: Vitam sancti Lamperti: li. 1 Ad Rupertũ epm Metensẽ: li. 1 Et quaedã alia. Scripsit etiam cantũ de sancta Trinitate ex Alcuino quo i octauis pẽ tecostes utimur: de inuentione sancti Stephani: & cantũ nocturnũ de sancto Lamp pertẽ epo et martyre: quos oẽ cui qbusdã alijs autentica et dulci modulatione co posituit. Claruit tẽporibũ Ludouici filij Arnoldi impato. Anno dũi. DCCCC.X. Adulphus Flauiacẽlis monachũ: ordinis sancti Benedicti: uir in divinis scri pturis eruditissimũ: & in oibũ lũs humanitatis suo tẽpore doctissimũ: inge nio subtilis: sensu: pfandus: eloquio dulcis: ornatũ et disertũ: in exponedis oluminibũ sacris acutũ et multũ egregiũ.
