On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 57

On ecclesiastical liberty: one book. The Life of the same Anselm: one book. And certain other things. He flourished in the times of Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1120.

Gratian, a monk of Bologna or Classe, of the Order of Saint Benedict, by birth, as some maintain, an Etruscan, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and burning with admirable zeal, ready in intellect and clear in eloquence, also distinguished in life and conduct, wrote, after Ivo, bishop of Chartres, a notable volume of Decrees from the statutes, enactments, and writings of the ancients, which professors of canon law use in the schools down to the present, approved by Pope Eugene III. Its title is: The Concordance of Discordant Canons: four books. The human race by two... He also composed certain other things. He flourished under Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1120.

Hugh, monk of Corbie, of the Order of Saint Benedict, called de Fouilloy, a man rich and learned in the Holy Scriptures through reading the ancients, distinguished in intellect and sweet in eloquence, and no less venerable for conduct than for knowledge, made his name known to posterity by his writings. For he wrote a notable volume, not so much useful as delightful to all religious persons and those fearing God, divided into four little books, designated beforehand as follows: On the material cloister: one book. On the arrangement of the cloister. On the spiritual cloister: one book. The contemplation of the soul’s cloister... On the cloister of the soul: one book. Into the heavenly [unclear] cloister. On the cloister of paradise: one book. Behold, a virgin shall conceive, etc. And certain other things. He flourished in the times of Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1120.

Richard, monk of Saint Victor in Paris, of the Order of Regular Canons of Saint Augustine, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in secular philosophy, excellent in intellect, scholastic in eloquence, outstanding in morals and conduct, wrote many and almost innumerable little works, by which he greatly benefited the usefulness of believers and consecrated his name to immortality. Among these the following are reported: On the Holy Trinity: five books. My righteous one lives by faith. On contemplation: one book. Arise, Lord, into your rest. On the twelve patriarchs: one book. Benjamin, a little youth. On the mystical ark: five books. That mystical ark of Moses. On the Song of Songs: one book. On my bed, etc.; the soul which God... On the extermination of evil: one book. What is it to you, sea, that you fled? On the promotion of good: one book. Every head is sick, etc. Against the Judaizers: one book. Behold, a virgin shall conceive, etc. On the tabernacle of the covenant: one book. Whatever you shall bind upon... On the forty-two stations: one book. In the regeneration, when he shall sit... On the study of wisdom: one book. Since to your question, etc. On the perfection of monks: one book. Bring to the Lord, sons of God, etc. On mental prayer: one book. Those things in the Gospel. On the threefold holocaust: one book. On the authority of Peter: one book. On judicial power: one book. On the difference of sins: one book. On the instruction of novices: one book. On the spirit of blasphemy: one book.

Eckardus primus abbas monasterij sancti Laurentij qđ Vraugia dicit:in diocefi Herbipolenfĩ in bircinia sylua:ordinis sancti Benedicti:natione teu tonicus:uir in diuinis scrturis eruditissimꝰ:&amp; infaecularibus litteris nulli inter germanos fuo tempore doctorũ inferior:metro excellens prosa.Scripfit non spernendae lectionis opufcula:quibꝰ ingenij fui uiacitatē declarauit.De qui bus ego tantũ uidi opus infigne:ad imitationẽ Boetij gemino ftilo cõpactũ ad in- ftuctionẽ consolationẽ monachorũ oīm fideliũ deū timentiũ ualde utile et amp; neceffarium: quod praenotauit: Laternam monachorũ: li.v Sermones quosdã elegantes uariafque epl'as ad diuerfos cõposuit. Claruit sub Conrado tertio imperatore:Anno dñi.Mill.CXXX. In medio ec-

Book

On the offices of the Church, one book. On diverse affections, one book. An epitome of the whole Bible, one book. On the Apocalypse of John, one book. On Daniel the prophet, one book. A chronicle from the beginning of the world, one book. On the double Pascha, one book. Of divisions or exceptions, twenty-four books. “O God, supremely good, unchanging.” On the vision of Nebuchadnezzar, one book. On the sacrifice of Abraham, one book. On the four winds, one book. On the words of Isaiah, one book. On the words of the Apostle, one book. On the Acts of the Apostles, one book. On violent charity, one book. On newness of life, one book. “Purge out the old leaven.” He also composed, besides these, many letters, sermons, and various treatises. He flourished under Conrad III, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1140.

Guigo, fifth prior of the Charterhouse, a man skilled in the divine Scriptures through long study, and not ignorant of secular letters either, mild in talent and distinguished in speech, and no less venerable in conduct than in learning, is said to have composed several little works, by which his name was given to immortality. Among these there is extant an excellent work, in lucid style, On the Life of Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, one book, written [unclear]; On the Institutes of the Carthusians, one book; and certain other things. He corrected with diligent study, according to the line of truth, the letters of the most blessed father Jerome, corrupted by the excessive fault of copyists. He died under the younger emperor Lothair, in the year of the Lord 1137, in the fifteenth indiction, on the sixth day before the Kalends of August.

Peter Lombard, bishop of Paris after being a scholastic, a man most devoted to the divine writings, nobly learned, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, transmitted his name by writing to posterity with such great glory that, down to the present day, the school of theologians everywhere, exercised in his little works, names and holds him as Master with singular veneration. For with sagacious study he wrote, from the sayings of the holy fathers, a commendable work: Sentences, three books. “Desiring something from.” On the whole Psalter, one book. “Since all the prophecies the Holy Spirit.” On all the letters of Paul, fourteen books. “The beginnings of things must be sought.” Various sermons, one book. He also composed not a few other things, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under Conrad III, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1140.

Eckard, first abbot of the monastery of Saint Laurence which is called Aura, in the diocese of Würzburg, in the Bircinian Forest, of the Order of Saint Benedict, a German by nation, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and, among the Germans in his time, inferior to none of the learned in secular letters, excellent in verse and prose. He wrote little works not to be despised in reading, by which he displayed the liveliness of his intellect. Of these I have seen only an excellent work, put together in a double style in imitation of Boethius, very useful and necessary for the instruction and consolation of monks and of all the faithful who fear God, which he entitled: The Lantern of Monks, five books. He composed certain elegant sermons and various letters to different persons. He flourished under Conrad III, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1130. In the middle

On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 58: buried in the church of the aforesaid monastery.

Engelbert, abbot of the monastery of Admont, of the Order of Saint Benedict, German by nation, a man very studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and sufficiently instructed in the disciplines of secular letters, distinguished in talent and speech, and no less venerable in conduct than in learning, made his name known by writing and expounding various works, and both by word and by example did things by no means insignificant for the edification of his brothers. For he wrote:

Elegant sermons, one book. On Vices and Virtues, one book.

He also published several other things, which have by no means come to my knowledge.

Peter, priest of the church of Troyes, surnamed Comestor or Manducator, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and excellently taught in secular letters, practiced in verse and prose, wrote certain distinguished little works in both styles, whose authority has long since been approved by the Church through usage. He was called Comestor or Manducator because, by citing the authorities of the Scriptures rather frequently in his sermons and little works, he seemed, as it were, to have eaten them into [the belly?] of his memory. Among the other volumes of his talent he wrote a notable work addressed to William, archbishop of Sens, briefly and usefully explaining all the historical books of the Bible, which from usage is now entitled:

The Scholastic History, twenty books. “Of imperial majesty is ...”

In Praise of Saint Mary, one book. Sermons on the season, one book.

Sermons on the saints, one book. And very many other things. He flourished under Frederick, the first emperor, in the year of the Lord 1160.

Peter the Parisian dialectician, called Abelard, French by nation, a man most learned in secular philosophy and nobly instructed in the divine Scriptures, delighting in novelty of terms and attempting to search into things too high for him, overcome by glory, fell into several errors. Through the action of the holy abbot Bernard, he was condemned together with his depraved doctrines in the council of Sens. From this time secular philosophy began to defile sacred theology with its useless curiosity. This Peter wrote several little works, which, if he had not mixed errors into them, could have been of use to posterity. Of these there exists a volume shadowed over with dialectical obscurity, varied in many opinions, which he wished to entitle:

His Theology, one book. Know Thyself, one book. And certain other things. He flourished under Conrad, the third emperor, in the year of the Lord 1140.

Adelphus, abbot of the Order of Saint Benedict, a man skilled in the divine Scriptures through long practice, not ignorant of secular letters, an indefatigable cultivator of regular observance, so that by word and example he might show himself a useful shepherd to the sheep of Christ committed to him, is said to have fashioned several little works for their benefit, in which a rich vein of talent recommends ornate speech. Of these there exist elegant works:

Sermons to the brothers, one book. Against the Saracens, one book. The rest which he is said to have composed have not come to my knowledge.

William, abbot of Saint-Thierry, afterward, as is said, a monk of Clairvaux under the blessed father Bernard of the Cistercian Order, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and also distinguished by holiness of life and conduct, for that reason especially beloved by him, published little works not to be despised in reading. Of these few have come to my knowledge. He began to write, but, forestalled by death, did not finish:

The Life of Saint Bernard the Abbot, one book. “About to write the life of your servant ...”

The Mirror of Faith, one book. The Enigma of Faith, one book. Sentences of Faith, one book. To Theophilus, On the Nature of the Soul, one book.

Book

On Contemplating God, one book.

On the Nature and Dignity of Love, one book.

On the Sacrament of the Altar, one book.

Meditations for Novices, one book.

Against Peter Abelard, one book.

On the Song of Songs, incomplete, one book.

On Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, one book.

And certain other things. There are some who say that this William, while he was still abbot of Saint-Thierry, wrote that widely known letter to the Carthusians, whose beginning is: “To the brothers of Mont-Dieu, an eastern light ...”; it is ascribed by many to blessed Bernard. He flourished under Conrad, the third emperor, in the year of the Lord 1140. And after he had completed one book on the life of Bernard himself, he died; Arnold, abbot of Bonneval, added four other books to it.

Conrad, monk of the monastery of Hirsau on the borders of the Swabians, of the Order of Saint Benedict, German by nation, of the diocese of Speyer, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and very skilled in secular letters, [unclear] musician and distinguished poet, composed many splendid little works under the name Peregrinus; in these, the ornate arrangement of thought and the cultivation of graceful discourse show their author inferior to none of the ancients. Of these, only the following have come to my knowledge. A notable work of dialogues under the name of Peregrinus the priest and Theodora, a virgin consecrated to God, which he entitled:

The Mirror of Virgins: 8 books. “As I am about to confer with you, O Theodore...” On the Gospels [unclear]: 1 book. “Since in the letter of the Old Testament...” On his life and the fruit of death: 1 book. “Since every discourse of the divine page...” On the matricularii: 1 book. “Since it is manifest to the world...” On the Praises of St. Benedict, in verse: 1 book. “Like light from the sun of virtues...” Didascalon: 1 book. “Since I see that you have long been at leisure...” On music and tones: 1 book. “Music is [unclear] of a certain [unclear]...” Of the rest I have seen nothing. There was another declaimer of the Order of Preachers, who, according to the custom of the moderns, composed sermons for the people under the name Peregrinus, much inferior to ours in eloquence and later than he in time. But whatever Conrad wrote in this way echoes Ciceronian eloquence, which the other could not do.

He flourished under Conrad III, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1140.

Arnold, abbot of Bonneval, of the Cistercian order, once a very close friend of the blessed abbot Bernard, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant also of secular writings, ready in talent and clear in eloquence, and no less distinguished in conduct than in doctrine, made his name known to posterity by writing. For when William, abbot of Saint-Thierry, died and left unfinished the work on the life of Saint Bernard, and when that saint himself also was already holding the heavenly realms, Arnold wrote and completed:

Life of Saint Bernard: 4 books. “The deeds of illustrious men do not...”

And some letters. He flourished under Frederick I, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1160.

Richard, monk of Cluny, of the Order of Saint Benedict, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and, by everyone’s report, most learned in secular letters in his time, subtle in talent and eloquent in speech, who, by writing and composing various treatises, transmitted his name with great glory to the knowledge of posterity. I do not recall that any of them have so far come into my hands. Yet his notable and famous work is reported:

Histories of the Times: 1 book. Letters to various persons: 1 book.

He flourished in the times of Frederick I, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1160.

Anfredus of Auxerre, monk of the Cistercian order, once a hearer and disciple of Peter Abelard, but, lest he should also become an imitator of his error, betook himself to the instruction of Saint Bernard of Clairvaux; under his discipleship, distinguished in doctrine and religion, he composed little works of reading not to be despised, by which he also made his name known to posterity:

Against Peter Abelard: 1 book. On the Apocalypse of John: 1 book. Letters to various persons: 1 book.

He flourished in the times of Frederick I, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1160.

On Ecclesiastical Writers Fol. 59

Peter, cleric of the church of Reims, called de Riga, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, and among all the teachers of his time most learned in the sacred letters, a notable grammarian and philosopher, excellent in verse and prose. He wrote not a few volumes in both styles, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these I have seen his notable metrical work on the Bible, which he entitled Aurora, as follows:

On Genesis: 1 book. “In the beginning, the world and what things in the beginning...” On Exodus: 1 book. “These twelve first [unclear]...” On Leviticus: 1 book. “But the voice of the Lord [to] Moses...” On Numbers: 1 book. “God addresses Moses and...” On Deuteronomy: 1 book. “These are the words of God by which...” On Joshua: 1 book. “After Moses, Joshua [unclear] the people...” On Judges: 1 book. “The Hebrew sins, says the Scripture...” On Ruth: 1 book. “Peter’s style hastens to Ruth...” On Kings: 3 books. “Dwelling on Mount Ephraim...” On the Song of Songs: 1 book. “Origen alone, with the learned...” On the Fourth Book of Kings: 1 book. “King Solomon reigned...” On Daniel: 1 book. “[unclear] the king, subjects to himself...” On Tobit: 1 book. “Whoever reads the history of Tobit...” On Job: 2 books. “Some attribute the book of Job to Moses...” On the Book of Judith: 1 book. “Eustochium, favoring Paula...” On the Book of Esther: 1 book. “All the way to the Ethiopians, who...” On the Books of Maccabees: 1 book. “Great Alexander, who...” On the Gospel History: 1 book. “Herod shone with the right of kings...” On the Acts of the Apostles: 1 book. “In the nineteenth year of Tiberius’ reign...” Recapitulations: 1 book. “These things concerning the new and old law...” On Grammar: 1 book.

He published many other works besides, which have not come to my knowledge. In the aforesaid little works he expounded the historical books of the Bible with marvelous brevity, and, carefully observing the law of meter, he explained each item in its historical and allegorical sense.

Oachim abbas Florēlis coenobii: ordinis sancti Benedicti: ex Calabria ori- undus: vir in divinis scripturis studiosus et exercitatus: qui ut ppheta suo tempore habitus: etiam futura praedicere conatus est. Sed mibi uideret (ut salua opinione sua uel suorũ loquar) ex coniecturis scripturarum illum magis lo- cutum q. pphetafe. Nam ut de caeteris interim taceā: Fredericũ imperatore ter- tiũ hoste ecclesiae futurũ somniauit: quē omnes nouimũ uelque ad morte pacificũ: & Ro- mano pontifici subiectũ et fidelẽ pleuerasẽ. Osuida nobilis mulier in Saxonia nata: in Gandeshemēsi coenobio qd̓ nō lōge ab Hildeshem distat sacromonialis: miro ingenio doctrina claruit: Ad uirgines em̄ sacratas castita- tem continentiam hortando latino sermone conscripsit: Comoedias: sex Vnica spes mūdi etcͣ De gestis Ottonū panaegyricū uersu hexametro. Item passionē sancti Dionysij carmine elegiaco. Item de sancto Gangolfo alijs sanctis plura. Graecae etiam linguae noticiam habuit. Coetanea Iohannis anglici fuit: quae doctri na sua papatum meruit. D Vdechinus p̄sbyter ecclesiae in Logenstein: natione teutonicus: uir in scri- opturis sanctis longa exercitatione doctus: in disciplinis saecularium litte rarum sufficienter instructus ob spem aeternae retributionis cum multis alijs sub Conrado imperatore tertio Hierosolymam profectus: cum faracenis na- uali procelio saepe dimicantibus: magna deuotione cōstantia ꝓ fide christi clarus effulsit. Reuersus aut̃ in patriā petente Cunone abbate mōtis sancti Disibodi tūc ordinis nr̄i: scripsit satis elegāti ẜmōe in modū epl̓ae siue libelli eādē pegrinatiōis Historiam: li. Epl̓aꝝ ad duersos: li. Et quaedam alia. ¶ Claruit sub Conrado imꝑatore tertio: Anno dn̄i Mill, C.XL. R Vpertus ep̄s Linconiēsis: uir in diuinis sscripturis eruditissimꝰ: in saecula- Qui bene praesūt p̄sbyteri. briū lrāꝝ disciplinis oīm suo tēpore doctoꝝ peritissimꝰ: ph̓us: astronomꝰ Intētio nrā in hoc tractatu. calculator inflignis: theologorū sui tēporis facile princeps: ingenio subti Cōputꝰ est scia numeratio. lis clarus eloquio: nomē suū multa uaria scribēdo cū gloria trāsmisit ad poste- ros. Joachim, abbot of the monastery of Fiore, of the Order of Saint Benedict, originally from Calabria: a man studious and practiced in the divine Scriptures, who, since he was regarded in his time as a prophet, also attempted to predict future events. But it would seem to me, speaking without prejudice to his own opinion or that of his followers, that he spoke more from conjectures drawn from Scripture than prophetically. For, to pass over the rest for the moment, he dreamed that the emperor Frederick III would be a future enemy of the Church; yet we all know that, right up to his death, he remained peaceful, subject to the Roman pontiff and faithful. He wrote a number of little works in clear language, in almost all of which he was accustomed to mingle, as if future and foreclosed, [unclear].

On Jeremiah the prophet: 1 book. On Daniel the prophet: 1 book. On the Gospel of John: 1 book. On the Apocalypse of John: 8 books. To Henry VI: 1 book. “You piously ask that something be explained.” On the Seven Seals: 1 book. “The first synagogical time.” The Psalter of Ten Strings: 2 books. The Book of Concord: [unclear] book(s). On the Fifteen Pontiffs: [unclear] book(s). On Future Times: [unclear] book(s). Letters to various persons: [unclear] book(s).

He also published many other works, especially against the Jews and other adversaries of the Catholic faith, which have not come into our hands. But the treatise which he wrote against Peter Lombard, bishop of Paris, was condemned in a general council, as is clear at the beginning of the Decretals, “We condemn.” He flourished under Henry VI, in the year of the Lord 1200.

Rui, of the fathers of Benedict, a Frenchman by nationality, a man practiced by constant study in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular disciplines, distinguished in talent and clear in eloquence, wrote several little works of his own genius, by which his name became known to posterity. Of these I have seen only the notable History of the deeds done in the Holy Land by Christians in the time of Urban II against the infidels: [unclear] book(s). “Among all the historiographers.”

I have seen nothing of the others. He flourished under Henry V, in the year of the Lord 1120.

Osuida, a noble woman born in Saxony, a nun in the monastery of Gandersheim, which is not far from Hildesheim, was distinguished by wondrous talent and learning. For the sacred virgins, exhorting them to chastity and continence, she wrote in Latin:

Six comedies. “The one hope of the world,” etc. A panegyric on the deeds of the Ottos, in hexameter verse. Also the Passion of Saint Dionysius in elegiac verse. Also, on Saint Gangolf and other saints, several works.

She also had knowledge of the Greek language. She was a contemporary of John the Englishman, who by her learning deserved the papacy.

Dudechinus, priest of the church in Langenstein, a German by nationality, a man learned in the holy Scriptures through long practice and sufficiently instructed in the disciplines of secular letters, for the hope of eternal reward set out with many others under the emperor Conrad III for Jerusalem. In frequent naval battles with the Saracens, he shone forth with great devotion and constancy for the faith of Christ. After he returned to his homeland, at the request of Cuno, abbot of Mount Saint Disibod, then of our order, he wrote, in sufficiently elegant discourse and in the form of an epistle or little book, the History of that same pilgrimage: [unclear] book(s). Letters to various persons: [unclear] book(s). And certain other works. He flourished under the emperor Conrad III, in the year of the Lord 1140.

Rupert, bishop of Lincoln, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and, in the disciplines of secular letters, the most skilled of all the learned men of his time; a philosopher, astronomer, and notable calculator; easily the foremost theologian of his time; subtle in talent and distinguished in eloquence, transmitted his name with glory to posterity by writing many and various works. Of his little works few have come into our hands. The following, however, are reported:

Summa of Theology: [unclear] book(s). On the Books of Dionysius: [unclear] book(s). A Summa which is called Numerical: [unclear] book(s). On the Celestial Sphere: [unclear] book(s). On Ecclesiastical Computation: [unclear] book(s). A beautiful Calendar: [unclear] book(s).

He published many other works besides, which have not come to my knowledge.

John, bishop of Chartres, a native of Salisbury, formerly clerk and disciple of blessed Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury: a man learned in the divine writings, nobly instructed in secular letters, subtle in talent, eloquent in speech, composed with fair grace, excellent in verse and prose, and no less religious

On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 60

nor venerable in learning. He wrote many excellent volumes, by which he made his name known to posterity, but few of them have come into our hands. I have read the distinguished work On the Trifles of Courtiers and Philosophers, which he wished to entitle Polycraticon, in eight books, “Most delightful, then, in many things.” Penitential, one book, “Since the mercies of the Lord are.” Life of Saint Thomas the Archbishop, one book. Letters to various persons, one book. He flourished under Frederick, the first emperor, in the year of the Lord 1140.

Petrus Blesensis, archdeacon of Bath, the close friend of the aforesaid bishop Iohannes Carnotensis, to whom he dictated some letters, was a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, and also exceptionally learned in secular letters; acute and forceful in talent, he knew how not to flatter the vices of princes and prelates, but to rebuke them. On account of his learning and the integrity of his life he was held in esteem among kings, princes, and bishops. He wrote many little works, among which these are reported: On Christian Friendship, one book, “Because true things have been diminished.” On Salutary Penance, one book, “You asked me that I might [write] something for you.” On Hastening the Passage, one book, “Who will give water to my head?” On the Quality of Penance, one book, “The excessive austerity of your severity.” “You are divided and your heart.” Against the Depraver, one book, “Your little exhortation.” Letters, 184 in number, in two books, “Most urgently elected, reverend father.” And On the Office of a Bishop, one book, “As often as I recall the words.” On the Danger of Prelates, one book, “I give thanks to your grace, since.” On the Life of Clerics of the Court, one book, “Asked by you, bishop.” Letters of Fortune, two books. He also wrote many other things. He flourished under Frederick, the first emperor, in the year of the Lord 1160.

Alexander, the third pope, a Sienese by origin, after Adrian IV sat in the chair of Peter for twenty-one years. He was a learned and energetic man, who endured many injuries from the emperor Frederick; while he resolutely crushed the three antipopes raised up by him against himself, and at last overcame the emperor himself. As a sign of his subjection, he trampled his neck with his foot, saying: “It is written: You shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you shall trample the lion and the dragon.” He wrote elegant letters to various persons, one book; and On Ecclesiastical Power, one book; and certain other things. He died in the times of Frederick, the first emperor, in the year of the Lord 1181, in the fourteenth indiction.

Crisolanus, archbishop of the church of Milan, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly learned in secular letters, distinguished in Greek and Latin eloquence, produced certain works of great authority, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. None of these has come into our hands. There is reported to be his Against the Greeks [unclear], one book; On the Holy Trinity, one book; letters, sermons, and other various treatises, which are unknown to me.

Hugo Eterianus, a Tuscan by nation, easily the most learned in the Scriptures among all learned men of his time, and exceptionally learned in secular letters, a most eloquent philosopher and rhetorician, perfectly instructed in Greek and Latin speech, whom all Greece admired as he wrote, most subtle in talent and second to none as a disputant. He wrote many excellent volumes both in Greek and in Latin, by which he transmitted his name with glory to posterity. Of these I have found only a certain work, brief indeed, but not to be despised, on the heresies which the Greeks heap upon the Latins, addressed to Cardinal Ardoinus, one book, “Your diligent prudence.” On the Immortal God, one book.

Concerning the rest I have found nothing.

He flourished in the times of Manuel, emperor of Constantinople, with whom he was of great authority, under Frederick, the first Roman Augustus, and Pope Alexander IV, in the year of the Lord 1160.

Christianus, archchancellor of Frederick, the first emperor, German by nation, a man most learned in secular literature, eloquent and industrious, whom the Italians admired when he spoke in his own time, also not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, whom Leo the Tuscan, notary of Manuel, emperor of the Greeks, extols with praises. He wrote certain excellent little works of his talent, of which there are extant:

The Deeds and Life of Frederick, the first emperor.

Of Various Letters, one book.

Certain Speeches, and other things.

He flourished under the same Frederick I, in the year of the Lord 1170.

Leo, Tuscan by nation, chief interpreter of the imperial letters under Manuel, prince of the Greeks, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, an excellent cultivator of secular letters, skilled in Greek and Latin speech. His office was to translate letters sent to the emperor, or to be sent to others, from one language into another. He published certain excellent volumes, and also transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these I have read only the distinguished work which he entitled:

On the Transgressions of the Greeks, two books: The intolerable [unclear] of the Greeks.

Against the Errors of the Greeks, one book.

He flourished at Constantinople in the times of Frederick, the first emperor, and Pope Alexander III, in the year of the Lord 1170.

John, archdeacon of a certain church of Horit[unclear], a man learned in the divine writings, not ignorant of secular letters, skilled in Greek and Latin speech, outstanding in talent, distinguished in eloquence. He wrote certain little works, not to be despised, for the edification of the faithful, by which he made his name known. Of these there is extant a distinguished and excellent work addressed to Stephen, a certain royal notary, against the Greeks:

On the Procession of the Holy Spirit, one book: Many things of the Greeks in rounded [unclear].

Also various letters.

But he is said to have written certain other things, which have not come into our hands.

Odefridus of Viterbo, priest, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular literature, outstanding in talent, distinguished, practiced in verse and prose. He wrote little works of reading not to be despised, by which he left the memory of himself to posterity. Of these there is extant a large volume addressed to Pope Urban III, in verse mixed with prose composition, on the beginning of the world, on the whole Old and New Testament, on the ages of the world, the times, deeds, and all histories, which he entitled:

Pantheon, eighteen books: On the beginning of the world.

Concerning the others I have seen nothing. He flourished under Frederick, the first emperor, and Henry his son, in the year of the Lord 1185.

Eckebertus, second abbot of the monastery of Saint Florin, of the order of the divine father Benedict, in the diocese of Trier, German by nation, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, no less venerable in conduct than in knowledge, was the brother of the blessed virgin Heliçabet, abbess of Schönau. He had formerly been a canon of the church of Bonn; called by his holy sister to Schönau, he first became a monk, and then was made abbot. He wrote little works of reading not to be despised, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among these I have found the following:

Against Heresies, one book: The prophets had long ago [unclear] times.

On the Beginning of the Gospel of John, one book: The mysteries of the divine word.

On the Magnificat, one book: The Spirit of the Lord is upon you, Mary.

On “The Angel Was Sent,” one book: The Gospel sermon [unclear].

For Virgins Consecrated to God.

On the Death of His Sister, one book: A word is to me for you, O king.

Meditations, one book.

On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 61

Sermons through the year, one book: “There shall be signs,” etc., the Advent of the Lord.

Praises of the Savior, one book. For he was a distinguished declaimer--

Letters to various persons, one book. --an outstanding declaimer, learned and eloquent, so much so that in a single disputation he overcame a certain heretic whom no one could refute.

He also published some other works, which have not come to my knowledge. For he was an outstanding declaimer, learned and eloquent, so much so that in a single disputation he overcame a certain heretic whom no one could refute. He flourished in the aforesaid monastery of Saint Florinus, which is called Schonau, in the diocese of Trier, under Emperor Frederick I, in the year 1160, and on account of his religion and learning he was held in esteem.

Elizabeth, nun and abbess of the sisters of the monastery of Schonau of the Order of Saint Benedict--for there are two monasteries, one of monks, the other of nuns, situated at the edge of the diocese of Trier, not far from the Rhine, in the Hircinian forest--sister of the above-mentioned Abbot Eckbert, was a virgin of most holy conduct, who had received many revelations from God and committed them to writing for the edification of posterity. Of these I have read the following:

The Way of God, a useful work, one book: “It happened at the beginning of the fifth.”

On the Eleven Thousand Virgins of Cologne, one book: “To you who [have] pious affections.”

Various Revelations, one book: “All who are going to read.”

To her brother Eckbert, one book: “You ask me, brother, for this.”

Letters to various persons, one book: “From the bishopric of Metz concerning the abbot.”

To Saint Hildegard, one book, and other similar works.

She died under Emperor Frederick I, in the year of the Lord 1165, in the thirteenth indiction, in the thirty-sixth year of her age, the twenty-fourth of her conversion, and the thirteenth of the vision of the heavenly splendor, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July. She was buried in the church of the monks of Saint Florinus, in the middle of the choir.

Hildegard, abbess of the monastery of Saint Rupert the Confessor opposite the town of Bingen, on the other side of the river Nahe, in the diocese of Mainz, of the Order of the divine father Benedict, German by nation, from the county of Sponheim, formerly a disciple of the blessed virgin Jutta, sister of Count Megenhard of Sponheim, our founder, was a virgin of most holy conduct, illumined from her childhood by divine revelations. Her life, confirmed by many miracles, spread the fragrance of her holiness into distant regions, so much so that the Roman pontiffs Eugenius III, Anastasius IV, Hadrian IV, and Alexander III, after the writings of her little work had been read publicly before all, approved them, and again strengthened her by letters so that she should persevere in the undertaking she had begun. Moreover, all that she wrote she learned from divine revelation. Among these works are the following:

On the Rule of Saint Benedict, one book: “And I, a poor little woman.”

Thirty Questions, one book: “Charity which with abstinence.”

Life of Saint Rupert the Confessor, one book: “For as in the true vision.”

Life of Saint Disibod the Bishop, one book: “In a mystical vision,” etc.

Fifty-eight Homilies on the Gospels, one book: “A certain man who [unclear].”

On the Sacrament of the Altar, one book: “In the vision which [unclear] of my soul.”

Scivias, a large volume, one book: “I, a poor little form.”

The Life of Merits, three books: “O crowds of men being born.”

Simple Medicine, one book: “And it happened in the sixth year after.”

Divine Works, one book: “He who was, who is, and who.”

To the People of Cologne, one book: “I, a poor little [unclear] form.”

An Exhortation of Secular Persons, one book: “O crowds of men being born.”

To her sisters: book 1. “O daughters, what footsteps of Christ...”

To the grey monks: book 2. “I, a poor little woman, in bed...”

Various poems: book 3. “Who are these who like clouds...”

To Saint Bernard: letters 4. “In the spirit of the mysteries of God...”

Letters to various persons, 135: book 5. “O gentle father, I, a poor little woman...”

She also wrote other things.

In all her little works Catholic doctrine shines forth, which either confirms faith or instructs morals; nor did she ever say or write anything that could be called into doubt. And although she was ignorant of the Latin tongue, nevertheless, by revelation of the Spirit of God, she dictated everything in Latin and fittingly, with notaries taking it down. We have seen many letters of Conrad III and Frederick I, emperors, and of the bishops of Mainz, Trier, Cologne, Bremen, Jerusalem, and almost innumerable others, who, moved by the fame of her sanctity and revelations from diverse regions of the world, commended themselves in writing to her prayers and sought answers to various questions. She died under Frederick, the first emperor, in the year of the Lord 1180, in the eighty-second year of her age, in the thirteenth indiction, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October.

[unclear] Hilbert, patriarch of Jerusalem, a learned and most holy man, who gave a rule to the Carmelite brothers while they were still dwelling in the Holy Land, which those same brothers, now established in Europe, profess everywhere after it had been modified and approved by the Apostolic See, at the request of Pope Innocent III described in lucid and truthful discourse:

The state of the Holy Land: book 1.

The rule of the Carmelites: book 1.

He flourished under Emperor Henry VI, in the year of the Lord 1190.

[unclear] Innocent, Pope III, by nation a Campanian, formerly called Lotharius, after Celestine, the third pontiff, presided over the Church for eighteen years: a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, since from his boyhood he had devoted himself to letters in the school of Paris, and in life he proved no less upright than learned. He left not a few little works of his talent. Of these, under the name of Lotharius the Levite, or also of Pope Innocent, the following are current:

On the utility of the human condition: books 3. “Why from the womb of the mother...”

On the seven penitential psalms: book 1. “There are chiefly three things in which...”

On the office of the Mass: book 1.

On the cloister of the soul: book 1.

The old decretals: book 1.

Several sermons: book 1.

Letters to various persons: book 1.

He flourished at the time of the discord that was between Philip, brother of Henry, and Otto, duke of Saxony, in the year of the Lord 1200.

[unclear] William of Auxerre, as they say a bishop, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, ascending the theological chair in the school of Paris, shone with renown for a long time, and among all the doctors of that time was celebrated with the greatest fame and reputation. He wrote a very distinguished and useful volume, or:

A Summa of Theology: book 1. “As the Apostle says: Faith...”

On the divine offices: book 1.

He is said to have written many other things also, which have not come to my knowledge.

[unclear] Cyril, priest and monk of Mount Carmel, and third prior general of the same order, by nation, as they say, a Greek, a holy man and illumined by a prophetic spirit, to whom almighty God is said to have disclosed his will by angelic ministry

On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 62, it is said: while he is honored with silver tablets written by the finger of God. He wrote, among other little works of his talent, to Abbot Joachim: On the Angelic Oracle, whose prologue begins thus: “To the house of the whole of divine wisdom.” The oracle itself begins thus, book one: “In the time of the years of Christ.” On the Progress of His Order, one book. Many letters to various persons. He flourished under Philip and Otto, in the year of the Lord 1200.

Helinandus, monk of Froidmont, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures through long practice, and nobly instructed in secular letters, sharp in intellect and eloquent in speech, appeared not least among the ecclesiastical doctors of his time because of the excellence of his learning and the integrity of his life. For he wrote several little works, by which he gave his name to immortality. Of these the following are reported: from the beginning of the world down to his own age, a great and notable volume of histories, forty-eight books; Lamentations and [unclear]; On the Restoration of the Fallen, one book; many sermons, one book; letters to various persons, one book; and many other things. He flourished under Henry VI, in the year of the Lord 1200.

Albertus, a monk of the Cistercian order and afterwards abbot of a certain monastery, a man studious in the divine Scriptures and exceptionally learned, subtle in intellect and clear in speech, after the death of the holy abbot Bernard wrote, where he had left off, namely from that place, “On my bed by night,” down to the end, forty-six subtle and most elegant sermons on the Song of Songs, one book. “Varied are the feelings of lovers.” And certain other things. He flourished under Henry VI, in the year of the Lord 1200.

Aelred, abbot of a certain monastery of the Cistercian order, a man exercised by constant study in the holy Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular philosophy, gentle in disposition, sweet in speech, outstanding in devotion. He wrote some little works for the benefit of his brothers, by which he both profited them and transmitted knowledge of his name to posterity. Among these there is extant a little work of great usefulness to religious men, filled with spiritual sayings, which he entitled The Mirror of Charity, one book, homily one: “When Jesus was twelve years old.” And other things which I have not seen. He flourished in the times of Henry VI, around the year of the Lord 1200.

Mauricius, bishop of Paris, very studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and nobly instructed in secular philosophy, inasmuch as before his episcopate he taught theology gloriously for many years at Paris; subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech; in delivering sermons to the people he was of excellent study. He is reported to have composed certain distinguished little works, by which he made his name known to posterity. Among these are reported, throughout the cycle of the whole year, both for Sundays and for feast days: Sermons to the People, two books; On the Care of Souls, to Priests, one book. But the other things which he is said to have written have not come to my knowledge. He flourished in the times of Henry VI, in the year of the Lord 1190.

Papias, a Lombard by nation, a man most learned in secular letters, the most famous grammarian of all in his time, fully [unclear] in Greek and Latin speech

well instructed; also not moderately practiced in the divine Scriptures. He wrote, in a twofold style in both literatures, certain distinguished little works, of which a few have come to my knowledge.

On the order of speaking, one book. [unclear] I found in this book. On a word of the Latin language, one book. Letters to various persons, one book. Of the rest I have found nothing.

He flourished in the times of Henry VI, in the year of the Lord 1200.

John Beleth, once a distinguished theologian of the Paris school, learned in the divine Scriptures and sufficiently instructed in secular philosophy, ready in talent, scholastic in speech, not unknown among the doctors of his time, brought his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity by writing and disputing. For he wrote a not useless:

Summa on the divine offices, one book. In the primitive Church. Also various sermons, one book.

He is said to have written besides not a few other things, but they have not come to my knowledge.

Theoderic, abbot of the Order of Saint Benedict, a German by nation, a man devoted to the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, no less distinguished in conduct than in knowledge, is reported to have composed some little works. Of these I have seen only, addressed to certain abbots:

Life of Saint Hildegard, four books. In the Roman commonwealth. And certain letters.

He flourished under Henry VI, in the year of the Lord 1200.

Werner, otherwise Irnerius, an illustrious and notable man, professor and most renowned interpreter of civil law and an excellent cultivator of the other humane letters, who was deservedly called the lamp of the law, because he was the first to expound civil law with glosses and, without example before him, gave to others an example of illuminating the law. And from this time professors of both laws always flourished in abundance and began to explain the volumes of his instruction down to the present day. He taught in both, at Rome as well as at Bologna, for a long time; there he had very many and excellent disciples, who by their learning spread the fame and glory of their master. His glosses and outstanding monuments on the laws are extant, very well known among professors of this field.

He flourished in the times of Henry VI, in the year 1200.

Peter, abbot of Cluny, of the Order of Saint Benedict, a man learned in the divine Scriptures by constant practice, gentle in talent, sweet and composed in speech, and sufficiently capable of persuasion, devout and praiseworthy in conduct, and a distinguished zealot for regular observance, making his name known to posterity by writing, composed certain devout little works for the benefit of readers. Of these the following are reported:

Revelations of many, one book. He received the letters of your affection. On eremitic life, one book. Letters to various persons, one book.

He also published some other works, which have not yet come to my knowledge.

Peter Cantor of Paris, and afterward, as they report, a bishop, a man most deeply learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in secular philosophy, presided gloriously for many years over the theological school at Paris and instructed many excellent disciples. He also wrote certain outstanding little works, of which I remember that a few have come into our hands. The volume entitled:

The Abbreviated Word, one book. He made the abbreviated word. Another book of distinctions, one book. Abel is called the beginning of the Church. Grammar of the theologians, one book. Various sermons, one book.

On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 63

On certain miracles, one book.

On the sacraments also, three books: "The people went about and gathered."

He flourished in the times of Henry VI, in the year of the Lord 1200.

Pileus of Modena, professor of both laws and a very celebrated interpreter, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, renowned in learning and cautious in counsel, held in the highest esteem among the older jurists, by writing and teaching various things in that faculty transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Of his little works there is found a certain notable and not to be despised summa, which he entitled:

On the order of trials, one book: "When the name of Christ has been invoked, the matter..."

But concerning the rest that he wrote, nothing has come to my knowledge.

Johannes Bosianus, by origin a Cremonese, a very famous expounder of the laws, teacher of Azo of Bologna, the most renowned jurisconsult, a man of great learning and reputation, who appeared first among the expositors of law, and by his example gave many both the spirit and the form of study. He is reported to have written in that faculty certain distinguished little works, by which he gave his name to immortality. Of these there survives a brief summa on the Pandects, which is entitled:

Ventosa, one book.

Lecture on the Code, nine books.

And certain other things. He flourished under Henry VI, in the year of the Lord 1200.

Stephen the Englishman, once the ornament and rector of the school of Paris, studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and in Aristotelian philosophy second to none in his time, taught theology gloriously for many years, and was the first to begin to expound sacred Scripture inwardly and morally. From this arose the custom that masters of theology should open the divine books more clearly to their disciples in the schools by their lectures. This Stephen, as I have learned, wrote the following little works:

On the five books of Moses, five books.

On Joshua, one book.

On the book of Judges also, one book.

On Kings also, three books.

On the twelve minor prophets, twelve books.

He published besides many other things, which have not yet come to my knowledge.

He flourished around the times of the rule of King Henry VI, but the fifth emperor crowned by the pope, in the year of the Lord 1200.

Bagorotus, distinguished professor of both laws and very celebrated interpreter, not ignorant also of other secular letters, whose authority among the old jurists was not small, on account of his excellent talent for teaching, and by his zeal for writing also made his name known to posterity. Of his little works there survives a notable summa which he entitled:

Of cavillations, one book: "Since it becomes dangerous for me."

On the order of trials, one book: "By the prayers and insistence."

He is said to have written several other things besides, but they have not come to my knowledge.

Placentinus, an Italian by nation, cultivator and very celebrated expounder of both laws, attained great glory at Montpellier by teaching and writing; he once held a place among the chief doctors among the professors of this art, because of certain highly commended volumes which he composed. Among these, among other things, are said to be:

A summa of trials, one book: "When I was at Mantua."

On the Code also, nine books. I have found nothing concerning the others. He flourished in the times of Henry VI, in the year of the Lord 1200.

Rofredus, by origin a Beneventan, a very renowned doctor in both laws, subtle in intellect, composed in speech after the scholastic manner, sufficiently capable, through long practice, of resolving doubts and questions of law, wrote in that faculty for students little works not to be despised, by which he consecrated his name and reputation to immortality. Yet of these we have been able to find only a few, which we have also set down: a useful volume containing:

Questions of civil law, one book: "If I were to consider my talent."

[…] Questions of canon law: 1 book. ["On all actions."] A Summa of law: 1 book. Whatever more he published has not as yet come to my knowledge.

Peter, archbishop of Sens, erudite by continual study in the divine Scriptures, rich in the reading of the ancients, and moreover nobly learned in secular letters, subtle in talent, renowned in eloquence: he wrote little works of no small usefulness, by which he both cultivated his own talent and prepared material for the edification of others. He wrote very subtly, with the sentences of the fathers appended: On all the Epistles of Paul: 14 books. Also various sermons: book. He diligently expounded also various books of the Bible, and is said to have written other various useful treatises, which have not come to my knowledge.

[Az]o, an Italian by nation, drawing the origin of [his] life from the city of Bologna, once hearer and disciple of John Bassiani of Cremona, a most learned man; a most famous interpreter of the civil law, a fountain of laws, an abundance of words, a lamp of law, who by his learning, erudition, [and] knowledge easily excels all the jurists who preceded him; he published many little works pertaining to the civil law, by which he acquired immortal praise [and] glory: A notable Summa of law: 1 book. On the Old Digest: 24 books. On the Code also: 9 books. Besides, he composed excellent apparatus on the laws, appended additions to several summas, and wrote various [things] which are not unknown to learned jurists. He flourished in the times of Frederick II, emperor, in the year 1230. And he left after him many distinguished disciples.

Giles de Fuscariis, a citizen of Bologna, a man most learned in canon law, nobly erudite as much in the imperial laws as in the other disciplines of humanity, subtle in talent, renowned in eloquence, a doctor of great authority among the ancient professors of this faculty. He wrote certain illustrious volumes in that discipline, of which I have seen only: On the order of judgments: 5 books. ["In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, I, Giles…"] On the office of the Notary: 1 book. ["[illegible]…"] Questions of law. The rest which he composed have as yet by no means come into our hands.

Francis, prince [and] founder of the order of Minors, an Italian by nation, sprung from Assisi, a city of Italy, a man of most holy conversation, a most ardent follower of evangelical poverty, who by word [and] example turned many from iniquity [and] directed [them] into the way of catholic justice; he was so great a lover of Christ that, in contempt of the world, he scarcely had an equal in any transitory consolation. In whose order many most learned men have thereafter become illustrious [the remainder of the page is illegible].

ON ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS. Fol. 64.

William, monk of the monastery of the divine martyr Dionysius [Saint-Denis] at Paris, of the order of Saint Benedict, a Gaul by nation, a man skilled by continual study in the divine Scriptures, and excellently learned in the disciplines of secular letters, renowned in talent and eloquence, and a distinguished knower of [his] time, transmitted his name to the notice of posterity by writing and teaching various [things]. Of these there is extant: A volume of Histories: 3 books. And several letters to various [persons]: 1 book. He is reported to have published commentaries on the divine Scriptures, which I have not yet seen.

[Jacobus] de Vitriaco, bishop of Acre, and afterwards cardinal of the most holy Roman Church, bishop of Tusculum: a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not unacquainted with secular letters; distinguished in morals and life. In declaiming sermons to the people he was of excellent talent, and, gloriously preaching the cross against the Albigensian heretics, he marked many of the faithful against them by apostolic authority. He wrote little works not unworthy of reading, by which he made his name known to posterity:

The Oriental History, 1 book. The Life of Mary of Oignies, 3 books. Against the Saracens, 1 book. On the Holy Women of Liège, 1 book. Letters to Various Persons, 1 book.

In addition he composed some other things which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under the emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1220.

Bonaguida of Arezzo, a man most learned in both laws in his time, of great authority among the old [teachers?] of this faculty, subtle in talent and clear in speech. He wrote, for the use of students of law, certain distinguished volumes, by which he made himself both useful to those then living and known to those to come. Of these there is extant a notable summa, which he entitled:

Introduction to Advocates, 2 books. “Since the office of advocacy ...” The Pearl of Law, 1 book. “After the discovery of knowledge ...” Declarations of Various Cases.

But he is also said to have composed certain other things, which have not come to my knowledge.

Petrus de Vineis, German by nation, secretary and chancellor of the emperor Frederick II: a learned and eloquent man, but especially reprehensible in this, that, adhering to the same Frederick and favoring him, he foolishly barked against the Roman Church. By him at last he was worthily rewarded, when in certain matters he had offended him, being deprived of the light together with his eyes. He wrote certain little works of his talent; of these I have found only:

Letters [explona?] of the Emperor, 6 books. “The pontiffs gathered ...” On Imperial Power, 1 book.

He flourished in the times of the same Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1230.

Antonius, called of Padua, but Spanish by nation, born from the city of Lisbon, of the Order of Minors and a disciple of blessed Francis: a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, since before his entry into the order he taught theology gloriously for a long time at Toulouse, Bologna, and Padua, and left distinguished disciples after him. He was of such holiness that he shone with many miracles both living and dead. He was an exceedingly excellent preacher, so that the supreme pontiff saw fit to call him the Ark of the Covenant, and Saint Francis was accustomed to call him his bishop. Among the other little works of his talent he wrote very elegant and most ardent:

Sermons for the Season, 2 books. “There shall be signs,” etc.; “Isaiah says ...” Certain Sermons on the Saints, 1 book.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1230. And because of the frequency of his miracles after death he was immediately enrolled by Pope Gregory IX, together with the saints of the Lord Dominic and Elizabeth, landgravine of Thuringia, in the catalogue of the saints.

Jordan, of the order of Preachers—after Saint Dominic, as they say, master general—a Teuton by nation, a man exercised and sufficiently erudite in the divine Scriptures, a distinguished preacher of the word of God, and venerable no less for sanctity than for knowledge; by his example and mellifluous teaching he instructed many unto piety. He is reported to have written some little works, the reading of which is judged not useless to preachers and devout brothers. Of these they report, [composed] from [his] office of priorate, to the brothers of his order: Several exhortatory letters: 1 book. Sermons to the people: 1 book. On the institution of the order: 1 book. He flourished under Frederick II, emperor, at the same time as also blessed Dominic, in the year of the Lord 1220.

Ubertus de Bobio, professor of both laws and a most sagacious interpreter, subtle in talent and luminous in scholastic eloquence, who among the ancient professors of this science was held among the principal doctors, transmitted his name with glory to the notice of posterity by teaching and writing, giving to the rest an example of learning and an aid to progress. For he wrote a notable Summa which he entitled: On the order of judgments: 1 book. ["Because the piety of the paternal name…"] Questions and determinations: And not a few others, which, however, have by no means come into our hands.

Bernard Dorna, a Provençal by nation, once hearer and disciple of Azo of Bologna, a most renowned man, a most learned professor and interpreter of both laws, who, provoked by the example of his most erudite teacher, accommodating himself wholly to letters, wrote various little works, by which he dedicated his name to immortality. Of these there is extant a volume On the conceptions of [legal] bills: A distinguished [work]: 1 book. And others which I have not seen. He flourished in the times of Frederick II, emperor, in the year 1240.

Accursius, an Italian by nation, sprung from the city of Florence, once hearer and disciple of Azo, a man most skilled in both laws, and not meanly learned in the other disciplines of secular letters, subtle in talent and renowned in eloquence—how great his authority is at this time among the professors of law, no one even moderately learned is ignorant. He wrote many illustrious little works, and was the first to gloss the whole civil law: On the Old Digest: 24 books. On the New Digest: 12 books. On the Inforciatum Digest: 13 books. On the Code: 11 books. On the Institutes: 3 books. He published, besides, not a few others, which are most well known to the students of law. He flourished under Frederick II, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1240.

Ubertus de Bonacurso, an Italian by nation, a man skilled in both laws and not ignorant of secular philosophy, prompt in talent and open in eloquence, who among the ancient expounders of law was of no obscure repute. He composed in that faculty certain illustrious little works, of which I do not recall that any has come into our hands. But there is reported [as] his: On the preludes of cases: 1 book. ["When, by imperial mandate…"] And certain [things] on judgments. But we believe that both these and his other works are not unknown to skilled jurists.

O Dofredus beneuentanus: Açonis bononiēsis auditor: Iacobi baldewini postmodum praeceptor: uir in utroqꝫ iure peritissimus: ingenio subtilis: clarus eloquio: qui multos insignes post se discipulos reliquit: propter do- ctrinam eruditionem tum iuris: tum aliarum littterarum humanitatis: in magna auctoritate habebat' apud ueteres: Cuius multa feruntur opuscula: quibus nomē suum notificauit posteritati: De libelloꝝ formatione: li. j Post q̄ opus notarie. De ordine iudiciario: li. j Quēadmodū christi fauēte De arte notariatus: li. j Et alia quae non uidī. Claruit sub Frederico imperatore secundo: Anno dn̄i Mill', CC.XXX. I Ohannes de Blanosco: natione burgundus: uir in utroqꝫ Iure doctissimꝰ: in phoꝝ saeculariū praeceptis sufficienter eruditus: ingenio acer prom- ptus: Scripsit aperto sermone professoribꝰ huiusce facultatis non spernē- da opuscula: quibus fama noīs sui tunc praesentibus post futuris longe lateqꝫ innoutit. Equibus extat uolumen magnae utilitatis quod praenotauit: De actionibus aduocatorū: li. J Ego Iohannes de Blano. Et uariae quaestiones. Caetera autem quae composuit: ad noticiam meā minime uenerūt. P Ohannes nomine natione teutonicus: ex ciuitate Friburgensi oriūdus: epūs Bossinensis in Vngaria: ordinis praedicatorum: uir in diuinis scriptu- rts multum exercitatꝰ doctus: in iure saeculari philosophia egregie pe- ritus: qui propter eruditionem uitae sanctitatem ex ordine ad episcopatū assū- ptus fuerat: quem postea deserens ad ordinē suum reuersus est: post Raymun- dum generalis magister ordinis constitutus: multa bona fecit. Scripsit notabilē Sũmam confessorum: li. v Qm̃ dubiorū noua quotī. k

On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 65.

Sermons on the saints: 2 books.

He also published many other things which have not come to my knowledge. He wrote the said sermons for the cycle of the year: first, indeed, brief ones, briefly expounding the Gospel and Apostolic readings. Afterwards, however, he published other sermons, both on Sundays and on feast days, so very lengthy, adducing so many testimonies of the Scriptures, that they can scarcely be committed to memory; yet these have now in part lost their value as newer ones have come upon the scene.

Raymundus de Pennaforte, a Catalan by nation, or a provincial, of the Order of Preachers, the third master general, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, ready in talent, distinguished for knowledge of canon law, made his name immortal by writing various works; by his little works he bound the Church to himself as a perpetual debtor, if I may so speak. For at the command of Pope Gregory IX he compiled:

The Decretals of law: 5 books. “The peaceful king, by pious mercy...”

A Summa on cases: 3 books. “Since, as Jerome says, the second...”

The Constitutions of his order: 1 book.

And certain other things.

He flourished under Emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1230.

Albertus Galioti, by homeland a Parmesan, professor and famous interpreter of canon laws, subtle in talent, cautious in counsel, scholastic in speech, who on account of his learning and experience in affairs was held among the foremost doctors by the old jurists, wrote certain little works in law not to be despised, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity with immortal praise. Of these there is extant a summa:

The Pearl of Questions: 1 book. “Since I, Albertus Galioti...”

And Declarations of Judgments: 1 book.

And certain other diverse works, unknown to us, are possessed by various people.

Odofredus of Benevento, hearer of Azo of Bologna, afterwards teacher of Jacobus Baldewinus, a man most skilled in both laws, subtle in talent, clear in speech, who left many distinguished pupils after him, on account of his learning and erudition both in law and in other humane letters was held in great authority among the ancients. Many little works of his are reported, by which he made his name known to posterity:

On the Formation of Libelli: 1 book. “After the work of notarial practice...”

On Judicial Procedure: 1 book. “In the manner in which, Christ favoring...”

On the Art of the Notariate: 1 book.

And other things which I have not seen.

He flourished under Emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1230.

Johannes de Blanosco, a Burgundian by nation, a man most learned in both laws, sufficiently instructed in the precepts of secular philosophers, sharp and ready in talent, wrote in clear language little works not to be spurned by professors of this faculty; by these the fame of his name became known far and wide, both to those then present and to those who would come afterwards. Of these there is extant a volume of great usefulness, which he entitled:

On the Actions of Advocates: 1 book. “I, Johannes de Blano...”

And various questions.

The rest, however, which he composed, have by no means come to my knowledge.

Johannes by name, a German by nation, born from the city of Freiburg, bishop of Bosnia in Hungary, of the Order of Preachers, a man much practiced and learned in the divine Scriptures, excellently skilled in secular law and philosophy, who on account of his erudition and the holiness of his life had been taken from the order to the episcopate; afterwards abandoning it, he returned to his order. Appointed master general of the order after Raymundus, he did many good things. He wrote a notable

Summa for Confessors: 5 books. “Since the new [unclear] of doubts...”

I Ohannes de deo:iuris utriusque professoꝛ enucleator eximius:atque in di-

And certain other things.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1250. He was buried in his own convent at Strasbourg, once, as they say, resplendent with many miracles.

Innocent, Pope IV, formerly called Sinibaldus, an Italian by nation, from the city of Genoa, sat in the pontificate after Celestine IV for eleven years. He was a man most learned in Holy Scripture and in law, a lover of religious, who held the general Council of Lyon, in which, with the consent of the fathers, he deposed Frederick from the empire; he made many statutes for the utility of the Church. He likewise wrote certain distinguished little works, on account of whose publication he is worthily numbered among ecclesiastical writers, and is to be transmitted with them to the knowledge of posterity.

Against Peter de Vinea.

On ecclesiastical power, one book.

An apparatus on the Decretals, five books. It begins: In Ezekiel [unclear].

The form of life of the Order of Sisters.

The rule of the Poor Clares, one book.

Authentics also, one book.

Letters to various persons, one book.

And certain other things.

He flourished under Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1250.

Rolandinus de Romanciis, a professor of both laws, a very celebrated interpreter, and nobly learned in secular philosophy, who among the old jurists was not among the least. He wrote in that faculty certain distinguished little works, by which he transmits his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Of these I have found only a summa: On the order of crimes, one book. It begins: A little book.

Determinations of questions.

The other works which he is said to have composed have not come to my knowledge.

Bernard, a priest of Compostela, a familiar of Pope Innocent IV, wrote in law certain distinguished little works, which in these times are held in great authority among jurists. Of them I have been able to find a few, namely, a notable apparatus:

On the Decretals, five books. In the beginning of this book [unclear]. The peace-making king, with pious [unclear].

Cases of the Decretals, five books.

Of the rest I have seen nothing.

He flourished under Emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1250.

Guido de Suzaria, a doctor most expert in law, sufficiently instructed in the other disciplines of secular philosophy, subtle and ready in intellect, cautious in counsel, whose authority was great among the old experts in these matters. He is said to have fashioned certain distinguished little works in law, among which there is extant a notable summa which he entitled:

On the actions of cases, one book. On the ordering of cases.

Various declarations also.

And very many other things, which have not yet come into our hands.

Bartholomaeus Brixianus, a professor of canon law, a most learned interpreter, and learned in the other branches of secular letters, subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech, wrote various distinguished little works both in law and on other matters, by which he gave his name to immortality. Of these the following are reported:

A repertory of the Decretum, three books. Since, with the old men supporting [unclear].

Disputations on the Decretals, five books.

Chronicle of Italy, one book.

Letters to various persons, one book.

And certain other things.

He flourished under Emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1240.

On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 66

...sufficiently learned in the disciplines of philosophy; subtle in intellect; scholastic in speech; who among the ancients was of great authority. He wrote many and various little works in both laws, by which the memory of his name came to the knowledge of many. Of these, a few have come to my knowledge. For I have found only the following:

A Summa of Cavillations, seven books: “For the honor of the supreme Trinity.” Another, entitled Judgment, four books: “At our beginning [unclear].” A table of the Decree, two books: “The book of the decrees of distinctions.” A table of the Decretals, one book: “For those wishing readily.” A concordance of the Decree and the Decretals, one book: “A treatise concerning constitutions.” Various questions.

He taught, however, in the city of Bologna, where he composed the aforesaid works and others.

Hugo of Barcelona, of the Order of Preachers, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Sabina of the most holy Roman Church: a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, who before entering the order had been a master of sacred theology, and had many distinguished disciples. He wrote several excellent little works, by which he consecrated his name to immortality. Shining no less in conduct and religion than in knowledge, he remained the same in dignity as he had been before. Of his books the following are listed:

On Genesis, one book. On Exodus, one book. On Leviticus, one book. On Numbers, one book. On Deuteronomy, one book. On Joshua, one book. On Judges, one book. On the book of Ruth, one book. On Kings, four books. On Chronicles, two books. On Ezra and Nehemiah, three books. On Tobit, one book. On Judith, one book. On Esther, one book. On the book of Job, one book. On the Psalter, one book. On Proverbs, one book. On the Song of Songs, one book. On the book of Wisdom, one book. On Ecclesiasticus, one book. On Isaiah the prophet, one book. On Jeremiah, three books. On Ezekiel, one book. On Daniel, one book. On the twelve minor prophets, twelve books. On the books of Maccabees, two books. On the Gospel of Matthew, one book. On the Gospel of Mark, one book. On the Epistles of the Apostle Paul, thirteen books. On the Acts of the Apostles, one book. On the Catholic Epistles, seven books.

U Incentius gallus natione burgundus: ordinis praedicatorũ dictus Beluaçẽ/ sis :uir in diuinis scripturis studiosus exercitatꝰ: ac ueterũ lectiõe diues: ingenio subtilis: ẜmone compositꝰ: tm̃ lr̃is studiũ adhibuit: ut nullis unqͣ laboribus: uiġilijs uel occupationibus ab earũ cultura potuerit euocari: quin semꝑ aut legeret: scriberet uel praedicaret.Tantus itaqƺ fuit ut post se necdũ habuerit parem:Sardua quae scripsit opuscule collecta: aequa lance cũ caeteris ponderemꝰ.Nam petente sumptꝰ ministrante rege Francoꝝ:g rãde admirabile opus speculorũ de om̃i:ut ita dixerim:re scibili in multis uolumini bꝰ maximis laboribꝰ comportauit:quod ita praenotauit atqƺ distinxit: Speculum historiale: li.xxxij Deꝰ est substãtia incorpo. Speculum Naturale: li.xxxiiij Qm multitudo libroꝵ. Speculũ Morale: li.iij In oṁbꝰ tuis memorare. Speculum Doctrinale. li.xiij Qm multitudo libꝛoꝝ. Book

On the Apocalypse of John: one book. A Summa on cases: one book. He also composed some other works besides, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under Frederick, the second emperor of that name, in the year of the Lord 1240.

Jacobus Balduini, formerly a pupil of Odofredus Beneventanus, a most distinguished man, a professor of civil law and an outstanding interpreter, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, eminent in counsel and action, wrote in that faculty certain excellent little works, by which he transmitted his name with praise to the knowledge of posterity. Of these the following are reported:

On the Code: twelve books. On the Old Digest: twenty-four books. On the New Digest: twelve books. On the Infortiatum: thirteen books. And certain other works. He flourished under Frederick, the second emperor of that name, in the year of the Lord 1240.

David, of the Order, as they say, of the Minors, German by nation, a man practiced in the divine Scriptures, distinguished in life and conduct, was of excellent talent in delivering sermons to the people. He wrote certain little works in plain style, whose reading is not to be despised by devout brothers. Of these the following are extant. To novices:

On the ordering of the outer man: one book. Religious progress, [seven?] [unclear]. On the ordering of the inner man: one book. My conferences which [unclear]. Sermons on the season: one book. Sermons on the saints: one book. And certain other works. He flourished not long after blessed Francis. He is buried at Augsburg.

Humbertus, of the Order of Preachers the fifth master general, from Vienne, a learned and excellent declaimer, evangelical in life, pure in conscience, eminent in action, sweet in eloquence and fit for persuasion, drew Hugo, once his teacher in sacred theology, to the Order. He wrote certain devout little works, by which his name came to the knowledge of posterity. Of these the following are reported:

On the Rule of Saint Augustine: one book. When I was thinking about the sermon. Summa for preachers: three books. Every man is to be exhorted. Deeds of the brothers of the Order of Preachers: five books. On the three substantial elements of religious life: one book. To the sons of grace, co-heirs. Letters to various persons: one book. And certain other works. He flourished while the empire was vacant, in the year of the Lord 1250.

Vincentius, a Gaul, Burgundian by nation, of the Order of Preachers, called Belvacensis, a man studious and practiced in the divine Scriptures and rich in the reading of the ancients, subtle in intellect, composed in speech, applied himself so much to the study of letters that he could never be called away from their cultivation by any labors, vigils, or occupations, without always either reading, writing, or preaching. He was therefore so great that after him he has not yet had an equal, if we weigh with an even balance the arduous little works which he wrote, gathered together with the others. For, at the request and with the expense supplied by the king of the Franks, he brought together with very great labors, in many very large volumes, the great and admirable work of the Mirrors concerning every, so to speak, knowable thing; and he entitled and divided it as follows:

The Historical Mirror: thirty-two books. God is an incorporeal substance. The Natural Mirror: thirty-four books. Since the multitude of books. The Moral Mirror: three books. In all your affairs remember. The Doctrinal Mirror: thirteen books. Since the multitude of books. Also On the grace of God: eight books. The book of the generation [unclear]. On the praises of Saint Mary: one book. If with prophetic mouth God commands.
