On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 67

On the praises of Saint John the Evangelist, one book: “Blessed John the Evangelist.”

On the instruction of children, one book: “If you have sons, instruct them.”

A consolation on the dead, one book: “First, therefore, observe.”

Letters to various persons, one book.

He also published several other things, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under Frederick, the second emperor, in the year of the Lord 1240.

Alexander of Hales, English by nation, of the Order of Minors, teacher of Cardinal Eustace, was a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, and second to none in his time in secular philosophy; subtle in intellect, a true [unclear] disciple of philosophy. He entered the order of the poor of Christ, which he wondrously adorned by his learning and holiness. At the command of Pope Innocent IV he wrote a distinguished work, divided into four volumes and usefully comprising many things, which he entitled:

A Summa of Theology, four books: “As Boethius says.”

A Declaration of the Rule of the Minors, one book: “To the reverend father in Christ.”

The rest of his works I have not seen.

It is said, however, that he expounded both the Old and the New Testament, and discussed many things subtly concerning the concord of divine and human law, and composed various other things, which have not come into our hands. He flourished under Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1240.

John of La Rochelle, of the Order of Friars Minor, master of sacred theology at Paris, learned in the divine Scriptures and magnificently taught in Aristotelian philosophy, who subscribed his name together with Alexander of Hales in the Declaration of the Rule of the Minors to the minister general, published certain excellent little works, by which he transmitted the fame of his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among these the following are reported:

On the Sentences, four books.

Summa of virtues and vices, one book.

Also On the Soul, one book.

He flourished under Frederick, the second emperor, in the year of the Lord 1250.

Henry, archbishop of Embrun, cardinal of the most holy Roman Church, commonly called Hostiensis, was a man most expert in both laws; because of the excellence of his natural ability and learning he was held in esteem by Pope Alexander IV. He wrote certain distinguished little works, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these I have seen only the distinguished work known to everyone:

On the titles of the Decretals, five books: “Alpha and O, one in essence.”

Also a concise Summa, one book.

The rest that he composed have as yet by no means come to my knowledge.

He flourished while the empire was vacant, in the year of the Lord 1250.

Walter, bishop of Poitiers, of the Order of Friars Minor, was a man learned in the divine Scriptures, nobly taught in the disciplines of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech; in delivering sermons to the people he was of excellent industry. He wrote certain works not to be despised; of these the following are reported. For at the command of Pope Alexander IV he arranged in style, very usefully, throughout the cycle of the year:

Sermons, two books.

On the Sentences, four books.

Quodlibets, one book: “It is asked in what way virtue.”

He flourished while the empire was vacant, in the year of the Lord 1250.

Walter, bishop of Maguelone, born from Lille, a town of Flanders, was a man exercised by long study in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, outstanding in intellect and clear in eloquence, who in his time, because of his learning and erudition, was of great reputation. At the request of the provost of the clergy of the church of Lille, he wrote:

On the Psalter, one book.

And certain letters.

He also published some other works, which have by no means come to our knowledge.

Alexander, called de Villa Dei, a native of Dol, of the order, as they say, of the Friars Minor, a man certainly trained in every respect, a grammarian, philosopher, astronomer, and distinguished calculator, wrote not a few little works both in verse and in prose, by which he transmitted his name to the memory of posterity. Of these I have so far found only the following: a volume written in leonine verse on grammar, whose use today in boys’ schools is constant; I do not know whether it is so useful, because of the deficiency of weaker age and the sloth of teachers. He entitled this very work:

Doctrinale for boys, three books: “I prepare to write for little clerics.”

On the ecclesiastical computus, one book: “Who now at the end of times.”

On the sphere, one book.

On the art of numbering, one book.

He is also said to have written many other things: sermons, letters, and various treatises, which have by no means yet come into our hands.

He flourished with great religion and learning under Frederick II, in the year 1240.

Eustachius, also called Bonaventura, born at Bagnoregio, minister general of the order of Friars Minor, and thereafter bishop of Albano and cardinal of the holy Roman Church, formerly hearer and disciple of Alexander of Hales, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in secular philosophy: his teacher Alexander, contemplating the gift of his intellect by nature and the purity of his life, used to say: “In brother Bonaventure Adam does not seem to have sinned.” He wrote many, profound, and most devout little works, in which, bringing forth burning words, he kindles the reader’s affection in the love of Christ no less than he illuminates the intellect with holy teachings. For he easily surpasses all the doctors of his time in the usefulness of his works, if you attend to the spirit of divine love and Christian devotion speaking in him. He is profound, not wordy; subtle, not curious; eloquent, not vain; bringing forth flaming, not puffed-up, words. Hence he is read more safely, understood more easily by one who loves, frequented more usefully, retained more sweetly and fruitfully. Many put forth learning; many preach devotion; few, by writing books, have taught both. But Bonaventure both surpassed many and few, since his learning instructs devotion, and devotion instructs learning. Therefore, if you wish to be both learned and devout, be intent upon his little works, which are:

On the Sentences, four books: “Explored by profound rivers.”

Breviloquium, seven books: “I bend my knees to.”

Soliloquium, one book: “Tell me, I ask, O man, if after.”

Itinerary of the mind into God, one book: “In the beginning, the first principle.”

The tree of life, one book: “I am fastened with Christ to the cross.”

Exhortatory work to a brother, one book: “Since, my beloved brother.”

On the reduction of the arts, etc., one book: “Every best gift, etc.”

Rule of conscience, that is, a small good, one book: “Behold, I have described it to you in threefold.”

Itinerary of the mind into itself, one book: “An evil thing occurs to consider.”

Compendium of the Scriptures, one book: “In the beginning of my conversion.”

On the instruction of novices, one book: “The question is about poverty.”

Centiloquium, four books: “Since according to venerable men.”

Pharetra, or scintillarium, one book: “First of all you must have.”

On the poverty of Christ against William, one book: [unclear].

On the five feasts of the infancy of Christ, one book: [unclear].

To Duchess Blanche, one book: [unclear].

On the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, one book: [unclear].

On the excellence of the Eucharist, one book: [unclear].

On the six-winged seraph, one book: [unclear].

On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 68

The notable work Illuminations: one book. On the Three Threes of Sins: one book. On the Seven Degrees of Contemplation: one book. On the Advancement of Religious: one book. On the Ten Commandments: one book. Apology for the Poor: one book. On the Lord’s Prayer: one book. The Legend of Saint Francis: one book. Constitutions of His Order: one book. On Genesis, seven visions: one book. On the Gospel of John: one book. On the Gospel of Luke: one book. On Three Questions: one book. On the Sandals of the Apostles: one book. On the Passion of the Lord: one book. Sermons through the Year: one book. Several letters to various persons. He also published some other works besides, which have not come to my knowledge. He died while the empire was vacant, under Pope Gregory X, at the Council of Lyons, in the year of the Lord 1283, indiction 1. He was buried in the cathedral church of Lyons. At length, because of his holiness and miracles, he was canonized in our own days by Pope Sixtus IV, under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1482, indiction 15.

Philip, chancellor of Paris, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in secular philosophy, since he was a famous master of sacred letters, presided gloriously for a long time over the theological school at Paris; there he splendidly instructed disciples by lecturing and the people by preaching. He wrote:

Two or three elegant sermons on each of the Psalms: one book. A Summa of Theology: one book. He also published many other works, which have by no means come to our knowledge.

Albert, bishop of Regensburg, of the Order of Friars Preachers, German by nation, Swabian by homeland, born at Lauingen, a man very studious and learned in divine writings, and second to none in secular philosophy in his own time; subtle in intellect, scholastic in eloquence, devout and most holy in life and conduct. Because of his doctrine and learning he was called “the Great.” He taught sacred letters and Aristotelian philosophy for many years, first at Paris, afterward at Cologne, where, among others, he had Thomas of Aquino as an outstanding disciple. Then, having been raised to the episcopate of the church of Regensburg, after he had governed it for some years he left it; for love of salutary study he returned to his convent at Cologne, where he persevered in teaching and writing until the end of his life. He wrote many, almost countless, little works, of which the following are reported:

A Summa of Theology: four books. “Your knowledge has become wonderful.” On the Sentences: four books. On the Four Coeval Things: one book. On Man: one book. On the Good: one book. He commented on all the books of Aristotle. He composed many [unclear], which have not come to my knowledge. He died under Emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1280, in the eighth indiction, in the eightieth year of his age. He was buried in the middle of the choir of his convent at Cologne. And after him there did not arise a man like him, who was so learned, instructed, and experienced in all letters, sciences, and matters. But whoever accuses him of necromancy does injury to a man beloved of God.

Simon of Tournai, priest, learned in the divine Scriptures, subtly taught in secular philosophy, a most acute dialectician and most skilled in all the liberal arts, was made master of the theological school and taught for many years in the school of Paris, where he instructed very many hearers. But while he followed Aristotle too much, he is found to have erred in certain matters. He wrote certain little works of his own talent, of which the following are reported: His own account of the Sentences. Various Questions: one book. On the Symbol of Athanasius: one book. He also published some other works, which have not come to my knowledge.

Thomas of Aquino, once a hearer and disciple in the convent at Cologne, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly taught in secular letters, subtle in intellect and clear in speech, distinguished in life and conduct, easily obtained first place among all the doctors of his time. Like another Augustine, he gave himself wholly to the study of the Scriptures, dwelling day and night in love and practice of it; he wrote so many and such great volumes that among the moderns he has few equals either in number or in usefulness: On the Sentences: four books. “I, wisdom, poured out rivers.” Summa of Theology: three books. “Because of Catholic truth.” Against the Gentiles: three books. “Truth shall be meditated by the throat.” A little book [unclear] “from the excellence” [unclear]. he commented on the books of Aristotle and Porphyry. He also published many other works, both on the divine Scriptures and on secular philosophy, which have by no means come into our hands.

He died under Emperor [Rudolf?], in the year of the Lord 1274, in the second indiction. And he was canonized by Pope John XXII.

Thomas of Cantimpre, by nation a Brabantine, of the Order of Friars Preachers, formerly, as they say, a disciple of Albert the Great, a devout man and outstandingly learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, ready in intellect, scholastic in speech, is said to have written certain excellent volumes, by which he brought his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among them there is extant a work on the mystical bees, which he entitled:

The Universal Good, one book. To the reverend father in Christ, Brother H.

On the Nature of Things, one book.

The Life of Saint Christina, one book.

And other works which I have not seen.

He flourished under Emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1270. And there are those who write that he had knowledge of the Greek language, and that he also translated the books of Aristotle which were then in use in the schools.

Alfonso, king of Castile and Leon, a philosopher and astronomer, most excellent among all men of his time, subtle in intellect and clear in speech, and a distinguished lover and cultivator of letters: after, following the long vacancy of the Roman Empire, he had been elected king of the Romans against Richard, brother of the king of England, and since he was a good and prudent man, when Richard had died in the fifteenth year after his election, with a view to peace, in the presence of Pope Gregory X, he voluntarily withdrew and completely renounced every right which he had had in his election. He wrote very useful and elegant works:

Tables in astronomy, one book.

Letters to various persons, one book.

He flourished during the time when the empire was vacant, in the year of the Lord 1270.

Peter, of the Order of Friars Preachers, by nation a Frenchman, and provincial prior of the same religious order in France, a man learned in the divine Scriptures through long study and not ignorant of secular philosophy, acute in intellect and ready in speech, was suited for delivering sermons to the people. Hence, for the benefit of readers, he composed, for the cycle of the year, works not to be despised:

Sermons on the Season, one book.

Sermons also on the Saints, one book.

But he is said to have written a number of other things as well, which have not come to my knowledge.

Consecrated canonically under the name of the fifth [unclear], he sat in the supreme pontificate for only five months; he was certainly a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in Aristotelian philosophy, who taught theology excellently for many years and acquired great praise for his learning. He wrote many excellent little works, by which he made his name known both to those then present and to those who would come afterward. Among them are extant:

On the Sentences, four books. Do you know the order of heaven?

On all the Epistles of Paul, fourteen books. The principles of things must be investigated.

Also on the Psalms, one book.

On the Song of Songs, one book.

He also wrote, as is said, several other lectures on the Bible, which I have not yet seen.

He flourished in the pontificate under Emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1275.

John of Ascoli, from Ascoli, of the Order of Friars Minor, after Saint Bonaventure minister general, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and an outstanding preacher of sermons, was sent to Constantinople by Pope Gregory X; by his exhortations he brought the Greeks back to obedience to the Roman Church, and persuaded them to come with him to the Council of Lyon. For the edification of the faithful he wrote sermons on the season, not to be despised, one book.

On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 71

Sermons on the saints: one book. Several letters to various persons: one book. And certain other things. He flourished while the empire was vacant, in the year of the Lord 1270.

Upertus of Rusia, of the Order of Friars Minor, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular literature, since indeed he taught theology excellently for many years and left after him many distinguished disciples. He wrote some excellent little works, by which he transmitted his name to posterity. Among these there is extant, addressed to Haymo the Englishman, minister general of his order, likewise a most learned man, a declaration On the rule of Saint Francis: one book. Also on the Sentences: one book. Various sermons: one book. And certain other things. He flourished while the empire was vacant, in the year of the Lord 1270.

Ulricus of Strasbourg, a German by nation, of the Order of Friars Preachers, once a hearer and disciple of Albert the Great, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, subtle in talent, scholastic in speech, composed little works of reading not to be despised, by which he became known both to present and to future generations. Among these there are extant: On the Sentences: one book. A Summa of theology: one book. Also On the Soul: one book. And many other things. He flourished under the emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1280.

Haymo, an Englishman by nation, minister general of the Order of Friars Minor, a man trained by long study in the holy Scriptures, since, having obtained the magisterial chair of the theological faculty, he instructed many disciples in it; at the command of Pope Alexander IV he corrected and rubricated the Roman Breviary. He is said, among other things, to have written concisely: On the Sentences: one book. And certain sermons: one book. And certain other things.

Otto, bishop of Freising in Bavaria in Germany, and, as some write, nephew of the emperor Frederick I, a German by nation, whom Pope Pius II, citing him in a certain oration, commends; a man learned in the divine Scriptures and by no means poorly taught in secular letters, subtle in talent and clear in eloquence. He wrote certain little works of reading not to be despised, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Among these there is extant an outstanding work, to be honored with every praise: Of Histories: one book.

Petrus Hispanus, a Portuguese, bishop of Tusculum and cardinal of the sacrosanct Roman Church, and finally supreme pontiff after Hadrian V, a man very learned in medicines and magnificently taught in secular philosophy, sat in the pontificate only eight months. He wrote little works in medicine not to be despised; among them the following are reported: The Treasury of the Poor: one book. On Problems: one book. Canons of Medicine: one book. Letters also to various persons: one book. And certain other things.

He flourished in the pontificate under the name of John the Twenty-first, in the times of Emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1275.

William, a citizen of Piacenza, a learned doctor of the art of medicine and not ignorant of other humane letters, who, hired at a public salary at Verona, held a school in that faculty for many years and instructed several excellent pupils. He wrote, for those who profess this science, little works not to be despised, by which he made his name known both to those present and to those to come. Among these there survives a notable volume which he wished to be entitled:

On the Whole of Medicine, four books. Also On Surgery, one book. Of the rest I have found nothing.

He flourished under Emperor Arnolph, in the year of the Lord 1270.

William, bishop of Paris, by homeland an Auvergnat, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, clear in speech, and venerable no less in conduct than in learning, composed not a few works of his erudition, by which, showing himself a learned and devout master, he rendered the memory of his name immortal. Of these, the following are reported: a notable volume entitled

On the Holy Trinity, one book. On the First Principle, one book. On the Sacraments, one book. Why God Became Man, one book. I shall set down four more. Summa of Vices, one book. In the order of divine wisdom. On Faith and Laws, one book. On Human Souls, one book. On Good and Evil, six books. On the Universe, six books. The second table after [unclear]. On the Profession of Novices, one book. After, by the help of God, thus far. On the Gift of Knowledge, one book. On the Works of Virtues, one book. On the Thirty Remedies for Temptations, one book. Against Plurality of Benefices, one book. On the Cloister of the Soul, one book. In sacred and signifying things. On Divine Rhetoric, one book. On Penitence, one book. On the Song of Songs, one book. On Demons, one book. On the Gospel of Matthew, one book. Various Sermons, one book. Letters to Various Persons, one book. He also published some other works which have by no means come to my knowledge.

He flourished under Frederick, the second emperor, in the year of the Lord 1230.

John Valensis, otherwise called Galensis, English by nation, of the Order of Friars Minor, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, who for a long time taught theology gloriously in the school of Paris, was of such erudition and eloquence that he was called the tree of life. He wrote many distinguished little works, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. But few of them have come into our hands. For I found a notable volume which is very [unclear] for preachers of the word

148

On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 72

I judge it necessary and useful; most people call it the Common Discourse, because it contains something concerning every state; but he himself entitled it Summa of Conferences, seven books: “When the teacher or preacher ...” On the Sentences, four books: “Since for every business there is a time ...” On the Ordering of Life, one book: “Abstinence is a good thing in food ...” Handful of Flowers, one book. On the Apocalypse of John, one book. Various sermons, one book. On Various Subjects, fifteen books. He flourished in the times of Emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1270.

William Durand, bishop of Mende, once a hearer and disciple of Henry of Susa, whom they call the Speculator, a doctor most skilled in law and very zealous for ecclesiastical observance, subtle in intellect and clear in speech, wrote to Ottobono, cardinal of Saint Adrian, later supreme pontiff Adrian V, an excellent work divided into three volumes, which he entitled Speculum of Law, four books: “To the reverend father in Christ ...” Rationale of Divine Offices, eight books: “Whatever things in ecclesiastical offices ...” Repertory of Law, one book: “By the rust of the first-formed man ...” And certain other works. He flourished under Emperor Rudolf. And he completed his work, the Rationale of Divine Offices, as he himself testifies, in the year of the Lord 1286.

Jacobus de Belviso, a most distinguished doctor of both laws and a cautious interpreter, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, profound in counsel and knowledge, and not ignorant of secular philosophy, is said to have written certain excellent little works in law, by which he transmitted his name to the memory of posterity. Of these I have not yet been able to see any. His works are said to include: On the Authentics, one book. On the Use of Fiefs, one book. Additions on the Novels, one book. And various disputations. And many other works. He flourished under Emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1270.

William of Lyon, of the Order of Friars Preachers, as they report bishop of the same church, a man much learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, sweet in intellect and subtle in speech, not affected, yet well arranged, was quite outstanding in delivering sermons to the people. He is said to have written some little works, by which he magnificently instructed both those then present and those who would come afterward. Among these are reported: On the Sentences, four books: “Since, concerning individual useful studies ...” Summa of Virtues, five books: “About to speak of individual vices ...” Sermons to the People, one book. He is also said to have written many other works, which have not come to my knowledge.

[Brother?] John Scotus, of the same order, a man sufficiently learned in the divine Scriptures and in Aristotelian philosophy by long study

149

Egidius de Roma:ordinis fratrum heremitarum sancti Augustini prior ge¬ neralis: ac deinde Bituricenfis archiepiscopus : beati Thomae aquinatis quondam auditor: uir in diuinis scriptris eruditissimus: in philofo¬ phia aristotelica nulli suo tempore secundus: ingenio subtilis: sermone schola¬ fticus: uita conuersatione deuotus: Scripsit multa pene infinita opuscula :

[unclear] very skilled: he wrote certain not-to-be-despised little works of his own talent, by which he made himself known to posterity. Of these there are extant:

On the Sentences, four books: “Since, as blessed Augustine bears witness ...”

Of the rest I have seen nothing.

He flourished in the time of the emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1270.

Erardus, monk of the monastery of Saint Quentin in Insula, a man devoted to the holy Scriptures, skilled through constant exercise, and sufficiently instructed in secular letters, quick in talent and distinguished in eloquence, wrote certain little works of no contemptible reading, by which he made his name known to present and future generations. Among these is said to be a history of the translation of the crown and of a portion of the Lord’s cross, relics which Louis, king of France, obtained from the emperor of Constantinople and brought to Paris. He also wrote, concerning blessed Elizabeth the landgravine:

Miracles Performed after Her Death, one book.

Chanted Responsories concerning the Same, one book.

And certain other things.

He flourished under the emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1270, and composed various little works in both kinds of letters.

[unclear], learned by long use and exercise, and sufficiently skilled in secular philosophy according to the custom of that time, distinguished in talent, scholastic in speech, composed various little works on the Scriptures, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among these the following are reported:

On the Sentences, four books.

Correctorium of the Works of Thomas, one book.

Additions on Bonaventure, one book.

And certain other things.

He flourished under the emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1280.

Richard, archbishop of Reims in Gaul, of the order of the Friars Minor, a man excellently learned in the holy Scriptures, inferior to none of the doctors of his time in delivering sermons to the people, subtle in talent, is said to have written many distinguished volumes, by which he made himself useful to those then present and known to those to come; but I do not recall that any of them has come into our hands. They report his:

Sermons on the Temporal Cycle, one book.

And also Sermons on the Saints, one book.

He flourished under the emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1270.

[unclear] of Mount Carmel, a Gaul by nation, a man learned in divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, distinguished in talent and eloquence, venerable no less in way of life than in learning, published several little works of great usefulness, by which he transmitted the memory of his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among these the following are reported:

A certain little work, not unprofitable for spiritual persons, which he entitled:

Decretals of Religious, one book.

On the Sentences, four books.

On the Rule of His Order, one book.

Chronicle of His Order, one book.

And many other things.

He flourished under the emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1280.

Egidius of Rome, of the order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, prior general, and afterwards archbishop of Bourges, once a hearer of blessed Thomas Aquinas, a man most learned in divine Scriptures, second to none in his time in Aristotelian philosophy, subtle in talent, scholastic in speech, devout in life and conduct, wrote many, almost countless, little works:

150

On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 73

Of these few have come into our hands. The following works of his are reported:

On the Hexaemeron: two books. On the Song of Songs: [one] book. On the Epistles of Paul: fourteen books. “May your own sound in your ears.” On the Sentences: three books. “For it is the brightness of the eternal light.” Exposition of the First Decretal: one book. “Firmly we believe,” and similarly. On the Rule of Princes: one book. “From the royal and most sacred.” Many Quodlibeta: one book. “Questions proposed.” On the Office of the Mass: one book. On the Possible Intellect: one book. Praises of Divine Wisdom: one book. On Divine Wisdom in the Blessed: one book. On the Subject of Theology: one book. On Good Fortune: one book. On the Body of Christ: one book. On the Measure of Angels: one book. On the Knowledge of Angels: one book. On the Dead: one book. A Distinction of the Articles of Faith: one book. On the Degrees of Forms: one book. On Predestination: one book. A Theory concerning Being and Essence: one book. On Generation and Corruption: one book. On Original Sin: one book. On the Formation of the Human Body: two books. On Ecclesiastical Power: two books. “Of theological truth.” On Prison: one book. “It will not please him when.” A Compendium of Theology: five books. “It was asked concerning God.” On the Renunciation of the Pope: one book. “The soul, as the philosopher bears witness.” Against the Corrupter of Thomas: one book. “I am dust.” Various Sermons: two books. “In which are set forth,” etc. On all the books of Aristotle. Notable Letters. And not a few other things.

He flourished under Emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1280.

Goffredus of Trani, subdeacon of the Roman Church and, as they report, chaplain of the supreme pontiff, a man nobly learned in canon law and secular philosophy, outstanding in talent and renowned for eloquence, who in his time was considered not the least among the doctors of this faculty, wrote little works of reading not to be scorned, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these there survives a notable summa, sufficiently widespread:

On the Titles of the Decretals: five books. “The diversity of glosses [unclear].” Various Questions: one book. Other works which he is said to have composed have by no means come to our knowledge.

Guido de Baysio, archdeacon of Bologna, a man very skilled in both laws, sharp in talent and renowned for eloquence, whose authority among professors of this science has remained great down to the present day, wrote many distinguished volumes, by which he rendered the memory of his name, so to speak, immortal. Of these only a few have so far come to my knowledge. For I have found only the following. A very large and notable volume which he entitled the Rosarium:

“To the reverend father in Christ.” On the Decree: two books. On the Decretals: five books.

151

Book

He flourished under the emperor Adolf, in the year of the Lord 1290.

[Thaddaeus?], a Florentine by nation, a most skilled doctor of the medical art, who taught that science excellently at Bologna for certain years, hired at a public salary, and, gathering an almost incredible treasure, acquired it by the great reputation of his experience. For when he was summoned by some prince, he wished to have no less than fifty gold pieces as his daily fee. Once summoned by Pope Honorius IV, he was unwilling to come until one hundred gold pieces a day were assigned to him; when he had been cured of a very serious illness, he gave him ten thousand gold pieces. He wrote:

On the Aphorisms of Hippocrates, one book; On the Prognostics of the same, one book; On his work On Acute Diseases, one book; On Galen’s Tegni, one book; On the Isagoge of Johannitius, one book; On preserving health, one book; Various counsels, one book; and certain other things.

He flourished under the emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1280. And at length he died at Bologna, an octogenarian.

John of Parma, from the territory of Bologna, minister general of the Order of Friars Minor, a man learned in the divine scriptures, devout in life and conduct, and an outstanding lover of holy poverty; from the Parisian school, where he had lectured on the Sentences, [unclear] he is said to have written many and various treatises, by which his name has come down to our memory. Of these I have found only:

On the Sentences, three books; On the conduct of religious, two books.

He flourished while the empire was vacant, in the year of the Lord 1260.

John Christophorus, of the Order of Friars Preachers, trained in the scriptures by long and continual study, and nobly learned in secular philosophy, ready in intellect and scholastic in speech, is said to have produced many little works on the holy scriptures; their publication, useful to those then present, made him known to those to come. For over a long time he publicly expounded the divine writings by lecturing on them, and explained them with subtle understanding. From his commentaries the following volumes are reported, namely:

On the Gospel of Matthew, one book; On Mark, one book; On Luke, one book; On John, one book; On all the epistles of Paul, fourteen books; and many others.

He flourished while the empire was vacant, in the year of the Lord 1260.

[Unclear], father [unclear] of the scriptures, subtle and vehement in intellect, and sufficiently suited to debating and solving their difficult questions, is said to have written certain excellent little works for the instruction of his students, by which he made his name known. Among these there are extant:

On the Sentences, three books; also Quodlibets, one book.

He flourished under the emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1270.

Henry of Ghent, archdeacon of Tournai, a German by nation, a man most learned in the divine scriptures among all the doctors of his time, and very subtle in Aristotelian philosophy, was of such reputation and authority in the school of Paris that he was called the Solemn Doctor throughout the whole Christian world. He was

On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 74

... subtle in intellect and most acute in scholastic disputations, as his distinguished little works testify. Of these I have found only the following at present: Summa of Theology, one book; On the Sentences, three books; On Virginity, one book; a compiler For Sacred Virgins; Quodlibets, two books; On Penance, one book; On Metaphysics, fourteen books; On the Books of the Physics, eight books. He composed many other things indeed, but they have not come to my knowledge. He died under Emperor Adolf, in the year of the Lord 1293, in the sixth indiction, on the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul. He was buried at Tournai in the church of Mary, the holy Mother of God.

Ugolinus, patriarch of Constantinople, of the order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, a man practiced by long study in the divine Scriptures and sufficiently learned, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, distinguished in conduct and life, is said to have written certain excellent little works, not to be despised in reading, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among these the following are said to be more important than the others: On the Sentences, three books; Quodlibets, one book; On the Difference of Idioms, one book; Sermons on the Season, one book; Sermons on the Saints, one book. He flourished under Emperor Adolf, in the year of the Lord 1290.

[Arlotus?], minister general of the order of the Friars Minor, Tuscan by birth, a man excellently learned in the divine Scriptures and sufficiently instructed in secular philosophy, a subtle dialectician and a very acute disputant, who won great praise for his learning by writing various works; in delivering sermons to the people he was of excellent talent. He is said to have brought together the New and Old Testament into one: Concordances, one book; Various Sermons, one book; and certain other things. He flourished in the times of Emperor Adolf, in the year of the Lord 1290.

Jacobus, bishop of Genoa, of the order of the Friars Preachers, a man practiced in the divine Scriptures, who because of his frequent citations of them is called a whirlpool; ready in intellect and clear in eloquence, he was sufficiently suited to delivering sermons to the people. He wrote not a few little works for the benefit of readers, by which he made his name known; of these a few have come to my knowledge, and I have set them down below. A volume of great size on the life and deeds of many saints, which he entitled The Golden Legend or Mirror of Saints, but which is now commonly called the Legend or Lombard History, one book, “The whole time of the present...” Mariale on Saint Mary, one book, “As I was thinking, the days of old...” Chronicle of the Genoese, one book, “Sacred Scripture, divinely...” On the Little Works of Saint Augustine, one book; Sermons on the Season, one book; Sermons on the Saints, one book, “He followed in his footsteps...” Lenten Sermons, one book. He also published some other things besides, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished in the times of Emperor Adolf, in the year of the Lord 1290.

Lucas, of the order of the Friars Minor, Italian by birth, originating from Padua, a man practiced by constant study in the holy Scriptures, an outstanding preacher of the divine word; in

153
genio clarus: & apertus eloquio: non minus opere q̃ sermone uiam dei populos docuit in ueritate: & multorũ corda ad amorẽ christi spũsancto cooꝑante conuer tit.Scripsit nõ cõtemnēdos quos ad populũ habuit: Sermones de tempore: li.j Sermones de sanƈtis: li.iij Alia quoqƺ nōnulla scripsisse dicitur: quae ad manus nostras nō uenerunt. Onradus de Halberstat:natiõe teutonicus:ordinis fratrꝰ praedicatoꝝ:uir tam in diuinis scripturis q̃ in foecularibꝰ lr̃s nobiliter doctus: philosophus theologus nō futulis:quippe ꝗ in ea facultate publice legens:multos do cuerit doctrinae suae laudẽ ingente acquisierit. Scripsit quaedã ĩ utraqƺ sciẽtia nō spernenda opuscula:quibus ad memoria posteritatis nomẽ suũ deductũ est. Sed pauca eorũ mihi innotuerunt.Reperi em̃ tantũ: Summā studentiū: li.iij Hoc opusculũ in tres. De Triuio quoqƺ. li.j In tribus beneplacitũ est. Lecturam in lob: li.j Vsqƺ in tempus sustinebit. Hic etiã fert cõcordantias totius Bibliae noui ue teris testamẽti primus ordinasse. Alchardus de mediauilla natiõe Anglieꝰ: ordinis fratrũ minorũ:uir in diui/ nis scripturis eruditissimꝰ: tam ĩ philosophia q̃ in iure canonico egregie doctus:ingenio clarus:sermone scholasticus:in quaestionibꝰ dubijs scri pturarũ soluẽdis subtilis promptus. Super dif.decreti: li.j Patres nr̃i om̃es sub nube. distinguished in talent and clear in eloquence; no less by deed than by speech he taught the peoples the way of God in truth, and, with the Holy Spirit cooperating, converted the hearts of many to the love of Christ. He wrote sermons, not to be despised, which he delivered to the people:

Sermons on the season: one book. Sermons on the saints: three books. He is also said to have written some other works, which have not come into our hands.

Conrad of Halberstadt, a German by nation, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a man nobly learned both in divine Scriptures and in secular letters, a philosopher and no mean theologian, since, lecturing publicly in that faculty, he taught many and acquired great praise for his learning. He wrote certain treatises in both sciences, not to be scorned, by which his name has been brought down to the memory of posterity. But few of them have become known to me. For I have found only:

Summa studentium: three books. This little work into three. On the Trivium also: one book. In three it has pleased. A reading on Job: one book. It will endure until the time. Sermons also: one book.

He is also said to have written commentaries on several books of the Bible, which, however, have not yet come into our hands. This man is also reported to have been the first to arrange concordances of the whole Bible, of the New and Old Testament.

Alchardus of Middletown, English by nation, of the Order of Friars Minor, a man most learned in divine Scriptures, excellently instructed both in philosophy and in canon law, distinguished in talent, scholastic in speech, subtle and ready in resolving doubtful questions of the Scriptures. He is said to have written many excellent volumes, by which he transmitted his name with glory to posterity. Of these I have found only the following:

On the Sentences: three books. He brought hidden things into the light. On the distinctions of the Decretum: one book. All our fathers under the cloud. On the order of judgments: one book. On the four Gospels: three books. On the Epistles of Paul: fourteen books.

It is said, moreover, that he published commentaries and readings on several books of sacred Scripture, but they have not come into our hands. He flourished in the times of Emperor Adolf and Pope Nicholas IV, in the year of the Lord's nativity 1290.

Nicholas of Bibra, German by nation, a man nobly learned in secular letters, not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, an outstanding philosopher and poet, who in his time, being held in esteem at Erfurt, acquired great glory for his learning. He wrote not a few treatises both in verse and also in prose, by which he also made his name known to posterity. Of these I have seen only the work whose title is hidden, which he composed at Erfurt in verse and in prose:

On Avoiding Evil: one book. Hearer and reader of the song. Letters to various persons: one book.

He flourished at Erfurt under Emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1290.

John of Paris, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a theologian, very learned in the holy Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, since in both sciences, having ascended the magisterial chair in the university of Paris, he taught publicly for a long time and left not a few disciples. He is said to have written certain excellent treatises, by which he made himself useful to those then present and later known to those to come. Of these I have found only one work, not to be scorned:

On the Sentences: four books.

Concerning the rest I have found nothing.

He flourished under Emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1280.

154

On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 75

Nicholas the Frenchman, of the Order of the Brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, the seventh prior general, a learned and holy man, after he had governed his order vigorously, as far as he was able, for nearly twenty years, resigned his office for love of Christ and returned to the quiet of the hermitage, where he persevered in holy conduct until death. Among other things he wrote a mournful work lamenting the condition of his order, after the brothers had been expelled from the Holy Land, which he entitled:

The Fiery Arrow, 1 book.

He also wrote other works. He flourished in the time of Emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1270.

Matthew of Aquasparta, of the Order of Friars Minor, the twelfth minister general, and afterwards bishop of Porto and cardinal of the holy Roman Church, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and, according to the custom of this time, magnificently learned in secular philosophy, composed certain distinguished little works of excellent talent, by which he made his name known far and wide. Of these the following are extant:

On the Sentences, 4 books. Inventory of Sentences, 1 book. On the Epistle to the Romans, 1 book. Several sermons, 1 book. And certain other works.

He flourished in the time of Emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1290.

William Peraldus, French by nation, of the Order of Preachers, a man devoted to and learned in the holy Scriptures, and also in secular letters, especially sufficiently distinguished in Aristotelian philosophy, ready in intellect and scholastic in eloquence, was of excellent industry in delivering sermons to the people. He published several well-ordered volumes in both faculties, by which he made his name known not only to those then present, but also to future generations. Of these the following are extant:

Summa of Virtues and Vices, 2 books. On the Instruction of Religious, 1 book. Sermons for the season, 1 book. Sermons on the saints, 1 book. And many other works which have not yet come to my knowledge.

Garcias, Spanish by nation, a man very practiced in both laws, subtle in intellect, ready and cautious in counsel, and acute in resolving questions of cases, was held in esteem in his time among the professors of this faculty; by teaching and writing he spread his name abroad. For he is said to have written several little works both on the laws and on canon law, which have not come into our hands. Of his there are extant:

On the Decretals, 5 books. And several works on the laws.

He flourished in the time of Emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1290.

Pope Nicholas IV, of the Order of Friars Minor, previously called Jerome, Picene by nation, born from the city of Ascoli, sat after Honorius IV in the chair of Peter for four years. He was a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and not meanly learned in secular letters, subtle in intellect and clear in eloquence, and no less venerable in life and goodness than in learning. He wrote a sufficiently distinguished work:

On the Sentences, 4 books. And certain sermons.

He is also said to have published useful commentaries on several books of the Bible. He died at Rome, while the empire was vacant after Rudolf’s death, in the year of the Lord 1291, in the fourth indiction.

Pope Boniface VIII, Campanian by nation, previously called Benedict, sat after the renunciation of Celestine V in the chair of Peter for eight years, [unclear] months

155
nouem: uir quidem doctus sed nimis arrogans et ambitiosus: qui pontificatū qui/ bus modis acquisierit chronographi non tacuerunt. Hic cū esset in iure peritissimus uideretqꝫ nouas causarum uarietates in foro contentioso: quae per decreta les non possent determinari: quotidie emergere cōposuit per tres eruditissimos in iure uiros nouas constitutiones quas appellari uoluit: Sextum decretaliū. li.j Sacrosanctae Romanae ec. Epistolas plures ad diuersos: li.j Mortitur sub Alberto imperatore: Anno domini Millesimo.CCC.III. Indictione prima.De quo fuerat ante prophetatum:Intrauit ut uulpis:uixit ut leo:mortuus est ut canis et c̃. g Vilhelmus mandagoti archidiaconus Nemasensis et postmodum Ebre- dunensis archiepiscopus:ac sacrosanctae ecclesiae Romanae demũ cardina lis:uir in utroqꝫ iure peritissimus:unus eorū qui iustu Bonifacij papae octa/ ui Sextum decretalium Codicem ediderunt: sicut in eiufdem uoluminis prin/ cipio patet:scripsit in ea facultate non spernenda opuscula: quibus nomen suum immortalitati consecrauit. Equibus ego tantum uidi opus insigne quod scri/ psit cum adhuc in ecclesia Nemasensi archidiaconatus teneret officiū: ad Berengarium Beterensis ecclesiae succentorem:postea episcopum: De electione praelatorū: li.j Quia dū electiōes imminent. Expositionē eiusdem: li.j Cū illius nō sim auctorita. De caeteris nihil uidi. Claruit sub Alberto imperatore: Anno domini Millefimo.CCC. b Erengarius Beterensis ecclesiae succētor:& postea episcopus : ac tandem sacrosanctae ecclesiae cardinalis:ad quem praefatus Guilhelmus mandagoti:cum adhuc ambo essent in minoribus constituti: librū de ele/ ctionibus praelatorum composuit: alter ex his qui Bonifacio octauo praecipiente librum sextum decretaliū comportarunt: uir in eadem facultate iuridica doctissimus:composuit ad eundem Guilhelmum tunc archidiacenum Nemasensem:insigne opus super summā Hostiensis secundum ordinem alphabeti:quod cum eiufdem fit quasi elucidarium summe praenotauit: Oculum: li.j De sententia excōmunicationis:li.j Alia etiam plura scripsisse dicitur: quae ad noticiam meam non uenerunt. Claruit sub Alberto imperatore: Anno domini Millefino.CCC. R ichardus de fenis Romanae ecclesiae uicecancellarius : & postea diaconus cardinalis tituli sancti Eustachij:doctor utriusqꝫ iuris:omniū laude suo tem pore celeberrimus:tertius eorum qui sextum decretalium iustu Bonifacĳ papae octaui cōportarunt:cuius nomen in principio eiusdem uoluminis expressū continetur.Fertur nōnulla in iure scripsisse opuscula:sed nihil eorū ad manus no/ stras meminipuenisse.Lector meꝰ studiosus illa inquirat. Claruit sub Alberto imperatore:Anno domini Millefimo .CCC. d Inus mugelanus utriusque iuris ꝓfessor enucleator insignis:ingenio subtilis:& in disputādis endandisque dubijs quaestionibus iuris ualde prom ptus acutus:qui docendo scribendo magnam sibi apud omnes Italiae doctores gloriā acquisiuit.Edidit in sua facultate multa praeclara opuscula.De qui bus feruntur subiecta.Super decretaliū: Super Codice: li.ix Super.ff.ueteri: li.xxiiij

nine: a man indeed learned, but excessively arrogant and ambitious; the chroniclers have not been silent about by what means he acquired the pontificate. Since he was very skilled in law and saw that new varieties of cases in the contentious court, which could not be determined by the decretals, were emerging daily, he composed, through three men most learned in law, new constitutions which he wished to be called:

The Sixth of the Decretals. One book, Of the holy Roman Church. Several letters to various persons, one book.

He died under the emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1303, in the first indiction. Of him it had previously been prophesied: “He entered like a fox, lived like a lion, died like a dog,” etc.

William Mandagot, archdeacon of Nimes and afterward archbishop of Embrun, and finally cardinal of the holy Roman Church, a man very skilled in both laws, one of those who, by order of Pope Boniface VIII, published the code of the Sixth of the Decretals, as is clear at the beginning of that volume, wrote in that faculty works not to be despised, by which he consecrated his name to immortality. Of these I have seen only the distinguished work which he wrote, while he still held the office of archdeacon in the church of Nimes, to Berengar, succentor of the church of Beziers and later bishop:

On the Election of Prelates, one book, “Because when elections are impending.” Exposition of the Same, one book, “Since I am not of that authority.”

Of the rest I have seen nothing.

He flourished under the emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

Berengar, succentor of the church of Beziers and later bishop, and at length cardinal of the holy Church, to whom the aforementioned William Mandagot, while both were still established in lesser offices, composed the book On the Elections of Prelates, was another of those who, at the command of Boniface VIII, compiled the sixth book of the decretals. A man most learned in the same legal faculty, he composed for the same William, then archdeacon of Nimes, a distinguished work on the Summa of Hostiensis according to alphabetical order; since it is, as it were, an elucidation of the same Summa, he entitled it:

The Eye, one book. On the Sentence of Excommunication, one book.

He is also said to have written many other things, which have not come to my knowledge.

He flourished under the emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

Richard de Senis, vice-chancellor of the Roman Church and afterward cardinal deacon of the title of Saint Eustachius, doctor of both laws, in his time very celebrated by the praise of all, was the third of those who compiled the Sixth of the Decretals by order of Pope Boniface VIII; his name is expressly contained at the beginning of that volume. He is reported to have written some small works in law, but I do not recall that any of them has come into our hands. Let my studious reader seek them out. He flourished under the emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

Dinus Mugelanus, professor of both laws, a distinguished elucidator, subtle in intellect, and very ready and acute in disputing and resolving doubtful questions of law, who by teaching and writing acquired great glory for himself among all the doctors of Italy. He published in his faculty many excellent works. Of these the following are reported:

On the decretals. On the Code, nine books. On the old Digest, twenty-four books.

156
DE SCRIPTORIBVS ECCLESIasticis Fol 76 Super.ff.nouo: li. xij Super.ff.inforciati: li. xiiij Consilia multa: — li. j Alia insuper non pauca praeter haec edidit: quae ad noticiam meam non uenerũt. Claruit sub Alberto imperatore: Anno domini Millefimo.CCC. IOhannes Duns:natione scotus: ordinis fratrum minorũ:Alexandri alen¬ sis anglici quondam Parisius auditor: uir in diuinis scripturis studiosus et eruditus: & in philofophia ariftotelica doctiffimus: & adeo profundus ut eiuf scripta paucis fint penetrabilia: & ob id quoqꝫ minus ufita. Claruit eodem tempore quo Dinus mugelanus sub Alberto imperatore Boni facio papa octauo:Anno dni Millefimo.CCC. I4 LIBER

On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 76

On the New Digest: 12 books. On the Infortiatum: 14 books. Many counsels: 1 book. He also published not a few other works besides these, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

John Duns, a Scot by nation, of the Order of Friars Minor, once at Paris a hearer of Alexander of Hales, an Englishman; a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and most learned in Aristotelian philosophy, and so profound that his writings are penetrable by few, and for that reason also less used. He published certain well-instructed volumes, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these there are extant:

Cupientes: On the prologue. Also Quodlibets: “All difficult things,” he says. On the knowledge of God: “Because the highest knowledge for us.” Questions on the Metaphysics: 1 book. Sermons on the season: 1 book. “There shall be signs,” etc. On this Gospel. Sermons on the saints: 1 book.

He is said to have written commentaries on the Gospel and the Apostle, and to have composed various other treatises, which have not come to my knowledge. He died in the time of Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1308, in the sixth indiction, and was buried at Cologne among the Friars Minor.

Simon, a monk of Haselgem, of the Order of Saint Benedict; a man most studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, subtle in talent, distinguished in eloquence. The counsel of our divine lawgiver Benedict, by which the monk is commanded to love the divine Scriptures, he so turned into practice that nothing in this life was sweeter than to read sacred letters and to turn over diligently the little works of the holy fathers with zealous study. He abridged:

The Moralia of Pope Gregory: 10 books. He wrote sermons on the Song of Songs: 1 book. The vision of a certain convert: [unclear] book. Several sermons: 1 book. Also letters to various persons: 1 book. And many other things.

He also collected excerpts from the sermons of blessed Pope Gregory on Ezekiel; also from the Conferences of the holy fathers, from Richard of Saint Victor on the contemplation of the twelve patriarchs, and from various sources various things not to be despised.

Peter of Bella Parthica, a Burgundian by nation; a man most ready in doubtful questions of law, both civil and canon. He wrote many excellent volumes on the laws, by which he transmitted the memory of his name to posterity. Of these the following are reported:

On the Code: 9 books. On the Institutes: 3 books. On the Old Digest: 14 books. On the New Digest: 1 book. One hundred disputations: 12 [books]. Several counsels: 3 books. And certain other things.

He flourished at the same time as Dinus Mugellanus, under Emperor Albert and Pope Boniface VIII, in the year of the Lord 1300.

Rainerius Pisanus, Italian by nation, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a man zealous and learned in the sacred writings, and sufficiently skilled in canon law, prompt in intellect, scholastic in speech, cautious in counsel, and no less venerable in [unclear] religion: in order to provide a path for his brothers less experienced in law in hearing confessions, he wrote a very great and distinguished summa on cases, in two large volumes, according to the order of the alphabet, which he entitled:

Pantheologia, two books. “Absolution. Concerning absolution.”

And certain other things.

He flourished under Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

Erardus, of the Order of Friars Preachers, German by nation, lector of the convent of Liège, a man zealous and learned in the divine scriptures, and an outstanding preacher in making sermons to the people, distinguished in intellect and adorned with scholastic eloquence. He wrote a very useful treatise for devout and religious persons, teaching seven dispositions to be made concerning the heart, gathering here and there with discernment from the divine scriptures many things pertaining to edification, which he entitled:

On the Teaching of the Heart, one book. “Prepare your hearts.”

Sermons on the Season, one book.

Sermons on the Saints, one book.

Besides these he published certain other things, which have not come to my knowledge.

Jacobus de Arena, from Parma by nation, a very celebrated consultant in both laws, profound in intellect, scholastic in speech; his opinions in explaining the laws, as Bartolus testifies, were so proper and fitting that he seemed to be writing from the mind of the founder of the law at the time. He published in civil law many excellent little works, by which his name [unclear] to the memory of posterity [unclear].

On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 77

Although there are many other things which he composed, they nevertheless have not come to me. He flourished in the times of Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

Nicolaus of Naples, a man skilled and most learned in civil law, and nobly instructed also in other secular letters, whose authority among professors of this faculty has in no small measure consigned him to immortality. But I have been able to find only the titles of the following:

On the Code, 9 books.

On the Infortiatum of the Digest, 14 books.

Concerning the other works which he is said to have composed, I have as yet been able to find nothing certain. He flourished under Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

Hubertinus of Casale, of the Order of Friars Minor, formerly a hearer of John of Parma, minister general; a devout man and sufficiently learned in the Holy Scriptures. When he saw that his order was falling away from its first institution, he began certain new separations under the guise of reform, and obtained their confirmation from the supreme pontiff. Yet at the petitions of the guardians and ministers they were at once revoked by the same pope, since they seemed to have been undertaken to the grave scandal and schism of the order. Therefore Hubertinus, being moved, entered the Carthusian order. He wrote a very renowned and distinguished volume, useful for religious and devout persons, which he entitled:

The Tree of the Life of the Crucified, 5 books. “To the universal true faith of Christ.”

Sermons and letters.

And certain other things.

Certain Catholic doctors warn us that Hubertinus, in the aforesaid volume, in certain places, especially where he takes up the Canticle of Simeon, must be read cautiously, because concerning certain articles he thinks otherwise than the Church, the mother of us all. Yet the author himself is to be excused, because it had not yet been determined, etc.

He flourished under Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

Jacobus of Ravenna, originally from the province of Lotharingia, a man most learned in civil law and the sacred canons, and easily the most skilled of all in his time both in divine Scripture and in secular letters; a professor of sacred Scripture, and a distinguished philosopher and dialectician, who, as Cinus says, converted what had been handed down by the elders in simple meaning into a dialectical mode of argument. He wrote many little works in both laws, among which are reported:

On the Code, 9 books.

On the Old Digest, 23 books.

On the New Digest, 12 books.

On the Infortiatum of the Digest, 14 books.

Various disputations, 1 book.

He flourished under Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1400.

Alanus of Lille, German by nation, a man most learned in divine Scripture and second to none in his time in secular letters; a theologian, philosopher, and most celebrated poet, who for a long time gloriously presided over the ecclesiastical school at Paris. There, shining clearly in all divine and human knowledge, he merited being called universal. He wrote in verse and prose almost innumerable little works, by which the memory of his name has been made immortal among posterity. But few of them have come to my knowledge. I find only the following under their titles:

On the Sentences, 3 books.

Quodlibets also, 1 book. “To the most reverend father and lord.”

The Eye of Sacred Scripture, 1 book. “Every science rests on its own principles.”

On Doctrine also, 5 books. “Since many for adorning.”

On the Five Books of Moses, 1 book. “In the five books of Moses,” 1 book.

On the Song of Songs, 1 book.

Albertus Patauinus: ordinis fratrũ heremitarũ sancti Auguftini:Egidij ro¬ mani quodã auditor atqꝫ discipłus:uir in diuinis scripturĩs studiofus eru ditus: faeculariu lrã nõ ignarus: in declamãdis ad populũ fermonibus excellētis ingenij fuit: multos ab iniquitate ad semitã iufticiae sta praedicatione pofteris memorabilẽ effecit.De quibus ifta feruntur: In Geneffim: li.j In Exodum: li.j In Leuiticũ. li.j

Book

On penitence, to the [prior?] of Bourges, four books: “By the grace of God, [unclear] of Bourges...” On mystical [equivocations?], one book. On the six wings of the Cherubim, one book. On the lament of nature, one book. A summa of virtues and vices, one book. On parables, one book. On the art of preaching, one book. The Anticlaudianus, one book. On the natures of animals, one book. Several sermons, one book. Letters to various persons, one book. Finally, he is said to have published notable commentaries and readings on many books of the Bible, especially on the prophets, on the Gospel, and on the Apostle. Concerning these I have not been able to find anything at all. Certain marvelous things are told about him, to which I neither lend support nor rashly refuse belief. He flourished under the emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

Wilhelm, a monk of the monastery of Affligem of the Order of Saint Benedict, German by nation, for some time prior in the same monastery, a man zealous in the divine Scriptures, learned through long practice, and sufficiently instructed in secular letters, capable in verse and prose, published in both kinds of writing certain little works not to be despised, by which he perpetuated the memory of his name. There are extant by him:

Useful sermons, one book. The visions of a certain nun, one book. On the life of Saint Lutgardis, one book. But other works which he composed have as yet by no means come to my knowledge.

Franciscus Accursius, Italian by nation, Florentine by homeland, son of the very learned Accursius, himself a man excellently learned in civil law and much instructed in the other disciplines of secular philosophy, whose works are extant in great authority among the professors of this faculty, made his times famous by teaching and writing, and gave his name to immortality. Of his little works I have as yet been able to see nothing. Various works of his are reported:

Glosses on the laws. Disputations also, one book. And many other things.

He flourished under the emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

Martinus de Fano, professor of both laws, the most celebrated interpreter of all in his own time, teacher of Johannes Andreae of Bologna, subtle in intellect, distinguished in eloquence, and very acute in pleading judicial cases, wrote excellent volumes in his faculty, by which he also made his name known to posterity. Of these I have found only:

On actions, one book: “I indeed, Martinus...” On the judgment of cases, one book: “Since to very many [unclear]...” Of the others I have seen nothing.

He flourished under the emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

Albertus Patavinus, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, formerly hearer and disciple of Giles of Rome, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, was of excellent talent in declaiming sermons to the people. By his preaching he recalled many from iniquity to the path of justice, and made his fame memorable to posterity. Of these the following are reported:

On Genesis, one book. On Exodus, one book. On Leviticus, one book.

Ekardus natione teutonicus: ordinis ut quidã uolunt praedicatorũ: uir in diuinis scripturis: ingenio subtilis et amp; clarus eloquio: sed dũ nimis philosophi¬ am insequẽs: nouitatẽ terminorũ cõtra theologorũ cõsuetudinẽ ubiqƺ curiose im miscuit: uarios errores inducit: inter quos extant decẽ et amp; septem articuli a summo põtisice damnati: &amp; ꝑ eundẽ magistrũ Eckardũ in fine uitae reuocati: quorũ in ex positione sua super euangeliũ lohãnis multi cõtinentur. On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 78

On Numbers: one book. On Deuteronomy: one book. On the Gospel: three books. On the epistles of Paul: thirteen books. Sermons for the season: one book. Sermons on the saints: one book. Sermons for Lent: one book. And certain other works.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

Dinus de Garbo, a Florentine by country, a most skilled doctor of the art of medicine, and also nobly learned in the principles of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, published in his field, for students, little works not to be despised, by which he transmitted the memory of his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these are reported:

Commentaries on Galen. On the harmfulness of varying complexion: one book. On Hippocrates, On the Nature of the Foetus: one book. A miscellany of questions: one book. On Avicenna also: one book. Various works also in philosophy. And certain other works.

His father Bruno, a most skilled physician in the art of surgery, handed this Dinus over to Thaddaeus, the Florentine physician, to be instructed in that science.

He flourished under Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

William of Cuneo, a Gaul by nation, a most learned interpreter of civil law, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, who in that faculty in his time had few more learned than himself, magnificently adorned the school of Orleans by teaching and writing. He published for professors of laws little works not to be despised, by which he made his name known to posterity:

On the Old Digest: twenty-four books. On the Code also: nine books. And various other works.

He flourished under Emperor Henry VII, in the year of the Lord 1410.

Jacobus of Viterbo, archbishop of Naples, of the order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, a man learned in the divine scriptures and not ignorant of secular literature, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, and no less venerable in conduct than in learning, wrote for the edification of readers little works not to be despised, by which he transmitted the memory of his name with glory to posterity. Of these I have not yet deserved to see any. But there is reported to be by him, addressed to Pope Clement V:

On the Governance of Christians: one book. On the Sentences: three books. Quodlibets also: one book. And some other works.

He flourished in the times of Henry of Luxembourg, the seventh emperor, and Pope Clement V, in the year of the Lord 1410.

Heinricus of Brussels, a monk of the monastery of Affligem, of the order of the divine father Benedict, a man studious in divine writings and skilled through continual exercise, an excellent philosopher and computist, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, wrote some commendable little works, by which he became widely known in his time. Of these are reported:

On the method of computus: one book. A calendar, on [unclear]: one book. And certain other works, which have not yet by any means come to my knowledge.

BOOK.

Alexander of Alexandria, of the order of Friars Minor, the sixteenth minister general, a man most erudite in the divine Scriptures, and in Aristotelian philosophy second to none of his time, subtle in talent, scholastic in speech, profound in sense and understanding. He composed certain little works in either science, by which, exercising his talent, he brought his name to the notice of posterity. Of these are reported: On the Sentences: 3 books. Various Questions: 1 book. On the Metaphysics of Aristotle: 12 books. On the books On the Soul: 3 books. He commented also on other books of Aristotle, and wrote various [things]. He flourished under Henry VII, emperor, [in the year 1]310.

Eckhart, a Teuton by nation, of the order (as some will have it) of Preachers, a man [versed] in the divine Scriptures, subtle in talent and renowned in eloquence; but, while pursuing philosophy too much, he curiously mingled everywhere a novelty of terms against the custom of the theologians, [and] introduced various errors—among which there are extant seventeen articles condemned by the supreme pontiff, and revoked by the same master Eckhart at the end of [his] life; many of which are contained in his exposition on the Gospel of John. Finally, the master-theologians of the faculty of the gymnasium of Heidelberg, in the year of the Lord [1]430, denounced the same errors, with certain others, as publicly condemned. But eleven articles were left as suspect, which all are wont to be appended separately to his little works as a caution. Nevertheless, where he wrote catholically, he gave dogmas profound and useful enough. Of his books I have found: On the Sentences: 3 books. On Genesis: 1 book. On Exodus: 1 book. On the book of Wisdom: 1 book. On the Song of Songs: 1 book. On the Gospel of John: 1 book. On the Lord's Prayer: 1 book. A sermon in the chapter of the Preachers: 1 book. Of his Positions: 1 book. Sermons on the [seasons of the] year: 1 book. Sermons on the saints: 1 book. [The incipits of these works:] "This beginning of Scripture"; "These are the names, etc.… because I feared"; "Love, etc.— The judge always"; "In the beginning, etc.— Aquila [an eagle]"; "Our Father— before the Lord's [day]"; "I, as the vine, [brought forth] fruit"…

162

Scripsit in medicinis multa ut ferunt egregia volumina:quibꝰ nomē fuū nō solū tunc praesentibus: sed etiā posteris cũ laude innotuit. Sed nihil eorū uidi.Feruntur autē: In Auicennā cōmentariorū: li. v Contra pestilentiā: li. j De febribus quoque: li. j De gradibus medicinae: li. j Et quaedam alia. On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 79

On the Code: nine books. On the old Digest: twenty-three books. On the new Digest: twelve books. On the Infortiatum: thirteen books. And certain other works.

He flourished under Henry VII, in the year of the Lord 1310.

William of Monte Laudinium, as they report abbot of the monastery of Poitiers, of the order of the divine father Benedict, a man exceptionally learned in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, of the greatest Aristotelian philosophy, and not ignorant of pontifical law; subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech. He published several little works of great authority, by which he made the memory of his name known to posterity. Of these the principal are reported:

On the Sacraments: one book. A Summa on Cases: [unclear] book(s). Various Declarations.

He also published many other little works, especially in law, and arranged various glosses of canons; concerning these I have so far been able to find nothing.

Guido, priest of the church of Ferrara and afterward, as they report, bishop, a man long practiced in the divine Scriptures, rich in reading of the ancients, and nobly learned in secular letters, a philosopher, a distinguished poet, wrote several little works, both in verse and in prose, of not contemptible reading, by which he made his name known. Of these I found only a volume written in verse to Pope Clement V, on the New and Old Testament, imitating Peter of Riga, which he entitled:

The Pearl of the Bible: one book. Its noble beginning: "Of the earth."

Of the others I have seen nothing.

He flourished in the times of Henry of Luxembourg, the seventh emperor, and Pope Clement V, in the year of the Lord 1310.

Peter of Saxony, a German by nation, of the order of Friars Minor, learned in the holy Scriptures, not ignorant of secular philosophy, and nobly learned in canon law, wrote certain excellent volumes of his intellect, which in his time were held in esteem. Of these there is extant a distinguished work useful to confessors:

A Summa of Cases: [unclear] book(s). Sermons on the Season: one book. Sermons on the Saints: one book.

The rest which he is said to have composed have not come to my knowledge.

Orusianus, an Italian by nation, a Florentine by homeland, formerly a hearer and disciple of the physician Thaddaeus, a man indeed learned and educated in philosophy and medicine, but by no means fortunate; for that reason, bidding farewell to the world, he entered the Carthusian order and profitably changed the art of the flesh into medicine of the spirit. He had previously written some little works in his faculty, by which he made his name known. Of these there is extant a commentary:

On Galen's Tegni: one book. And certain other works.

He flourished in the Carthusian order in the times of Albert, Roman emperor, in the year of the Lord 1300. And thereafter he is reported to have written various treatises pertaining to spiritual edification.

Peter of Verberia, called Aureoli, of the order of Friars Minor, archbishop of Aix, doctor of the Parisian school, very learned in the divine Scriptures, very skilled in Aristotelian philosophy according to the custom of this time, subtle in intellect, acute as a disputant, was outstanding in declaiming sermons to the people. He wrote many excellent little works, by which he magnificently spread his name. Of these there are extant:

163

Sunt qui scribant hunc Martinū ordinis diuipr̄is noftri Benedicti extitisse: quos mea sententia nominis Mariani Scoti ordinis nr̄i cuiꝰsupra memini fimilitudo fe/ fellit:qui et ipse chronicā scripfit. Sunt item alij qui Cisterciensis ordinis collegio cum exiftiment aggregandum:quos aut ignorantia rerum obfuscauit aut liuor. g Erardus Odonis:ordinis fratrûm minorum octauufdecimꝰ minister ge- neralis:uir in diuinis scripturus eruditissimus: & in philosophia fcholaftica nobiliter doctus:ingenio subtilîs:fermone apertus:& ad difputandùm fa- tis idoneus.Fertur quaedā in scripturis sancta lucubrafle opufcula.De quibus mi- hi pauca innotuerunt: Super sententias: li. iij De Logica quoque li. j m 2

Book

On the Sentences: 3 books, “Because it belongs to a disciplined [unclear].” A Breviary of the Bible: 1 book, “Come, let us ascend to the mountain.” On the Conception of Saint Mary: 1 book, “The depths were not yet,” etc. Sermons on the Season: 1 book. Sermons on the Saints: 1 book. And other things which I have not seen.

He flourished before his pontificate, lecturing on the Sentences at Paris, in the time of Louis the Bavarian, the fourth emperor, in the year of the Lord 1317.

Gentilis of Foligno, a distinguished professor of medicine and magnificently learned in other disciplines of secular philosophy, had no small skill in that faculty. He wrote many excellent volumes in medicine, as they say, by which his name became known with praise not only to those then present but also to posterity. But I have seen none of them. The following, however, are reported:

Commentaries on Avicenna: 5 books. Against the Pestilence: 1 book. Also On Fevers: 1 book. On the Degrees of Medicine: 1 book. And certain other things.

He flourished under Henry VII, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1310.

Dante Alighieri, Italian by nation, Florentine by homeland, a man inferior to none in his age in divine scriptures, a philosopher and poet, subtle in intellect and brilliant in eloquence, the keenest disputant of all, wrote many splendid volumes both in meter and in prose, by which he transmitted his name to posterity. Driven from his homeland, he lived in exile all his days: for some time in Gaul, and afterward with the king of Aragon; and on his own misfortune he composed various works. Of his little works these are reported:

Of Comedies: 1 book. On the Monarchy of the World: 1 book. Several letters. And certain other things.

At last he died in exile at Ravenna, under Louis the Bavarian, the fourth emperor, in the year of the Lord 1321, in the fourth indiction, and in the fifty-sixth year of his age.

Michael of Cesena, the seventeenth minister general of the Order of Friars Minor, a man most learned in divine scriptures, ready in intellect and brilliant in eloquence, and no less venerable for religion than for knowledge, published in the holy scriptures little works of exposition not to be despised, by which he became widely known far and wide both to those then present and now to posterity. Of these I have so far been able to find very few, namely:

On the Sentences: 4 books. On the prophet Ezekiel: 1 book. Sermons on the Season: 1 book. Sermons on the Saints: 1 book.

He published lectures and commentaries on many books of the Bible, which I have not yet seen.

He flourished under Louis IV, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1320.

Bertrand, of the Order of Friars Minor, Milanese by homeland, born of a noble family, and, as some hold, priest cardinal of the most holy Roman Church, was certainly a man outstandingly learned in divine scriptures and not moderately instructed in secular philosophy. In delivering sermons to the people he was of excellent talent. He wrote several little works of great usefulness. Of these I found:

On the Sentences: 4 books. Sermons on the Epistles: [unclear] books. Sermons on the Gospels: [unclear] books, “They will see the Son,” etc., “the word.”

164
