On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 80

Sermons on the saints: book(s) [unclear]. The other works that he composed have not yet come to my knowledge. He flourished in the times of Louis the Bavarian, the fourth emperor, and Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1325.

[Gerardus?] of Bologna, of the order of the Brothers of the Blessed Virgin Mary of Mount Carmel, the eleventh prior general, a Parisian doctor, most learned in the divine Scriptures, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, venerable no less for his way of life than for his knowledge, governed his order energetically for twenty years. He wrote several volumes of reading not to be despised, by which he transmitted the memory of his name even to posterity. Of these the following are reported:

On the Sentences: three books. Quodlibets: one book. Ordinary Questions: one book. Sermons on the season: one book. Sermons on the saints: one book. And many others.

He began an excellent Summa of theology, which nevertheless, overtaken by death, he left unfinished. He died under Louis the Bavarian, the fourth emperor, in the year of the Lord 1317, in the fifteenth indiction. He was buried at Avignon.

John of Colonna, Roman by country, of the order of the Preaching Friars, archbishop of Messina, a man possessing talent in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular letters, a most sagacious investigator of the histories of past time, wrote works of noble talent not to be despised, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these there exists the volume that he entitled:

Sea of Histories: ten books. Various letters to various persons: one book. He also produced some other works, which have not come to my knowledge.

Martinus, of the order of the Preaching Friars, penitentiary of the lord pope in the city of Rome, and afterwards, as they report, bishop of a certain city, a man studious and learned in the holy Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, was of excellent talent in delivering sermons to the people. He wrote certain excellent works, by which he transmitted the memory of his name to posterity. Of these I have seen only:

A Table of the Decretum: one book. Among all other things of the faithful. A concise Chronicle: two books. Since to know the times of the highest ones. Sermons on the season: one book. Knowing that now the hour is. Sermons on the saints: one book. Confession is made with the mouth unto salvation. On various miracles: one book. A certain householder. Of the rest I have seen nothing.

He flourished under Louis, the fourth emperor, in the year of the Lord 1320. There are some who write that this Martinus was of the order of our father Benedict, but in my judgment they have been deceived by the resemblance of the name of Marianus Scotus, of our order, whom I mentioned above, who himself also wrote a chronicle. There are likewise others who think he should be joined to the college of the Cistercian order; these either ignorance of the facts or spite has clouded.

Gerardus Odonis, of the order of Friars Minor, the eighteenth minister general, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly taught in scholastic philosophy, subtle in intellect, clear in speech, and quite suitable for disputing, is said to have composed certain works in the holy Scriptures. Of these few have become known to me:

On the Sentences: three books. Also on Logic: one book.

Various Questions: one book. On the books of the Ethics: ten books. On Moral Philosophy: one book.

He also composed the office of the stigmata of Saint Francis, founder of the Order of Minors. Finally, he is said to have published commentaries on many books of the Bible, which have not yet at all come into our hands. He flourished under Louis the Bavarian, the fourth emperor, and Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1430.

Nicolaus de Lyra, English by nation, of the Order of Minors, a man most devoted to the sacred Scriptures and skilled through long practice, perfectly instructed in the Hebrew language, ready in intellect, scholastic in speech, and no less venerable in manner of life than in knowledge, wrote many distinguished little works on the sacred volumes, by which his name came to the knowledge of posterity. And how useful and necessary they are for all who desire to learn sacred Scripture, no one knows better than one who has exercised himself in reading them. For there are some who judge him contemptible because of the simplicity of his eloquence; they seem to me both vain and unskilled, and unworthy of sacred knowledge and salutary philosophy, since they censure ecclesiastical simplicity and embrace words, not things.

Concerning the little works of this devout and learned man, the following are reported:

On the Sentences: three books. On Genesis according to the literal sense: one book. “In the beginning,” etc. “Omitting.” On Exodus: one book. “According to what Isidore says.” On Leviticus: one book. “And he called Moses,” etc. “As the Lord spoke,” etc. “Ex.” On Numbers: one book. “The declaration of your words.” On Deuteronomy: one book. “You will bring them in,” and [unclear]. On Joshua: one book. “The Lord raised up judges.” On Judges: one book. “In the days,” etc. “Here follows.” On Ruth: two books. “Through me kings reign.” On Kings: two books. “Gather up the fragments.” On Chronicles: two books. “He will be priest over Solomon.” On Ezra and Nehemiah: two books. “These things ought to have been done,” etc. On Tobit: two books. “Arphaxad,” etc. “After the histories.” On Judith: two books. “In the days,” etc. “After.” On Esther: two books. “Have patience with me,” etc. On Job: two books. “A great prophet has arisen.” On the Psalter: two books. “Behold, I have described it to you threefold.” On the Song of Songs: two books. “The words of Ecclesiastes, as it says.” On the Book of Wisdom: two books. “Let him kiss me,” etc. “It is expedient.” On Ecclesiasticus: two books. “All wisdom,” etc. “Here begins.” On Isaiah the prophet: two books. “Jerusalem, evangelist, give.” On Jeremiah: two books. “I have made you a prophet to the nations.” On the Lamentations of Jeremiah: two books. “How she sits.” “In the preceding.” On the Book of Baruch: two books. “These words,” etc. “After the book.” On Ezekiel: two books. “The heavens were opened,” etc. On Daniel: one book. “But to Daniel God gave.” On the Twelve Minor Prophets: one book. “The bones of the twelve prophets.” On Maccabees: two books. “And it came to pass,” etc. “After the history.” On the Gospel of Matthew: one book. “Four faces to one,” etc. On Mark: one book. “The face of a lion on the right.” On Luke: one book. “The face of an ox on the left.”

Besides these he published several other works, which have not yet come into our hands. He flourished in the times of the emperor Louis IV and of Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1320.

Guido Perpignanus, a Catalan by native land, of the Order of the Brothers of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, the twelfth bishop, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular literature, outstanding in ability, sweet in speech, an acute disputant, distinguished no less in conduct than in knowledge. He wrote many very distinguished little works, by which he commended his name to posterity. Among these the following are reported: a polished, notable three-part work: On the perfection of the Catholic life:

BOOK

To Pope John XXII: three books. On the Sentences: three books. Six Quodlibets: one book. Ordinary Questions: one book. On the Concordance of the Evangelists: one book. Correctorium of the Decretum: three books. To the Cardinal of Albano: one book. On the books of the Physics: eight books. Questions on the Soul: one book. He also composed many other works, which have not come to my notice. He flourished in the times of Louis IV, emperor, and Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1430.

Augustinus of Ancona, of the order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, a man devoted to the divine scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, ready in intellect, scholastic in speech, wrote many volumes not unworthy of reading, by which he commended the memory of his name to posterity. Of these the following are reported: To Pope John XXII, a work of no small size, On Ecclesiastical Power: three books. “Most holy and most reverend...” On the Sentences: one book. Quodlibets also: one book. On the Holy Spirit against the Greeks: one book. On the Ten Strings: one book. On the Entry into the Promised Land: one book. On the Powers of the Soul: one book. On the Resurrection: one book. On Matthew: one book. On Mark: one book. On Luke also: one book. On John: one book. On Missus est: one book. On the Magnificat: one book. On the Epistles of Paul: fourteen books. On the Canonical Epistles: seven books. On the Acts of the Apostles: one book. On the Apocalypse: one book. And very many others.

This man began a distinguished volume from the writings of the divine father Augustine, which he entitled the Milleloquium; but, overtaken by death, he left it unfinished. Afterwards Bartholomaeus of Urbino, of the same order, completed it. He flourished under Louis the Bavarian, the fourth emperor, and Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1440.

Petrus de Apono, an Italian by nation, a Paduan by homeland, a man devoted to and learned in secular letters, a distinguished philosopher, renowned for knowledge of many languages, is reported to have worked out many little works both in philosophy and in medicine, by which he transmitted the memory of his name to posterity. There are, however, some who write that he was a magician, and showed many marvels through that superstitious art; whether this is true I would not dare to affirm, since indeed I know nothing certain about it. For I do not recall that I have read anything from his little works, or ever seen them. Concerning these, however, the following are reported. A distinguished work divided into 110 distinctions, which he entitled On Every Kind of Medicine: one book. To Pope John XXII: one book. “In our first disputation...” Whether the Word in divine things is.

Quiad Ludouicum imperatorē aeque excōmunicatũ fugiens dixit ei: O imperator defendā te uerbo. On Ecclesiastical Writers

On the book of Johannes Mesue; On Aristotle’s Problems; And certain other works. He translated Galen on black bile and on the regimen of health, with many other works. He flourished under Louis IV, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1320.

Albertus de Beka, a German by nation, from Guelders by homeland, of the Order of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, provincial prior of Lower Germany, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and outstandingly learned both in canon law and in Aristotelian philosophy, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence; he shone in his time no less brightly for his manner of life than for his learning. He wrote certain commendable little works, by which he brought his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among these are reported:

On the Sentences; A Summa of the censures of the new law; On the rule of his order; And certain other works.

He also corrected the ordinal of his order with discerning care. He flourished in the times of Louis the Bavarian, the fourth emperor, and Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1320.

Clement V, pope, born in Gascony, formerly called Bernard, bishop of Bordeaux, sat after Benedict XI in the chair of Peter for eight years and ten months. He was a learned and energetic man. By his command the Order of the Templars was destroyed throughout the whole world in one day. He celebrated the Council of Vienne, in which he enacted many things for the benefit of the Church. He composed the seventh book of Decretals, which John XXII, his successor, published, as is contained at the beginning of the same work. It is commonly called:

The Clementine Code; Also letters to various persons.

He died while Henry VII was governing the Roman Empire, in the year of the Lord 1313, in the twelfth indiction.

Petrus de Perpiniano, called Riminatione, a Catalan, of the Order of the Brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man most learned in the sacred Scriptures and a subtle expounder of scholastic philosophy, quick in intellect and an outstanding declaimer, produced many little works of reading not to be despised; by exercising in them the abundant vein of his talent, he made his name known also to posterity. Among these are reported:

Questions on the Sentences; On the whole Psalter; Various sermons.

Concerning the other works that he composed, however, nothing has come to my knowledge.

Derricus, of the Order of Friars Minor, a holy and learned man and an outstanding preacher of the divine word, assuming a pilgrimage on account of his most fervent love for it, penetrated Asia and India, where by preaching and teaching the evangelical faith of Christ he converted many from iniquity to the path of justice. His most holy life was confirmed by many signs both in the flesh and after death. Among other little works of his talent he wrote:

The history of his pilgrimage; Also various sermons; And certain letters.

He flourished in the times of Louis IV, emperor, and Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1320.

Book

Francis Maronis, of the Order of Friars Minor, formerly a hearer of John Scotus, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in the teachings of the philosophers, subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, composed in style, constant in study, and sufficiently acute and very well suited for debating and resolving questions of the Scriptures. He wrote not a few excellent volumes of his talent, in which he both showed himself most learned and transmitted his name with glory to posterity. Of these, the following are reported:

On the Sentences, four books: Around the prologue of the first book. On formalities, one book. Various questions, one book. Sermons on the season, one book. Sermons on the saints, one book.

It is also said that he composed certain commentaries on the divine volumes and various other treatises, which have not yet at all come to my knowledge.

He flourished in the times of Louis the Bavarian, the fourth emperor, and of Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1320.

Bonaventure of Padua, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, once prior general and thereafter priest-cardinal of the holy Roman Church with the title of Saint Cecilia, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, ready in intellect and clear in eloquence, revered no less for his manner of life than for his knowledge, of great reputation in delivering sermons to the people; when he was most vigorously defending the liberty of the Church against tyrants, he was at last pierced by an arrow by the lord of Carrara and was crowned with martyrdom. He wrote very useful and elegant works:

Sermons on the season, one book: The desired one will come to all. Sermons on the saints, one book: But far be it from me to glory.

And certain other things.

He flourished under Louis, the fourth emperor, in the year of the Lord 1320.

William Ockham, English by nation, of the Order of Friars Minor, formerly a disciple of John Scotus, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in Aristotelian philosophy, subtle in intellect and clear in eloquence. He wrote certain little works on the Scriptures, by which he transmitted his name to posterity. Acting and writing against John XXII, who condemned the heresy of the Fraticelli, together with Peter of Picenum, whom the emperor Louis had set up as an idol and had caused to be called Nicholas V, and declaring him to be a heretic, he was excommunicated by him. Fleeing to the emperor Louis, likewise excommunicated, he said to him: “O emperor, I will defend you with the word.” And so he remained excommunicated with the excommunicated man until the end of his life, and at last was absolved at death. He was a most vigorous opponent of Scotus his master, and attacked almost all of his sayings. He wrote:

An Apology, one book. On the Sentences, four books. Quodlibets also, one book. On the supporters of heretics, six books: In all curious matters. On the sacrament of the altar, one book.

And certain other things.

He flourished in the times of Louis, the fourth emperor, and of Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1320. And he was buried in the Munich convent of his order, in the province of Noricum, which is now called Bavaria, of which the emperor Louis had previously been duke.

Alvarus, of the Order of Friars Minor, Spanish by nation, a hearer of John Scotus, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, held in esteem by John XXII, acted against William Ockham the Englishman in writings and in words. He published certain distinguished volumes of his talent, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among these there is a great and notable work, describing the defects of ecclesiastical persons, which he entitled:

On the Lamentation of the Church, one book. Also The Mirror of Kings, one book. On the Sentences, one book. An Apology, one book. And certain other works.

He flourished at the same time as Ockham, under Louis, the fourth emperor, and Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1320.

[unclear]

Matthew Silvaticus, Mantuan by homeland, noble by birth, a physician by art and profession, in which faculty in his time he was considered both learned and experienced before many others; subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence. He wrote in that science volumes not to be despised, by which he brought his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among these I have seen only a notable work, addressed to Robert, king of Sicily and physician, on all simple medicines and their properties, which he entitled:

Pandects, one book. Aaron in Greek; in Arabic.

Of the rest I have seen nothing.

He flourished under Louis, the fifth emperor, in the year of the Lord 1420.

[unclear]

John Canonicus, of the order, as they say, of the Friars Preachers, and afterward, as [unclear]; once a hearer and disciple in the academy of Paris; a man learned in the divine Scriptures, and subtly instructed in secular philosophy; also not ignorant of both pontifical and imperial law. He is said to have composed certain distinguished little works, by which, exercising his talent, he also made his name known to posterity. But I have seen none of them. They are said to be:

On the Sentences, one book. Disputed Questions, one book. And certain other works.

He flourished under Louis, the fourth emperor, in the year of the Lord 1330.

[unclear]

Durandus of Saint-Pourçain, of the Order of Friars Preachers, and afterward, as [unclear]; and not meanly instructed in secular philosophy; ready in intellect and distinguished in eloquence; an excellent declaimer of sermons; at first a defender of the writings of Saint Thomas Aquinas, but afterward a very fierce assailant of them. A certain shifting cause is reported for this change, to which I ought neither readily to give credence nor rashly to deny it. He wrote certain volumes not to be spurned, by which he made his name known. Among them are reported:

On the Sentences, one book. On the Instruction of the Clergy, one book. A Notable Summa, one book. Various Questions, one book. Diverse Sermons, one book.

The other things which he is said to have composed have not yet come to my knowledge.

Erenus of Boyo, Breton by nation, of the Order of the Friars of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel; a man most learned in every respect; a notable professor of sacred Scripture; of sharp and forceful intellect; sufficiently fit for solving questions of the Scriptures. He is said to have written several distinguished little works, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity with glory. Among these is found a notable work, as his followers report:

Book [unclear]. iii

On the Sentences; and Various Questions.

But he is also said to have composed certain other works, which have not come to my notice.

Petrus, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a man learned in the divine Scriptures through long practice, and a subtle and profound interpreter of scholastic philosophy, an acute disputant, an excellent preacher of sermons, sharp in intellect, scholastic in speech, published certain little works not to be despised. By fruitfully and usefully exercising his talent in them, he made his name known not only to those then living but also to future generations. Of these there are extant:

On the Sentences, four books; Sermons on the Season, one book; Sermons on the Saints, one book.

In addition, he adorned many books of Aristotle with most elegant commentaries. He flourished under Emperor Louis IV, in the year of the Lord 1320.

Stephanus of Asti, of the Order of Friars Minor, a man nobly learned in the divine Scriptures, a philosopher, an eminent jurist, distinguished in knowledge, profound in intellect, cautious in counsel, firm in judgment, composed in speech, is said to have forged various little works of his excellent talent, by which he made his name known both to those then living and to future generations. Of these I have seen only the necessary:

Summa on Cases:

On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 84

On the Clementines: one book. Various Questions: one book. Of the rest I have found nothing. He flourished around the times of Louis the Fourth, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1330.

Johannes Andreas, an Italian by nation, a native of Bologna, a jurist most celebrated to the admiration of all, a fountain of canons and a most cautious interpreter of doubts, distinguished in talent, profound in knowledge, orderly in speech, who, contrary to the custom of men of our time, although he was bound by the ties of a wife, nevertheless devoted incredible zeal to letters, so that nothing could have been sweeter to him than to write something for the edification of posterity, as his distinguished volumes bear witness; by them he won eternal memory for his name. Of these I have been able to see a few:

On the Decretals: five books. On the Sixth Book of the Decretals: one book. On the Novellae, in two forms: three books. Additions to the Speculum: one book. The prefatory Mercuriale: one book. A Summa on betrothal and marriage: one book. On the Clementines: one book. On the praises of Saint Jerome: three books. On the tree of consanguinity: one book. Of the rest I have seen nothing.

At length he died of the plague and was buried at Bologna, under Charles the Fourth, emperor, and Pope Clement the Sixth, in the year of the Lord 1348, in the first indiction.

Cinus of Pistoia, born of the noble family of the Symbaldi, formerly hearer and disciple of the most distinguished man Dino of Mugello, and a close friend of Johannes Andreas, certainly the most learned of all in civil law in his time, subtle in talent, ready and very abundant in knowledge, published many little works in that faculty, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these the following are reported:

On the Code: nine books. On the first part of the Old Digest: one book. On the second part: one book. Additions on the remaining parts: one book. And many other things.

He flourished under Louis the Fourth, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1430.

Monaldus, of the Order of Friars Minor, a theologian and most learned jurist, subtle in talent, cautious in knowledge, scholastic in speech, a man of outstanding industry in delivering sermons to the people, published, for the benefit of the simple, little works not to be scorned even by a doctor; through them he usefully provided both for those then present and for those who would come long afterward. Of these the following are reported, necessary and very fine:

A Summa of canon law: one book. “Since one who is ignorant [unclear].” Questions on the Sentences: three books. Various sermons: one book. And very many other things, which have by no means come to our knowledge.

Oldradus de Laude, an Italian by nation, formerly a hearer of the very learned man Dino of Mugello, a very close friend of Johannes Andreas, a man highly skilled in both laws and also excellently imbued with the disciplines of philosophy, who for many years was a consistorial advocate, acquired great praise and glory for his learning. He wrote several distinguished little works in both laws, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these I have seen only:

A volume of counsels: one book. “In the name of the Lord, amen. In the case.” Of the rest I have seen nothing.

Book

He is said to have left behind many lectures on civil law, which I have not yet seen. He flourished under Emperor Louis IV, in the year of the Lord 1330.

Johannes de Blomendal, a German by nation, of the Order of Friars Minor, was a man devoted to the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy; outstanding in talent, distinguished in eloquence, and an excellent teacher in delivering sermons to the people. For the edification of the faithful he wrote volumes not to be despised, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these I have so far found only:

Sermons on the season, one book, “Take your weapons, your quiver.” Sermons on the saints, one book. Sermons for Lent, one book.

He flourished under Louis the Bavarian, the fourth emperor, and Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1330.

Guido de Monte Rocherii, a man very devoted to the holy Scriptures, rich in reading of the ancients, distinguished in talent, scholastic in speech, wrote little works of his talent not to be scorned, by which he also made the memory of his name known among posterity. Of these I have seen only that well-known work, published in print, which he composed for the direction of simple priests and wished to be entitled:

The Handbook of Curates, three books, “Since, as the prophet says.”

I could not find any others. He flourished in the times of Emperor Louis IV and Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord [unclear].

Johannes de Lineriis, a philosopher and the most celebrated astronomer of all in his time, magnificently restored this discipline, which had by now been almost erased from human memory. In this faculty he had as co-workers and associates men most learned in mathematical science: Johannes de Saxonia, Johannes de Muris, and Bernard, distinguished philosopher-astronomers, who themselves wrote various little works. As for the little works of this Johannes de Lineriis, although he wrote many splendid things, I have seen very few, namely:

Canons of the Primum Mobile, one book, “Of any arc set forth.” Tables of the same, one book. On the Sphere also, one book.

Of the rest I have found nothing. He flourished in the times of Louis the Bavarian, the fourth emperor, and Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1330.

Johannes Danck of Saxony, a German by nation, contemporary of the aforesaid Johannes de Lineriis and associate in his studies, a man most learned in every respect, a philosopher and astronomer, among all of his time most celebrated, subtle and outstanding in talent, published many splendid and admirable little works, by which he transmitted his name with glory to posterity. But up to now I have found very few:

Canons on eclipses, one book, “The quantity of the eclipse of the sun.” Canons of the tables, one book, “The time of the fourth aspect.” On the Astrolabe, one book. On ascensions, one book.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Louis IV and Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord [unclear].

Petrus de Palude, a Frenchman by nation, of the Order of Preachers, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy and canon law, an acute disputant and excellent declaimer, published certain splendid volumes on the holy Scriptures, by which he consigned his name to immortality. Of these

174
domini Millesimo.CCC.ac.XL. Claruit temporibus Ludouici imperatoris quarti: Benedicti papae. xij. Anno domini Millefimo.CCC.XL. BArtholomaeus de Ofa:patria Pergomēsis:uir in diuinis scripturis studio/ sus: in foecularibꝰ litteris egregie doctus:philosophus historiographꝰ insignis: ingenio praeftans clarus eloquio:Fertur nonnulla excellentis doctrinae cudiffe uolumina:quibus nomen suum ad noticiam posteritatis transmi fit.In quibus praecellit opus: Historiarū insigne: li.xvj Claruit sub Ludouico imperatore quarto:Anno domini Millefino.CCC.XL. b Artholomaeus Pisanus:ordinis fratum praedicatoꝝ:uir in diuinis scriptoru ris eruditus: in utroque iure peritissimꝰ:ac in phiae foecularis scia nobiliter

are reported: On the Sentences: four books. Various Questions: one book. And diverse sermons: one book. And many other things. He is also said to have adorned and expounded many books of the Bible with his commentaries.

Johannes Calderini, an Italian by birth, from Bologna as his native city, formerly a hearer and disciple of Johannes Andreae, a professor of canon law and a very [unclear] interpreter, not ignorant of secular philosophy and the divine Scriptures, ready in talent and clear in speech, wrote not a few volumes in his own faculty; by these, proving his talent through diligent exercise, he transmitted his name to the memory of posterity. Among these I have found a great and distinguished work, divided into three volumes of no small size, which he entitled: Repertory of Law: two books. A. This expression “a” sometimes. On the Decretals: five books. On ecclesiastical interdict: one book. Although many doubtful matters concerning. Many opinions: one book. Of the others I have seen nothing. He flourished under Louis the Bavarian, the fourth emperor, and Pope Benedict XII, in the year of the Lord 1340.

Paulus de Liazariis, a hearer of Johannes Andreae of Bologna, a fellow-student of Johannes Calderini, a man most skilled in both laws, nobly instructed in the precepts of the philosophers, distinguished in talent and speech, who among the doctors of law in his time was not the least. He wrote, among other little works of his talent, a distinguished volume, as is said: On the Clementines: one book. And certain other things. He flourished in the times of Louis the Bavarian, the fourth emperor, and Pope Benedict XII, in the year of the Lord 1440.

Lupold of Bebenburg, bishop of Bamberg, German by birth and, as they report, formerly a hearer of Johannes Andreae of Bologna, a very celebrated jurist, nobly learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, subtle in talent and distinguished in speech. He published little works not unworthy of reading, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity with great glory. Among these there is extant a distinguished work on the zeal of the Christian religion of the ancient princes of the Germans: one book. On the rights of the Roman Empire: one book. And certain other volumes on diverse subjects, which have not yet come to me. He flourished in the times of Louis, the fourth emperor, and Pope Benedict XII, in the year of the Lord 1340.

Nicolaus Mutinensis, a man nobly learned in both laws, especially in the laws, subtle in talent, scholastic in speech, cautious in knowledge and counsel. So that he might leave monuments of his talent to posterity, he wrote certain excellent volumes in civil law, by which he had made himself useful to those then present and known to those to come. Among these are reported: On the Code: nine books. On the Old Digest: twenty-four books. On the New Digest: twelve books. On the Infortiatum: thirteen books. And certain other things. He flourished in the times of Louis the Bavarian, the fourth emperor, and Pope Benedict XII, in the year

De.iiij.fensibus scripturae: li. Manuale facerdotū: li. De uitij capitalibus: li. Claustrū animae: li. De cōceptione sanctae Mariae: li. De modo studendi: li. Introductoriu iuris: li. in the year of the Lord 1340.

Lapus de Castellione, abbot of San Miniato, of the Order of the holy father Benedict, a jurist most learned among all men of his time, trained from his earliest age, as they say, in the disciplines of the courts, distinguished in talent, scholastic in speech, and an outstanding disputant of scholastic questions, whose authority among jurists is to be reckoned by no means slight. He wrote several treatises in his field. Of these there is extant a distinguished work:

His Allegations, one book. On the Clementines, one book. And many other things.

He flourished in the times of Louis IV, emperor, and Pope Benedict XII, in the year of the Lord 1340.

Guericus, abbot of Igny, a man by no means lowly learned in the divine Scriptures, easy in talent, sweet and composed in eloquence, sufficiently apt for persuasion, distinguished no less by his life and love of regular observance than by knowledge of the Scriptures. For the edification of simple devout brothers he wrote treatises not to be despised; in them, showing himself a useful and faithful shepherd of Christ’s sheep, he also made his name known to posterity. Of these I have found only a work of sermons on the temporal cycle and the saints through the circuit of the year, which he delivered:

To his brothers, one book. “We await the Savior.”

He also wrote letters.

As for the other things which he is said to have composed, I have so far been able to find nothing.

Henricus de Vrimaria, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, by nation, as they report, a German, a man from boyhood most studious and very learned in the holy Scriptures, second to none in his time in Aristotelian philosophy. For many years he was an outstanding doctor in the Parisian school; he shone forth, renowned for celebrated learning. He wrote many excellent volumes, among which the following are said to be:

On the Sentences, four books. Also Quodlibets, one book. On the Ten Commandments, one book. Flowers from the Conferences of the Fathers, twenty-four books. “Hear, O Israel, the commandments. In [unclear].” On the Perfection of Man, one book. “Because many things suitable for preaching.” On the Incarnation of the Word, one book. On the Fourfold Instinct, one book. “Other seed fell into the earth.” Exposition of the decree on the celebration of Mass, one book. Sermons on the Temporal Cycle, one book. On the Books of the Ethics, ten books. And many other things.

He flourished in the times of Louis IV, emperor, surnamed the Bavarian, and Pope Benedict XII, in the year of the Lord 1340.

Bartholomaeus de Osa, by homeland Bergomensis, a man studious in the divine Scriptures, notably learned in secular letters, a distinguished philosopher and historiographer, outstanding in talent and bright in eloquence. He is said to have produced some volumes of excellent learning, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among these the following stands out:

A distinguished work of Histories, sixteen books.

He flourished under Louis IV, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1340.

Bartholomaeus Pisanus, of the Order of Preachers, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, most skilled in both laws, and in the knowledge of secular philosophy nobly

learned, distinguished in talent, clear in speech, cautious in knowledge and counsel. He is said to have written certain excellent little works, of which I have seen only the Summa which they call the Pisan, a work indeed not to be rejected, which a few years ago was in use among plebeian confessors. The author entitled it:

The Summa [unclear], a book.

Of the rest I have seen nothing.

He flourished under Emperor Louis IV, and completed his Summa, as he himself testifies, in the year of the Lord 1338.

Albertus Brixianus, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a man zealous and learned in the holy Scriptures, and not slightly learned in both laws; also an outstanding declaimer of sermons, and no less holy than learned, since he is said to have shone even in life with miracles. Among the other monuments of his talent he wrote the notable:

Summa on cases, a book. Various sermons, a book. And certain other things.

He flourished under Emperor Louis IV, in the year of the Lord [1340?].

Ludolphus, of the Carthusian Order in the house of Strasbourg, a German by nation, sprung from the Saxon land, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters; gentle in disposition, sweet and well-ordered in speech, and also distinguished in life and conduct. He produced certain excellent little works of great devotion and deep learning, by which, nobly exercising his talent, he bestowed his name upon immortality. Of these I have seen only the following: a great and distinguished volume on the Gospel, which he entitled:

The Life of the Lord Jesus, “No one [can lay] another foundation.” Also on the Psalter, “As once manna [unclear].” Other works of his are also reported.

He flourished under Emperor Louis IV, in the year of the Lord [unclear].

Hermannus de Schildis, of the Order of Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, a man most zealous and very skilled in the divine writings, outstanding in talent, and no less distinguished in life than in learning and knowledge. He produced many excellent volumes, by which he showed the abundant vein of his talent and transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity with great praise and glory. Of these the following are reported:

On the First Book of the Sentences, a book. A reading on Genesis, a book. A double Hexaemeron, a book. On the Song of Songs, a book. On the subject matter of the Song of Songs, a book. On the Lord’s Prayer, in two ways, a book. On the Ave Maria, a book. A Breviloquium, a book. On the four senses of Scripture, a book. A Manual for Priests, a book. On the capital vices, a book. The Cloister of the Soul, a book. On the Conception of Saint Mary, a book. On the Method of Studying, a book. An Introduction to Law, a book. On True and False Friendship, a book. On the Canonical Hours, a book. On the Five Senses, a book.

Book

On the forty-two mansions: one book. Against the flagellants: one book. On the comparison of the Mass: one book. On the division of [unclear] of meter: one book. On the chapter Omnis utriusque: one book. Various sermons: one book. Preachable collations: one book. Of diverse questions: one book. On Aristotle's Rhetoric: one book. He published many other things besides, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished in the time of Louis IV, emperor, and Pope Benedict XII, in the year of the Lord 1340.

William of Kayotho, of the Order of Friars Preachers, provincial prior in France, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed both in canon law and in scholastic philosophy, subtle in talent and distinguished in eloquence, of excellent ability in delivering sermons to the people, wrote certain works not to be despised, by which he transmitted his name with praise to the knowledge of posterity. Of these there is said to be:

An abbreviation of the Summa of John the Teuton, which is called that of confessors: one book. “What is simony? [unclear].” Various sermons: one book. The rest that he composed have by no means come to our knowledge.

Peter de Casa, of Limoges, of the Order of the Friars of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, the fourteenth prior general, and afterward bishop of [Basionensis], and finally, as they say, patriarch of Jerusalem, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, ready in talent, distinguished in eloquence, learned and eloquent in delivering sermons to the people, published certain excellent volumes, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these there are said to be:

On the Sentences: three books. Sermons for the season: one book. Sermons on the saints: one book. And certain other things. He flourished when he was elected prior general of his order from the convent of Limoges, under Louis IV, emperor, and Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1330, in the thirteenth indiction. He vigorously ruled his order for twelve years.

Paul of Perugia, of the Order of Friars of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount [Sophia], sufficiently instructed, subtle in talent, scholastic in speech, published several works of great authority; by exercising his brilliant talent in them, he transmitted the memory of his name to posterity with great glory. Of these there survives a very celebrated, almost divine work, which he recited in the Paris school:

On the Sentences: three books. Concerning the first book of the Sentences. Quodlibets also: one book. And certain other things. He flourished at Paris and completed his lectureship under Louis the Bavarian, fourth emperor, and Pope Clement VI, in the year of the Lord 1354, in the twelfth indiction. And not long after that same lectureship of his he died at Paris and was buried there in the convent.

Bernardus Parentinus, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a man devoted to the divine Scriptures, skilled through long practice and not moderately learned in scholastic disciplines, subtle in talent, distinguished in eloquence, of excellent reputation in delivering sermons to the people, wrote for the instruction of simple priests certain volumes not to be despised, by which he transmitted his name to posterity. Of these there survives:

On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 87

An Exposition of the Mass, one book: “Since the wise man cries out.” Various Sermons, one book. And many other things. He flourished under Louis, the fourth emperor, in the year of the Lord 1340.

Carmel: certainly a man most learned in the Holy Scriptures, and excellently instructed in secular philosophy; of sharp and vigorous intellect, scholastic eloquence, subtle in debating and resolving questions of the Scriptures. He wrote certain distinguished little works, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Of these there are extant:

On the Sentences, three books: “One conclusion having been proposed.” Various Determinations, one book: “It is asked whether [unclear].” Also Various Sermons, one book. The rest which he composed have not come to the knowledge of our reading.

John Estuidi, English by nation, a man easily the most learned of all in secular letters in his time, a philosopher and astronomer second to none, outstanding in talent, sweet in eloquence. He wrote certain distinguished little works of his talent, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among these there is extant a notable work of judicial astrology, on the accidents of the world, which is commonly called:

The English Summa, two books: “My intention in this book.” Concerning the rest I have seen nothing. He flourished and completed the same Summa, as he acknowledges at its beginning, under Charles, the fourth emperor, and Pope Clement VI, in the year of the Lord 1347, in the fifteenth indiction, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of January.

Bernard, abbot of the monastery of Cassino, of the order of the holy father Benedict, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, outstanding in talent, distinguished in life, and an eminent cultivator and propagator of regular observance. He wrote certain distinguished little works for the edification of monks, by which he made his name known. Of these the following are extant:

Mirror of Monks, one book: “He reads in Proverbs: teaching.” On the Rule of Saint Benedict, one book. On the regular precepts, one book. Sermons to the Brothers, one book. He is also said to have composed many other things, which have by no means come down to us.

Simon of Cremona, of the order of the hermit friars of Saint Augustine, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of the liberal arts, outstanding in talent, renowned in eloquence, quite excellent in declaiming sermons to the people; indeed he labored at this office for a long time at Venice, where by word and example he instructed very many. He wrote little works, not to be despised, for the instruction of the aforementioned simple people. Of these the following are extant. To Antonius, his brother, a priest:

Sermons. On the Gospels, one book: “Lift up your heads, because.” Also On the Epistles, one book: “Let us cast off the works of darkness.” The rest which he composed have not yet come to the knowledge of our reading.

Peter Raymundi of Insula Grassa, French by nation, of the order of the friars of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, fifteenth prior general, who after Peter de Casa of Limoges vigorously ruled his order for ten years; a man learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular philosophy. He wrote elegantly:

On the Sentences, four books. And certain other things. He flourished, and was elected general from the convent of Carcassonne in the province of Narbonne

Book

...sis: under Emperor Louis IV and Pope Clement VI, in the year of the Lord 1343, the eleventh indiction.

Reinerus of Forlì, a jurist most celebrated among all men in his time, teacher of Bartolus of Saxoferrato, a man distinguished in talent and eloquence, is said to have composed various little works in civil law, by which he transmitted the memory of his name with glory to posterity. But I have not been able to find any of them anywhere. He died under Emperor Charles IV and Pope Innocent VI, in the year of the Lord 1358, the eleventh indiction.

Simon of Cascia, of the order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, and no less venerable for the holiness of his life than for his knowledge, since he is said to have been illumined by the spirit of prophecy in the Florentine convent, produced several volumes of great usefulness, in which he shows himself a learned and devout man. Among these I have found a notable work on the whole Gospel, commonly entitled:

The Deeds of the Savior, fifteen books. [A bono super bono creato?] On Christian Doctrine, one book. On Patience, one book. An Exposition of the Creed, one book. On the Mirror of the Cross, one book. On the Discipline of Spiritual Men, one book. Letters to Various Persons, one book. And certain other things.

He flourished under Emperor Louis IV, in the year of the Lord 1340.

Simon of Speyer, German by nation, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, master of Paris, very learned in the holy Scriptures and skilled in Aristotelian philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in discourse, taught theology gloriously for a long time in the school of Cologne, and gained from all men great praise for his learning. He wrote a notable volume:

On the Sentences, four books. Also Against the Jews, one book. A Postil read at Cologne, one book. Besides these he produced some other works, but they have by no means come to our knowledge.

Ertorius, whom some call Fortanerius, of the order of Friars Minor, the nineteenth minister general, English by nation, Welsh by homeland, afterward archbishop of Ravenna and finally patriarch of Grado, cardinal of the most holy Roman Church, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, produced certain distinguished volumes, by which he made his name known also to posterity. Among these there exists a notable work:

On Augustine’s City of God, twenty-two books.

Of the rest I have found nothing. Finally, he is also said to have labored over compilations of the books of the Bible. He flourished; he was elected minister general of his order in the chapter at Marseille, under Emperor Charles IV and Pope Innocent VI, in the year of the Lord 1356, the ninth indiction.

Albericus Roxiatus, of Bergamo by homeland, an eminent professor of both laws, a very illustrious interpreter, also excellently learned in the other secular letters, ready in intellect and orderly in eloquence, produced many well-instructed volumes on the laws, by which he transmitted the memory of his name with praise to later generations. Of these the following are reported:

On the Code, twelve books. On the Old Digest, twenty-four books. On the New Digest, twelve books. On the Infortiatum, thirteen books. On the Institutes, four books.

LIBER ALphonsus episcopus Hispalensis: ordinis fratrū heremitarū sancti Augu- stini: uir tam in diuinis scripturis: q̄ in saecularibus litteris multū eruditus: &amp; inter Ecclesiasticos doctores suo tempore celeberrimus: ingenio et amp; elo- quio clarus. Edidit nōnulla magnae auctoritatis volumina: quibꝰ nomen suū etiam posteris notificauit. Equibꝰ ego tantū reperi: opus subtile et amp; insigne: Super sententias: li. De caeteris nihil percepi. iiij Claruit sub Ludouico imperatore quarto: Anno dn̄i Mill̓. CCC.XL. Obannes de Bachone: anglicus: ordinis fratrū beatae Mariae semper virgi- nis de monte Carmeli: uir in diuinis scripturus eruditissimus et amp; tam in iure canonico q̃ in philosophia saeculari egregie doctus : in gymnasio parisien̄. nō minus cōuersationē q̃ scientia clarus effulsit: ac deinde in prouincialem angliae promotus: ordinē suum uerbo et amp; exemplo strenue gubernauit. Scripsit multa et insignia volumina: quibꝰ nomē suū ad posteros trāsmisit. Equibꝰ ista ferunt̉: In euangeliū Matthaei: li. In euangeliū Marci: li. In euangeliū Lucae: li. In euangeliū Iohannis: li. In epistolas Pauli: li. In Actus apostolorū: li. In epistolas canonicas: li. In Apocalypsin: li. Super sententias: li. Quodlibeta uaria: li. Speculū ordinis sui: li. Defensoriū ordinis sui: li. Contra iudaeos: li. De paupertate christi: li. In regulā sui ordinis: li. Et alia multa. Explanatiōes insup̄ edidit: suꝑ libros beati Augustini de sancta trinitate: &amp; de Ciui tate dei: &amp; Anselmi: Cur deus homo: &amp; de incarnatiōe uerbi: in quibus omnibus ingeniū suū magnifice exercitauit. Claruit temporibus Caroli imperatoris quar- ti: &amp; Clemētis papae sexti: Anno domini. Mill̓. CCC.L. Obannes eligerus de Gonderbleuen: natione teutonicus: Iohannis de Sa- xonia clarissimi astronomi q̃dā auditor: uir in saecularibus lr̄is eruditissi- mus : philosophus et amp; astronomꝰ inter omnes sui temporis celeberrimus: ac diuinis scripturis sufficiēter imbutus: ingenio subtilis: &amp; clarus eloquio. Scripsit in Mathematica scientia nō spernēda volumina: quibus nomen suum ad posteri- tatem transmisit. Equibus subiecta ferunt̉: De cōpositione astrolabij: li. De utilitate astrolabij: li. De utilitate quadrātis: li. De magnetē quoqꝫ: li. De astrogemetro: li. Rex astrorū Ptolemaeus. Zelo prīcipali intellectuqƺ. Vtilitates noui quadrātis. Tractaturus de magnetē. Summa rorāte nobis. Et alia plura. Claruit temporibus Caroli imperatoris quarti: &amp; Clemētis papae sexti: Anno dn̄i Millesimo. CCC.L. BVpertus natione Gallus: ordinis fratrū beatae Mari ae semper uirginis de monte Carmeli: uir in diuinis scriptruris studiosus et amp; eruditus atqꝫ in philo- sophia scholastica egregie doctus: ingenio clarus: sermone apertus. Edidit

On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 88

On the sixth book of the Decretals, one book. On Dante’s Comedies, one book. He also composed some other works, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under Louis, the fourth emperor, in the year of the Lord 1340.

Johannes de Saxonia, of the Order of Friars Minor, German by nationality, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, sufficiently instructed both in canon law and in scholastic philosophy, and of excellent reputation in delivering sermons to the people. He published certain distinguished volumes of his talent, by which he made his name known also to posterity. Of these there is extant: A Summa on cases, one book. And other works which I have not seen. He flourished under Louis, the fourth emperor, in the year of the Lord 1340.

Gerardus de Senis, Italian by nationality, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, a man by no means moderately learned in the holy Scriptures, skilled through long exercise in both laws, subtle and acute in intellect; Johannes Andreas, his contemporary, often commends and cites his learning. He wrote some distinguished little works, by which he transmitted the memory of his name to posterity. Of these, the following are said to be the more important: On the first book of the Sentences, one book. On contracts of usury, one book. On prescriptions, one book. I have found nothing concerning the rest. He flourished with Johannes Andreas, under Louis the Bavarian, the fourth emperor, and Pope Benedict XII, in the year of the Lord 1340.

Johannes de Rupe Scissa, of the Order of Friars Minor, very zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular philosophy; led astray by some spirit, lest I say induced, he began, as though a prophet, to foretell the desolation of the Catholic Church and certain other terrible things. He was cast into prison by the ministers of his order; a lying spirit was found in his mouth. He wrote in chains to a certain cardinal: His Revelations, one book, beginning: “Most reverend father in Christ.” Also on the four books of the Sentences. And certain other things. He flourished under Louis, the fourth emperor, in the year of the Lord 1340.

Gerardus, bishop of Savona, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, Bergamasque by homeland, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures, nobly instructed in canon law, subtle in intellect, renowned in eloquence, no less distinguished in life than in learning, composed for the use of readers little works not to be despised. By profitably exercising his talent in these, he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these they report: On the Sentences, three books. Two quodlibets, one [book]. On the Song of Songs, one book, beginning: “The two wings of the cherubim.” On the Epistle to the Hebrews, one [book]. On the sixth book of the Decretals, “On relics and the veneration of saints,” [unclear], in the year of the Lord 1340. He is also said to have written many other little works, which have not come to my knowledge. In the Parisian school he ascended the magisterial chair. He flourished under Louis, the fourth emperor, in the year of the Lord 1340.

Thomas de Garbo, Florentine by homeland, son of Dino, once a physician, a man learned and skilled in medicine, nobly instructed in the disciplines of the philosophers, adhering to the footsteps of his most learned father. He published, in his own faculty, little works not to be spurned by physicians, by which he transmitted his name with glory to posterity. Of these there is extant a very notable Summa of medicine, one book. And certain other works. He flourished in the times of Louis the Bavarian, fourth emperor of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 1340.

181
DE SCRIPTORIBVS ECCLESIASTICIS Fol.89 uaria in scripturis sanctis opuscula: quibus ingenii sui magnifice exercitās: memoria nomis sui etiam posteris notificavit. Erat autē praedicator verbi divini egregius: & multa scriptit declamatoribus sermonū utilia. De quibus ista ferunt: Super sententias: li. iiiij In epistolas Pauli: li. xiiiij Sermones de tempore: li. i Sermones de sanctis: li. i Alia insuper multa composuit: quae ad noticia meā non uenerunt. Lemens papa sextus: patria Lemonicensis: Petrus Rogerijante uocatus: abbas Filcaniēlis ordinis sancti Benedicti: sedit in cathedra Petri post Benedictū duodecimū annis decē: mēlib. sex: uir in divinis scripturis eruditus: & sacerlīi litteras: nō ignarus: iuris canonici doctor insignis: nō min. cōver, satione q. scīetia uenerādus: in declamādis sermonī ad popūl excellētis inge, nīn fuit. Edidit quaeda praeclara opuscula: quibus uitacitāte ingenii sui ostendit. E quibus ferunt: Sermones uarii: li. i In canonicatione yuonis. li. i In approbatioe Caroli regis: li. i Collationes multae: li. i Epistolarũ ad diuersos: li. i Et quaedam alia. Moritur Auiniōne sepultus sub Carolo imperatore quarto: Anno domini Mill'. CCC.LI. Indictione.v. Regorius Arimīnēsis: ordinis fratrũ heremitarũ sancti Augustini prior ge generalis: uir in divinis scripturis doctissim. & in phia scholaistica multũ eru, ditus: ingenio et eloquio clar. in gymnasio parisiēlĩ magnā eruditiōs suae gloria ab omnib. cōmeruit: quippe q. uita et doctrina celeberrimus effulsit: Scri, psit nō spernēdae lectionis opuscula: de quib. ista ferunt potiora: Super sententias: li. iiiij In epistolas Pauli apōl: li. xiiiij Et quaedam alia. Claruit temporibus Caroli quarti imperatoris: & Clemētis papae sexti: Anno do, mini Mill'.CCC.ac.L. Hilippus de Pergamo prior monasteriũ sancte Mariae de Auancia in Pā, dua: ordinis sancti patris nostri Benedicti: uir in divinis scripturis studio, fus et erudit. & sacerlīi philosophiae nō ignarus: ingenio praestas et cla, rus eloquio. Scripsit nōnulla doctrinae sancte opuscula: quibus nomē suũ ad noticia posteritatis trāmislit. E quib. ego reperi tĩ volumẽ magnũ: Super Ethicā Catonis. li. i Sermones etiam scripsit dicie. li. i Caetera quae composuit: ad noticia nostrae lectionis minime uenerũt. Obannes de Beka: natione teutonicus: clericus ecclesiae Traiectensis: uir in scripturis sanctis admodũ studiosus et doctus: & sacerlīi philosophiae nō ignarus. Edidit quaedam ingenij sui nō cōtemnēda opuscula: de quib. ego uidi tĩ: opus simplici et aperto sermōe cōscriptũ ad dũm Johanne epm Tra, iectis ecclesiae: & Guilhelmũ ducē Hollandiae: de gestis pontificũ Traiectensiũ: & co mitũ Hollandinorũ: quũa tēpore sancti willebrordi primi epi uisũ ad annũ domini Mill'.CCC.ac.XLVI. deducens praenotari uoluit: Chronica Traiecten. eccliae: li. i De caetens nibil uidi. Claruit temporibus Ludouici quarti: & Caroli similiter quarti imperatorũ: Anno LIBER

Book

Alphonsus, bishop of Seville, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, a man very learned both in divine Scripture and in secular letters, and among the ecclesiastical doctors most celebrated in his own time, distinguished in intellect and eloquence. He published some volumes of great authority, by which he made his name known also to posterity. Of these I have found only the subtle and notable work:

On the Sentences, four books.

Of the rest I have learned nothing.

He flourished under Louis, the fourth emperor, in the year of the Lord 1340.

Johannes de Bachone, an Englishman, of the Order of the Friars of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man most learned in divine Scripture and excellently instructed both in canon law and in secular philosophy; in the school of Paris he shone with no less distinction in conduct than in learning, and afterwards, promoted to provincial of England, he vigorously governed his order by word and example. He wrote many notable volumes, by which he transmitted his name to posterity. Among them the following are reported:

On the Gospel of Matthew, one book. On the Gospel of Mark, one book. On the Gospel of Luke, one book. On the Gospel of John, one book. On the Epistles of Paul, one book. On the Acts of the Apostles, one book. On the Canonical Epistles, one book. On the Apocalypse, one book. On the Sentences, one book. Various Quodlibets, one book. Mirror of His Order, one book. Defense of His Order, one book. Against the Jews, one book. On the Poverty of Christ, one book. On the Rule of His Order, one book. And many others.

He also published explanations on the books of blessed Augustine On the Holy Trinity and The City of God, and of Anselm, Why God Became Man and On the Incarnation of the Word; in all these he exercised his talent magnificently. He flourished in the times of Charles, the fourth emperor, and Pope Clement VI, in the year of the Lord 1350.

Johannes Eligerus de Gonderbleuen, a German by nation, once a hearer of Johannes de Saxonia, the most distinguished astronomer; a man most learned in secular letters, a philosopher and astronomer most celebrated among all those of his time, and sufficiently imbued with divine Scripture; subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence. He wrote volumes in the mathematical science that are not to be despised, by which he transmitted his name to posterity. Among them the following are reported:

On the Construction of the Astrolabe, one book. On the Usefulness of the Astrolabe, one book. On the Usefulness of the Quadrant, one book. Also On the Magnet, one book. On the Astrogemeter, one book.

Ptolemy, king of the stars. With principal zeal and understanding. The uses of the new quadrant. About to treat of the magnet. The highest [unclear] for us. And several others.

He flourished in the times of Charles, the fourth emperor, and Pope Clement VI, in the year of the Lord 1350.

Bvpertus, a Frenchman by nation, of the Order of the Friars of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man devoted to and learned in divine writings and excellently instructed in scholastic philosophy; distinguished in intellect, clear in speech. He published

182
domini.Millesimo.CCC.L. Hancifcus Petrarcha: natioe Etrusca: uir in divinis scripturis eruditus: & in faecularib. liris omni sui tèporis longe doctissim: phus: rhetor: & po eta celebrim: qui liras humanitatis post longa silètia mortuas: ut ita dixe rim: ab inferis reuocavit ad superos: nó minus sancta còuerstatione q sciètia clarus emicuit. Amore nàq christi et phia salutaris uità solitaria aggreslus é: in qua uifq ad mortè:meditado:oràdo et scribèdo pleuerans: totò múdo eius fama ferebat. De cuius opusculis reperi: De uita solitaria: li. i. Paucos homines notui. De remedijs fortunae: li. ii. Cum res fortunalsq. In, vín. plal', poenitètiales: li. i. De conflictu curarù: li. i. De praelenti múdo: li. i. De bistoria Grisildis: li. i. Bucolicoru metrice: li. i. viii Monice tranquillo. Epistolarũ ad diueros: li. i. Africa ad Rupertũ regem: li. i. Vita Scipionis africani: li. i. De rebus memorabilib: li. i. De pomerijs ad Sagemor: li. i. Alia quoq multa edidit: quae ad manus nostras minime uenerút. Morìe in here, mitorio suo agri Patauini sub Carolo imperatore quarto: & Gregorio papa unde, cimo: Anno dni Mill'. CCC. LXXIII. Indìstione uero.xii. Ichael de Masha: ordinis fratrũ beremitarũ sancti Augustini: uir in diuinis in scripturis studiosus:eruditus: & ueterũ lectione diues:atq in faecularibus litteris nobiliter doctus:ingenio subtilis:eloquio clarus: & fermonũ decla/ mator egregius:uita quoq et còuerfatiõis bonestate insignis. Edidit multa praecla ra uolumina ad aëdificatione fidelũ:quibus nomẽ luũ cum gloria transmifit ad no ticia posteritatis. Equibus subiecta ferunt: Super sententias: li. iiiij In Elsia pphetam: li. i. In euangeliũ Matthaei: li. i. In euangeliũ Marci: li. i. In euangeliũ Lucae: li. i. In euangeliũ Iobannis: li. i. De uita christi: li. i. De passione domini: li. i. De quattuor uirtutib: li. i. Sermones uarii: li. i. Etalia multa. In multos denicq libros bibliae còmetarios elegãtes lucubrasse diciç. Claruittem, poribus Ludouici quarti: & Caroli similiter quarti imperatorũ: & Clemétis pape fexti: Anno domini Mill'. CCC.L. Richardus de Bury: episcopus Dilmelmëlis: Eduardi Anglorũ regis tertij cancellarius:ad quẽ Francisci Petrarchae: de insula Tile interrogatis extat epistola:uir in divinis scripturis studiosifimus et ualde eruditus atq in fae, cularib. litteris sufficiëter instructus:libros et amator singularis et celebrim: mul tis expèsis et laborib. i uniuersitate Oxoniësi insignẽ bibliothecã fundauit: quam ad publicã utilitate inibi studentiũ incredibili studio instituit. Scripsit de amore li broru et institutione dictae bibliothecae pulcherrimu tractatu:qui iam impressus es quae graeco fermone praenotauit:

On Ecclesiastical Writers Fol. 89

various little works on the Holy Scriptures; in these, splendidly exercising his talent, he made the memory of his name known even to posterity. He was also an excellent preacher of the divine word, and wrote many things useful to declaimers of sermons. Of these they report the following:

On the Sentences: 4 books On the Epistles of Paul: 14 books Sermons on the Season: 1 book Sermons on the Saints: 1 book

He composed many other things besides, which have not come to my knowledge.

Clement, the sixth pope, by homeland a Lemovician, formerly called Petrus Rogerii, abbot of [Fiscaniensis?] of the order of Saint Benedict, sat in the chair of Peter after Benedict XII for ten years and six months. He was a man learned in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular literature; an outstanding doctor of canon law, venerable no less in conduct than in knowledge; in delivering sermons to the people he was of excellent talent. He published certain distinguished little works, in which he showed the liveliness of his talent. Of these they report:

Various sermons: 1 book On the canonization of Yvo: 1 book On the approval of King Charles: 1 book Many collations: 1 book Letters to various persons: 1 book

And certain other things.

He died at Avignon, and was buried, under the emperor Charles IV, in the year of the Lord 1351, indiction 5.

Gregory of Rimini, prior general of the order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, was a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and very learned in scholastic philosophy, distinguished in talent and eloquence. In the school of Paris he won from all men great glory for his learning, since he shone forth most famously in life and doctrine. He wrote little works of no contemptible reading; of these they report the following as the more important:

On the Sentences: 4 books On the Epistles of Paul the Apostle: 14 books

And certain other things.

He flourished in the times of Charles IV, emperor, and Pope Clement VI, in the year of the Lord 1350.

Philippus de Pergamo, prior of the monastery of Saint Mary de Avancia in Padua, of the order of our holy father Benedict, was a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular philosophy, excellent in talent and distinguished in eloquence. He wrote some little works of holy doctrine, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these I found only one large volume:

On the Ethics of Cato: 1 book He also wrote sermons for speaking: 1 book

The rest that he composed have by no means come to the knowledge of our reading.

Johannes de Beka, a German by nation, cleric of the church of Utrecht, was a man very devoted to and learned in the Holy Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular philosophy. He published certain little works of his talent that are not to be despised; of these I have seen only one work, written in a simple and open style, addressed to lord Johannes, bishop of the church of Utrecht, and to Guilhelmus, duke of Holland, concerning the deeds of the bishops of Utrecht and the counts of Holland. Bringing it down from the time of Saint Willebrord, the first bishop, as I have seen, to the year of the Lord 1346, he wished it to be entitled:

Chronicle of the Church of Utrecht: 1 book

Of the rest I have seen nothing.

He flourished in the times of Louis IV and likewise Charles IV, emperors, in the year

Book

IbObannes de Erfordia:natiōe teutonicus:patria thoringus: ordinis fratrū minorū:doctor in diuinis scipturis illuminatus tam in utroqƺ n 4

in the year of the Lord 1350.

Francis Petrarch, of Tuscan nationality, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, and in secular letters by far the most learned of all in his time, a philosopher, rhetorician, and very celebrated poet, who, after long silences, called the letters of humanity, dead, so to speak, back from the lower world to the upper, shone forth no less clearly for holy conduct than for knowledge. For from love of Christ and of salutary philosophy he entered upon the solitary life; persevering in it until death by meditating, praying, and writing, his fame was carried through the whole world.

Of his works I have found:

On the Solitary Life, one book, “I have known few men.” On the Remedies of Fortune, two books, “When things and fortunes...” On the Seven Penitential Psalms, one book. On the Conflict of Cares, one book. On the Present World, one book. On the Story of Griselda, one book. Bucolics, in meter, one book, “Eight...” [unclear] “in tranquil...” Letters to various persons, one book. Africa, to King Robert, one book. The Life of Scipio Africanus, one book. On Memorable Matters, one book. On the [pomeria?], to [Sagemor?], one book.

He also published many other works, which have by no means come into our hands. He died in his hermitage in the territory of Padua under Emperor Charles IV and Pope Gregory XI, in the year of the Lord 1373, in the twelfth indiction.

Michael de Massa, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, a man devoted to the divine Scriptures, learned, rich in reading of the ancients, and nobly instructed in secular letters, subtle in talent, distinguished in speech, and an excellent declaimer of sermons, also notable for the goodness of his life and conduct. He published many excellent volumes for the edification of the faithful, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Among them the following are reported:

On the Sentences, four books. On Isaiah the Prophet, one book. On the Gospel of Matthew, one book. On the Gospel of Mark, one book. On the Gospel of Luke, one book. On the Gospel of John, one book. On the Life of Christ, one book. On the Passion of the Lord, one book. On the Four Virtues, one book. Various Sermons, one book. And many other works.

Moreover, he is said to have labored elegantly on commentaries on many books of the Bible. He flourished in the times of Louis IV and likewise Charles IV, emperors, and of Pope Clement VI, in the year of the Lord 1350.

Richard de Bury, bishop of Durham, chancellor of Edward III, king of the English, to whom there is extant a letter of Francis Petrarch in response to an inquiry about the island of Thule, a man most devoted to and very learned in the divine Scriptures, and sufficiently instructed in secular letters; a singular and very celebrated lover of books. With many expenses and labors he founded a distinguished library in the University of Oxford, which he established there with incredible zeal for the public benefit of the students. He wrote a very beautiful treatise on the love of books and the establishment of the said library, which has now been printed, which he entitled in the Greek language:

184
iure q̃ in saeculari philosophia nobiliter et egregie doctus. Edidit magnae auctori- tatis plura opuscula:in quibus uim ingenij sui praestantissimi etiā posteritati osten dit.E quibus ego uidi tm̄ volumē magnū quod praenotauit: Tabulã iuris: li.j Qm ut scriptũ est.xij.q. ij. Summã de casibus: li. ij Rogatus a fratribus ꝙ eis. De alijs nihil uidit.Fert aut elegãtes cõposuisse sermones:sed ad me nō uenerunt. Iohannes Taceßphale:natiõe anglicus:ordinis fratrũ beatae Mariae semp̄ uirginis de mõte Carmeli: doctor diuinaꝝ scripturaꝝ eruditꝰ:& saeculariũ lr̄aꝝ nō ignarus:ingenio subtilis:sermone cõpositus:declamator sermonũ omniũ suo tꝑe celeberrimꝰ.Edidit nō cõtemnẽdae lectiõis opuscula:quibꝰ ingeniũ utiliter exercitãs nomē suũ ad noticiã posteritatis cũ laude trāsmisit.E quibꝰ subie Super sententias: li. iiij (cta ferunt: In Apocalypsin lobãnis: li.j Sermones de tempore: li.j Sermones de sanctis: li.j Et quaedam alia. Claruit in cõuentu suo Norwicẽsi:ubi sepultus in pace quiescit. Rupertus Holkoth:natiõe Anglicus:ordinis praedicatorũ:uir in di- ruinis scripturis eruditissimꝰ:& saeculariũ lr̄aꝝ nō ignorans:ingenio praestãs et amp; clarꝰ eloquio:declamator quoqꝫ sermonũ egregius.Scripsit multa prae- clara opuscula:quibꝰ nomē suũ posteris notificauit.E quibꝰ ista ferunt: Vtrum quilibet uiator Dn̄s petra mea et amp; robur. Haec est uia:ambulate in. Theodosius de uita all̓. Super sententias: li. iiij In librũ sapiẽtiae: li.j De.vij.peccatis mortalibꝰ: li.j Moraliçationes: li.j De imortalitate aiae. li. In Canticacanticoꝝ:li. In Ecclesiasticũ imp̄fecte: li. Et alia plura. Moritur ex peste:postea q̃ lecturā sup librũ Eccłiastici inchoauerat:sub Carolo im peratore qrto:&amp; Clemẽte papa sexto:Anno dn̄i Mill'.CCC.XLIX. Indictõe. ij. N Icolaus Dorbin:natiõe Anglicꝰ:ordinis fratrũ beatissimae Mariae semp̃ uir- ginis de monte Carmeli:uir in diuinis scripturis eruditꝰ et amp; in saeculari ph̄ia egregie doctus:qui in uniuersitate Oxonien̄.legēdo et amp; disputãdo magnas ab omnibꝰ laudes cõmeruit:Scripsit nō spernẽdae lectioĩs opuscula:quibꝰ ingenij sui uiuacissimi uenā omnisariã locupletẽ ostẽdit.E quibus extant: Vtrum quilibet uiator Dn̄s petra me a et amp; rob ur. Haec eft u ia ambulate i n. Theodosius d e uit a all̓. Super sententias: li. iiij Determinatiões quaestionũ:li.j Et quaedam alia. Claruit in gymnasio Oxonien̄.&amp; uaria multaqƺ cõscripsit volumina. P Aulus de perusio: utriusqƺ iuris professor et amp; celeberrimꝰ interpres: atqƺ in alijs lr̄is hūanitatis egregie doctus: graeco et amp; latino ad ꝑfectũ instructꝰ elo- quio:cuftos et amp; magister bibliothecae Ruperti regis Siciliae doctissimi et amp; stu diosissimi principis multo tempore fuit.Scripsit quaedã praeclara opuscula: quibꝰ nomē suũ notificauit posteritati.E quibꝰ extat uolumẽ insigne:in quo multa sunt et amp;iocũda et amp; utilia de dijs gentiliũ et amp; aliorũ:quod praenotauit: Collectionum: li.j Et quaedam alia. B Claruit temporibus Caroli imperatoris quarti:Anno dn̄i Mill.CCCL. Onominus natiõe Pergomensis:ex Clusono oppido natꝰ:medicꝰ doctus et amp;oim suo tꝑe facile peritissimꝰ atqƺ ĩ caeteris ph̄iae disciplinis nō mediocris

On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 90.

Philobiblon, one book, “A desirable treasure.” Several letters, one book. And certain other works. He flourished under Emperor Charles IV, in the year of the Lord 1350.

John [Walßgram?], an Englishman by nation, of the Order of the Friars of the Blessed Virgin Mary of Mount Carmel, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly taught in secular philosophy, subtle and acute in intellect, adorned with the master’s cap in the school of Paris, shone forth as most celebrated in lecturing and disputing. He wrote certain excellent volumes, by which he made his name known. Among these there exists a distinguished work:

On the Sentences, three books. Various Questions, one book. The rest which he is said to have composed have not yet come to my knowledge.

John de Saxo, of the Order of the Friars Minor, learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly taught both in canon law and in secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, an outstanding preacher in delivering sermons to the people and very famous in his time. He produced certain small works of reading not to be despised, which are necessary for the instruction of simple priests. Of these I have found only:

A Summary of Law, one book. Sermons on the Season, one book. Sermons on the Saints, one book.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Charles IV and Pope Clement VI, in the year of the Lord 1350.

Thomas of Argentina, a German by nation, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, after Gregory of Rimini prior general, a man most learned in the holy Scriptures and an excellent cultivator of secular philosophy, distinguished for his life and the honesty of his conduct, who wonderfully exalted his order by word and example. He wrote some excellent volumes on the Scriptures, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Among these there exists a very lucid work:

On the Sentences, three books, “The deep gave its voice.” Constitutions of his order, one book. And certain other works.

He flourished under Emperor Charles IV, in the year of the Lord 1350.

John Bramart of Aachen, a German by nation, of the Order of the Friars of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, provincial prior of Lower Germany, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and a most celebrated expounder of secular philosophy according to the custom of the scholastics of this time; distinguished in intellect and eloquence, an outstanding teacher in delivering sermons to the people. He wrote, for the usefulness of the faithful, small works not to be despised, by which, exercising his talent, he transmitted the memory of his name to posterity. Among these there are:

On the Sentences, four books. Various sermons, one book.

He is also said to have written many other works, which have not come to my knowledge.

Henry of Erfurt, a German by nation, [unclear] in the divine Scriptures by long study, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence. He wrote some volumes for the edification of the Church, by which he made his name known to many by report. Among these an historical work is reported:

On Memorable Deeds, one book. And certain other works.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Charles IV and Pope Clement VI, in the year of the Lord 1350.

John of Erfurt, a German by nation, a Thuringian by homeland, of the Order of the Friars Minor, an enlightened doctor in the divine Scriptures both in

185
DE SCRIPTORIBVS ECCLESIASTICIS Fol.9j eruditus: in medendis corporibus humanis expertissimus. Scripsit in ea faculta te non spernenda opuscula: quibus nomen suū ad noticiā posteritatis cum gloria transmisit.Sed ego nihil eorū uidifisse me memini.Fertur autē eius: De uenenis: li.j Quaestionū diuersarū: li.j Et quaedam alia. Claruit temporibus Caroli imperatoris quarti:& Clemētis papae sexti: Anno dn̄i Millefimo.CCC.L. Hilmannꝰ Aquensis:natione teutonicus:ordinis fratrū beatae Mariae sem per uirginis de mōte Carmeli:facratur litterarū insignis professor: ingenio praestans et declamator egregius : atqƺ in philosophia foeculari quā aristo- telicā appellant satis admodū eruditus:Scripsit ad utilitatē legentiū nō cõtemnē da syntagmata:quibꝰ famā nominis sui ad longinquos destinauit.E quibus fertur lectura una singulariter notabilis:quā Coloniae legerit publice: In euangeliū Matthaei: li.j Super sentētias quoqƺ: li. iiij Sermones etiam uarios in bibliam cõmentarios composuisse dicitur: De quibꝰ cum sim incertus:nihil certi possum iudicare. B artholus de faxoferrato: Cini Iacobi bothigarij doctorū quodā audi tor saecula nō habuerūt:ingenio subtilis acutus:eloquio cõptus diser tus.Edidit quaedā praeclara uolumina maxime in legibus:quae quantae auctorita tis hodie sint apud iuristas:nemo uel tenuiter doctus expertꝰ qui ignorat.E qui bus ferunt̃ cõmentaria insignia iuris ciuilis subiecta: Super Codice: li.ix Super.ff.ueteri: li.xxiiij Super.ff.nouo: li.xij Super.ff.Inforciati: li.xiij Super Institutis: li.iij Tyberiadis quoqƺ: li.j Consiliorū etiā: li.j De Guelphis Gibellinis: li.j Et multa alia.
