B Etrusthomas:ordinis fratrū beatae Marię semper uirginis de monte Carmeli:primū ep̄us Pacensis:deinde Cretēsis archiep̄us:nouissime uero pa triarcha Cōstantinopolitanꝰ:uir in diuinis scripturis eruditissimus:uita cõuersatione sanctissimus:quippe qui uiuus mortuus:signis miraculis multis legitur coruscasse:in declamandis sermonibus ad populū excellentis ingenij fuit. Scripsit quaedam praeclara uolumina:de quibus ista ferunt̃: Super sententias: li.iij Sermones quoqƺ uarij: li.j Et quaedā similita. Claruit temporibus Caroli imperator is quarti:& Clemētis papae sexti: Anno domini Millefimo. CCC.L.Et in Cypro sepultus est. B Artholomaeus ordinis fratrū sancti Francisci:natione anglicus: uir in diuinis scriptoris studiosissimus:& non infime doctus:atqƺ in foecula tribus lr̄is sufficiēter imbutus:nec minus religiosa cõuersatiōe q̄ sciētia insigne.Edidit nō spernēdae auctoritatis opuscula:quorū lectio simplicioribus fratribus necessaria iudicat̃.E quibꝰ ego reperi tantū uolumē qđ praenotauit:

in law as well as in secular philosophy, nobly and excellently learned. He published several works of great authority, in which he showed even to posterity the power of his most excellent talent. Of these I have seen only the large volume which he entitled:

A Table of Law: book 1. “Quoniam, as it is written, XII, question II.” A Summary on Cases: book 2. “Asked by the brothers that to them.”

I have seen nothing of the others. It is said, however, that he composed elegant sermons, but they have not reached me.

John Tacesphale, an Englishman by birth, of the order of the brothers of blessed Mary ever virgin of Mount Carmel, a learned doctor of the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, subtle in talent, composed in speech, the most celebrated preacher of all sermons in his time. He published works not to be despised in reading; by these, exercising his talent usefully, he transmitted his name with praise to the knowledge of posterity. Of these the following are reported:

On the Sentences: books 4. On the Apocalypse of John: book 1. Sermons on the Season: book 1. Sermons on the Saints: book 1. And certain others.

He flourished in his convent at Norwich, where, buried, he rests in peace.

Rupert Holkoth, an Englishman by birth, of the order of preachers, a man most learned in divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, outstanding in talent and distinguished in eloquence, and also an excellent preacher of sermons. He wrote many outstanding works, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these the following are reported:

Whether every wayfarer. “The Lord is my rock and my strength.” “This is the way; walk in it.” Theodosius on the Life [unclear]. On the Sentences: books 4. On the Book of Wisdom: book 1. On the Seven Deadly Sins: book 1. Moralizations: book 1. On the Immortality of the Soul: book [unclear]. On the Song of Songs: book [unclear]. On Ecclesiasticus, unfinished: book [unclear]. And many others.

He died of the plague, after he had begun his lecture on the Book of Ecclesiasticus, under Charles, fourth emperor, and Pope Clement VI, in the year of the Lord 1349, in the second indiction.

Nicholas Dorbin, an Englishman by birth, of the order of the brothers of most blessed Mary ever virgin of Mount Carmel, a man learned in divine Scriptures and excellently taught in secular philosophy, who in the University of Oxford, by lecturing and disputing, earned great praise from all. He wrote works not to be scorned in reading, by which he showed the rich and varied vein of his very lively talent. Of these there are extant:

Whether every wayfarer. “The Lord is my rock and my strength.” “This is the way; walk in it.” Theodosius on the Life [unclear]. On the Sentences: books 4. Determinations of Questions: book 1. And certain others.

He flourished in the school at Oxford, and wrote many various volumes.

Paul of Perugia, professor of both laws and a most celebrated interpreter, and excellently learned in other humane letters, perfectly trained in Greek and Latin eloquence, was for a long time keeper and master of the library of Rupert, king of Sicily, a most learned and most studious prince. He wrote certain outstanding works by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these there is extant a distinguished volume, in which there are many pleasant and useful things concerning the gods of the gentiles and of others, which he entitled:

Collections: book 1. And certain others.

He flourished in the times of Charles, fourth emperor, in the year of the Lord 1350.

Bonominus, a native of Bergamo, born in the town of Clusone, a learned physician and easily the most skilled of all in his time, and in the other disciplines of philosophy of no mediocre

On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 9[unclear] learned, most experienced in healing human bodies. In that faculty he wrote works not to be despised, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. But I do not remember having seen any of them. The following of his are reported:

On Poisons, one book; Various Questions, one book; and certain others.

He flourished in the time of Charles IV, emperor, and Pope Clement VI, in the year of the Lord 1350.

Hilmannus of Aachen, a German by nation, of the Order of the Brothers of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a distinguished professor of sacred letters, outstanding in talent and an excellent declaimer, and also quite sufficiently learned in secular philosophy, which they call Aristotelian, wrote, for the use of readers, treatises not to be despised, by which he sent the fame of his name to distant places. Of these, one particularly noteworthy lecture is reported, which he read publicly at Cologne:

On the Gospel of Matthew, one book; also On the Sentences, four books. He is also said to have composed various sermons and commentaries on the Bible; about these, since I am uncertain, I can judge nothing certain.

Bartolus of Saxoferrato, once a hearer of the doctors Cinus and Jacobus Bothigarius, had few equals in the age: subtle and acute in talent, polished and eloquent in speech. He published certain excellent volumes, especially on the laws; how great their authority is today among jurists, no one even slightly learned and experienced is ignorant. Among them are reported the following distinguished commentaries on civil law:

On the Code, nine books; On the Old Digest, twenty-four books; On the New Digest, twelve books; On the Infortiatum, thirteen books; On the Institutes, three books; also Tiberias, one book; also Counsels, one book; On the Guelphs and Ghibellines, one book; and many others.

He died under Charles IV, emperor, and Pope Innocent VI, in the year of the Lord 1355, in the eighth indiction, and in the fifty-sixth year of his age.

Bertrus Thomas, of the Order of the Brothers of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, first bishop of Patti, then archbishop of Crete, and most recently patriarch of Constantinople, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, most holy in life and conduct, since indeed, alive and dead, he is read to have shone with many signs and miracles, was of excellent talent in delivering sermons to the people.

He wrote certain excellent volumes, of which the following are reported:

On the Sentences, three books; also various sermons, one book; and certain similar things.

He flourished in the time of Charles IV, emperor, and Pope Clement VI, in the year of the Lord 1350. And he was buried in Cyprus.

Bartholomaeus, of the Order of the Brothers of Saint Francis, an Englishman by nation, a man most devoted to the divine writings and not slightly learned, and sufficiently imbued with secular letters, and no less distinguished in religious conduct than in knowledge. He published works of authority not to be despised, whose reading is judged necessary for the simpler brothers. Among these I found only the volume which he entitled:

A book, "Since the properties of things follow..."

On the properties of things: nineteen books. Various sermons: one book. He is said also to have written many other things, but they have by no means come into our hands.

Petrus Boherius, abbot of Saint Avianus, of the order of the divine father Benedict, a jurist, an eminent cultivator of sacred Scripture, subtle in intellect, distinguished in speech, a most celebrated director of monastic discipline, produced for the edification of his brothers several little works, by which he transmitted his name to posterity. Of these I have found only:

On the Rule of Saint Benedict: one book. On the Mirror of Monks: one book. On the signs of utterances: one book. Of the rest I have seen nothing.

Since he was a most celebrated doctor of decrees, he commented on the Rule of the holy father Benedict in a new and unusual kind of exposition, comparing all its chapters, judgments, doctrines, and also, what requires greater diligence, its words, counsels, and precepts with pontifical law, and with admirable subtlety confirmed them by the canons of the fathers. He flourished in the times of Charles IV, emperor, and Pope Innocent VI, in the year of the Lord 1360.

Jacobus de Altavilla, German by nation, of Rinaugia by homeland, of the diocese of Mainz, a most learned professor of sacred letters, nobly instructed in secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, produced several notable little works on the divine Scriptures, by which he destined his name for the knowledge of posterity. Of these I have hitherto been found worthy to see only a notable volume:

On the Sentences: four books. Also various Questions: one book.

He flourished in the times of Charles IV, emperor, and Pope Innocent VI, in the year of the Lord 1360.

Johannes de Ymenhusen, German by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, ready in intellect, cautious in knowledge, scholastic in speech, an outstanding teacher no less by example than by word, wrote certain excellent volumes, not to be despised in reading; by these, magnificently exercising his intellect, he also made known to posterity the memory of his name. Of these I have found only:

On the Sentences: three books. Elegant sermons: one book. Of the others I have seen nothing.

He flourished under Charles IV, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1360.

Petrus Berthorius, French by nation, of Poitiers by homeland, prior of the monastery of Saint Eligius at Paris, of the order of the divine father Benedict, a man most studious in the divine writings, very learned, and notably instructed in secular letters, of excellent intellect in declaiming sermons to the people, an outstanding philosopher, historian, and cosmographer, wrote many excellent volumes, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Of these the following are reported. To Johannes de Pratis, bishop of Palestrina, cardinal of the holy Roman Church, he wrote a great and distinguished work, now printed in three volumes, not useless for the simpler preachers, which they call the Dictionary, but he himself wished it to be entitled:

Moral Repertory: three books. "To the reverend father in Christ, lord..." Also Moral Reductory: four books. "See how not only in the..." Moral Inductory: one book. "Considering the beginning of history..." He wrote a Cosmography: one book. Various sermons: two books. And many other things.

Finally, at the instance of Johannes, king of France, he translated Titus Livius into the French language.

And it should be noted that of the three moral works which we marked down in the first place, each one of the three

consists of large volumes; of these, one part of the moral Reductorium, embracing in a moral sense all the historical books of the Bible, has been printed, and it begins from Genesis thus: “God, in the creation of the world,” etc. Letters of his to various persons are reported, and small but many treatises.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Charles IV and Pope Innocent VI, in the year of the Lord 1360.

Johannes de Tambacho, a German by nation, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a man much practiced and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular philosophy either, outstanding in talent, composed in expression with scholastic brilliance, published certain volumes not to be despised, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these I have found only the following: a great work, not to be rejected, against the weapons of raging adverse [fortune?], no less useful than pleasant, which he wished to be entitled:

The Consolation of Theology, 15 books. “Whatever things have been written,” etc. On the Sensible Delights of Paradise, 1 book. “You were in the delights of the paradise of God.” He published Sermons, 1 book. And certain other works.

He flourished under Emperor Charles IV, in the year of the Lord 1360.

Leonardus de Chifano, of the Order of Friars Minor of Saint Francis, the twenty-fourth minister general, and thereafter priest-cardinal of the Roman Church, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, very skilled in secular philosophy, subtle in talent, distinguished in eloquence. He is said to have left many monuments of his talent. Of these I have found very few:

On the Sentences, 3 books. On the Song of Songs, 1 book. A notable Summa, 1 book. Various Sermons, 1 book.

He flourished under Emperor Charles IV, in the year of the Lord 1370.

Johannes Balistarii, a Catalan by country, of the Order of the Brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, the seventeenth prior general, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, who governed his order vigorously in deed and word for sixteen years, composed distinguished monuments of his talent. Of these there are reported:

On the Sentences, 4 books. On the War of the Church Militant, 1 book. Various Sermons, 1 book. And certain other works.

The aforesaid distinguished work On the Strong War of the Church Militant, against Antichrist assailing it, he sent dedicated to Pope Gregory XI. He died in the times of Emperor Charles IV and Pope Gregory XI, in the year of the Lord 1373, in the twelfth indiction, in his convent of Majorca.

Johannes Boccacius of Certaldo, an Italian by nation, a Florentine by country, a man easily the most learned of all in secular letters in his time, not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, a poet, philosopher, astronomer, subtle in talent, eloquent in speech, published many distinguished volumes, by which he brought his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these the following are reported. To Robert, king of Sicily:

On the Genealogy of the Gods, 14 books. “If sufficiently from the things reported, lord.” On Illustrious Men, 1 book. “As I was seeking what.” On Famous Women, [unclear] book. “On the day before, distinguished among women.” On the Heresies of the Bohemians, [unclear] book. “I had indeed risen weary.” On the Victories of Sigismund, [unclear] book. On the Wars of the Emperors, [unclear] book. On Mountains, 1 book. “Afterwards concerning mountains [unclear].” On Springs, 1 book.

R Ichardus archiepiscopꝰ Ardmacensis et primas Hyberniae:uir ĩdiuinis scrip- turis eruditus secularis philosophiae iurisqꝫ canonici nō ignarus: inge- nio clarus: sermonem scholasticum: in declamandis sermonibꝰ ad populũ ex- cellentis industriae:scripsit ingenij sui nōnulla opuscula:quibus nome̅ suũ ad poste- ros transmisit. On rivers: one book. On the wars of the Florentines: one book. On the rebellion of the lands of the Church: one book. On the victory of the Tartars: one book. On pools and marshes: one book. On the names of the sea: one book. Bucolics: one book. On the capture of Constantinople: one book. Letters to various persons: one book. And many other things.

In the vernacular language, moreover, many books of his are extant, full of jests and vanities, such as the book of the Hundred Tales; Corbatius; Philostratus. He died under Emperor Charles IV and Pope Gregory XI, in the year of the Lord 1375, in the thirteenth indiction, at the age of sixty-two.

Johannes Hildesheimensis, German by nation, of the Order of the Brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, learned in the Holy Scriptures, nobly instructed in secular letters, an outstanding philosopher and poet, was of excellent talent in delivering sermons to the people. He was formerly at Avignon the devoted household servant of blessed Peter Thomas, the General, a most holy man, of whom we made mention above. He wrote many distinguished little works in verse and prose, by which he transmitted his name with glory to posterity. Of these, the following are reported. To Florentius, bishop of Münster, he published a lengthy volume:

On the Three Holy Kings: one book. A Chronicle of Histories: one book. A Defence of His Order: one book. On Monsters in the Church: one book. On the Fountain of Life: one book. On Antichrist: one book. Against the Jews: one book. Against One Painting Shameful Things: one book. Eighty Letters: one book. Various Sermons: one book. And certain other things.

He flourished in the time of Emperor Charles IV, in the year of the Lord 1370.

Johannes Marronis, English by nation, of the Order of the Brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, outstanding in secular philosophy [unclear]. He composed certain distinguished little works commending his talent, by which he also made his name known to posterity. Among these there is said to be the notable work which he entitled:

A Table of Originals: one book. Against the Wycliffites: one book. And certain other things.

He flourished in the school of Oxford, where by teaching, disputing, and writing he earned great praise from all, at about the time when the errors of John Wyclif were condemned by the archbishop of Canterbury.

Johannes Golein, Norman by homeland, of the Order of the Brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, prior of the convent of Rouen, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures and sufficiently instructed in secular letters, subtle in talent and distinguished in eloquence, wrote little works of no contemptible authority, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among these there is extant a notable work:

[unclear] by poetic fiction. And if sometimes from pools. A modest portion of the labor undertaken. Tyndarus was not better. When of the most venerable men.

On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 93

On the Sentences: three books. On the office of the Mass: one book. Sing to the Lord a new song. Various questions. He also published some other works besides, which have by no means come into our hands.

Heinricus de Dolendorp, of the Order of the Brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man learned by long exercise in the divine Scriptures and perfectly instructed in the disciplines of worldly philosophy, which they call Aristotelian; acute in intellect and very capable at debating and unraveling scholastic questions. He wrote, for the instruction of readers, certain excellent volumes. Of these I have found only four books: On the Sentences. Of the rest I have found nothing. He flourished in the times of Charles IV, emperor, and Urban V, pope, in the year of the Lord 1370.

Gallus, abbot of the monastery of Aula Regia in Bohemia, of the Order, as they say, of the Cistercians, German by nation, a man skilled by long exercise in the divine Scriptures and rich in reading of the ancients; an outstanding contemplator of divine things, subtle in intellect, clear and orderly in speech, and also distinguished in the regular conduct of life. For the edification of his brothers he published certain excellent volumes, by which he sent his name on to the knowledge of posterity. Of these there is extant a great and notable dialogue between father and son, which he entitled: The Pomegranate: three books. Son, when you approach service. Sermons to the brothers: one book. Today there is great use of this volume, The Pomegranate, among truly devout religious, because it is suitable for beginners, for those making progress, and for the perfect.

Richard, archbishop of Armagh and primate of Ireland, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy and canon law; eminent in intellect, scholastic in discourse, and of excellent industry in delivering sermons to the people. He wrote some little works of his intellect, by which he transmitted his name to posterity. When he once preached to the people on the matter of mendicancy, he put forward nine conclusions; offended by these, the mendicant friars appealed before the people to the Apostolic See. Therefore, when both the archbishop and the friars appeared at Avignon before Pope Innocent VI and the cardinals, in the year of the Lord 1357, on the eighth of the month, Archbishop Richard publicly set forth, read, and pronounced: his Propositions: book [unclear]. He also wrote Sermons: book [unclear]. Questions on the Sentences: book [unclear]. And certain other things. Do not judge according to... He flourished in the times of Charles IV, emperor, and Innocent VI, pope, in the year of the Lord 1370.

Matthew of Kraków, Polish by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy; ready in intellect, scholastic in speech. Raised to the master's chair in the Prague school, he earned great praise from everyone for his learning. He wrote many excellent little works, though only a few of them have come into our hands. I have seen his work, not to be rejected, addressed to Heinrich, bishop of the church of Warmia, on predestination, namely that God made all things well; the speakers in this dialogue are father and son. He entitled it: Rationale of Divine Works: seven books. I should like it to be explained how. Also On Contracts: one book. On the transfer of temporal things. On the celebration of Mass: one book. To the bishop of Warmia: one book. Letters to various persons: one book.

Book Sermons, conferences. He flourished first in the Prague studium; then, when he was driven out for a time with the other Germans by the Hussites, he taught letters in the Parisian academy.

Johannes Fust, a German by nationality, from the town of Kreuznach in the county of Sponheim, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, prior of Strasbourg, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, of excellent talent in delivering sermons to the people, wrote, while he was still lector in the convent of Kreuznach, some not contemptible little works for the instruction of simple preachers, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these we have seen:

Sermons on the Season: one book. Sermons on the Saints: one book. Weekday Sermons for Lent: one book.

But of the other things which he composed, nothing has yet come into our hands. He is said to have flourished at Kreuznach around the time of Emperor Charles IV. The convent at Kreuznach has the originals of the sermons of the said Fust.

Gerardus Magnus of Deventer, a German by nationality, of the diocese of Utrecht, a man excellently learned both in the divine Scriptures and in canon law, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, who first established at Deventer the house of the brothers whom they call “of the Common Life.” He wrote several little works of not contemptible reading, by which, exercising his talent, he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. For he was renowned throughout all Germany not only for learning, but also for religious life and praiseworthy conduct. Of his little works they report these:

On Contracts and [Usury?]: one book. On the Instruction of Novices: one book. On the Letting of Pastoral Care: one book. On the Interior Life: one book. On the Government of Nuns: one book. On the Disadvantages of Marriage: one book. Letters to Various Persons: one book. Various Sermons: one book. And many other things.

He died under Emperor Wenceslaus and Pope Urban VI, in the year of the Lord 1384, in the seventh indiction, in the forty-fourth year of his age.

[unclear], [of the order of the brothers of Blessed Ma]ry ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, learned in the divine Scriptures, of excellent and vigorous talent in preaching to the people. He wrote not contemptible little works for preachers of the divine word, by which he made his name known to many. Of these the following notable items are extant:

A Certain Lecture: one book. Sermons on the Season: one book. Sermons on the Saints: one book.

He flourished in the [Cambridge?] academy in England, where by writing and disputing he acquired great glory for his learning.

Franciscus Martini, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a Catalan by nationality, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, an outstanding declaimer. He published a distinguished volume, furnished with much diligence, on the holy and most pure conception of the glorious Virgin Mother of God, which he entitled:

Compendium: seven books.

And certain other things. He flourished in the convent of Barcelona, where the aforesaid golden work

James of Lausanne, of the Order of Preaching Friars of St Dominic, and, as they report, bishop of a certain city, a man most devoted to the divine Scriptures and skilled by long practice, ready in intellect, scholastic in speech, and quite distinguished in delivering sermons to the people. He wrote little works of no contemptible usefulness, by which he made his name known to posterity. Among these they report:

On Genesis, one book: “In the beginning God created.” On Exodus, one book: “I shall come to you,” etc. On Leviticus, one book. On the Book of Numbers, one book. On Deuteronomy, one book: “As in the day [unclear].” Sermons on the season, one book: “I am fixed with Christ to the cross.” Sermons on the saints, one book. Lenten sermons, one book. He also published many other things: lectures on the sacred books, conferences, various determinations, and treatises, which have not come into our hands.

[unclear]

Conrad of Alzey, a town of the diocese of Mainz in the Palatinate, three miles distant from Worms, a German by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and excellently taught in secular letters, a philosopher, poet, and mathematician most celebrated among the Germans in his time, subtle in intellect and clear in eloquence, excellent in verse and prose. In both styles he wrote certain distinguished little works, by which he made his mind known. Among these there is extant a volume, adorned with beautiful variety in verses and rhythms, concerning the most holy and most pure Mary, Mother of God, and the redemption of the human race, entitled:

The Work of Figures, one book. Letters to Various Persons, one book. Poems also, one book. And many other things.

He flourished around the times of Emperor Charles IV, in the year of the Lord 1370.

[unclear]

Stephen Petringon, an Englishman by nation, of the Order of the Friars of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect and a most acute disputant, and very renowned in delivering sermons to the people. He published little works not to be spurned, by which he brought his name to the knowledge of many. Among these are:

Against the Wycliffites, one book. A Repertory of Arguments, one book. A Certain Notable Lecture, one book. Sermons on the season, one book. Sermons on the saints, one book. And not a few other things.

He flourished in the University of Oxford, at the time when John Wycliffe was [unclear].

[unclear]

Bertram, bishop of Thessalonica, of the Order of Preaching Friars, a German by nation, vicar in pontificals of the bishop of Metz, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and among the most famous doctors of his time, outstanding in intellect and clear in eloquence, and also an excellent declaimer of sermons. He wrote to Cuno, archbishop of Trier, a distinguished work entitled:

On the Illusions of Demons, one book: “To the most reverend father in Christ.” To the same, On Schism, one book: “The wise shall possess glory.” Various sermons, one book. And several other things.

He died under Emperor Wenceslaus and Pope Urban VI, in the year of the Lord 1387, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February, in the tenth indiction. He was buried in his convent at [Coeluestinum?].

Thomas Lombe, of the Order of the Friars of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, an Englishman by nation, a man learned in the holy Scriptures by long practice and daily study, and well instructed in the precepts of the philosophers, subtle and keen in intellect; in the school of Oxford, after attaining the magisterial chair, he earned great praise for his learning. He wrote an excellent work:

On the Sentences, four books. Against the Lollards, one book. On the Incarnation of the Lord, [unclear]. Sermons, [unclear] books. And various questions. And certain other things.

He flourished in the University of Oxford, especially at the time when John Wycliffe in England was exhumed and publicly burned.

Philip Riboti, a Catalan by nation, of the Order of the Friars of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, and provincial prior of Catalonia, a man devoted to and learned in the holy Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular letters, venerable also in life and conduct, and an excellent lover and cultivator of the Carmelite Order. For the edification of the brethren he wrote little works by no means contemptible; in these, showing the fervor of a spiritual heart toward his religion, he also commended the memory of his name to posterity. Among these there is extant a volume not to be rejected, concerning the first institution, enlargement, and confirmation of his order, which he entitled concerning the deeds:

Of the Carmelites in Particular, ten books: “When the Israelite people.” On Illustrious Men of the Carmelites, one book. Sermons and letters.

193

Claruit temporibus wencislai imperatoris: Bonifacij papae noni: Anno domini Millesimo.CCC.ac.XC.

Moreover he composed several other works, which have not come to my knowledge.

Nicolaus Rizonis, by homeland a Toulousain, of the order of the brothers of blessed Mary ever virgin of Mount Carmel, and provincial prior in the kingdom of Sicily: a learned man, distinguished in life and conduct, an excellent preacher of sermons, subtle in intellect and lucid in speech. He published some little works on the Scriptures, whose [unclear] will not be contemptible to preachers of the word. Of these they report:

Sermons on the Temporal Cycle, book 1. Sermons on the Saints, book 1. A twofold Lenten collection, books 2.

Concerning the other things which he composed, nothing has yet come to my knowledge.

Henricus de [Kalkar?], by nation a German, of the Carthusian order, and prior of the house of Saint Barbara in Cologne Agrippina: a man having an intellect enlightened in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant either of secular letters, notable in life and conduct. He published little works not to be despised in reading, whose [unclear] is judged very useful for religious and devout brothers. Among them they report these:

Monastic Exercises, book [unclear]. A [Loquagum?] on Rhetoric, book [unclear]. A [Cantuagum?] on Music, book [unclear]. On the Origin of His Order, book [unclear].

And certain other things, pertaining especially to the cleansing of consciences. He flourished under the emperor Wenceslaus, in the year of the Lord 1390.

Richardus Maydescon, of the order of the brothers of blessed Mary ever virgin of Mount Carmel, by nation an Englishman: a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, and excellently taught in secular philosophy, which they call Aristotelian; bright in intellect, scholastic in speech, and a distinguished preacher. He wrote many commendable little works, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among these I have found:

Against the Lollards of Wycliffe. Sermons on the Temporal Cycle. Sermons on the Saints. The rest are unknown to me.

He flourished in the school of Oxford especially at that time when the heresy of John Wycliffe began to spring up in England; and he wrote various things.

Marsilius de Inghen, by nation an Englishman: a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and most nobly taught in secular philosophy; the first founder of the Heidelberg school, which Rupert, duke of Bavaria and count palatine of the Rhine, magnificently endowed when he established it, and Pope Urban VI confirmed on the model of Paris; also, as Wimpheling testifies, canon and treasurer of the church of Saint Andrew of Cologne. He published little works not to be despised, by which he made his name known to posterity. Among these, in the library of Heidelberg, they have today, written in his own hand:

Questions on the Sentences. A Notable Dialectic. Commentaries on Aristotle. And certain other things.

He died under the emperor Wenceslaus and Pope Boniface IX, in the year of the Lord 1393, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of September, in the second indiction. He was buried at Heidelberg in the church of Saint Peter. There are some who write that he was a German; to them I freely grant their judgment. It is certain, however, that he was called from the school of Paris to Heidelberg for the beginning of the university.

Johannes, monk of the monastery of Castell, in the diocese of Eichstatt, of the order of Saint Benedict, by nation a German: a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular letters; excellent in intellect and eloquent in speech; a distinguished theologian, philosopher, and rhetorician. He wrote many excellent volumes, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among these I have found only: a great and most famous work, divided into two volumes, which with immense and commendable study [unclear]

On the Rule of Saint Benedict. A Breviary of the Bible. Sermons on the Temporal Cycle. Sermons on the Saints. Sermons on the Passion of the Lord, 42. Letters to Various Persons.

Moreover he published many other things, which have not yet come to my knowledge.

Conradus de Monte Puellarum, by nation a German, canon of the church of Regensburg: a man learned in the divine Scriptures and most learned in secular philosophy, subtle in intellect and bright in eloquence. First, receiving the rudiments of the liberal arts in the school of Erfurt, he then betook himself to the university of Paris, where, publicly lecturing to students on philosophy and sacred letters for eight years, he was adorned with the badge of the doctorate. He wrote to Lord Lupold, bishop of Bamberg, a great and noble work which he entitled [Concerning?] the Greeks:

Economics. Monastics, to the duke of Austria. Politics also. Various Questions.

And many other things. He flourished in the times of the emperor Wenceslaus and Pope Urban VI, in the year of the Lord 1390.

Henricus Boyc, by nation a Breton, from the diocese of Leon, as he testifies at the beginning of his work on the Decretals: a man most learned in canon law and in scholastic philosophy

[unclear] nobly learned; outstanding in ability and renowned for eloquence; diffuse and copious in thought. He wrote in that faculty volumes not to be despised, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these the following are reported:

On the Decretals, five books, “Venerabilibus discretis.” On the Sixth of the Decretals, one book. On the Clementines, one book.

It is also reported that he published commentaries on the Decrees, and various other treatises on diverse matters, which have by no means come into our hands.

Johannes Ruysbroeck, prior of the regular canons of Groenendaal in Brabant, in the diocese of Cambrai, of German nation, a man, as they say, devout but little learned, wrote in his native tongue certain little works for the edification of the simple. These were afterward turned into Latin by another; in some respects they are excellent, but in certain points they are said by the doctors to be erroneous. And concerning these Johannes de Gerson, chancellor of Paris, composed advisements. Of them these are reported:

On the Adornment of Spiritual Nuptials, three books, “Ecce sponsus venit ex.” On the Progress of Religious, one book. Exhortatory Letters, one book. And certain others.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Wenceslaus and Pope Boniface IX, in the year of the Lord 1390.

Johannes Schodehouen, of German nation, of the Order of the Brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, prior of Mechelen, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular philosophy, of excellent talent in delivering sermons to the people, wrote for the use of preachers of the word of God volumes not to be despised. Of these the following are extant: a distinguished work on vices and virtues, and on every preach-able subject according to alphabetical order, in two volumes, which he entitled:

Polypodium, three books, “Abscondunt se multi.” Various Sermons, one book. He also published some other works, which have by no means come into our hands.

Ostemper [unclear] Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, nobly instructed in secular philosophy and canon law, whom Pope Urban VI first appointed vicar of the whole order; finally elected general in the year of the Lord 1381, he governed the order under the obedience of Pope Urban for nine years. He wrote many excellent volumes, of which these are reported. To the Cardinal of Santa Maria in Trastevere, a distinguished and excellent work:

On the Conception of Saint Mary, one book. Questions on the Sentences, one book. On the Whole Psalter, five books. On the Gospel of Matthew, one book. A Table of the Sentences, three books. On the Gospel of Luke, one book. Lenten Sermons, one book. He began a Dictionary, three books. On Valerius Maximus, one book. And certain others. A Table of the Moralia of Gregory, one book, “Erant ambo [unclear] Isidorus.” On the Ethics of Aristotle, one book.

On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 96

Prevented by death, he did not complete this divine work of the new dictionary, but brought it through only from A as far as C inclusive, in three volumes. He died in the last year of the emperor Wenceslaus, under Pope Boniface IX, in the year of the Lord 1416, on the Kalends of December, in the seventh indiction. And, honorably buried before the high altar of his convent at Bologna, he rests in the peace of Christ.

Philippus Ferrariensis, of Toulouse, bishop of the church of Pax in Spain, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, an excellent declaimer of sermons, ready in talent, distinguished in eloquence, once preaching in the kingdom of Sicily, converted many from iniquity and brought forth great fruits of his learning for God. He wrote elegant works:

Sermons on the season, one book. Sermons on the saints, one book. And certain other things.

There are some who write that, because of his exceptional learning and the uprightness of his life, he was raised to the honor of the cardinalate; of this I am not certain.

Alterus Disse, English by nation, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, nuncio and legate of Pope Boniface IX in the kingdoms of England, Spain, Portugal, and Aragon, in the parts of Gascony, and in the other lands and kingdoms, preaching the cross against infidel schismatics; a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, an excellent declaimer of sermons. He wrote not-to-be-despised little works, by which he made his name known. Of these there are extant:

Against the Lollards, one book. On the schism also, one book. On some psalms, one book. Sermons on the season, one book. Sermons on the saints, one book. And certain other things.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Wenceslaus and Pope Boniface IX, in the year of the Lord 1390.

Gerardus Zutphaniensis, German by nation, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant also of secular letters, subtle in talent, distinguished in eloquence, and no less to be preferred for his manner of life than for his knowledge of the Scriptures. He published certain little works pertaining to the instruction of devout brothers, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Of these I have seen only:

On Interior Reformation, one book, “A certain man went down from...” On Spiritual Ascent, one book, “Blessed is the man whose help is...” Various sermons, one book. Concerning the rest I have found nothing.

From his writings it appears that he was a devout and religious man, of some order, though it is not known by us. There are indeed those who write that he was a canon regular; we pass this over as probable. He flourished in the school of Cologne. He wrote various things.

Johannes de Hisdinio, of the order of the brothers of the Hospital of Saint John of Jerusalem, a man learned in the divine writings, not ignorant of secular philosophy, a distinguished doctor of sacred Scripture, an excellent declaimer of sermons, acute in talent and composed in eloquence. He published many splendid volumes; at the University of Paris he delivered many elegant lectures. Of these the following are extant:

On the Gospel of Mark, one book, “He was made like a lion in...” On the Gospel of John, one book. On the Epistle to the Romans, one book. On the Epistles to the Corinthians, one book. On the Epistle to the Galatians, one book.

196

Book

On the Epistle to the Ephesians: one book. On the Epistle to the Philippians: one book. On the Epistle to the Colossians: one book. On the Epistles to the Thessalonians: one book. On the Epistles to Timothy: one book. On the Epistle to Titus: one book. On the Epistle to Philemon: one book. On the Epistle to the Hebrews: one book. On the Annunciation of the Lord: one book. Various sermons: one book. And many other things. “Teach your son: because that.” “Hail Mary, full of grace.”

He is also said to have written commentaries and lectures on many books of the Bible, which have not yet come into our hands at all. He flourished in the times of Emperor Wenceslaus and Pope Boniface IX, in the year of the Lord 1390.

Philippus de Monte Galerio, of the Order of the Friars of Saint Francis, a man practiced in sacred Scripture, a great and distinguished preacher of the word of God, wrote little works in which, nobly exercising his talent, he also transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these I have found only the following:

Sermons for the season: one book. Sermons on the saints: one book. Lenten sermons: one book.

He is further said to have composed various other treatises and to have explained some of the divine books, but none of them has come to me.

Johannes, surnamed Grossus, of the Order of the Friars of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, nineteenth prior general; others have twenty-first; by homeland a Toulousain; a studious and learned man. He wrote, in a clear style, volumes not to be despised, by which, having magnificently exercised his practiced talent, he also made his name known to posterity. Of these I have seen only a distinguished work, which contains the foundation and progress of the Carmelite Order, entitled:

Viridarium: three books. “By what things [unclear].”

His sermons are reported: one book. And certain other things.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Wenceslaus and Pope Boniface IX, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1400.

Nicolaus de Gorran, of the Order of the Friars Preachers of Saint Dominic, a man most studious in the holy Scriptures, nobly learned, outstanding in talent, published in a scholastic and clear style many volumes, the reading of which will not be to be rejected by those who desire to be instructed in the holy Scriptures. Of these I recall that few have come into our hands. They report, however, the following among many:

On the Sentences: four books. On the five books of Moses: five books. On Isaiah the prophet: one book. On Jeremiah also: one book. A large work on Ecclesiasticus: one book. On the Song of Songs: one book. On the Gospel of Matthew: one book. On the Gospel of Mark: one book. On the Gospel of Luke: one book. On the Gospel of John: one book.

197

On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 97

On the Epistles of Paul: fourteen books. “I have given you as a light to the nations.”

Various sermons: one book. And certain other things.

He is reported, besides, to have produced notable commentaries and lectures on almost the whole Bible, which have not come to the notice of my reading.

Jacobus de Theramo, an Aprucine canon, archdeacon of Aversa, a very celebrated jurist, a distinguished doctor of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, ready, clear and well-ordered in speech, whose authority among the professors of this faculty was great in his time, produced in that discipline certain excellent volumes, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these I have found only the dialogue on the redemption of the human race, commonly called Belial, which the author entitled:

The Consolation of Sinners: one book. “After through the tree of knowledge.”

On the Clementines he is said to have written: one book. And certain other things.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Wenceslaus and Pope Boniface IX, in the year of the Lord 1390.

Wilhelmus de Oppenbach, a German by nation, a distinguished doctor learned in the holy Scriptures, and nobly trained in scholastic philosophy, sharp in intellect, vigorous and well suited to disputing and resolving questions of the Scriptures, wrote in the theological faculty some not negligible little works, by which he made his name known in the University of Paris. Of these I have found:

On the Sentences: three books.

Disputed Questions: one book.

He is also reported to have written certain sermons and other treatises, and to have composed lectures in the schools, which have not come to my notice.

Heinricus de Langenstein, called de Hassia, a German by nation, a man learned in the aforesaid Scriptures, nobly instructed in secular philosophy, outstanding in intellect, abundant and expansive, since, after spending many years in lecturing on Genesis and scarcely reaching the fourth chapter of the book, he completed as many volumes. For he was resolved on all matters, copious in speaking and writing, so much so that for him it was a greater difficulty voluntarily to reject noteworthy things that occurred to him than to find new things to say. As I have found from a certain letter of his, I would believe that he was a canon of the church of Worms. He first flourished in the University of Paris, where he earned the laurel of the doctorate; then, for the adornment of the new planting of the University of Vienna, he betook himself there, and by both teaching and writing acquired great glory for his learning. Of his little works the following are reported:

On the Sentences: three books. “In the beginning God created.”

A Prologue on Genesis: five books. “To the reverend father and brother in Christ [unclear].”

On the Schism of Antichrist: one book. “To you I will give the keys of the kingdom.”

On the Contemplative Soul: one book.

On Contemplation: one book.

The Mirror of the Soul: one book. “Seven times in the day I have spoken praise.”

On the Canonical Hours: one book. “Many great princes.”

Against the Astrologers: one book. “Divine wisdom in all things.”

On the Lord’s Prayer: one book. “Hail Mary, full of grace.”

On the Hail Mary: one book. “I believe in God the Father almighty.”

On Contempt of the World: one book. “To the reverend lord Johannes de [unclear].”

Against Brother Thelefforus: one book.

Scripsit inter caetera ingenij sui monimēta: prae/ dicatoribꝰ uerbj dei necessaria ualde opuscula: quibꝰ nomē suū ad noticiam poste/ ritatis transmisit. Equibus extant: Sermones de tpe duplices: li. De alijs nihil uidi. Illustrissimi principis. Claruit temporibus wencislai imperatoris: Bonifacij papae noni: Anno domini nostri iesu christi: Millesimo.CCCC. Fertur quaedā praeclara cudiisse opuscula: quibꝰ nomē suu̇ ad noticiam posteritatis cū gloria trāsmisit.Equorū numero extare phibent̉ ualde notabiles: Sermones de tempore: li. Sermones de sancta: li. Caeteriorū uero quae composuit titulos operū inuenire nō potui. Book

Against a certain Wycliffite, one book, [incipit:] “Behold, we have left all things.” To the Canons Regular, one book. On the property of monks, one book. Sermons for the Temporal Cycle, one book. Sermons on the Saints, one book. On the Song of Songs, one book. Letters to various persons, one book, [incipit:] “H., called de Lagensteyn.” Various Questions. He also published many other things which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished in the times of Rupert, the Bavarian palatine, king of the Romans, and of Pope Boniface IX, in the year of the Lord 1400.

Johannes de Bromyard, of the order of Friars Preachers, a holy man, devoted to the divine Scriptures and learned by long practice, also not ignorant of secular letters, excellent in talent, an outstanding declaimer, wrote certain distinguished volumes by which he established the memory of his name among posterity. Of these, the following are reported: a great and very lucid work, very useful to preachers, which he entitled: A Summa of Preachers, one book, [incipit:] “The life of preachers, etc.” A Summa of Moral Law, one book, [incipit:] “In the following little work [unclear].” Sermons for the Temporal Cycle, one book. Sermons on the Saints, one book, [incipit:] “Lay up for yourselves treas[ures].” He is said besides to have written many other things which have not come to my knowledge.

Johannes Gluel, German by nation, of the order of the Friars of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, prior of Cologne, sprung from Aachen, an imperial city, a man outstandingly learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular literature, of excellent and distinguished talent in delivering sermons to the people, wrote, among the other little works of his study, a volume not to be rejected by the cultivators of this religion, on the origin and progress of his order, which he entitled: Mirror of the Carmelites, one book. Sermons for the Temporal Cycle, one book, [incipit:] “Lay up [unclear].” Lenten Sermons, one book. Sermons on the Saints, one book. He flourished in his convent at Cologne, writing and composing various little works, where at last, when his strength failed, he ended his day and was buried in peace.

Heinricus Euta, or Oyta, German by nation, the unique ornament and co-founder from the beginning of the University of Vienna in Austria, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, nobly instructed in Aristotelian philosophy, subtle in talent, scholastic in speech, an outstanding declaimer of sermons, wrote many distinguished volumes, of which very few have so far come into our hands. For I have read only: On the Sentences, four books, [incipit:] “Concerning the prologue of the first [book] of the Sentences [unclear].” On Contracts, one book, [incipit:] “Love justice, you who judge.” On the Conception of Saint Mary, [incipit:] “A virgin shall arise from Israel.” And certain sermons. Of the rest I have seen nothing. He flourished in the University of Vienna under Emperor Wenceslaus, together with Heinricus de Hassia, in the year of the Lord 1390.

Heinricus de Andernacho, German by nation, of the order of the Friars of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man devoted and learned in the divine Scriptures, an outstanding interpreter of Aristotelian philosophy, excellent in talent, famous among all men of his time as a declaimer of sermons, published little works of authority not to be lightly esteemed; of these the following are reported. A distinguished work:

Sermones uarij li.j Alia uero quae scripsisse dicitur:ad noticiã nostrã minime uenerũt. Inter oĩa genera signorū. Homa de Haselbach:natione teutonicus: in scripturis sanctis eruditꝰ:

On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 98

On the Sentences: four books. Sermons for the season: one book. Sermons on the saints: one book. Questions of philosophy: one book.

And certain other works which have by no means come to the notice of our reading. He flourished especially in the convent at Cologne, where he is said to have been buried.

Lasius Andernarius, a Gaul by nation, of the order of the brothers of blessed Mary ever virgin of Mount Carmel, a man learned in the holy Scriptures, nobly exercised in the arena of scholastic discipline, distinguished in talent, an outstanding disputant. He wrote some notable volumes, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Among these the following distinguished, splendid work excels:

On the Sentences: four books. Questions and Collations: one book.

He is also said to have written some works on moral philosophy, but they have not come to me.

Bartholomaeus de Saliceto, jurist, the most celebrated of all in his time, subtle in talent and distinguished in eloquence, whose sayings are held in great authority among professors of civil law. He published certain splendid little works on laws, by which he consecrated the memory of his name to immortality among posterity. Of these the following are reported:

On the Code: nine books. On the Institutes: four books. On the Use of Fiefs: one book.

And many others. He flourished in the times of the emperor Wenceslaus and of Pope Boniface IX, in the year of the Lord 1390.

Johannes, abbot of the monastery of Saint Bavo, of the order of the divine father Benedict, a German by nation, an outstanding doctor and professor of the divine Scriptures, subtle in talent, polished in eloquence, distinguished no less for religious conduct than for knowledge of letters. He wrote certain notable little works for the instruction of monks. Of these the following are extant. A work which he entitled:

On the Eating of Meat: one book. Explanations on the Rule: one book. Questions on the Sentences: one book.

Besides these, he is said to have written various and numerous treatises; but I do not recall that any of them have come into our hands, except that little book which he wrote on the eating of meat, in which he beautifully sets out and rightly concludes that, for a healthy monk professed according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, the eating of meat is illicit and therefore wholly forbidden.

Richardus Lauinham, of the order of the brothers of blessed Mary ever virgin of Mount Carmel, an Englishman by nation, a man excellently learned in the holy Scriptures, an eminent interpreter of secular philosophy, and also of excellent talent in delivering sermons to the people. He also wrote some volumes, of which these are reported:

Against the Lollards: one book. On the Foundation of His Order: one book. For the Book of Bridget: one book. Various Sermons: one book. Also On Logic: one book. And Various Questions: one book.

He flourished in the University of Oxford, especially at the time when the heresy of John Wycliffe and of the Lollards began in Bohemia.

Johannes de Werdena, of the order, as they report, of the Friars Minor, a Teuton by nation, a man zealous and learned in the holy Scriptures, rich in the reading of the ancients, and sufficiently learned in natural philosophy, in talent

Romasinus patria Ferrarienfis:ordinis fratrũ proedicatorũ sancti Domīni/ tci:uir in scripturis fanc̄tis ftudiosus doctus:in delictis populorū corripiē- dis declamator egregiùs:fert̉ quaedadā ad instructionē simpliciū sacerdotū pꝛaeclara cudisse oputuscula:quibꝰ nominis fu noticiã cũ laude transmisit ad pofte- ros.De q̃rũ numero potiffime ferunt: Sermones de tempoꝛe. li.j Sermones dę sanctĩs: li.j Sermones Ꝑ quadragesimã: li.j Caetera uero que composuit:ad noticiã nostrâ hucufqƺ non ue

excellent; composed in speech with scholastic simplicity; in his time a very celebrated preacher of popular sermons. Among the other monuments of his talent he wrote very useful little works necessary for preachers of the word of God, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these there are extant:

Sermons on the Temporale, in two sets: book. Sermons on the Saints, in two sets: book. Sermons also for Lent: book. But the other things which he composed have by no means come to our knowledge. Let us put on, etc. We see [unclear].

Jacobus, who is called the Great, by country a Toledan, of the order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, distinguished for his knowledge of natural philosophy, and rich in reading of the ancients. He is said to have issued various treatises and commentaries on the divine books, which have not yet come into our hands. I found one excellent, notable volume of his, entitled On the discourse of the inquiry of wisdom:

Sophilogium: book.

Of the others I have seen nothing.

Of the most illustrious prince.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Wenceslaus and Pope Boniface IX, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1400.

Johannes Campscen[us?], of the order of the Friars of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, an Englishman by nation, long exercised in the holy Scriptures by study, rich in talent through continual reading of the ancients, an excellent preacher of sermons. He is said to have forged certain distinguished little works, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Among these, the following are reported to be extant and very notable:

Sermons on the Temporale: book. Sermons on the Saints: book.

But I could not find the titles of the other works which he composed.

Thomas Gualensis, of the order of the Friars Preachers, an Englishman by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, very studious, and also nobly learned in secular letters, especially in scholastic philosophy; subtle in talent, clear in eloquence; likewise an excellent preacher of sermons, an acute disputant in scholastic lectures. He wrote many distinguished little works on the holy Scriptures, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Yet of these few have come into our hands. For I found only the following:

On the whole Psalter: book. On the Proverbs of Solomon: book. On Augustine’s City of God: book. On the Song of Songs: book.

He flourished in the University of Oxford, where he is said to have composed many volumes, especially various lectures on several books of the Bible.

Philippus, abbot of the monastery of Otterburg, in the diocese of Worms, of the Cistercian order, a German by nation, a man studious in the divine Scriptures, learned by long exercise, not ignorant of secular literature. For the edification of readers he issued volumes not to be despised; by them, exercising his talent properly, he also left to posterity the memory of his name. Among these the following are reported. A distinguished, notable work:

Sermons on the Temporale: book. Sermons on the Saints: book. Book of letters to various persons.

If he issued anything further, it has as yet by no means come to my knowledge.

Nicolaus, a physician of exceptional learning, an Italian by nation, by country a Florentine, a man most learned not only in medicine but also in the other letters of secular philosophy, clear in talent, elegant in eloquence; how great his learning may be among physicians

DE SCRIPTORIBVS ECCLESIASTICIS Folijoo Homas de Kempis:natiōe teutonicus: ordinis canonici san/ t Augustini montis divae martyris et uirginis Agnetis prope Zwollis in diocesi Traiectensi:uir in scripturis divinis studiosus et eruditus: uita et co uerlatio deuotus: & beatae Mariae semp uirginis amator praecipuus. Claruit temporibus Ruperti Bauari regis Romanoruũ:& Gregorũ papae.xii. An, no domini Mill.CCCC.X. Icolaus monachus coenobiũ sanctae crucis in Austria:ordinis Cifterciensis: n natione Germanus: uir in diuinis scripturis studiosus et eruditus ac uete, ru lectione diues:ingenio excellẽs et clarus eloquio. Scriptit quaedam no sperneda utilitatis opuscula: quibus ingenii lui memoria ad posteros transmisit. Equibus ferunt subiecta. Opus no absciendũ in laude beatiflimae dei genitricis et uirginis Mariae: praedicatoribus utile:quod praenotauit: Imaginẽ sanctae Mariae: li. ii Nomẽ uirginis Maria: Lu. Sermones uariũ: li. i Caetera:& si multa ferũ:quae cosopusuit:ad nos minime uenerũt. Artholomaeus de Vrbino:ordinis fratru heremitarũ sancti Augustini:uir i b diuinis scripturis studiosus et eruditus: & saeculariũ litterarũ non ignarus: operũ sanctoũ patru diligens perscrutator. Scriptit no sperneda uolumia: de quib' ferunt subiecta. Ex opuclulis sancti Ambrosiũ et Augustini opus singula/ ri studio fm alphabeti ordinẽ in unũ coportauit: cui titulũ imposuit: Milleloquiũ Augustini: li. i Milleloquiũ Ambrosiũ. li. i De bello quoqũ spirituali: li. i Etalia complura. Claruit temporibus Ruperti regis Romanoruũ:& Gregorũ papae duodecimi: An, no domini Mill.CCCC.X. Ranciscus de Plataea: ordinis fratrum minorũ sancti Francisci: uir in diu/ nis scripturis eruditus: & tam in iure s in philosophia saeculari notabiliter doctus:ingenio excellens: & declamator sermonum egregius: multa prae clara dicitur lucubrasse opuclula: quibus nominis lui memoria cu laude transmi/ sit ad posteros. De quorum numero subiecta ferunt. Opus insigne et praeclarum quod praenotauit: De restitutionibus: li. i Vtrũ restitutio sit de ne. LIBER De censuris: li. 5 Sermones uarii: li. 1 Caetera uero quae cōposuit: ad noticiā nostrā lectionis nō uenerūt. Etrus de Candia: natīone Cretensis: ordinis frātrū minorū: primo epus No/ p/ uariensis: deinde Mediolanēlis archiepūs: postea sacrosanctae ecclesiae Ro/ manae cardinalis: & postremo fūmus pontifex Alexander quintus nomi/ natūr: vir in diuinis scripturis eruditissimus: & in philosophia scholastica magnifice doctus: declamator sermonū celeberrimus: qui olim in gymnasio Parisiēnli publi/ cae scholae praefuit: & docēdo ac scribēdo magnas et ingētis laudes acquisiuit. De/ cuius elegantissimis opusculis extant luculentī utiles et cōmentariī: Super sententias: li. uij Sermones uarii: li. 1 Et quaedam alia. Moritur ultimo Ruperti regis Romanorũ anno: sepultus in cōuentu minorũ Bo/ noniae: Anno dn̄s Milleseimo. CCCC.X. Indictione tertia. Ranciscũ de bachone: patria Cathalanũ: ordinis frātrũ beatae Mariae sem/ per uirginis de mōte Carmeli: cōuentus Gerundēsis: vir in diuinis scriptu/ ris eruditus et in philosophia ōculari nobiliter doctus: tantũ docēdo et di/ sputādo in Parisiēnli uniuersitate ualuit: ut doctor sublimis cognomiauit sit. Scri/ ptũ inter alia ingenii sui monimēta opus magnũ et insignẽ ex scriptis sancti/ trum declamatoribus sermonũ ad populi latũs utile: quod praenotare possimus: Repertoriũ praedicantiũ: li. 1 Super sententias quoqũ: li. uij Fertur praeterea et quaedam alia scripsiisse: sed ad manus nostras non uenerunt.

On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 99 ... of this time is confirmed not by my words but by their testimonies. He published certain distinguished little works in that faculty. Among these there is said to be an excellent work: Summa medicinae, one book; and certain others.

He died in the time of Rupert, king of the Romans, and Pope John XXIII, in the year of the Lord 1412, indiction 5.

Johannes de Duren, of the Order of Friars Minor of Saint Francis, German by nation, a man studious in the Holy Scriptures and nobly practiced in them, of great and distinguished reputation in delivering sermons to the people. He is said to have fashioned certain little works for the guidance of simple priest-preachers, by which he left the memory of his name to posterity. Of these there survive: Sermones de tempore, one book; Sermones de sanctis, one book; Quadragesimale, one book, “Sanctificate the fast ...”; “When a suitable confessor ...”; De septem peccatis mortalibus, one book, “There is a way which seems right to a man”; De occultis vitiis, one book; De confessione, one book.

He is also said to have written many other things, which have not come to my knowledge.

Hilmannus de Hachenberg, of the Order of Friars Minor, German by nation, from the diocese of Trier, a man studious in the divine Scriptures and learned by long practice, having a polished tongue through practice in speaking; in delivering sermons to the people he shone forth as a very great and most renowned man. He wrote certain little works, not to be despised by simple persons, by which, fruitfully applying his talent, he left the memory of his name to posterity. Of these there survive: Sermones de tempore, one book, “There shall be signs ... he foretold”; Sermones de sanctis, one book; Sermones per quadragesimam, one book.

And certain others.

He flourished in his convent at Koblenz, where he died and was buried.

Johannes de Lignano, a very celebrated jurist, well instructed in the disciplines of the philosophers, outstanding in talent, renowned for eloquence. He is said to have fashioned certain distinguished little works in canon law; by applying himself to these he spent his time usefully and also left the memory of his name to posterity. Of these, as Franciscus de Zabarellis testifies in the prologue on the Clementines, there survive compilations: Super Clementinis, one book; and certain others.

He flourished under Rupert the Bavarian, king of the Romans, and Pope Boniface IX, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1405.

[Hugo?] de Sletstadt, German by nation, a man studious and very learned in the divine Scriptures, and excellently learned in the disciplines of the philosophers, subtle in talent and an outstanding disputant of scholastic questions. He wrote certain, as they say, distinguished volumes, by which he left the memory of his name to posterity. Of these there survives: Quaestiones sententiarum, three books, a work [unclear]; and certain others. He was, moreover, in his determinations, a follower of the Order of Friars Minor of the holy father Bonaventure, a clear interpreter, explaining those things which in that man’s singular philosophy could have seemed obscure and rather uncommon to simple persons.

Paulus Venetus, of the Order of Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and, in Aristotelian philosophy, second to none in Italy in his time; subtle in talent, scholastic, and an excellent declaimer. He composed many little works, especially in philosophy, by which he left the memory of his name to posterity. Of these they report:

Ichael berbrant de Duren: ordinis frātrũ beatae Mariae semper uirginis de/ monte Carmeli: natīone teutonicus: facrũ theologiae lector: & prior con/ uentũ Crucēnacensi in diocesi Moguntina: uir doctũ et declamator adeo/ insignẽ ut nō solũ i uicino: sed etũ ad remota loca: & cathedrales ecclesias euoca/ tus omnīu admiratiũ habitus praedicaret. Hic apud Iohanne comiti Španhemẽ/ sem ultimũ: magnũe familiaritatiũ et auctoritatiũ erat: & multa ab eo suo cōuentu/ bonũ obtainuit. Scripsiit inter caetera elegantes: Sermones de tempore: li. 1 Sermones de sanctis: li. 1 Collationes synodales: li. 1 Et quaedam alia. Claruit temporibus Ruperti regis Romanorũ: & Sigismundi imperatoris: Anno/ dn̄s Milleseimo. CCCC.X. Etrus de spira ordinis frātrũ heremitarũ sancti Augustini: natīone teutoni/ cus: uir in diuinis scripturis studiosũs et eruditus: & in ōculari philosophia/ magnifice doctus: ingenio praestans et clarũs eloquio: in declamandũs ser/ monibus ad populi celeberrimũs opinionis. Scripsiit quaedam praeclara opuscula: q/ bus nominũ sui memoriaũ ad posteros transmisit. E quorũ numero feruntur: Sermones de tempore: li. 1 Sermones de sanctis: li. 1 Super libros Ethicorũ: li. uij Alia uero quae cōposuit: ad noticiā nostrā lectionis nondum uenerunt. Einardus de Fronthouen: natīone teutonicus ordinis ut ferunt frātrũ prae/ dicantũ: uir in diuinis studiosũs et longa exercitatione peritus scripturũs: & ōcularis litteraturũ nō ignarũ: Scripsiit praedicantũbũ uerbi dei nō ab/ iencia opuscula: quũ nominũ suũ etũ posteris notificauit. Equibũego uidi tantũ: Sermones de tempore: li. 1 DE SCRIPTORIBVS ECCLESIATICIS Fol.ioj Sermones de sanctis: li. De alijs nihil uidi. Claruit (ut sui dicũt) in cõuentu Cõfluentino: ubi mortuus est. Iohannes Capreolus: ordinis fratrũ praedicatorũ: patria Tholosanus: uir̃ in scripturis sanctis eruditus: in disciplinis aristotelicae phiae egregie do¬ ctus: ingenio acutus: ad disputandũ satis idoneꝰ: dictorũ sancti Thomae Aquinatis ꝓpugnator defensor acerrimus. Scripsit ingenij sui monimenta cla¬ rissima: quibꝰ nomẽ suũ notificauit. Equibꝰ extant multa volumina: Super sententias: li. iij Et sermones uarij: li. j Ac quaedam alia. Claruit sub Sigismũdo imperatore: Anno domini Mill̃.CCCC.XV. Deinricus de Cosueldia: natiõe teutonicus: ordinis Carthusien̄: prior domꝰ sanctae Mariae: prope montẽ diuae Gertrudis in Hollãdia: uir in diuinis scripturis eruditiffimꝰ: uita cõuersatiõe deuotus: magnae famae: ingenio subtilis clarus eloquio: declamator quoqƺ sermonũ celeberrimus. Scripsit ml̃ta praeclara uolumina: quorũ deuotis fratribꝰ: suae salutis amatoribus utilis frequẽ¬tatio iudicatur. Equibus subiecta ferunt̾: In Exodum mystice: li. j In epistolã Pauli ad Romanos: li. j De tribꝰ uotis substãtialibꝰ: li. ij Nolite diligere mũdum. Contra uitium proprietatis: li. j De tribus custodijs monasticis: li. j De institutione nouitiorũ: li. j Circũcisoriũ mysticum: li. j De sacramẽto altaris: li. j De annũciatione dñica: li. j Eulogiũ Pauliberemitae: li. j Sermones de tempore: li. j Epistolarũ ad diuerfos: li. j Et alia complura. Guilhelmi parisiensis epĩ arduũ opus de uniuerso corporeo incorporeo seu spiritali: mira industria plustrans: breui compendio pulchre cõclusit. Morit̃ in domõ Vallis gratiae prope Brugas: uisitatiõis actu salubriter occupatus: temporibꝰ Sigismũdi imperatoris: Anno dn̄i Mill̃.CCC.XII Indictione. iij. vj. Idus Iulij. Deinricus Hachenburg: ordinis fratrũ praedigatorũ: natione teutonicus uir in diuinis scripturis magnifice exercitus probe instructus: in declamãdis ad populũ sermonibꝰ excellẽtis ingenij celeberrime opinionis. Scripsit ꝓ directiõe simpliciũ sacerdotũ nõ abijcienda uolumina. Equibꝰ extant: Sermones de tempore: li. j Ego ueniã curabo eum. BOOK.

Against the Jews: 1 book. ["Bound by [the testimonies] of very many…"] A Summa on natural [philosophy]: 1 book. Sermons on the [seasons of the] year: 1 book. Sermons on the saints: 1 book. Sermons for Lent: 1 book. On the [books of] Posterior [Analytics]: 3 books. ["All doctrine, etc."] On the Physics: 8 books. ["By natural philosophy…"] On the Metaphysics: 12 books. ["With you, most wise…"] On [the books] On the Soul: 3 books. ["So great [a study] of letters, etc."] A Summa of philosophy: 3 books. ["A colloquy below, etc."] A twofold Logic: 3 books. ["Completing the rest…"] On [the book] On Generation [and] Corruption: 3 books. ["Of human and divine [things]…"] On the [book] of Porphyry: 1 book. ["Greatest, to the strong, etc."] On the book of the Categories: 1 book. ["To me, seeking, etc."] On the Consequences of Strode: 1 book. ["[I take] Jesus, God [and] man…"] And several others. He flourished under Wenceslaus the emperor, in the year of the Lord 1400. And, dying young, he was buried in the sacristy of his order at Venice.

James of Thessalonica, of the order of Friars Preachers, a man erudite in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular letters, excelling in talent, polished and composed in speech, second to none of his time in declaiming sermons to the people. He published certain illustrious volumes, by which he left to posterity a praiseworthy memory of his name. Of these there is extant a notable work, entitled "On the morals of men and the offices of the noble and of the common people," setting forth [its] subject: On the game of chess: 3 books. ["Among all kinds of signs…"] Various sermons: 1 book. But the others which he is said to have written have by no means come to our knowledge.

Thomas de Haselbach, a Teuton by nation, erudite in the holy Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, outstanding in talent, scholastic in speech, but too diffuse [and] prolix, and on that account liable to the reproach of certain [persons]. For when he was the ordinary lector of sacred theology in the gymnasium of Vienna, reading for twenty-one years on the prophet Isaiah, he did not reach the end of the first chapter. He wrote some little works on the divine Scriptures, of which the following are reported—many volumes: On Isaiah the prophet: 1 book. ["After [that], by God's gift, in such wise as…"] On the Sentences: 3 books. On the Ten Precepts: 1 book. On the five senses of man: 1 book. Sermons on the [seasons of the] year: 1 book. Sermons on the saints: 1 book. But the others which he is said to have written have by no means come to our knowledge.

Thomasinus, of Ferrara by country, of the order of Friars Preachers of Saint Dominic, a man studious [and] learned in the holy Scriptures, a distinguished declaimer in correcting the sins of peoples. He is reported to have forged certain illustrious little works for the instruction of simple priests, by which he transmitted to posterity the notice of his name with praise. Of whose number these are foremost reported: Sermons on the [seasons of the] year: 1 book. Sermons on the saints: 1 book. Sermons for Lent: 1 book. But the rest which he composed have not come to our knowledge hitherto. He flourished in the times of Rupert, king of the Romans, and of Gregory XII, pope, in the year of the Lord 1410.

[The source here repeats the Thomasinus of Ferrara entry verbatim; not re-translated.]

On Ecclesiastical Writers Folio 100

Thomas de Kempis, a German by nation, a canon of the order of Saint Augustine, of the Mount of the holy martyr and virgin Agnes near Zwolle in the diocese of Utrecht, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, devout in life and conduct, and an especial lover of blessed Mary ever virgin. He wrote little works, not to be despised, for the instruction of simple brothers. Among them the following are reported:

On contempt of the world, three books, “He who follows me shall not.” Sermons to novices, two books, “Behold how good and pleasant.” Sermons to the brothers, one book, “He who has not renounced.” Dialogue of novices, one book, “I ask you, dearest father.” On the solitary life, one book, “Dearest, since you were in.” On the three tabernacles, one book, “It is written in the prophet.” On true compunction, one book, “Weep with me, all you friends.” The little garden of roses, one book, “With the holy you will be holy.” The valley of lilies, one book, “I am the flower of the field and the lily.” The alphabet of a monk, one book, “Show me your ways, Lord.” Consolation of the poor, one book, “Be comforted, be comforted.” The epitaph of a monk, one book, “The way of the just has been made straight.” What a monk ought to be like, one book, “Listen, religious monk.” Manual for beginners, one book, “Let the little children come.” Instructional book for youths, one book, “Son, from your youth receive.” Another work on contempt of the world, one book, “The Lord rules me, and nothing.” Letters to various persons, one book, “Dearest brother, gladly.” And certain other works.

He flourished in the times of Rupert, Bavarian king of the Romans, and of Pope Gregory XII, in the year of the Lord 1410.

Nicolaus, monk of the monastery of the Holy Cross in Austria, of the Cistercian order, a German by nation, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures and rich in the reading of the ancients, excellent in talent and distinguished in eloquence. He wrote certain useful little works, not to be despised, by which he transmitted the memory of his talent to posterity. Among them the following are reported: a work not to be despised in praise of the most blessed mother of God and virgin Mary, useful to preachers, which he entitled:

The Image of Saint Mary, two books, “The name of the virgin Mary: Lu.” Various sermons, one book.

The rest, though many works which he composed are reported, have by no means come down to us.

Bartholomaeus of Urbino, of the order of the hermit brothers of Saint Augustine, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, a diligent investigator of the works of the holy fathers. He wrote volumes not to be despised, among which the following are reported. From the little works of Saints Ambrose and Augustine he gathered into one work, with singular zeal, according to the order of the alphabet, and gave it the title:

The Milleloquium of Augustine, one book. The Milleloquium of Ambrose, one book. Also, On Spiritual Warfare, one book. And very many others.

He flourished in the times of Rupert, king of the Romans, and of Pope Gregory XII, in the year of the Lord 1410.

Franciscus de Platea, of the order of the Friars Minor of Saint Francis, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and notably learned both in law and in secular philosophy, excellent in talent and an outstanding preacher of sermons, is said to have composed many splendid little works, by which he transmitted the memory of his name with praise to posterity. Of their number the following are reported: an outstanding and splendid work which he entitled:

On Restitutions, one book, “Whether restitution is of necessity.”

Book

On censures, five books. Various sermons, one book.

The other works that he composed have not come to our knowledge by reading.

Petrus de Candia, Cretan by nation, of the order of the Friars Minor, first bishop of Novara, then archbishop of Milan, afterwards cardinal of the most holy Roman Church, and finally supreme pontiff named Alexander V, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and splendidly learned in scholastic philosophy, a very celebrated preacher of sermons, who once presided over a public school in the university of Paris, and by teaching and writing gained great and immense praises. Among his most elegant little works there survive clear and useful commentaries:

On the Sentences, seven books. Various sermons, one book. And certain other works.

He died in the last year of Rupert, king of the Romans, and was buried in the convent of the Friars Minor at Bologna, in the year of the Lord 1410, in the third indiction.

Franciscus de Bachone, a Catalan by homeland, of the order of the brothers of blessed Mary ever virgin of Mount Carmel, of the convent of Girona, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly learned in secular philosophy, had such strength in teaching and disputing in the university of Paris that he was surnamed the Sublime Doctor. Among other monuments of his talent he wrote a great and notable work from the writings of the saints, widely useful to preachers of sermons to the people, which we may entitle:
