On the eternal Gospel: a book. On the Christian religion: a book. On the conception of Saint Mary: a book. On the Passion of the Lord: a book. Sermons for the Temporal cycle: a book. Sermons for the Sanctoral: a book. And certain other works.

He died at Aquila, a city of Abruzzo, in the reign of Emperor Frederick III, under Pope Eugene IV, in the year of the Lord 1443, in the sixth indiction, in the sixty-fourth year of his age. And because of his frequent miracles he was enrolled in the catalogue of the saints by Pope Nicholas V, in the year 1450, the seventh after his death. His feast is kept on the twentieth day of the month of May.

Antonius Gaynerus, of Pavia by origin, a very celebrated doctor of medicine, nobly learned also in the precepts of the philosophers, excellent in talent, and notably distinguished in skill in his profession, wrote in that discipline certain lucid little works, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these the following are reported:

On illness of the stomach: one book. Also on fever: one book. On illnesses in general: one book. On pleurisy: one book. On the womb: one book. On fluxes: one book. On arthritis in the joints: one book. On the afflictions of stone: one book. On the third of Avicenna: one book. And many other works.

He flourished at the time of the Council of Basel, in the year of the Lord 1440.

Gerardus Stredam, a German by nation, of the Carthusian order, prior of the house of All Apostles near Liège, a man most zealous in the divine Scriptures and excellently learned by long practice, venerable also for religion, prudence, and authority, wrote for the edification of simple brothers certain excellent little works, of which the following are reported. To the abbot of Saint Hadrian of Giraldus’s Mount:

On pastoral care: one book. On the Ten Commandments: one book. On the seven sacraments: one book. The Mirror of Religious: one book. A Dialogue on the virtues: one book. A Dialogue on the vices: one book. Sermons for the Temporal cycle: one book. Sermons for the Sanctoral: one book. And certain other works.

He died at the beginning of the reign of Emperor Frederick III, under Pope Eugene IV, in the year of the Lord 1443, in the sixth indiction.

Matthaeus Palmerius, an Italian by nation, a Florentine by native city, a historian, philosopher, and most eloquent orator, who in the Council of Florence, which Pope Eugene IV celebrated against the Synod of Basel, was counted among the illustrious men, wrote a book on the angels full of error. Persistently defending it, he was condemned as a heretic and was burned at the city of [unclear]. Carefully examining the Chronicle of Eusebius of Caesarea, he corrected it; and, completing it down to the year of the Lord 1448, he inscribed it to Piero di Cosimo de’ Medici: one book. It begins: “That it is innate in our minds.”

Letters to various persons: one book.

He flourished in the times of the Council of Basel and of Pope Eugenius IV, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1440.

Johannes Ernesti, German by nation, once rector and ornament of the University of Heidelberg, learned in the holy Scriptures, rich in his reading of the ancients, subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech with singular charm, an outstanding disputant of questions, wrote, as they say, certain distinguished little works, by which he transmitted the memory of his name with glory to posterity. Of these the following are reported:

Questions on the Sentences, one book. Disputed Questions, one book. Many Sermons, one book. On the Nativity of the Lord, an oration, one book: “And if of speaking concerning the greatest [unclear].” On Fasting, to the University, one book: “Most sacred [unclear] desires.” Many Various Orations, one book. On the Authority of the Council, one book. And many other things.

He flourished at the time of the Council of Basel, at the beginning of the reign of Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1440.

Bartholomaeus, of the Carthusian order, prior of the house of Bethlehem in the town of Roermond in Guelders, German by nation, acute in sacred letters, a devout and celebrated interpreter, wrote for the edification of his brothers certain distinguished little works, by which he magnificently exercised his intellect and left to posterity the memory of his name. Of these the following are reported:

Exercise of Devotion, one book. Summary of Vices, one book. On Abstinence from Meat, one book. On the Proclamations of the Brothers, one book. On Rash Judgments, one book. On the Oath, one book. On the Vow also, one book. And certain other things.

He died under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1046, in the ninth indiction, on the third day before the Ides of July.

Heinricus de Werlis, German by nation, of the Order of Friars Minor, minister of the province of Cologne, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular philosophy, excellent in intellect, scholastic in eloquence, an acute disputant, an outstanding declaimer of sermons, composed certain lucid volumes, by which he left to posterity the memory of his name. Among these there is an outstanding work:

On the Sentences, four books. On Ecclesiastical Power, one book. Various Sermons also, one book. And many other things.

He flourished in the times of the Council of Basel and of Pope Eugenius IV, in the year of the Lord 1490.

Andreas de Traiecto, German by nation, a monk of our monastery of Sponheim, of the order of Saint Benedict, which is situated within the borders of the diocese of Mainz, between the Rhine and the Hercynian forest, which is called the Soonwald, stretching westward toward Trier, certainly a studious man, learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant also of secular letters, outstanding in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, wrote both in meter and in prose little works not to be despised, of which the following are extant:

Soliloquies of a man to God: one book, “When once [unclear] of the divine calling.” On the progress of virtues: a book, “Having gone out [unclear] a trench of a cubit.” On abstinence from meats: a book, “The authority of your fraternity.” On the use of flocks: a book, “Reverend father, recently by me.” Letters to various persons: a book, “Although among all things which, wrongly.” Various conferences: a book, “Although there is nothing in me which.” Poems and rhythms. And certain other short works. He flourished in the aforesaid monastery of Sponheim before the introduction of the latest Bursfeld reform, in the year of the Lord 1445.

Anthony, of the Order of Friars Preachers, archbishop of Florence, an Italian by birth, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, excellent in talent, distinguished in eloquence, famous in delivering sermons to the people, of celebrated reputation, and no less venerable for his life and conduct than for his learning. He wrote many splendid volumes, by which he labored magnificently for the edification of the Church militant. Among these there is a very famous great work, divided into four volumes of no small size, which he entitles: A Summa of cases of conscience: three books, “They have been magnified.” A huge and notable Chronicle: three books, “I shall speak propositions from [unclear].” A Directory for confessors: one book, “Those who search have failed.” On ecclesiastical censure: a book, “Turn to the Lord.” Sermons on the season: a book. And certain other works. Sermons on the saints: a book. Leonardus of Udine, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a man indeed in the divine writings [unclear]. He died after many labors of sacred study, not without a reputation for sanctity, under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1459, in the seventh indiction, on the sixth Nones of May. He was buried at Saint Mark, the convent of his order.

Leonardus of Udine, of the Order of Friars Preachers, not ignorant of secular philosophy; devoted and learned in [divine?] writings; not ignorant of secular philosophy; in delivering sermons to the people, of excellent talent and lofty reputation. He wrote, for the benefit of preachers, certain splendid little works, by which he transmitted the memory of his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Among these the following are reported: Sermons on the season: a book, “Interpreter of divine mysteries.” Sermons on the saints: a book. On covetousness: a book, “Do not lay up treasures for yourselves.” On the laws for Lent: a book. Against the Hussites: a book. Various sermons: a book. On the Passion of the Lord: a book. And certain other works. He flourished under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1445.

John of Capistrano, from the town of Capistrano in Abruzzo, not far from the city of L’Aquila, of the Order of Friars Minor, formerly a disciple of Saint Bernardino of Siena, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, excellently instructed in canon law, outstanding in talent and distinguished in eloquence, and also devout in religious life and conduct, a most celebrated preacher of the divine word, who by word and example converted many from iniquity. He wrote certain little works of no small usefulness, of which few have come to me: Some letters. And certain other works. He flourished under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1450, not without a reputation for sanctity.

The Most Recent Dawn: 1 book, “Scribes and notaries.” Various consultations: 1 book. He is said also to have written some other things, but they have not come to my knowledge.

Henry of Herp, of the Order of Friars Minor of Saint Francis, a German by nationality, of the province of Cologne, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of pontifical law, outstanding in intellect and clear in speech, of a very celebrated reputation in delivering sermons to the people, no less venerable for his religious life than for his knowledge of the Scriptures, wrote little works of authority not to be rejected, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of their number the following are reported. A large and notable volume: On the Precepts of the Decalogue: 1 book, “I find another law in...” Sermons on the Season: 1 book, “Behold, your king comes.” Sermons on the Saints: 1 book, “Rabbi, where do you dwell?” according to [unclear]. Sermons for Advent: 1 book, “Who will be able to think...” On the Three Parts of Penitence: 1 book, “No one can serve two masters.” And certain other things. He flourished under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Pius II, in the year of the Lord 1460.

Johannes de Turrecremata, of the Order of Friars Preachers, bishop of Sabina and cardinal priest of the Holy Roman Church, a man zealous in the divine Scriptures and an excellent preacher of sermons, ready in intellect and clear in speech, wrote many little works of his intellect, by which he made his name known. Of these the following are reported. To Arsenius, monk of the monastery of Saint Benedict at Lando, which he himself held in commendam, he composed a large work, not to be rejected: On the Rule of Saint Benedict: 1 book, “Since, with the help of our Lord...” On the Whole Psalter: 1 book, “To the most blessed father and merciful...” Questions on the Sunday Gospels: 1 book, “To the holy and most venerable...” Questions on the Gospels for Saints: 1 book, “Recently the reverend father enjoined upon me...” On Blessed Water: 1 book, “Divine Scripture teaches us...” On the Salvation of the Soul: 1 book. Sermons on the Season: 1 book. Sermons on the Saints: 1 book. And many other things. He flourished under Emperor Frederick III and the supreme pontiffs Pius and Paul, in the year of the Lord 1460.

Johannes of Mechelen, a German by nationality, a man trained by long study in the divine Scriptures and not moderately learned in scholastic philosophy, excellent in intellect and renowned for knowledge, taught theology publicly for many years in the school of Cologne and acquired great praise for the light of his erudition. He wrote certain distinguished little works of his intellect, by which he transmitted the memory of his name to posterity. Of these the following are reported. A notable work: On the Sentences: 4 books. On the Psalter: 1 book. Various Questions: 1 book. Sermons and Collations: 1 book. And many other things. He flourished in the times of Emperor Frederick III and Pope Pius II, in the year of the Lord 1460.

Dionysius Rykel, otherwise of Leeuwen, a German by nationality, of the Order of Carthusians, of the house of Bethlehem in Roermond, a man most zealous in the divine Scriptures and skilled through continual exercise, not ignorant also of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, singularly devout in life and conduct, so much so that he was even deemed worthy of divine revelations, to whom there are extant several letters of Nicholas of Cusa, cardinal and most learned man, wrote so many and so great works that in the number of his little works, apart from Augustine, among the Latin...

Nicholas of Cusa, bishop of Brixen, and cardinal-priest of the holy Roman Church of the title of Saint Peter in Chains, a Teuton by nation, from the diocese of Trier, a man most erudite in the divine Scriptures, and easily the prince of the theologians of his time, and excellently learned in secular letters: a philosopher, rhetorician, and most celebrated mathematician, subtle in talent and eloquent in speech, skilled in the three languages—Hebrew, Greek, and Latin—most upright in life and conversation and singularly devout, a sincere and fervid lover of the salvation of souls; who, sent as legate into Germany, did and established many useful things for the reformation of the Church, and especially of our order. He wrote many illustrious volumes, of which the following are extant: On the vision of God: book. ["I will now disclose what [things] to you…"] On the peace of the faith: book. ["He was of those who, among…"] The Reparation of the Calendar: 2 books. ["Receive, most holy pope…"] On mathematical complements: book. ["To the praise of the omnipotent God…"] A Sifting of the Koran: 3 books. ["So great is the power of the supreme…"] On the hunting of wisdom: book. ["It is [my] purpose [to set forth] my [things]…"] On the game of the mystical globe: 2 books. ["Since I see you [going] to the [Apostolic] See…"] A Compendium: book. ["Receive a brief compendium…"] A Trialogue on Possest [actualized-possibility]: book. ["Since to us is granted…"] On mathematical perfection: book. ["The noble mind is solicitous…"] Against the Bohemians: book. ["Nicholas, by [God's] mercy…"] On the Beryl: 1 book. ["Whoever shall have read the [things] which [are] in…"] On the gift of the Father of lights: book. ["And if already before, [as] above…"] On seeking God: book. ["According to your desire, as far as possible…"] On the summit of contemplation: [book]. ["I see you [pondering] a certain profound [matter]…"] On Learned Ignorance: book. ["He will wonder, and rightly…"] On Conjectures: 2 books. ["Now, such as it is, [the work] being given…"] On the filiation of God: [book]. ["At length [it] compelled me…"] On Gene[sis]

Book. The archbishop of Trier, judging that man to be learned, experienced, and zealous, by the authority of the supreme pontiff took him from the Charterhouse and appointed him abbot in the aforesaid monastery; through him he reformed many monasteries in his diocese. He himself also, by the authority of the Council of Basel, magnificently extended the reform. He wrote, for the reform of monks: Useful Constitutions, one book, “When the divine office [unclear].” On the Quality of an Abbot, one book, “Since every [unclear] proceeds from on high.” And certain other things. He died under Emperor Albert and Pope Eugene IV, in the year of the Lord 1439, the twentieth of his abbacy, in the first indiction, on the first day of the month of December. He was buried in the said monastery of Saint Matthias the Apostle at Trier, before the altar of the protomartyr Stephen, in the right apse of the choir, under a stone inscribed with his name.

Guarinus of Verona, once a hearer of Chrysoloras the Byzantine philosopher, a man not ignorant of Greek letters and most skilled in Greek and Latin speech; through his labors the studies of the liberal arts were aroused and called back into the light, which had seemed weakened and already almost extinct. He taught first at Venice, afterwards at Ferrara; in both places he had very famous pupils. He wrote to Prince Leonello a work entitled On the Difference between a Flatterer and a Friend, one book; also a brief Grammar, one book; A Comparison of Scipio and Gaius, one book; Letters to Various Persons, sixteen books; several Orations, one book; many Poems; and not a few other things. By order of Pope Nicholas V he translated into Latin Strabo’s Geography, a work no less useful than delightful. From Plutarch he made Latin versions of the lives of many illustrious men; but Plutarch himself On the Education of Children, with many other works, he translated most elegantly, which are partly extant. He died under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Pius II, in the year of the Lord 1460, in the eighth indiction, on the day before the Nones of December. He was buried at Ferrara in the convent of the Carmelites, honorably endowed with a marble tomb.

Heinrich Kalteisen, archbishop of the churches of Nidaros and Caesarea, of the Order of Friars Preachers, German by nation, a native of Koblenz, where he entered the order; first lector of the sacred palace, preacher of Holy Cross, inquisitor of heretical depravity, afterwards, as we have said, consecrated chief bishop of two provinces by apostolic authority; through his learning and preaching he became famously known to the whole world. Since he was a very celebrated doctor of sacred theology, he wrote, among other notable things: Sermons on the Season, one book; Sermons on the Saints, one book; Sermons through Lent, one book; On the Magnificat, one book; Various Questions, one book; Conferences to the Clergy; and many other things. He died under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Paul II, in the year of the Lord 1466, in the fourteenth indiction, on the sixth day before the Nones of October. He was buried in his own convent at Koblenz.

Johannes Bertachinus of Fermo, a very celebrated jurist, singularly devoted to that faculty, outstanding in talent and distinguished in eloquence, wrote certain excellent little works in law, by which he transmitted the memory of his name to posterity. Of these there survives a very distinguished work, divided into three large volumes, which

Pius II, pope, Tuscan by nation, Sienese by native city, formerly called Aeneas Silvius, sat in the supreme pontificate after Calixtus III for six years: a man most learned in every respect, a philosopher, orator, and distinguished poet; he left to posterity many monuments of his talent. Once, when poor, he served a certain prelate at the Council of Basel. Then, after being taken on as a scribe in the chancery of Frederick III, emperor, and after receiving the poet’s laurel, he was made first bishop of Trieste, afterward of Siena, then cardinal, and most recently was elected pope by the vote of all. Concerning his writings, the following are reported, composed with great force of eloquence:

On the Miseries of Courtiers, one book.

On the Education of Children, one book.

Solution of Questions, one book.

On Two Lovers, one book.

Against the Taborites, one book.

To Nicholas of Cusa, one book.

On Faith, to the Turk, one book.

On the Expedition against the Turks, one book.

To the Bishop of Cracow, one book.

On the Council of Basel, one book.

On the Source of the River Nile, one book.

On the Practice of Hunting, one book.

On Fate also, one book.

Abridgments of Blondus, one book.

On the Origin of the History of the Bohemians, one book.

Precepts of Rhetoric, one book.

Europe, to Cardinal Antonio, one book.

On the Foreknowledge of God, one book.

Dialogue against the Turks, one book.

On Grammar, one book.

An Unfinished Work of Histories, one book.

Letters to Various Persons, one book.

On the Fall of Constantinople, an oration, one book.

On the Fall of the Universal Church, one book.

In the Assembly at Mantua, an oration, one book.

An Oration to Pope Calixtus, one book.

An Oration before the Gathering of Cardinals, one book.

On the Deeds Done by Himself, one book.

Various Orations.

Many epigrams and certain other very elegant little works, which I have not seen, he is said to have written; by these he made his name known to posterity. He died under Emperor Frederick III, at Ancona, as is said, in the year of the Lord 1464, in the twelfth indiction, on 1 September. He was buried at Rome in the church of Saint Peter, beside the altar of Saint Andrew.

Lanfrancus de Oriano, a very celebrated jurist, not ignorant of secular literature, excellent in talent and renowned for eloquence, wrote in his profession certain volumes not to be despised, by which he transmitted the memory of his talent to posterity and proved himself in many ways magnificently in study. He also published many other things, which have not come to my knowledge.

Henricus Gorrickem, German by nation, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and notably learned in secular philosophy, distinguished in talent, scholastic in speech, and an acute disputant, was regarded in his own time as distinguished in the University of Cologne by lecturing and composing. He wrote little works of no contemptible reading, by which he transmitted his name to posterity with glory. Of these there are extant:

Conclusions on the Sentences, three books: “Desiring something concerning ...”

On Superstitions, one book: “In the reading ...”

Against the Hussites also, one book.

On the Celebration of Feasts, one book.

A summary of Saint Thomas, one book.

Sermons and conferences, one book.

In addition he published various questions, determinations, lectures, different books, and treatises, which have by no means come to the knowledge of our reading. He flourished under Frederick III, emperor, and Pope Pius II, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1460.

Johannes Kanneman, of the Order of Friars Minor, German by nation, a man learned in the holy Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, subtle in talent, distinguished in eloquence, was excellent in declaiming sermons to the people. Since, thinking wrongly about ecclesiastical power, he was being sought by the minister of Saxony for prison, he slipped away in flight and took refuge with the Observantines; thereafter he amended his error together with his life. Johannes de Hagen, a Carthusian and most learned man, had already long before corrected him and recalled him to the paths of justice. He wrote:

A defense of himself, one book.

On the Passion of the Lord, one book.

Various sermons, one book.

Certain questions, one book.

And many other things.

He flourished in the times of Frederick III, emperor, and Pope Pius II, in the year of the Lord 1460.

Jacobus Luterbuck, German by nation, of the Order of Carthusians, vicar of the house of Mount Saint Savior near Erfurt, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, distinguished in talent, clear in speech, a cautious interpreter of doubtful matters, and devout also in life and conduct, wrote many various little works, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Concerning these the following are reported:

On the Jubilee Year, one book.

On the Causes of Many Sufferings, one book.

On the Threefold State of Men, one book.

Consolation for the Evils of This World, one book.

On the Manner of Observing an Interdict, one book.

Apologeticus of Religious, one book.

On the Precautions of Diverse Estates, one book.

On the Knowledge of Secrets, one book: “For cutting away errors ...”

He died in the times of Emperor Frederick III and Pope Paul II, in the year of the Lord 1466, in the fourteenth indiction.

Nicolaus Dorbellus, of the Order of the Friars Minor of Saint Francis, of the province of Tours, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, second to none in scholastic philosophy, renowned for his intellect, and sufficiently fitted for disputing and disentangling questions of the Scriptures, wrote certain excellent volumes, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. In the school at Poitiers, both by teaching and by writing, he earned great praise for his learning. Concerning his little works the following are reported: an outstanding and most celebrated work, almost divine, pleasing in its singular usefulness:

On the Sentences. Four books. “Because, as the Wise Man bears witness, [unclear].”

On the Summulae of Peter of Spain. Seven books. “As the Philosopher says in the sixth [book] of the Metaphysics.”

On mathematical science. One book. “The first part having been dispatched.”

On the books of Aristotle’s Physics. Eight books. “Nature.” Here begins the book [unclear].

On the books On the Heavens and the World. Two books. “On generation”; here begins the book.

On the books of the Meteorology. Two books. “On the first things.” The book begins.

On the books On the Soul. Three books. “Of good and honorable things.”

On the books of the Metaphysics. Twelve books. “The second part of this having been dispatched.”

On the books of the Ethics. Ten books. “By a concise treatise according to [unclear].”

And certain other things. He was, moreover, a profound interpreter and most keen defender of the sayings of John Scotus; from his writings, expounding philosophy, he named this very work a compendium, dividing it into three parts: mathematical, theological, and ethical. He flourished in the times of Emperor Frederick III and Pope Callixtus III, in the year of the Lord 1455.

Petrus de Unçola, a citizen of Bologna, a very celebrated jurist, well instructed in the disciplines of the liberal arts, outstanding in intellect, renowned in eloquence, distinguished by experience in military affairs and especially in judicial matters, wrote, for the use of notaries studying legal science, an excellent volume on the continuation of the fifth, sixth, and seventh chapters of the Summa of Master Rolandinus, which he entitled:

Aurora novissimae: one book. Scribarii et tabellionii. Various consultations: one book. He is said also to have written some other works, but they have not come to my knowledge.

Henricus de Herph, of the Order of Friars Minor of Saint Francis, a German by nation, of the province of Cologne, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of pontifical law, excellent in talent and clear in speech, of very celebrated reputation in delivering sermons to the people, venerable no less for his religious life than for his knowledge of the Scriptures, wrote little works of authority not to be rejected, by which he made his name known to posterity. Among them the following are reported. A large and distinguished volume:

On the precepts of the Decalogue: one book. I find another law in. Sermons for the season: one book. Behold, thy king comes. Sermons on the saints: one book. Rabbi, where dwellest thou: [unclear]. Sermons for Advent: one book. Who will be able to think. On the three parts of penitence: one book. No one can serve two lords. And certain other works. He flourished under Frederick III, emperor, and Pope Pius II, in the year of the Lord 1460.

Johannes de Turrecremata, of the Order of Friars Preachers, bishop of Sabina and cardinal priest of the holy Roman Church, a man devoted to the divine Scriptures and an outstanding preacher of sermons, ready in talent and clear in speech, wrote many little works of his talent, by which he made his name known. Among these the following are reported. To Arsenius, monk of the monastery of Saint Benedict, which he himself held in commendam, he composed a large and not-to-be-rejected work:

On the Rule of Saint Benedict: one book. With the help of our Lord. On the whole Psalter: one book. To the most blessed father and most merciful. Questions on the Sunday Gospels: one book. To the holy and most reverend. Questions on the Gospels for the saints: one book. The reverend father lately enjoined me. On blessed water: one book. Divine Scripture teaches us. On the salvation of the soul: one book. Sermons for the season: one book. Sermons on the saints: one book. And several other works. He flourished under Frederick III, emperor, and under Pius and Paul, supreme pontiffs, in the year of the Lord 1460.

Johannes de Mechilinia, a German by nation, a man trained by long study in the divine Scriptures and not moderately learned in scholastic philosophy, excellent in talent and distinguished in knowledge, taught theology publicly for many years in the academy of Cologne and acquired the praise of great erudition. He wrote certain distinguished little works of his talent, by which he transmitted the memory of his name to posterity. Among them the following are reported. A distinguished work:

On the Sentences: four books. On the Psalter: one book. Various questions: one book. Sermons and conferences: one book. And several other works. He flourished in the times of Frederick III, emperor, and Pope Pius II, in the year of the Lord 1460.

Dionysius Rikel, otherwise of Leuwis, a German by nation, of the Order of Carthusians, of the house of Bethlehem in Roermond, a man most devoted to the divine Scriptures and skilled through continual exercise, not ignorant also of secular philosophy, subtle in talent, scholastic in speech, singularly devout in life and conduct, so much so that he was even held worthy of divine revelations, to whom several letters of Nicholas of Cusa, cardinal and most learned man, are extant, wrote so many and such great works that in the number of his little works, apart from Augustine among the Latins

On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 117 ...had no one equal to him. He applied himself to contemplation and prayer with such fervor that one would never have thought he could have written anything. Conversely, in writing and reading he was so diligent that one would have judged him never able to pray or contemplate. He slept very little; he was admirable in abstinence from food and drink, for, following the example of blessed Jerome, he judged it sweet to meditate day and night on the law of the Lord, always either writing something useful or reading, so that prayer often interrupted reading, and sacred reading frequently followed prayer. Concerning his little works he himself, on his own, reviewed them in the following index:

Bessarion, commonly so called, patriarch of Constantinople, a man most learned in every respect, a philosopher, an orator, second to none in both languages, wrote certain distinguished volumes of his genius, by which he transmitted his name to posterity with great glory. Among them the following are reported. Against Mark, bishop of Ephesus, who, after the manner of the Greeks, held erroneous views concerning the Holy Spirit at the Council of Florence, he wrote a distinguished and excellent work, which he entitled:

Confutation, 1 book. On that passage, “Thus I wish him to remain,” 1 book. In Praise of Plato’s Philosophy, 5 books. Praises of His Own Country, 3 books. To the Greek Emperor, of Consolation, 3 books. Several Orations and Letters. And certain other things.

He also founded at Venice a notable library, most richly furnished with many books, both Greek and Latin; over it was placed, with no small stipend, Marcus Antonius Sabellicus, a most learned man, of whom we shall speak later. At length he died after many days, while on an embassy to France, under Emperor Frederick and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1473, in the sixth indiction.

Johannes Hagen, otherwise “de Indagine,” a German by nation, of the Carthusian order, of the house of Mount Saint Savior near Erfurt, prior in Eisenach, in Stettin, a man most devoted to the divine Scriptures, very learned, and excellently taught in canon law, brilliant in talent, ready and prudent in counsel, wrote in clear language many distinguished volumes to princes, bishops, and other prelates of churches, when asked about various and diverse questions; of these I remember that only a few have come into our hands. For, as I learned from the writings of a certain devout father of the same order, he published more than three hundred treatises; of all these I myself have seen and read only those which I have set down below in order. A notable work which he entitled:

Finally, on many books of the Bible he composed elegant commentaries, and other notable treatises and almost innumerable solutions of questions. He flourished under Frederick III and Pope Pius II, in the year of the Lord 1460.

Johannes, abbot of the monastery of Neuzelle, studious and learned in the sacred scriptures, nobly learned in canon law, subtle in intellect, distinguished in eloquence, wrote many diverse little works of his intellect, by which he transmitted to posterity with glory the memory of his most celebrated name. Of these the following are extant:

A very distinguished notable work, which is entitled Concordance of the Canon of the Bible, one book: “In the beginning God created.”

Sermons on the season, one book: “Look, lift up your heads.”

Sermons on the saints, one book: “Having left the nets, Saint Peter.”

Letters and various questions.

Obannes de Lutrea:natione teutonicq: uir in diuinis scripturis studiosus et eruditq: & in phia scholastica egregie doctus:ingenio acer: uita praeclara/ rus:& declamator sermonũ celeberrimus: q primu in gymnaio Erfordēsi

Book. The other things that he composed have not come to the notice of our reading.

Jacobus de Gruytrode, German by nation, of the Carthusian order, prior of the house of All Apostles near Liège, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, devout in life and conduct, excellent in talent and sweet in speech, wrote certain distinguished and devout little works, the reading of which is considered not unprofitable for religious persons and lovers of their own salvation.

On True Virtues, 2 books. On the Seven Deadly Sins, 1 book. On the Four Last Things, 1 book. On the Life of the Lord Jesus, 1 book. On Preparation before Mass, 1 book. On the Definition of the Name Monk, 1 book. Meditations on the Passion of the Lord, 1 book. Lectionary [of the table?], 1 book. Mirror of Prelates, 1 book. Mirror of Subjects, 1 book. Mirror of Priests, 1 book. Mirror of Secular Men, 1 book. Mirror of Old Age, 1 book. Contemplation of Saint Mary, 1 book. Colloquy of Jesus and the Monk, 1 book. Colloquy of Jesus and the Prelate, 1 book. Colloquy of Jesus and the Old Man, 1 book. Colloquy of Jesus and the Hermit, 1 book. Colloquy of Jesus and the Disciple, 1 book. Contemplation of Saint Mary, 1 book. Little Crown of Saint Mary, 1 book. Dialogue of the Crucified One and the Sinner, 1 book. Dialogue of Mary and the Sinner, 1 book. Another dialogue of Mary and the [sinner?], 1 book. Meditations on the Compassion of Mary, 1 book. On the Name of Jesus and Mary, 1 book. Sermons on the Temporale, 1 book. Sermons on the Saints, 1 book. Letters to Various Persons, 1 book.

A Bundle of Myrrh, beloved. Eat, friends, and drink.

Deal with me, sweetest Jesus. Do not be angry, I beg you, Lord. You have wounded my heart, sister. Forgive, I beg you, most kindly one. I have a word for you, O [unclear].

Of these the items placed below are reported: and many others. He died most devoutly under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1472, in the fifth indiction, on the day before the Ides of February.

Jacobus Zenus, a Venetian patrician, bishop of the church of Padua, a man studious and learned in the holy Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular letters, subtle in talent, eloquent in speech, ready and circumspect in counsel, and distinguished by experience of many things, wrote certain distinguished volumes, by which he transmitted his name to posterity with glory. Among these there is a most elegant work:

On the Deeds of the Supreme Pontiffs, 1 book, and certain other things.

He died under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1476, in the ninth indiction.

Guilhelmus Forleon, Breton by nation, of the order of the brothers of Saint Francis, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and exceptionally instructed in secular philosophy, distinguished in talent, scholastic in speech, who in the Paris gymnasium, both by teaching, by disputing, and also by writing, earned great praise for his learning, published certain distinguished little works on the Scriptures. Among these there is a very celebrated work:

DE SCRIPTORIBVS ECCLESIASTICIS fol.123 theologiā gloriose docuit: & postea in ecclesia Moguntina praedicatoris officium strenue gessit. Scripsit quaedam non spernendalectionis opuscula: quibus memoriām sui posteris reliquit. E quibus ferunt subiecta: Super sententias: li. iiiij Sermones uarii: li. i Questiones disputatae: li. i Et quaedam in phia. li. Moritur sub Frederico imperatore tertio: & Sixto papa quarto: Anno dñi Mille CCCC.LXXIX. Indictione duodecima. H Lanus de rupe: natione teutonicus: ordinis frarum praedicatorum: vir in diuinis scripturis eruditus: in declamādis sermonibus ad populum excel lentissimae opinionis: uita et conversatione deo deuotu et beatae Marīae femp uirginis amator praecipuus: eiusq rolarij et famulatus pmotor uenerand: a qua etiam singulari dono supernae consolationis aliquotiens meruit recreari: & iam in aeterna foelicitate refoueri. Scripsit inter alia ingenii sui opera: Compendiũ platerij Mariani. li. i Quia catholicae ueritatis. De miraculis rolarij: li. i Quis speciosa laus nō. Sermones quoq uarios: li. i Et quaedam alia. O Onradus de Zabernia: natione teutonicus: vir in scripturis diuinis studi osus et exercitatus: & saecularis litteraturae praesertim musicae non igna rus: ingenio docilis: & uita exemplaris: in declamandis sermonibus ad po pulum clarus et deuotus. De quorum numero extant subiecta: De monochordo: li. i Cũ ut quidam sapiens. De modo bene cantandi: li. i In fauorem totius cleri. De fine collectarum: li. i Quãq plariq de. Aurentius calcaneus brixianus: vir nobilis: eques aurat: & legum doctor celeberrimus: phus et historiologus luculentissimus: ingenio et eloquen tia clarus: ac disputator quaestionũ acutissim. On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 120

On the Sentences: four books. Various Questions: one book. And very many other works.

His hearer and disciple once was a very learned man and easily the foremost of the theologians of our age: Master Stephanus, called Bruleffer, a Gaul by nation, of the same order. He first taught theology in the convent at Paris; afterwards, betaking himself to the observance of the order at Mainz in Germany, he began there to lecture on the Sentences, which he is continuing in the convent at Metz with no small praise. This William flourished under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Paul II, in the year of the Lord 1470.

Albertus de Eybe, a German by nation, canon of the church of Bamberg and chamberlain of Pope Pius II, was a man zealous and learned in secular letters, not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, an outstanding rhetorician and poet. He wrote little works not to be despised in reading, of which the following are extant. To Lord Johannes, duke of Bavaria, bishop of Münster and afterwards primate of Magdeburg, an outstanding work entitled:

The Poetic Pearl: one book. You have very often wished, reverend father. Also, On Matrimony: one book. Letters to Various Persons: one book. And very many other works.

He flourished under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Pius II, in the year of the Lord 1460.

Rodericus, bishop of Zamora, was a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular letters, outstanding in intellect and distinguished in eloquence. He wrote little works of no contemptible authority, products of his intellect, by which he commended the memory of his name to posterity. Of these I have so far seen only one volume, which he entitled: Mirror of Human Life: two books. Above all human things.

The rest he has not seen.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Frederick III and Pope Paul II, in the year of the Lord 1470.

Ambrosius Choriolanus, of the order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, prior general, a Roman by country, was a man learned in the divine Scriptures and distinguished in knowledge of secular letters, excellent in intellect and eloquent in speech, learned and eloquent. He wrote certain splendid little works, by which he commended his name to immortality. Of these, however, only a few came to my knowledge through reading; I have set them down below:

On the Rule of Saint Augustine: one book. From the parent of all doctors. A Commendation of the Same Rule: one book. After blessed Augustine. On the Second Rule: one book. Keen in intellect, splendid in life. On the Life of Saint Augustine: one book. Very often, when in great. On the Praises of the Same: one book. They have been accustomed, most blessed father. Various Orations: one book. He also wrote many other works.

He flourished under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Paul II, in the year of the Lord 1470.

Benedictus Stendel of Halle, a town of Saxony, a German by nation, was a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in secular philosophy, excellent in intellect and clear in speech. In the academy of Erfurt he gloriously taught theology for many years, and shone forth distinguished both in life and in doctrine. He wrote certain little works not to be despised in reading, from which in the said university he lectured ordinarily, the following:

On Genesis: one book. On Exodus: one book. On Leviticus: one book.

Book [unclear]: one book. On Numbers: one book. On Deuteronomy: one book. Various sermons: one book. Different conferences: one book. And certain other things, in logic, philosophy, and the remaining scholarly studies and exercises. He flourished under Frederick III, emperor, and Pope Paul II, in the year of the Lord 1470.

Ilfridus, titular bishop of Cyrene, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a German by nation, vicar in pontificals of Theoderic, archbishop of Mainz, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, skilled in the Hebrew and Latin languages, subtle in talent, distinguished in speech, an acute disputant, an outstanding preacher of the divine word, ready in counsel, and illustrious in life, wrote certain little works worthy of reading, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these, the following are extant, addressed to the aforesaid Archbishop Theoderic:

On the Usury of the Jews: one book. It asks in the forum of conscience. On the Redemption of Rents: one book. It first asked whether [unclear]. Sermons and conferences: one book. Various questions: one book. And certain other things. He flourished under Frederick III, emperor, and under Pius and Paul, Roman pontiffs, in the year of the Lord 1470.

Godescalcus of Meschede, a German by nation, a Westphalian by homeland, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, excellently taught in secular philosophy, keen in talent, illustrious in life, a profound doctor of sacred theology, who for many years taught that science gloriously in the academy of Erfurt, earned from all great praise for his learning. In the same university he wrote and lectured on certain excellent little works, by which he made his name known to posterity. Among them are reported:

Questions on the Sentences: three books. Sermons and conferences: one book. Various disputed questions: one book. And many other things.

His brother Theodericus Gresmundt of Meschede, doctor of arts and medicine, a man most learned in every respect, still surviving, resides at Mainz; he himself, among other things, composed an elegant treatise On the Regimen of Health in Time of Pestilence. He has a son called Theoderic after his own name, scarcely completing three lustrums of age; his admirable talent, and his singular learning as well as eloquence, far surpass many of mature age, even doctors. There is extant, addressed to me, his distinguished book On the Seven Liberal Arts. For he wrote, both to me and to others, almost countless letters, most ornate on every sort of subject, and various orations displaying Ciceronian eloquence, so that, like another Adeodatus, once the son of most holy Augustine, by his talent, readiness, and skill in writing and arguing he is an object of admiration and astonishment to many, even learned men. But Godescalcus, his father’s brother, flourished under Frederick III, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1470, and died before this decade.

Stephanus Hoest of Ladenburg, formerly canon of the church of Speyer, a German by nation, a man learned in secular letters, not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, a very celebrated philosopher and orator, keen in talent, eloquent in speech, distinguished in delivering sermons to the people, since for some years he held the office of preacher in the castle of Heidelberg, wrote little works not to be despised, by which he commended the memory of his name to posterity. Among them is extant:

On the Books of the Ethics: ten books. Sermons and conferences: one book.

On Ecclesiastical Writers, folio [unclear]

Poems and certain other things.

He died under Frederick, the third emperor, and Pope Paul II, in the year of the Lord 1471, in the fourth indiction.

Bernardus Justinianus, a Venetian by homeland, a very celebrated philosopher and orator, outstanding in talent and eloquent in speech, who, because of his singular grace in speaking, was held in esteem not only among his own Venetian senate, but also among the Roman pontiffs, cardinals, and the other princes of Italy and senators of cities. Among the other monuments of his talent he wrote, on Laurentius Justinianus, Venetian patriarch, his maternal uncle:

The Life and Most Holy Conduct, one book. Also Histories, one book. Several elegant Orations, one book. Letters and certain other things.

He flourished under Frederick, the third emperor, and Pope Paul II, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1470.

Henricus de Piro, a German by nation, born from the city of Cologne, of the order of the Carthusians, professed of the house of Saint Barbara in the same city; before entering the order a subtle and famous doctor of both laws, and afterward also practiced in the divine Scriptures. He wrote certain distinguished volumes, of which the following are reported:

On the Institutes, three books. “With the lawgiver of all granting me...” Also, To Novices, one book. Counsels in Various Cases, one book. Sermons on the Season, one book. Sermons on the Saints, one book. And certain other things.

He flourished in the times of Frederick, the third emperor, and Pope Paul II, in the year of the Lord 1470.

Nicolaus Donis, a German by nation, of the order of the divine father Benedict, a man studious and learned in secular letters, and not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, a distinguished philosopher and mathematician, a most vigilant discoverer and most sagacious restorer of Ptolemy’s Cosmography, excellent in talent and clear in eloquence. He wrote volumes not to be despised, by which he transmitted his name to posterity. Among them there exists a wonderful and very celebrated work, with pictures and new tables most elegantly arranged and most diligently corrected:

On the Cosmography of Ptolemy, to Pope Paul II, seven books. “It does not escape me, most blessed father...” Also On Marvelous Places, one book. “Since, as Augustine says...” Various Letters to different persons. And certain other things.

He flourished, moreover, under Frederick, the third emperor, and Pope Paul II, in the year of the Lord 1470.

Georgius de Burbach, a German by nation, a man very experienced in secular letters and knowledge, and not ignorant of the holy Scriptures, a philosopher and easily the most brilliant astronomer of all men of his time. In the university of Vienna he publicly taught philosophy and the science of the stars for a long time; there, among countless other pupils, he instructed Johannes de Regiomonte, afterward a most learned man. He wrote certain distinguished little works of penetrating talent. Of their number I have seen only:

The New Theorics of the Planets, one book. “The sun has three orbs from itself...”

Of the others I have as yet seen nothing. He flourished under Frederick, the third emperor, and the Roman pontiffs Pius and Paul, in the year of the Lord 1470.

Domitius Calderinus, a Veronese by homeland, a most brilliant rhetorician and perfectly imbued with the disciplines of all the good arts, of Greek and Latin speech s

excellently skilled; subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech. He wrote many distinguished little works in humane letters, by which he transmitted the memory of his name to posterity. Of these, the following are reported:

On Juvenal, one book: “There are two kinds of satires [unclear].” On Martial, one book. On Suetonius, one book. On the Ibis of Naso, one book. On the letters of Cicero, one book. Against Brotheus the grammarian, one book: “Would that Heli and Marcus [unclear].” Letters to various persons, one book. Various orations. And many other things.

He died under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, whose secretary he had been, in the year of the Lord 1477, in the tenth indiction.

Johannes Tinctoris, German by nation, of Cologne, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in secular philosophy; acute in intellect and an outstanding disputant. He taught theology publicly for a long time in the University of Cologne, and gained great praises for his learning. He wrote little works not to be despised, of which the following are reported:

Dissensions of Thomas and Scotus, which he began to reconcile, in one book. Questions on the Sentences, one book. Also various collationes. And certain other things.

He flourished in the aforesaid university under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Paul II, in the year of the Lord 1470.

Nicolaus Perotus of Sassoferrato, and bishop of Siponto, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and second to no one in his time in secular letters; an outstanding theologian and a most eloquent rhetorician; keen in intellect and distinguished in life. He wrote certain lucid little works, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these there survives a notable work divided into two volumes, on the poet Marcus Valerius Martialis, very beautifully comprising all the elegance, method, and explanation of Latin speech, which he entitled The Volume of Commentaries on the Language, or, as it is commonly called:

Cornucopia, two books: “Barbara and [unclear] flatters [unclear].” On the Education of Boys, one book. On the Kinds of Metres, one book. Orations and various letters.

He is said to have written many other things besides, both in divine letters and in humane letters, and to have translated some things from Greek into Latin; but they have not come into our hands.

He flourished under Emperor Frederick III and the Roman pontiffs Pius and Paul, in the year of the Lord 1470.

Antonius Rosellus, Tuscan by nation, an eminent professor of both laws and a very celebrated interpreter, and greatly adorned with the discipline of other good arts; outstanding in intellect and eloquent in speech. He taught law for many years in the University of Padua. He wrote many distinguished little works, by which he commended the memory of his name to posterity. But I do not recall that I have ever seen any of them. There is reported, however, his notable work:

On the Monarchy of the World, three books. And many other things.

He died under Emperor Frederick III, in vigorous old age, and was buried at Padua.

On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 122.

In the year of the Lord 1467, indiction 15.

Johannes Beatus, by nation a German, of the Order of the Brothers of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular literature, an excellent theologian and subtle philosopher, sharp in intellect, distinguished in life, an outstanding disputant of questions, and notable in delivering sermons to the people, wrote certain excellent little works. Among these the following are reported:

On the Epistle of Paul to the Romans, one book: “Sacred Scripture divinely in ...”

A Preceptory of the Divine Law, ten books.

On the Sacrament of the Altar, one book.

Sermons on the Season, one book.

Sermons on the Saints, one book.

Various Disputed Questions, one book.

He also published a number of other things, which have not come to the knowledge of our reading. He died under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV in his convent of Tenen, in the year of the Lord 1476, indiction 9, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of August.

Bartholomaeus Cepolla, a Veronese by nation, a very celebrated jurist and a distinguished cultivator of other disciplines of secular literature, acquired great praise for his learning by lecturing, disputing, and writing in regular course in the gymnasium of Padua. He wrote many excellent little works, and commended the memory of his name to posterity. Among these there is extant a work indeed most subtle, which he entitled:

Cautelae of Law and of Civil Cases, one book: “It is to be noted especially that ...”

On Simulated Contracts, one book.

On Urban Estates, one book.

On Rural Estates, one book.

Also On Military Affairs, one book.

And very many others.

He died in the time of Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1477, indiction 10.

Johannes de Regiomonte, by nation a German, once a pupil of the astronomer Georgius Burbachius, no less than Anaximander of Miletus or Archimedes of Syracuse, very learned in Greek and Latin eloquence, the glory of the Germans, endowed with a perpetual stipend by Matthias, king of Pannonia, and by the consulship and citizens of Nuremberg on account of astronomy and the other mathematical disciplines, gained great praise for his learning not only among his own Germans, but also among the Italians and the French. For, having been summoned to Rome by the supreme pontiff Sixtus to correct the Dionysian paschal computus, while he was preparing many things for posterity, he perished of disease, to the very great loss of scholars. He wrote certain excellent little works, of which the following are extant:

A Very Beautiful Calendar, one book.

Ephemerides, that is, a daily register, one book: “After we have sent out the index ...”

Against Gerardus of Cremona, one book.

Letters and Orations, one book.

And very many others.

He died at Rome under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1476, indiction 9.

Gerardus de Elten, by nation a German, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular philosophy, sharp in intellect, distinguished in life: after he had taught theology gloriously for many years in the gymnasium of Cologne, having held the vanities of the world in contempt, in his old age he entered the Order of Preachers for the love of God in the same city of Agrippina, and was soon appointed inquisitor and exterminator of heretical depravity. He wrote, among other things, as they report:

Questions and Sentences, one book.

Book

Disputed Questions, one book.

Sermons and Conferences, one book.

Various things also in philosophy.

And very many others.

He flourished under Emperor Frederick III and the supreme pontiff Sixtus IV, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1475.

Alexander Tartagnus de Imola, a jurist both devoted to study and learned, and well experienced in the rudiments of other secular disciplines, excellent in intellect and of distinguished eloquence, wrote, for the usefulness of those who labor in the study of both laws, certain excellent volumes, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of their number the following are reported:

On the Sixth Book of the Decretals, one book.

Also On the Clementines, one book.

Also On the Code, nine books.

On the Old Digest, twenty-four books.

On the New Digest, fourteen books.

On the Infortiatum, fourteen books.

And certain others.

He flourished in the time of Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1470.

Johannes Soreth, a Norman by nation, of the Order of the Friars of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, the twenty-fifth prior general; a man most learned in the divine scriptures, and not ignorant of secular philosophy; subtle in talent, sweet and clear in speech, devout in life and conduct, and singularly religious and holy; the ornament, glory, splendor, and reformer of the Carmelite order, such as past ages have rarely seen and future ages will more rarely behold; wholly given to God, wholly intent on reading and prayer; a despiser of the world; a lover, model, and mirror of monastic conduct; an imitator of angelic purity, guardian of virtues, and keenest enemy of vices. He wrote many commendable little works of his excellent talent, of which the following are extant:

On the Sentences, four books. Various sermons, one book. On the rule of his order, one book. A larger commentary on the same, one book. He arranged the Constitutions, one book. He also wrote many other things.

He died at Angers under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus, in the year of the Lord 1471, in the third indiction, on the eighth day before the Kalends of August.

Theodore Gaza of Thessalonica, a man excellently learned in secular letters and not ignorant of sacred scripture, most learned in Greek and Latin, outstanding in talent and eloquent in speech, wrote many little works; he translated many things from Greek into Latin, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Of his writings nothing has yet come to the knowledge of our reading. But among his translations are reported:

Theophrastus, On Plants, one book. Aristotle’s Problems, one book. The same author, On Animals, one book. And certain other things.

He died at Rome under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1478, in the eleventh indiction.

Johannes de Lutrea, a German by nation, a man studious and learned in the divine scriptures, and excellently learned in scholastic philosophy; keen in talent, distinguished in life [unclear], and a very celebrated declaimer of sermons, who first in the gymnasium of Erfurt

he taught theology gloriously, and afterwards in the church of Mainz vigorously discharged the office of preacher. He wrote certain little works of no contemptible reading, by which he left the memory of himself to posterity. Among them they report the following:

On the Sentences, four books. Various Sermons, one book. Disputed Questions, one book. And certain things in philosophy, [unclear] book[s].

He died under Frederick III, emperor, and Sixtus IV, pope, in the year of the Lord 1479, in the twelfth indiction.

Alanus de Rupe, a German by nation, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, of most excellent reputation in delivering sermons to the people, in life and conduct devoted to God and a special lover of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin, and a venerable promoter of her rosary and service; by her, too, he sometimes deserved to be refreshed with a singular gift of heavenly consolation, and now to be revived in eternal happiness. Among the other works of his talent he wrote:

A Compendium of the Marian Psalter, one book. It begins: “Because of catholic truth.” On the Miracles of the Rosary, one book. It begins: “[unclear].” Also Various Sermons, one book. And certain other things.

He died in his convent at Zwolle, under Frederick III, emperor, and Sixtus IV, pope, in the year of the Lord 1479, in the seventh indiction, on the vigil of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary. Her rosary, and the psalter commemorative of Christ’s Passion, which had long now been neglected, he recalled to the minds and practices of men; in its honor he founded a confraternity, which, confirmed by the apostolic see, increases daily and provides many with a salutary exercise.

Conradus of Zabern, a German by nation, a man studious and practiced in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular literature, especially music; teachable in talent and exemplary in life, distinguished and devout in delivering sermons to the people. He wrote in plain speech certain little works not to be despised, by which, usefully and fruitfully exercising his talent, he also commended the memory of his name to posterity. Among their number the following are extant:

On the Monochord, one book. It begins: “Since, as a certain wise man...” On the Method of Singing Well, one book. It begins: “In favor of the whole clergy...” On the Ending of Collects, one book. It begins: “Although very many concerning...” Many and Various Sermons, one book. And certain other things.

He flourished in the year of the Lord 1470, under Pope Sixtus IV, under whom he also died.

Laurentius Calcaneus of Brescia, a noble man, a knight of the golden spur, and a most celebrated doctor of laws, a most lucid philosopher and historian, distinguished in talent and eloquence, and a very acute disputant of questions. He wrote certain distinguished volumes, by which he transmitted his name to posterity; among these they report the following:

On the Commendation of Studies, one book. On the Seven Mortal Sins, one book. On the Conception of Saint Mary, [unclear] book[s]. Also Several Counsels, [unclear] book[s]. And certain other small works.

He died under Frederick III, emperor, and Sixtus IV, pope, in the year of the Lord 1478, in the eleventh indiction.

Johannes de Dorstein, a German by nation, of the Order of Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and

Book [unclear]

... not ignorant of philosophy; subtle in intellect; sufficiently suited to disputing and resolving questions of the Scriptures; also of outstanding reputation in delivering sermons to the people; who, teaching and preaching in the school at Erfurt, was held in esteem. He wrote works not to be despised, by which he commended the memory of himself to posterity.

Of these there are reported:

Sermons on the season: one book. Sermons on the saints: one book. And certain other things.

He flourished in the convent of Erfurt under Frederick III, emperor, and Sixtus IV, pope, in the year of the Lord 1475.

Angelus Saxo of Brunswick, a German by nationality, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, excellently instructed in secular philosophy, keen in intellect, distinguished in life, of very celebrated reputation in delivering sermons to the people, since after obtaining the magisterium of teaching in the school at Erfurt he performed the office of preacher for a long time at Mainz. Among other things he wrote a certain notable work:

On the Canon of the Mass: one book. Various sermons: one book. Diverse questions: one book. And certain other things.

He died at Strasbourg, buried in the monastery of the penitents, under Frederick III, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1481, in the fourteenth indiction.

Franciscus Philelfus, born from the ancient town of Tolentino, a golden knight and poet laureate, a philosopher and very celebrated orator, once in his youth at Venice a pupil of Chrysoloras, the Byzantine philosopher, from whom he learned Greek and Latin eloquence most perfectly; a man so studious of the good arts, an untiring lover and cultivator of them, that, like another Pliny, amid the continual occupations of wars he was always either reading something to himself or dictating something to others. For he wrote in both languages, in prose as well as in verse, many excellent volumes, by which he left to posterity the memory of a very celebrated intellect. Of these there survive:

Eutyphro, on piety: one book. On moral discipline: eight books. Life of Pope Nicholas V: two books. A consolatory work to a friend: one book. On the diversity of laws: one book. The Sforziad, in heroic verse: nine books. Satires, in the same meter: ten books. On jests and serious matters, in hexameter: six books. Lyric poems in every kind of meter: six books. Various orations, sixty: one book. Incipit: “Since I desire something to...” Latin letters: twenty-one books. Incipit: “Because of many laws...” Greek letters: thirty-nine books. In Greek verses, in odes: three books. Banquets, in prose: two books. Also On Exile: three books. And many other works.

Besides these he translated many things into Latin, among which the following are reported: Aristotle’s Rhetoric to King Alexander: one book. From Plato: two books. Hippocrates, On winds and the sufferings of the body: two books. Of Latin letters: the lives of Theseus, Galba, and Otho. Also Apophthegms: two books. And many other things. This Franciscus, as we have said, was the pupil and son-in-law of Chrysoloras the Byzantine, a most distinguished man; and after he had become most learned from him, first among the Venetians, afterward among the Florentines, the Sienese, the Bolognese, and finally the Milanese, under

Moritur Coloniae in maiori eccl̓ia sepultꝰ:sub Fre¬derico imperatore tertio: Anno dn̄i Mill̓.CCCC.XCII. Indictione decima. septimo Calend̓.septembris. On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 124

... under four dukes, with an annual pension, he gloriously taught Greek and Latin letters to very many. He died at Bologna, ninety years old and poor, indeed as a philosopher and a Christian, under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus, in the year of the Lord 1481, the fourteenth indiction, in the year after the death of his son Marius. Book [unclear].

Marius Philelphus, son of the aforesaid Francis Philelphus, a knight with golden spurs, such as our people call knights, and a laureate poet, a doctor of philosophy and the arts of very celebrated reputation, and distinguished by knowledge both of the divine Scriptures and of both laws, was engaged for a public salary to lecture in the gymnasium of Mantua; there also he brought to an end his life and his studies. Among other things he wrote:

A distinguished work of precepts of the art of rhetoric, two books. Elegant orations, one book. Letters to various persons, one book. Songs and rhythms. “I had already long ago determined...”

But he also composed many other things in verse and prose, which have not come to me. He died at Mantua under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1480, the thirteenth indiction.

Theodericus de Herxen, a German by nation, visitor of the order of the brethren of the clerics living in common, a devout man, and studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, ready in intellect, clear in speech, outstanding in life and conduct. For the edification of simple brethren he wrote many devout volumes, in which, usefully exercising his talent, he left the memory of himself to posterity. Of these the following are reported:

On the whole Psalter, one book. On the Lord’s Prayer, one book. On the Ave Maria, one book. On the Passion of the Lord, one book. On the desire of dying, one book.

And many other things. He flourished under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1476.

Dominicus de Dominicis, a Venetian by homeland, first bishop of Torcello and afterwards bishop of Brescia, and apostolic referendary, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and most learned in secular letters, excellently adorned with philosophy, dialectic, astronomy, and eloquence. Because of his great virtues he was held in high esteem among the Roman pontiffs Pius, Paul, and Sixtus, and often fulfilled the office of legation. He wrote several excellent little works of excellent talent, but I do not recall that any of them have come into our hands. The following elegant works of his are reported:

Orations on various subjects, one book. Also various sermons, one book. And many treatises.

He died at Brescia under Emperor Frederick III and Sixtus IV, supreme pontiff, in the year of the Lord 1478, the eleventh indiction, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of March, in the sixtieth year of his age.

Ludovicus Donatus, a Venetian patrician and bishop of Bergamo, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of scholastic philosophy, distinguished also in piety, religion, clemency, and mildness, subtle in intellect and clear in eloquence. He wrote certain lucid little works, by which he left the memory of himself to posterity. Of these I have never deserved to see any. His notable work addressed to Paul II is reported:

On the Sentences, four books. Also various orations, one book.

He died under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the second indiction. He was buried in the church of Saint Vincent the Martyr. 1484.

Book

Conradus of Rodenberg, German by nation, abbot of the monastery of Saint John the Baptist at Rheingau, in the diocese of Mainz, of the order of the divine father Benedict, a devout and learned man, and a particular guardian and lover of regular observance, who previously for many years held the office of prior at Saint Matthias the Apostle in Trier and at Saint Martin in Cologne. Since he was a most ardent lover of the blessed Mary ever virgin, he wrote in her honor, in plain discourse, a very celebrated volume, taking the material of praise from each of her members, under the figure of a cluster of grapes, to which he gave the very apt title:

On the vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth: one book. Its foundations are in the mountains. The exercise of novices: one book. Consider your calling, brothers. On preparation before Mass: one book. Our Lord Jesus Christ. On the ruin of the order, an oration: one book. The crown has fallen from our head. On the causes of the ruin, an oration: one book. Catch us the little foxes. On pastoral care, an oration: one book. Blessed is the servant whom he finds. And various collections in chapters.

He died under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Innocent VIII, in the year of the Lord 1486, in the fourth indiction, on the eighth day before the Kalends of January. He was buried in the right apse of the choir before the altar of Saint Benedict, toward the ambulatory.

Stephanus of Gaeta, a Neapolitan, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, and a most learned professor and interpreter of both laws, acute in intellect and sufficiently capable in debating and resolving questions of the Scriptures, clear and orderly in speech. He wrote to Johannes Baptista de Bentivoliis of Sassoferrato, counselor of Ferdinand, king of Sicily, a very celebrated work:

On the sacraments: seven books. To the thresholds of blessed Peter the Apostle. And certain other works.

He flourished in the time of Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1470.

Georgius Molitoris of Neuenburg, German by nation, a man trained by long study and excellently learned in the divine Scriptures, and not moderately instructed in scholastic philosophy, which they call Aristotelian; keen in intellect, distinguished in life. In the academy of Erfurt he taught theology publicly for several years and won great praise for his learning. He wrote certain distinguished little works of his intellect, by which he commended his memory to posterity; among them they report the following:

On the Sentences: four books. On the Passion of the Lord: one book. Many sermons: one book. Various questions. And several other works.

He died under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1484, in the second indiction.

Bartholomaeus, surnamed Platina, a Cremonese by homeland, formerly an apostolic abbreviator, a man most learned in every respect, a very celebrated philosopher and rhetorician, subtle and forceful in intellect, eloquent and pleasing in speech, steadfast and strong in spirit. He suffered many calamities from Paul II, to such an extent that, stripped of all his goods and dignity, after suspension on the rack he was most cruelly thrust into prison, and was detained until the death of that Paul. When he was soon freed by Sixtus, in imitation of Eutrandus, deacon of Pavia, who suffered similar things from Berengar, king of Italy, he not ineptly marked the character and vices of Paul by a counter-reckoning. For he wrote to Pope Sixtus IV:

On the deeds of the Roman pontiffs: one book. On the natures of things: one book. Letters to various persons: one book.
