On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 125

And certain other things.

He died at Rome of the plague, under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1481, in the fourteenth indiction.

Nicolaus of Wachenheim, a German by nation, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and excellently instructed in secular philosophy, outstanding in intellect and renowned for eloquence, who, in the Heidelberg academy, for almost fifty years, by teaching, lecturing, and disputing, was as it were the chief among theologians and was held in the highest esteem, wrote some little works not contemptible in reading, by which he also commended the memory of his name to posterity. Of these a few have come down to me:

Questions on the Sentences, one book. Many sermons, one book. Several conferences and orations, one book. “Because, with the approval of the sacred [unclear].” And certain other things.

He flourished at Heidelberg under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1480, already very old, and under Pope Sixtus IV; he died almost seven years before this.

Michael of Milan, of the Order of Friars Minor, studious and learned in the holy Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular literature, subtle in intellect, distinguished in life and conduct, of very celebrated reputation in preaching sermons to the people, wrote, for the benefit of those who devote themselves to preaching, some little works not to be despised, by which he also made his name known to posterity. Of these there are extant:

Sermons on the season, one book. Sermons on the saints, one book. Sermons for Advent, one book. Sermons on penitence through Lent, one book. Sermons on sins, one book. Sermons on the Ten Commandments, one book. And certain other things.

He flourished under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1480, and died under Pope Innocent VIII.

Sixtus, Pope IV, a Ligurian by nation, born in Savona, a maritime city, formerly called Franciscus, minister general of the Order of Friars Minor, sat after Paul II in the chair of Peter for thirteen years. He was a man learned in the divine Scriptures, an excellent disputant, a lover of the clergy, a promoter of religious, and a singular benefactor, especially of those whom a life of observance commended. When Pope Paul once heard him disputing, he admired him so much that he deemed him worthy of the honor of the cardinalate. Before his pontificate he wrote certain distinguished little works, among which these are reported:

On future contingents, one book. On the power of God, one book. On the blood of Christ, one book. On the conception of Saint Mary, one book. And certain other things.

He died under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1483, in the second indiction.

Johannes Consobrinus, Portuguese by nation, of the Order of the Brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular literature and canon law, outstanding in intellect, of very celebrated reputation in preaching sermons to the people, first in England and then in Portugal gave great and effective barkings against the enemies of the faith; by disputing, preaching, and writing he rejected and refuted very many heresies and errors. At the request of the provost of the royal college of Saint Mary of Ambten in England, he wrote a notable work in three parts on contracts and exchanges, which he entitled:

254
Rupertus de Licio: epus Aquilae marfori seu Aprucij urbis: ordinis fratrum minorum: vir in divinis scripturis studiosus et eruditus: & saecularis litterae non ignarus: ingenio excellens: eloquio dulcis et compositus: vita et conversatione praeclarus: declamator sermonum celeberrimus: & universo christiano in orbe famosus: qui verbo et exemplo multos ab iniquitate conversit: Scriptit ad aedificationem legentium et maxime praedicator verbi divini quaedam praeclara volumina: de quibus feruntur subiecta: Sermones de tempore: li. Nox praeceps, etc. verba sunt. De laudibus sanctis: li. No gloriet sapiens in. De poenitentia p. quadragesimā: li. Multi sunt uo. etc. ppter ni. De peccatis quod: li. Et quaedam alia. Claruit sub Frederico imperatore tertio: & Sixto et Innocentio pontificibus: Anno domini Mill. CCCCLXXXVI. Nescio si adhuc uivit. Obannes pheffer de widenberg: natione teutonicus: patria francus orientalis: vir in divinis scripturis longo studio eruditus: & in saeculari phia egregie doctus: ingenio excellens: vita et conversatione deuotus: mansuetus: & praeclarus: qui de universitate Heydelbergenis missus: principium Friburgelis gymnasijs sua eruditione illustravit: in quo iam pannos plurimos theologia gloriose docuit: & multos auditoris suos pbe eruduit. Scriptit quaedam praeclara opuscula: de quibus extat opus insignis sup eplis Pauli: quod publice lectu praenotauit: Directorium sacerdotale: li. xiiij. Circa lecturae eplax beati. Et alia complura. Claruit adhuc in humanis sub Frederico impatore tertio: Anno dñi. MCCCC. XC. Poteat adhuc uivere. Obannes britannicus ex palatiolo agri Brixianī oppido ortus: vir in saecularibus eruditissimus: & divinarũ scripturae non ignarus: plus clarus: poeta insignis: & rhetor luculentus: qu apud Brixianos suos bodie in precio habetur: quos inestimabili eruditione: doctrina et scriptis in dies clariores: multa ac uaria scriptit: quibus nomen suũ posteritati notum praesentibũ efficit uenerandũ. De quibus subiecta ferunt: Commentarioe opus celeberrimũ: In Persium: li. j In Statum quodg: li. j In metamorpho. Ouidij: li. j Epistolae quodg uariae: Et alia complura: Claret in civitate Brixiana et maria cōponit opuscula: sub Maximiliano Romano rum rege: & Alexandro pontifice sexto: Anno domini Mill. CCCCLXCLIII Aptista Ferrariensis: ordinis fratrum beatae Mariae semp uirginis de mon te Carmelit: vir in divinis scripturis eruditus: & in saeculari litteratura egregie doctus: metro excellens et prola: & in utraq: lingua peritus: in declamandis sermonibus ad populum celeberrimi ac prope divini ingenij: Scriptit multa praeclara uolumina: quibus utilem praesentibus et notum posteris reddit. Equibus subiecta feruntur: Opus luculentissimũ historiarum a christi temporibus usũ ad nos:quod praenotauit Floridam: Chronica sui ordinis: De ruina Romani imperij: De monte Syna: Vita Mechtildis: Chronica Ferrarien.

Book [unclear]

On commutative justice, four books. Various sermons, one book. And certain other works. He abridged the Conflatus of Francis Maro in a pleasing compendium. He flourished in the year of the Lord 1475. And under Pope Sixtus IV he died at Lisbon, poisoned for the faith.

Henry, surnamed the Prudent, of the Carthusian order, prior of the house of the Valley [of God?] near Bruges in Flanders, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, brilliant in intellect, devout in life and conduct, singularly devoted to God, wrote for the instruction of religious certain distinguished little works, by which he made his name known to posterity. Among these there is a very celebrated work, especially suitable for devotion, divided into three parts according to the distinctions of states: of beginners, of those advancing, and of the perfect; in the manner of a dialogue, in which the interlocutors introduced are: an angel, a monk, Jesus the heavenly father, and Mary, the loving mother-in-law of holy souls; and he entitled it:

Tetralogue of Devotion, three books. And certain other works.

He died in the new house of Saint Sophia of Constantinople near Buscum Ducis, in which for some years he held the office of prior, under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1484, in the second indiction.

Franciscus Diedus, a noble Venetian patrician, a man excellently learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, a philosopher, rhetorician, distinguished in learning and eloquence, a very celebrated interpreter of pontifical and civil law, an ever-loving and tireless guardian of the Venetian commonwealth, wrote certain distinguished little works both in verse and in prose, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Among these the following are reported:

History of Saint Roch the Confessor, one book. Various orations and letters. And certain other works.

He died at Verona under Emperor Frederick III and Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1483, in the first indiction.

Rudolph Agricola of Groningen, a Frisian by nation, a man most learned in secular letters, not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, a philosopher, rhetorician, and the most celebrated poet of all his time, skilled in Greek and Latin speech, not ignorant of the Hebrew language, excellent in intellect, eloquent in speech, formerly the teacher of Johannes Camerarius of Dalberg, bishop of Worms, a man likewise most learned: in the Heidelberg school, by teaching and writing, he easily obtained the first place among all the doctors, even those of any faculty. He wrote certain most excellent little works of his intellect, by which he consecrated his name to immortality and left it to posterity. Among these the following are extant:

Life of Francis Petrarch, one book. A poem on Saint Anne, one book: “Anna, mother of the highest [unclear].” A most subtle Dialectic, three books. Various letters and orations, one book.

He also published various most elegant poems, by which he showed his intellect to be almost divine. He translated the Psalter from Hebrew, and certain works of Plato from Greek. Beginning to translate the volumes of Dionysius the Areopagite, he was overtaken by an untimely death and left them unfinished. He also wrote other works.

He died at Heidelberg, his mind most fully extended toward God, under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Innocent VIII, in the year of the Lord 1485, in the third indiction. Hermolaus Barbarus, patriarch of Aquileia, wrote this epitaph for him: “Envious fates have enclosed beneath this marble Rudolph Agricola, the hope and glory of the Frisian soil. Indeed, while he lived, Germany deserved whatever

On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 123

Latium has whatever glory Greece has. He was buried at Heidelberg among the Friars Minor, not without loss to Latin letters.

Thilmannus, of the order of regular canons of Saint Augustine, provost of the monastery of the divine martyr Christopher in Ravengiersburg, at the edge of the diocese of Mainz, beside the Hercynian Forest, which extends its tail from the river Rhine toward the Mediomatrici and the Treveri, in a place that from antiquity is called the Retreat of the Huns; a German by nation, zealous in the divine Scriptures, devout in life and conduct. He wrote, in a simple and plain style, for the edification of the brothers, certain little works full of devotion and charity, in which he exercised his talent. Of these the following are extant:

On the Spiritual Vineyard, one book. “I should wonder, dearest...”

On the Instruction of Novices, one book. “Having entered, dearest, upon the warfare...”

And certain small exercises.

He died an old man and full of days, under Frederick, the third emperor, and Pope Innocent VIII, in the year of the Lord 1485, indiction 3.

[Henricus?] Arnoldi, a Saxon by nation, by profession a Carthusian monk of the house of Basel; a man devout in religion, distinguished in talent, sincere in affection, grave in manners, sweet in speech, affable in conduct, pious, gentle, shining by example, very much practiced in sacred letters, and not ignorant of pontifical law. When he was performing the office of notary in the holy Council of Basel for many years, he was approved by the testimony of all as faithful, just, and prudent. At length, seeing that all things are vanity, he despised everything for the love of Christ, choosing and entering the enclosure of the Carthusians; there, appointed prior of the same house, he ruled laudably in peace and tranquility for many years the monks subject to him, the lay brothers, and the others, pursuing them with paternal love. He wrote many little works, very devout and salutary. Of these, those that have come to our knowledge are set down below:

Many devout prayers concerning various saints, one book. “The following prayers...”

Several sermons, one book.

Histories concerning various saints, one book.

A Concordance of the Evangelists on the Passion of the Lord, one book.

Meditations on the Life of Christ, one treatise.

On the Instruction of Novices, one treatise.

A Dialogue between Jesus and Mary, one treatise.

A Dialogue on Exercises, that is, between a saint and his little servant, one treatise.

Another dialogue between the same persons on the cross, one treatise.

On the Commendation of Charity, one treatise. “The excellence of charity...”

On Holy Humility, in the form of a prayer, one treatise. “Of perfect humility...”

Again on humility, one treatise. “Dearest brothers, humble...”

A Chronicle of the Carthusian House in Basel, one treatise.

He happily departed from this life under Frederick III, emperor of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 1487.

Jodocus of Calw, a German by nation, a Swabian by homeland; a man practiced by long study in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of scholastic philosophy; prompt and vigorous in talent. In the Heidelberg school he was held in esteem for many years by reading, teaching, and preaching; there also, according to custom, he for some time carried out the office of preacher in the church of the Holy Spirit. He wrote, as they say, certain treatises not to be rejected, but they have not come to the knowledge of our reading. There are extant by him, on various matters:

Various sermons, one book.

A Vocabulary for Preachers, one book.

And various treatises.

Book C

He flourished under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1480; and under Pope Innocent VIII he died three years before this.

Nicolaus of Kreuznach, German by nation, from the diocese of Mainz and the county of Spanheim, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, distinguished in life, an acute disputant and an outstanding preacher of sermons, taught theology publicly for many years in the university of Vienna, and both among the scholars there and with Emperor Frederick III obtained great praise as the reward of his learning. He wrote certain excellent little works, by which he made his name known to posterity; among them these are reported:

Questions on the Sentences, four books. Various Sermons, two books. Many Collations and Orations, one book. On the Conception of Saint Mary, one book.

And many other things, which, since he kept them hidden until his death, have not yet been able to come to the knowledge of our reading; yet they will come day by day. He died at Vienna in Austria under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Innocent VIII, in the year of the Lord 1491, in the ninth indiction.

Petrus Scotus, German by nation, a native of Strasbourg, canon of Saint Peter there, a man practiced in the divine Scriptures and very learned in both laws, and also highly educated in the other humane arts; a most celebrated philosopher, rhetorician, and poet; excellent in intellect, distinguished in life and conduct. He wrote certain modest and most elegant little works, both in verse and prose, by which he commended himself to posterity. On Saints John the Baptist, John the Evangelist, and John Chrysostom he wrote a beautiful and delightful work:

In elegiac verse, one book. Praises of Jean Gerson, one book. Most elegant Letters, one book.

He died at Strasbourg and was buried in the church of Saint Peter, under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Innocent VIII, in the year of the Lord 1491, in the ninth indiction, and in the thirty-first year of his age. Brought to perfection in a short time, he fulfilled many times; he was taken away, lest wickedness should change his understanding.

Nicasius of Voerda of Mechelen, German by nation, a Brabantine by homeland, deprived of his eyes from the third year of his age and therefore naturally wholly ignorant even of all letters, displayed, as it were, a great miracle in our time, a second Didymus of Alexandria, when he became most learned in every doctrine and science, both divine and human. For in the university of Cologne, where he died, he taught law publicly; the books of both laws, which he had never seen, he learned by hearing, retained in memory, and recited openly. In the university of Leuven he first received the degree of master in arts; afterwards he directed schools for some time in Mechelen; then, having returned to Leuven, he was made licentiate in sacred theology; by a special apostolic dispensation he was ordained priest; he preached publicly, heard confessions, ministered at the altar, and, though blind, recited the Gospel before everyone, using his mind as his book; only at the altar did he not celebrate the divine offices by himself. Finally, in the academy of Cologne, by the consent of all the doctors, he was made doctor of canon law, and also a cautious interpreter of the imperial laws. He published a very celebrated work, which he read extraordinarily in that same university of Cologne, with many taking it down:

On the Institutes, four books. “Because those things which are well begun...” On the Sentences, four books. Various Sermons, one book. Diverse Questions.

On Ecclesiastical Writers, folio 27

He wrote to me certain not inelegant letters, in one of which, rather fully, he wove together the whole history of his fortune; and, when questioned by me some time ago, he humbly confessed that he had made the aforesaid little works.

He died at Cologne and was buried in the greater church, under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1492, the tenth indiction, on the seventh day before the Kalends of September.

Christophorus Persona, a Roman, prior of Saint Balbina in the City, of the order of the hermit brothers of Saint William, was most devoted to the divine Scriptures and very learned, highly skilled in the Greek and Latin languages, since from his earliest age he had imbibed those letters in Greece itself under Greek teachers, so that he seemed to have been born from Greece; subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech. Among other things he wrote:

Letters to various persons, one book.

And many other things.

He translated into Latin Origen against Celsus the philosopher, eight books, for Pope Sixtus IV. Also twenty-five moral sermons of Saint John Chrysostom, which he dedicated to Marco Barbo, cardinal of Saint Mark. But certain little works of Athanasius of Alexandria, with many others, he translated [unclear] and gave them to be read by Latins.

He died at Rome, carried off by plague, under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Innocent VIII, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1486, the fourth indiction.

Hermolaus Barbarus, a Venetian by nation, a patrician by birth, archbishop patriarch of Aquileia, and at last bishop cardinal of the most holy Roman Church, was a man devoted to the divine Scriptures, most learned in secular letters, a very celebrated philosopher, rhetorician, poet, astronomer, and geometer, highly skilled in Greek and Latin speech, subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, devout and distinguished in life and conduct, and most worthy of every ecclesiastical honor. From adolescence he devoted zeal and labor to good letters and holy morals; he became such and so great that he left no second after him. Beginning to write in the eighteenth year of his age, he composed many very elegant little works, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Of their number the following are reported: a very beautiful work:

On Celibacy, one book.

Plinian Corrections, one book.

Against Barbarous Philosophers, one book.

On the Married Estate, in verse, one book.

Questions of Geometry, one book.

The Agreement of Astronomy and Medicine, one book. His Lucubrations.

Precepts for Writing History, one book.

Compendium of Philosophy, one book.

Compendium of Galen, one book.

Letters to various persons, one book.

Multiple Orations, one book.

Of poems, more than twelve [unclear], one book.

And many other things.

The Plinian Corrections, a large work, which he began at Rome as Venetian ambassador and completed as patriarch, he dedicated to Pope Alexander VI; in it he healed nearly five thousand wounds of copyists. Once, in the year of the Lord eighty-six, when he was passing through Cologne on his way to Mainz, at the request of Theodericus [Flas?] of Neuss, a physician, he composed a little book on how far astronomy agrees with medicine. To Marcus Antonius Sabellicus, the historiographer, he published a book on the precepts for writing history. He interpreted Aristotle’s Rhetoric, the whole Dialectic, and also Dioscorides; he composed elegies, letters, metrical orations, up to twelve thousand poems, as we have said. He translated into Latin the responsal treatise of the patriarch of Constantinople on the Catholic faith, in reply to the questions of Mehmed, the great Turk; also Plutarch On Isis and Osiris, and the same author’s Why Oracles Ceased.

258

Book

A certain little work of Dionysius the Areopagite, for Arnold Bostius, Carmelite of Ghent. He translated very many other things as well. His work On Marriage contains about six hundred verses; in it he argues most elegantly whether it is expedient for a wise man to take a wife, concluding that it is not.

He died, not without the very great loss of scholars, under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord 1493, in the thirty-ninth year of his age, in the eleventh indiction.

Junianus Maius, Parthenopaean, a Neapolitan, a man certainly most devoted to secular letters and excellently learned, not ignorant also of the divine Scriptures, a very celebrated philosopher and rhetorician, outstanding in talent and distinguished in eloquence, wrote certain little works of reading not to be despised, by which he left the memory of himself to posterity. Of these there survives a large and distinguished volume addressed to Heinrich, archbishop of Acerenza, confessor of Ferdinand, king of Naples, and chiefly to the king himself, which, gathering it from the books of the ancients, he entitled:

On the Property of Ancient Words, one book. Letters to Various Persons, one book. And certain other things.

He flourished under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1480. And I am uncertain whether he is still alive.

Benedictus Capra, of Perugia, a man most celebratedly learned in both laws, well exercised both in the divine Scriptures and in the precepts of the philosophers, subtle in talent, an excellent disputant, and distinguished also by knowledge of many ancient matters, publicly taught law for a long time in the university of Perugia and acquired a great reputation for his learning. Among other things he wrote:

On the Decretals, five books. Also very many Counsels, one book. And certain other things.

He flourished under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1480.

Johannes Andreas, bishop of Aleria, secretary of the apostolic library, formerly a companion of Cardinal Nicholas of Cusa, a man devoted to the divine Scriptures and very learned in secular letters, a jurist, a most eloquent orator, excellent in talent, outstanding in life and conduct, skilled in both Greek and Latin speech, wrote certain little works of no middling authority, by which he transmitted the memory of his name with glory to posterity. Of their number the following are reported:

On the Fourth Book of the Decretals, one book. On the Use of Fiefs, one book. On Appeals, one book. Letters to Various Persons, one book. And very many other things.

He died under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Innocent VIII, in the year of the Lord 1451, in the eleventh indiction.

Johannes Campeius of Bologna, a very celebrated jurist, not moderately learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular philosophy, excellent in talent and distinguished in eloquence, publicly taught law for a long time in the university of Bologna, where, instructing many very distinguished pupils, he gained great fruit and praise for his knowledge. He wrote in that faculty many excellent commentaries and treatises, as they report, by which he commended his name to posterity. But none of them has come into our hands. There is reported to be his distinguished:

Treatise on Dowry, one book. And very beautiful Counsels, with many other things.

On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 128

He flourished under Frederick III, emperor, and Sixtus IV, pope, in the year of the Lord 1484. And I do not know whether he is still alive.

Dominicus Bolanus, a Venetian by nation, a man practiced in divine Scripture and excellently learned in secular letters, a philosopher and rhetorician not to be dismissed, sharp and forceful in talent, composed in speech, published some fine little works of his talent. In these he showed himself a devoted and faithful worshiper of the Christian name, and commended his memory to posterity. Of these I have seen only a notable little work against the detractors of Mary’s purity, which he dedicated to Nicolaus Marcellus, the seventy-first doge of the Venetians:

On the Conception of Saint Mary, one book, “With no small grief.”

Of the rest I have seen nothing.

He flourished at Venice under Frederick III, emperor, and Sixtus IV, pope, in the year of the Lord 1485. I hear that he is still living.

Franciscus Niger, a Venetian priest, a man studious and learned in divine Scripture, a most learned professor of the arts and philosophy, a poet and orator of no slight worth, outstanding in talent and eloquent in speech, wrote various little works of his talent, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these there is extant a work not to be scorned, but to be extolled with great praises, addressed to Leonardus Botta, a Milanese knight, entitled Grammar, fourteen books, “From Annaeus Seneca in the letters.”

Letters of his are reported.

And certain other things.

He flourished at Venice under Frederick III, emperor, and Sixtus IV, pope, in the year of the Lord 1480. I do not know whether he is still alive.

Jacobus de Stralen, a German by nation, a man most learned in divine Scripture and excellently learned in secular philosophy, excellent in talent and distinguished in eloquence, who for many years taught theology gloriously in the school at Cologne, deserved great praise from everyone for his learning. He wrote many splendid little works, various lectures and questions, of which I have seen only:

On the Apocalypse of John, one book, “Jacob saw a ladder in his sleep.”

Of the others I have seen nothing.

He flourished at Colonia Agrippina under Frederick III, emperor, and Innocent VIII, pope, in the year of the Lord [unclear]. He was a very old man, being about eighty years of age. And I believe he is still alive.

Marsilius Ficinus, an Italian by nation, Florentine by homeland, a man most learned in secular letters and not ignorant of divine Scripture, a very celebrated philosopher and rhetorician, most skilled in both languages, the singular glory, ornament, and crown of Platonic theology, wrote many splendid little works in an ornate style, among which are:

[On the excellence?] of Plato, one book, “Just as in [unclear].”

Letters, several books, “Plato, father of philosophers, [unclear].”

And many other things.

From Greek, moreover, he translated many things into Latin. For Petrus de’ Medici, a Florentine, he translated fifty-six treatises of Plato. Also Mercurius Trismegistus, On the Power and Wisdom of God. The book of Xenocrates the Platonist, On the Doctrine of Plato. In addition he translated many other things too, which have by no means come to the notice of our reading. He flourished at Florence under Frederick III, emperor, and Sixtus IV and Innocent VIII, Roman pontiffs, in the year of the Lord 1490. And I believe that he is still among the living.

Rupertus of Licio, bishop of Aquila, a city of the Marsi or of Abruzzo, of the Order of Friars Minor: a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular literature; excellent in talent, sweet and well-ordered in speech, distinguished in life and conduct, a very celebrated declaimer of sermons, and famous throughout the whole Christian world, who by word and example converted many from iniquity. He wrote, for the edification of readers and especially of preachers of the divine word, certain excellent volumes, of which the following are reported:

Sermons on the Temporale, a book beginning: “Nox praeceps,” etc.; these are the words. On the Praises of the Saints, a book beginning: “Let not the wise man glory in ...” On Penitence for Lent, a book beginning: “Many are ...” etc. [unclear]. On Sins, [unclear], a book beginning: “And certain other things.”

He flourished under Frederick III, emperor, and under the pontiffs Sixtus and Innocent, in the year of the Lord 1486. I do not know whether he is still living.

Johannes Pfeffer of Widenberg, German by nation, by homeland an East Franconian: a man learned by long study in the divine Scriptures, and excellently trained in secular philosophy; outstanding in talent, devout, gentle, and distinguished in life and conduct. Sent from the University of Heidelberg, he adorned with his learning the beginning of the schools at Freiburg, in which he has already taught theology gloriously for very many years and has instructed many of his hearers uprightly. He wrote certain excellent little works, among which there exists a distinguished work on the Epistles of Paul, which he marked out for public reading:

Priestly Directory, fourteen books, beginning: “Concerning the reading of the epistle of blessed ...” And many other things.

He was still flourishing among men under Frederick III, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1490. He may still be living.

Johannes Britannicus, born at Palazzolo, a town of the Brescian territory: a man most learned in secular studies and not ignorant of divine Scripture; [unclear] famous, an outstanding poet and splendid rhetorician, who among his own Brescians is today held in honor. By invaluable learning, teaching, and writings he makes them daily more renowned. He wrote many and various works, by which he makes his name known to posterity and venerable to those now living. Of these the following are reported:

A very celebrated work of commentary: On Persius, one book. On Statius, likewise one book. On Ovid’s Metamorphoses, one book. Likewise various letters. And many other things.

He is distinguished in the city of Brescia and composes many little works, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, and Pope Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord 1493.

Battista of Ferrara, of the Order of the Friars of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel: a man learned in the divine Scriptures and excellently trained in secular literature; outstanding in verse and prose, and skilled in both languages; in declaiming sermons to the people very celebrated and of almost divine talent. He wrote many excellent volumes, by which he makes himself useful to those now living and known to posterity. Of these the following are reported:

A most lucid work of histories from the times of Christ down to us, which he entitled Florida. Chronicle of his Order. On the Fall of the Roman Empire. On Mount Sinai. Life of Mechtild. Chronicle of Ferrara.

On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 129

Various sermons: three books. He published very many epigrams, and various ones, which we hope will soon be made public. He also translated from Greek into Latin several sermons of blessed John Chrysostom; and many other things unknown to us. He is still living at [Ferrara?], and is composing various works under Maximilian, most merciful king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1494.

Peter Brutus, Venetian by nation, bishop of Cattaro, certainly a man most learned in divine Scripture, excellently instructed in secular letters, outstanding in talent, eloquent in speech, distinguished in life and conduct, skilled in the Hebrew and Latin tongues, who, for the confirmation of the Christian faith, undertook many contests of disputations against the perfidious Jews, always as victor. Among other little works of his talent he wrote to the senate of Vicenza a very celebrated and notable work, abundantly furnished with authorities from the holy Scriptures:

Against the Jews: one book. “As I was reading the letters of very many.”

And certain other things.

He flourished under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1485. And I do not know whether he is still living.

Ubertinus, a cleric of Crescentino, a man most learned in secular letters, not ignorant of divine Scripture, a philosopher, rhetorician, distinguished poet, most skilled in both languages, outstanding in talent, eloquent in speech, who in the very celebrated university of Pavia lectured publicly for seven years on a stipend, with the greatest attention and profit of his hearers. He wrote many excellent little works, both in verse and in prose, of which the following are extant:

On the Letters of Cicero: sixteen books. “The letters of this volume.”

On the Duties of the same: three books. [unclear]

On the Metamorphoses of Naso: one book.

Also a book of letters: one book.

Many poems: one book.

He flourished under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1480. And I do not know whether he is still living.

William of Aachen, German by nation, a man learned in divine Scripture, not ignorant of secular philosophy, subtle in talent, scholastic in eloquence, distinguished in life and conduct, who formerly held the office of preacher in the church of Basel. He wrote many commendable little works, by which he commended his memory to posterity; from these, in the university of Erfurt, he publicly lectured on certain ones, with everyone’s attention and praise. He wrote:

On the Gospel of John: one book.

On the Canon of the Mass: one book.

On the Passion of the Lord: one book. “He handed Jesus over to their will.”

Disputed Questions: one book.

Itinerary of the Holy Land: one book.

Various sermons: one book.

And many other things.

He flourished under Emperor Frederick III and Sixtus IV, supreme pontiff, in the year of the Lord 1485. And I believe that he is still living.

Johannes de Lapide, German by nation, a monk of the Carthusian order of the house of Basel, a man most learned in divine Scripture, not ignorant of secular literature, outstanding in talent, eloquent in speech, distinguished in life and conduct. Having formerly obtained the mastership in the faculty of arts in the university of Paris, he governed in the same for several years; and, diligently pursuing the study of sacred letters by teaching, lecturing, and disputing, he deserved to be adorned with the doctoral dignity in the school of theologians. [unclear]

Book

Diuersi generis carminae. Et alia complura. Observans Nuenburgensis quondam auditor: uir in diuinis scripturis studiosus et Maximiliano Romanorũ rege: Georgij Molito/ erudit⁹:&amp; foecularis philofophiae nō ignarus:ingenio clarus:sermone scho lasticus:primũ Erfordiae:&amp;nũc in gymnasio Moguntino theologiam publice do/ cens:ac multos erudiens:Scripsit in ea facultate quaedam praeclara opuscula: qui/ bus nomẽ suũ notificauit.Equibus extat opus grande: In prologum bibliae: li.j Cogitanti mihi in prisciqꝫ. De eadẽ re:prosaice:li.j Nemo christianae religiõis. De misera hominis cõditiõe:li.j Inter multa ꝗbus se mens.

He first transferred to the University of Basel the doctrine of those Parisians who are called Realists; there he planted, strengthened, and increased it. He was also one of the chief initiators and founders of the Tübingen school. Finally, after freely resigning several benefices, he was called to a canonry and the office of preaching in the distinguished church of Basel; and at length, after a few years had passed, leaving everything for the love of Christ, he took the habit of the holy Carthusian order. He wrote many excellent little works, by which he made himself useful to those then living and memorable to those to come. Of these, we have obtained access to only a few. The following, however, are extant:

An Introduction to Grammar, one book. “Since grammar is [the art] of speaking correctly.”

A Dialogue on the Art of Punctuation, one book. “Student: Greetings, master.”

On Exponible Propositions, one treatise. “So that from youth in the art of logic.”

On the Art of Resolving Sophistical Arguments, one treatise. “Since for every science.”

An Explanation of All the Books of Aristotle’s Logic, one book. “To investigate and to discover.”

An Explanation of the Books of the Same Author’s Physics, one book. “The book of the Physics.”

An Explanation of the Six Books of the Same Author’s Metaphysics, one book. “Because first philosophy.”

On the Things Required for a Worthy Priest, one treatise. “Man to the image.”

A Resolver of Doubts Occurring Concerning the Mass, one treatise. “The greater the office.”

A Summary of the Passion of Jesus Christ, one treatise. “At night Jesus, being sorrowful.”

On the Ascension of the Lord, among the sermons of Meffret, one sermon. “Arise, O Lord.”

On Meffret’s Sermons concerning the Immaculate Conception, one treatise. “Since the Lord and Redeemer.”

Very many sermons, both to the clergy and to the people, one book.

Various orations and letters, one book.

Also several other things of which no mention is made here.

Moreover, he divided many books by various authors into treatises and chapters, placing summaries before each, by which what the writer’s intention is in them can clearly be known. Among these are Cicero’s books On Duties, On Friendship, On Old Age, and On the Dream of Scipio. Likewise the books of Aristotle’s Logic. The books of the same author On the Soul, and the books of the Metaphysics. Likewise the books of Ephrem the deacon. The books of John Chrysostom On Compunction of Heart. The book of Saint Augustine On Contrition of Heart; the book of the same author’s letters. And almost all the books of Saint Ambrose the bishop. He is still living in the Basel Charterhouse, and is composing various works; by his example and writings he calls many to holy studies, under Maximilian, most merciful king of the Romans, and the supreme pontiff Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord 1493.

Angelus de Clavasio, an Italian by birth, of the order of the Friars Minor of Saint Francis, a man devoted to and learned in the study of the divine scriptures, and a very celebrated jurist; outstanding in talent, renowned in eloquence, devout in life and conduct. He is also said to have produced certain excellent little works, by which he spread his name far and wide. Among these there is extant a notable summa on cases, very useful and necessary for simple confessors, and nevertheless for learned men who are occupied, now already dispersed everywhere, which he titles from the author’s name:

The Angelic Summa, one book. “Although the angelic spirits.”

Additions to the Same, one book.

And certain other things.

He completed this summa under Frederick III, emperor, and the supreme pontiff Sixtus IV. And I hear that he is still alive while Maximilian governs the kingdom of the Romans and Germans, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1493, the twelfth indiction.

Iason de Mayno, Milanese by homeland, ducal senator, a man most learned in both laws, and learned both in the divine scriptures and in the other secular disciplines [unclear].

263

Viuit adhuc Parisius apud sanctũ Maturinũ residens. On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 130

he says that he had before Pope Alexander VI (which circulates in print); I do not recall that any of these came into our hands. But, as I have learned for certain, he wrote elegantly:

On the title De actionibus in the Institutes, 1 book. Also on the Code, 9 books. On the Digest he wrote various things, 50 books. Orations, letters, and certain other things.

He is renowned today among the Milanese princes, in the highest esteem, under Maximilian, most illustrious king of the Romans, and Alexander VI, supreme pontiff, in the year of the Lord in which I wrote these things, 1493, indiction 11.

Laurentius Burellus of Dijon, of the order of the brothers of blessed Mary ever virgin of Mount Carmel, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, very excellently instructed in secular letters, outstanding in talent, distinguished in eloquence, practiced in verse and prose, wrote certain notable volumes in both kinds, by which he made his name known. Among these the following are reported: a very celebrated work in praise of Elijah, patriarch of the Carmelites, which he entitled:

Helias, 1 book. On the illustrious men of his order, 1 book. And very many others.

He is still living, in great esteem among his own, writing and composing many things, under Maximilian, most unconquered king of the Romans, and Alexander VI, supreme pontiff, in the year of the Lord 1494.

Christophorus Landinus, an Italian by nation, a citizen of Florence, a man especially learned in secular letters, not ignorant also of philosophy and sacred Scripture, for many years presided over the chair of the Muses and by public office taught poetry. Distinguished in talent, he wrote works held in great esteem by all, especially: commentaries on P. Vergilius Maro; likewise commentaries on Q. Horatius; Camaldulenses; Ethics.

He is reported still to flourish among his Florentines, whom he adorns with all the flowers of literature.

Jacobus of Bergamo, of the order of the brothers of Saint Augustine, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, nobly instructed in the disciplines of secular letters, outstanding in talent, eloquent in speech, distinguished in life and conduct, a very celebrated historiographer, wrote certain very lucid little works, by which he made posterity beholden to the memory of him. Among these there is extant a work of histories from the beginning of the world down to the years of the Lord 1486, a large and notable volume, which, bringing together material from diverse sources with much long labor, he entitled: Supplementum chronicarum, 11 books. Pro Ciceronis vestri [unclear]. Of the others I have learned nothing.

He is still living among his own people of Bergamo, in esteem, nearly sixty years old, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, and Pope Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord 1494.

Baptista de Sancto Blasio of Padua, a man very skilled in both laws, distinguished for the learning of the philosophers, subtle in talent and adorned with eloquence, who in the Paduan gymnasium publicly taught laws excellently, where he instructed a great number of pupils, wrote in that faculty certain notable little works, by which he showed the force of his talent to those present and to posterity. Among these I have read:

On dotal privileges, 1 book. “Since many things concerning dowries...” Also Correlatives, 1 book. “In this work of correlatives...” Questions on arbitration, [unclear] book. “In the name of Christ...” On the first part of the Decretals, 1 book. “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ...”

Et certa alia. Viuit adhuc in Italia multa et uaria scribens tam metro s prosa: sub Maximiliano Romano rege: & Alexandro papa sexto: Anno dñi Mill'. CCCC. XCIII. Obannes de keyberfberg: natio teutonicus: air in diuinis Icripturis stu- diosus et eruditus: & saecularis philosophia sno ignarus: ingenio praestans: uita et conuersatio praeclarus: declamator sermonũ celeberrimũ: qui in ca- thedrali ecclesia argentineli: a multis annis praedicatoris gerit officiũ: Scriptit no- nulla cõmendada opuscula: sed ad noticia nostrae lectionis adhuc minime uene- gunt: Ferunt aũt eius elegantes: Sermones ad populi: li. Orationes uariae ad clerus: li. Et quaedam alia. Magnis hic sumptibus et labore diuturno collegit opera lohannis Gerson: quorũ multa ex Gallia stand ad nos perduxit: diuident ea in tris partes ordine pulcher, rimo: ac tabula utile admodũ cõficiẽs: id totũ impressurae donauit. Viuit adhuc i ciuitate Germaniae Argentineli: ac uaria componit: sub Maximiliano Romanog rege clariffimo: Anno domini Mill'. CCCC. XCIII. Obannes Picus natione Italus Comes Mirandula et Cõcordiae dominus: uir omnis bonae literaturae studiosiffimus: & sicut praeclaro sanguine:ita diu/ no admodũ ingenio nobiliffimũ: magna familiae omnigenũ artium stipatũ caterua: cui quibũ liris et studũs latinis pariter hebraicũs et graecis palaestrũ exercet: dignus et optime meritũ cuius pfectionẽ musũ seuantũ: doctiffimũ nostra aetate phus est atqũ disputator acerrimũ: Scriptit stilo elegatiffimo nũnlla quũ aetas nũ tũ cõprobare: tũ uel maxime admirari habebit: quũ nomis et gloriae luũe memo/ ria sno indigne sempiterna reddidũt. De quũ extant quũ sã pdiere: Heptaplus sup principiũ Genesis. Item Nongẽtae cõcluiones philosophicae. Apologia. Item super psalmos: li. Et plura alia quũ nũdum cõspectũ nostro seũ exhibuere. Viuit adhuc hodie in ingeniosiorũ adolescentũ suorũ gregẽ apud Italos: neqũ altiora scribere: neqũ bũfa/ cere posteritati cẽstat: sub Alexandro sexto pontifice maximo: regeũ Romano, ru Maximiliano: anno quo haec scribimus Mill'. CCCC. XCIII. Obannes Capnion alias Reuchlin: natione teutonicus ex Phorcen oppũ i do Sueuia: legum imperialiũ doctor eximius: Illustriffũ comitis Eberbar/ di de wirtenberg consul cui facũdiffimũ: tum iuris fideiũ integerrimũ: om- nis antiquiffimũ philosophiaũ: & litteraturũ indagator sollertiffimũ. Triũ principi- paliũ linguarũ Hebraicũ scilicet silũ et Chaldaicũ: Graecũ pariter et latiniũ sinpres peritiffimũ. Gallicanũ etũ atqũ politioris linguaũ nostra uernacula suũ imprimis clarũ: Et ťa in diuinis Icripturũ secretariũ: ťũ in saeculariũ liris eruditiffimũ. Quinimo i om- ni genere doctũna haec stempestate praecipuũ: putũ qui graecoũ hebraorũ secre- ta mysteria multũs iã annis enixiffime penetrauit. Dignũ pfesto q solis liris: no etũ pstrepenți populari curiũ incũberet. Nullũ em nobũs no mo Italia: sed necũculũ quidũ nostrũ: buic tanto uiro pare obiũceret. Scriptit nũnlla opa quũ suũ memorũ ũi praesentibũ cõmendauit et posterũs. Ad eũm Vangionũ camerariũ Dalburgi: Dialogum in quo omia secreta phũa graeca hebraicũ et christiũnũ portentiffica uerba explicat: quem praescriplũ Capnion:uel de Verbo Mirifico: De praeexercitamẽtis rhetoriciũ: De diuersitate ţtuor idiomatũ graecaeling. Orationẽ funebrem in mortẽ Rudolphi agricolae.

Book C.

He also wrote other things. He completed these same works in the academy under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1480, indiction 13. And I believe that he is still alive.

[Marcus Antonius Sabellicus?], the most celebrated poet of all our age, adorning Venice with books by his learning, excellent in talent, eloquent in speech, skilled in both languages; to him Hermolaus Barbarus, the Venetian archbishop and patriarch of Aquileia, once composed a book on the precepts for writing history. He wrote, both in verse and in prose, certain distinguished volumes, by which he secured perpetual memory for his name among posterity. Of these I have seen the following: a very celebrated work addressed to the Venetian senate, containing, from the beginning of the city: History and Deeds of the Venetians, 34 books, beginning: “I, about to write from the city...” On the Antiquity of Aquileia [unclear], 6 books, beginning: “And if from all the writers...” On the Sontian Flood, a poem, one book, beginning: “The swift [river] pours forth from Illyrian [unclear]...” On the Sontian Slaughter, a poem, one book, beginning: “Whither, headlong Fortune, do you rush?” On the Carnic Fire, one book, beginning: “[unclear], night set forth on spread wheels...” On the Shipwreck of Peter’s Boat, one book, beginning: “The gracious vessel is tossed.” On the Inventors of Things and Arts, one book, beginning: “Among the pleasing things of study you are accustomed...” On the Origin of Udine, a poem, one book, beginning: “These things [unclear] on the ground...” In Praise of Mary, fourteen elegies, one book, beginning: “The gracious day of the Virgin [unclear].” I have seen nothing of the rest. He is renowned today among the Venetians in very high esteem, composing many and various things, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, and Pope Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord in which we write this, 1494.

Hubertus Leonardus, bishop of Dariensis, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man learned in divine scriptures, not ignorant of secular literature, outstanding in talent, famous for eloquence, who once taught theology with distinction in the Paris academy, wrote many highly commendable little works, by which he made his name known with glory. Of these the following are reported: On the Genealogy of the Noble Franks and Their Deeds, to Louis, bishop of Liege, one book. On the Gospel of Luke, one book. On the Governance of Princes, three books. On Ecclesiastical Immunity, three books. Against the Heretics of Nivelles, one book. Various Sermons, one book. A Notable Lenten Collection, one book. And many other things. When he was inquisitor of heretical depravity against certain heretics of Nivelles through the diocese of Liege, he confuted and defeated them with the sword of the Holy Spirit, writing the aforesaid very celebrated work, containing twenty-eight principal propositions; in it, vigorously and eloquently attacking just as many erroneous articles of theirs, he rejected them. He flourished in Germany, from which he came, under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Innocent VIII, in the year of the Lord 1490. And I believe that he is still alive.

Gabriel Biel, German by nation, of the order of those who call themselves Brothers of the Common Life, or those living in common, a man learned in divine scriptures, excellently taught in secular philosophy, outstanding in talent, distinguished in life and conduct, who presided over the academy of Tubingen from the beginning of its foundation for many years, where he instructed many disciples both in philosophy and in sacred letters, wrote certain little works of authority not to be despised, by which he made his name known. Of these, [unclear] are regularly read in the aforesaid academy:

DE SCRIPTORIBVS ECCLESIATICIS Fol.i34 li. Epistolas quoqꝫ et oratiōes scholasticas sine numero plures. Epigrāmaton elegiarū: li.j Epistolas quoqꝫ oratiōes scholasticae sine numeroplares. Multa praeterea utilitati nostrae cõmuni e graeco in latinũ uertit opuscula: Xeno- phontis apologiã ꝓ Socrate:Nestoriũ haerericũ: Confessionẽ Cypriani: Proclum de beata uirgine: Luciani aliquos mortuorũ dialogos: Eiusdē dialogũ de concilio deorũ: Monomachiã Iliados Homeri de Paridis Menelai duello in lingua Ger- manica metrice. Epiphaniũ de uita morte ꝓphetarũ. Maximũ Tyriũ Platoni/ cũ philosophũ: in or̃one: Si deus fecit bona: unde ueniant mala. Viuit usqƺ hodie litteris incubens sub Maximiliano rege: principeqƺ suo Eberhardo de wirtẽberg: cuiꝰ illustre nomen: insignis ille Capnion ingenio suo illustrius reddit: Anno quo haec scribimus Mill'.CCCC.XCIIII. Onradus Leontorius: vulgariter de Leonberg: natioe teutonicus : mona- chus coenobij Mulbronnensis: ordinis Cisterciensis: uir ĩ diuinis scripturis studiosus eruditus: in saecularib⁹ egregie doctus: philosphus: orator poeta non abijciēdus: triũ (ut ferunt) principaliũ linguarũ peritus: ingenio subtı- lis disertus eloquio: Scripsit metro prosa nonnulla opuscula: quibus nomẽ suũ notificauit. On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 131

On the canon of the Mass, one book. On the passion of the Lord, he wrote one book. Also various sermons, one book. And certain other things.

He is distinguished today, an old man and advanced in age, at the court of the count of Württemberg, in the highest esteem; and he is said to be writing certain things, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, and Pope Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1494.

Georgius of Gemmingen, a German by nation, provost and canon of the renowned church of Speyer, a learned and noble man, professor of both laws and a most celebrated interpreter, and in the other disciplines of the liberal arts excellently skilled, an outstanding philosopher and rhetorician, subtle in talent and eloquent in speech, excellent in verse and prose: he wrote certain distinguished little works, in which, laudably exercising his talent, he also made his name known to posterity. Yet he conceals what he writes, so that he may avoid the appearance of empty glory, or may correct what he has written with the file of a more mature examination. Of these, however, the following have become known to us:

On the method of duel, one book. On engines of war, one book. On the care of soldiers’ horses, one book. Certain orations.

In addition, he has produced many letters, both to me and to others; from these, how much he is worth, both in learning and in eloquence, and also in experience of many matters, is easily perceived by the person who reads them. He is distinguished, in manly age, in the city of Speyer, intent upon sacred letters and writing various things, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, and Alexander VI, supreme pontiff, in the year of the Lord 1495.

Johannes Venetus, of the Carthusian order, of the house of Saint Andrew the Apostle de Litore, near Venice, a man zealous and learned in the divine scriptures, excellent in talent, devout in life and conduct, and an outstanding cultivator of regular observance: he wrote, for the instruction of the simple, little works not to be despised, by which he made his name known. Of these there is an excellent work, which he entitled:

Know Thyself, three books; “Since nothing [unclear], nothing...” On Patience and Humility, one book; “Brothers most dear in Christ...” The Mirror of the Dying, three books; “After the manner of good parents...” Also The Crown of Old Men, one book; “While the human mind...” Various Sermons, one book. Several devout letters. And certain other things.

He flourished at Venice under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV; he completed the works written above in the year of the Lord 1482, in the thirteenth indiction. And I am uncertain whether he is still living.

Johannes of Mylbach, a German by nation, a man zealous and learned in the divine scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy either, distinguished in talent, scholastic in speech, who formerly taught theology gloriously for a long time in the school of Erfurt, and instructed very many disciples in that faculty: he wrote some distinguished little works, in which he magnificently exercised his talent and commended knowledge of himself to posterity. Among these he regularly lectures on:

On the Epistles of Paul, fourteen books. Various Sermons, one book. In Praise of Saint Jerome, one book. Various Questions. And certain other things.

He is distinguished at Erfurt, an old and feeble man, a prebendary in the monastery of Saint Peter, in the year of the Lord

In quo cauṣam et radice omniũ stul- ticiarum adeo eleganter expressit: mores hominũ carpit: & quaedã salutaria reme- dia lingulis tradit: ut nó iure stultorũ libru: sed divinã potius satyrã opus illud ap- pellaslet. Acobus Vymphelingus Sletstetelũs:natiũe teutonicus: psbyter ecclesiae Spireũs:uir i divinis scripturis eruditifũm?: & in saeculariũ iiris egregie do/

[of the Lord?] in which we write these things: 1493.

Johannes de Arundine, a German by nation, bishop of [Usbitensis?], of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, vicar in pontifical matters of David of Burgundy, bishop of Utrecht; a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, an outstanding preacher of sermons, subtle in intellect, distinguished in life and conduct. He wrote many excellent volumes, by which he made his name known. Of these the following are reported:

A notable lecture On the Book of Wisdom, one book. On Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, one book. Sermons on the Blessed Immaculate One, one book. Sermons for the season, one book. Sermons on the saints, one book. And certain others.

He flourished at Utrecht, under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Innocent VIII, in the year of the Lord 1490. And I believe that he is still alive.

Georgius Valla of Piacenza, a man most learned in every respect, a very celebrated rhetorician and poet, excellent in intellect and eloquent in speech, who, now adorning all Italy with his learning, teaches both languages most brilliantly at Venice. He wrote many excellent volumes, by whose elegance and usefulness he may deservedly feel that learned men everywhere are indebted and bound to him. Of these the following are extant:

On orthography, one book. On the quantity of syllables, one book. On the figures of orators and poets, one book. On Cicero’s On the Universe, one book. Plato’s book called Timaeus. On the same author’s On Fate, one book. Cicero’s work On Fate. On the book of the Topics of the same author, one book. A particularly good observation. On the Rhetoric to Herennius, one book. “Long ago I had looked ahead.” On Juvenal, one book. On Horace’s Poetics, one book. On the method of disputing, one book. On things to be sought and avoided, one book. A book of letters to various persons. Various orations. And many other works.

He translated from Greek into Latin Aristotle’s little work On Virtue; also two books of the same author’s Ethics; likewise the work of Nemesius, the Christian philosopher, On the Nature of Man; also the little book of Athenagoras, a very acute philosopher, On the Resurrection; likewise the book of dialectic of Bristo; in addition, the treatise of Galen the physician On the Sects of Physicians; the same author’s Introduction to Medicine; also four books of the Problems of Alexander; and many other works.

Johannes Camerarius of Dalburg, bishop of Worms, a German by nation, a very celebrated jurist and most learned both in divine Scriptures and in secular letters; once a pupil of Rudolf Agricola, that most learned man; skilled in both languages, a very distinguished rhetorician and poet, subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, and notable for much experience of affairs, magnificently ennobling the nobility of his lineage by his character and learning. He has written and is writing, both in verse and in prose, certain little works of excellent talent, which he has not yet allowed to come to light, because, occupied with the affairs of the commonwealth, he has not been able to complete them quite as he had intended. Yet some of these have become known to us:

A Sapphic poem On the death of Rudolf Agricola, one book. Also On Coinage, one book. An oration before Pope Innocent VIII, one book.

On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 132

Various poems and orations; and several very elegant letters.

He is distinguished today, in mature age, in the see of the church of Worms, a prelate worthy of God, and he is writing various works, under Maximilian, most gracious king of the Romans, and the supreme pontiff Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things concerning him, 1494.

Baptista Guarinus of Verona, son of Guarinus, a most learned man, of whom we have made mention in his proper place: certainly a man not inferior to his father, but most learned in every branch of letters and in the discipline of the liberal arts, a philosopher, orator, and poet most celebrated among all, very skilled in the Greek and Latin languages and very eloquent in both. He wrote and translated many excellent little works, by which he commends to those now living and to posterity the almost divine force and keenness of his talent. Among these the following are reported:

A very beautiful work of dialogues. On the Epicurean sect, one book. On the order of teaching, one book. On administering a kingdom, one book. On Cicero’s Letters, one book. On Ovid’s Fasti, one book. On Lucan’s Pharsalia, one book. On the poet Catullus, one book. Letters to various persons, one book. Several orations also, one book. And poems of various kinds.

He translated the following into Latin: from Xenophon, the Praise of Agesilaus, which he dedicated to Hermolaus Barbarus the elder, bishop of Verona; also certain orations of Demosthenes and of Dio the historian; and also some orations of Gregory Nazianzen to Christ [and] Mary. He published and translated many other things besides, which have not come to my knowledge. He is distinguished to this day at Ferrara, where, succeeding his father, he has now for thirty-three years taught both languages most brilliantly, and he is writing various works, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, and Pope Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1494, in the twelfth indiction. He himself has a son learned in Greek and Latin, following the discipline of his forefathers.

Angelus Politianus, a man skilled in every respect and most learned, a celebrated grammarian, a distinguished philosopher, orator, and poet, perfectly equipped in Greek and Latin eloquence, excellent in talent, who for a long time illuminated Italy by his learning and teaching. He wrote various excellent volumes, by which he commended the memory of his name to posterity. Among these the following are reported:

Certain Centuries, one book. On the errors of the Latin language, one book. Various letters to various persons, one book.

And he is said to have written certain other things, which have not come to my knowledge. This man dared to present Homer’s Iliad in verse for Latins to read. He is still distinguished in Italy, as I have learned, writing various works, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, and Alexander VI, supreme pontiff, in the year of the Lord 1494.

Baptista Mantuanus, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, second to none in knowledge of secular letters, doctor of sacred theology, distinguished philosopher, most celebrated poet and orator, excellent in talent, eloquent in speech, outstanding in life and conduct, an ornament of the Latin language, a renowned interpreter of Greek, excellent in verse and prose. He wrote many outstanding volumes in both styles, by which he acquired for his name a celebrated fame throughout the whole Christian world. Of these the following are reported:

To his father:

Georgius Molitor, an Observant of Neuenburg, formerly a hearer, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular philosophy, distinguished in talent, scholastic in speech, first publicly teaching theology at Erfurt and now in the gymnasium of Mainz, and instructing many, wrote certain excellent little works in that faculty, by which he made his name known. Of these there is extant a large work:

On the prologue of the Bible, one book. As I was thinking, in ancient and [unclear].

Many conferences to the clergy, one book. Most reverend father in Christ.

On the value of masses, one book. Various questions.

And certain other things.

He is flourishing in manhood in the gymnasium of Mainz, teaching theology in ordinary course and composing various works, under Maximilian, the most illustrious king of the Romans, and the supreme pontiff Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord in which we are writing these things, [1493?].

Robertus Gaguinus, a Frenchman by nation, minister general of the Order of the Holy Trinity, an outstanding doctor of Decrees, and most learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, a distinguished poet and a most eloquent orator, who often left the Italians stunned by his eloquence, excellent in talent, devout in life and conduct, wrote many excellent little works in both kinds, by which he made his name known far and wide. Of these the following are extant. A work in distinguished verse to Arnoldus Bostius, a Carmelite living at Ghent, against Vincentius de Castronovo, of the Order of Preachers:

On the conception of holy Mary, one book. My mind is [unclear] you.

On the same subject, in prose, one book. No one of the Christian religion.

On the art of versifying: three books, "The things concerning the making of verses..." Many very elegant orations: one book. Also a book of letters: one book. Countless epigrams. And many other works.

He is still living at Paris, residing at Saint-Mathurin. And day by day he writes various works to be published, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, and Alexander VI, supreme pontiff, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1494.

Darynghus Sifridi Sinnama, born at Hagis in Frisia, who is commonly called Hermannus, German by nation, a very celebrated professor and interpreter of both laws, eminently learned both in divine Scripture and in secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, prompt and firm in counsel, whose authority is held in great esteem among the princes and prelates of the churches: in the university of Cologne, by teaching, writing, and giving counsel, he easily holds the first place. Among other things he wrote a great and very celebrated work, explaining legal titles with the utmost clarity, very useful and necessary for all beginning to study in both laws or in one of them:

On the titles of the Code: twelve books, "And if verbosity without [unclear]..." On the title of the Old Digest: twenty-four books, "But what new [unclear]..." On the title of the Infortiatum: fourteen books, "It will have to be known here in..." On the title of the New Digest: twelve books, "Because there are seven parts..." On the title of the Authenticae: one book, "Who the constitutions..." On the usages of fiefs: one book, "Because this book of fiefs..." On the Peace of Constance: one book, "Because the emperor Frederick..." On the title of the Institutes: four books, "Because from this book..." On the title of the Decretals: five books, "All, as the emperor says..." Certain other works are extant.

He is living in manhood in the city of Cologne, illuminating it by that learning of his, under Maximilian, most illustrious king of the Romans, and Alexander VI, supreme pontiff, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1494, in the twelfth indiction.

Raphael Regius, Italian by nation, a man most learned in every respect, a distinguished philosopher, a celebrated poet, an eminent orator, skilled in both languages, excellent in intellect, eloquent in speech, who in the university of Padua acquired the greatest praises for his learning by teaching, disputing, and composing. He is said to have fashioned many excellent little works, by which he made his name and intellect known with great glory. Of these the following are extant:

Corrections on Quintilian: one book, "Great-hearted men are wont kindly..." On the praises of eloquence: one book, "If anyone ever of an excellent work..." On one letter of Pliny: one book, "In the inscription of this work..." Against Johannes Calphurnius: one book, "Although by the very grave..." A dialogue against the same: one book, "Yesterday a crowd of boys [unclear]..." Various orations. Also many letters. And many other works.

He is still living at Padua, as I have learned, and is composing various works, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, and Alexander VI, supreme pontiff, in the year of the Lord 1494.

Laurentius Bonincontrius, an eminent philosopher and astronomer, and excellently learned in the other disciplines of the liberal arts, outstanding in intellect, distinguished in eloquence, strong in verse and prose. He is said to have fashioned many excellent little works, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of many; but I have not yet been able to see any of them. There is said, however, to be an eminent work of his for the cycle of the year:

Entitled Fasti: one book. And certain commentaries.

And certain other works.

He is still living in Italy, writing many and various things both in verse and in prose, under Maximilian, King of the Romans, and Pope Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord 1493.

Johannes of Kaysersberg, a German by nation, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular philosophy, outstanding in talent, distinguished in life and conduct, a very celebrated declaimer of sermons, who for many years has held the office of preacher in the cathedral church of Strasbourg. He has written some commendable little works, but they have not yet come to the notice of our reading. They report, however, that the following elegant works are his:

Sermons to the People, one book. Various Addresses to the Clergy, one book. And certain other works.

This man, at great expense and with long labor, collected the works of Johannes Gerson, many of which he brought to us from France; dividing them into three parts in a very fine order, and preparing a very useful table, he gave the whole to the press. He is still living in the German city of Strasbourg, and composes various works, under the most renowned Maximilian, King of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 1493.

Johannes Pico, an Italian by nation, Count of Mirandola and lord of Concordia, a man most devoted to every kind of good letters, and, as he was most noble by illustrious blood, so also by a truly divine talent; surrounded by a great retinue [unclear] of arts of every kind, with whom he exercises the arena of books and studies, Latin as well as Hebrew and Greek; worthy and most deserving, whose perfection the Muses [unclear]. He is the most learned philosopher of our age and a very acute disputant. He has written in a most elegant style some works which the age will both approve and especially admire, since they have not unworthily made the memory of his name and glory everlasting. Of him there are extant the following, which have already appeared:

Heptaplus on the Beginning of Genesis. Also Nine Hundred Philosophical Conclusions. Apology. Also On the Psalms, one book.

And several other works which have not yet presented themselves to our sight. He is still living today among the Italians in the company of his more gifted young men, and he does not cease either to write loftier things or to benefit posterity, under Alexander VI, supreme pontiff, Maximilian, King of the Romans, in the year in which we write these things, 1493.

Johannes Capnion, otherwise Reuchlin, a German by nation, from the town of Pforzheim in Swabia, an excellent doctor of imperial law, a most eloquent counselor of the most illustrious Count Eberhard of Württemberg, and at the same time of the utmost integrity in law and faith; a most skilled investigator of all the most ancient philosophies and literatures. He was always most expert in the three principal languages, namely Hebrew together with Chaldean, and likewise Greek and Latin. He was also especially distinguished in French and in his own more polished vernacular tongue; and most learned both in the secrets of the divine Scriptures and in secular books. Indeed, in every kind of learning he is foremost in this age, as one who for many years has most earnestly penetrated the secret mysteries of the Greeks and Hebrews. Worthy indeed to devote himself to books alone, and not also to the noisy public court. For not only Italy, but not even our age, could offer us anyone equal to so great a man. He has written some works by which he has commended his memory to those now living and to posterity:

A dialogue addressed to Dalberg, chamberlain of the Vangiones, in which he explains all the secret, wonder-working words of Greek, Hebrew, and Christian philosophy; he entitled it Capnion, or On the Wonder-Working Word. On Rhetorical Preliminary Exercises. On the Diversity of the Four Idioms of the Greek Language. A funeral oration on the death of Rudolf Agricola.

Also letters and scholastic orations, more than can be numbered. Of epigrams and elegies: one book. Also scholastic letters and orations, more than can be numbered.

Moreover he translated many little works from Greek into Latin for our common benefit: Xenophon’s Apology for Socrates; Nestorius the Heretic; the Confession of Cyprian; Proclus On the Blessed Virgin; some of Lucian’s Dialogues of the Dead; a dialogue of the same author On the Council of the Gods; the Monomachia from Homer’s Iliad, on the duel of Paris and Menelaus, in the German language, in verse; Epiphanius On the Life and Death of the Prophets; Maximus of Tyre, the Platonic philosopher, in the oration: If God Made Good Things, Whence Do Evils Come? He lives to this day, devoted to letters, under Maximilian the king, and under his own prince Eberhard of Württemberg, whose illustrious name that distinguished Capnion renders still more illustrious by his talent, in the year in which we write these things, 1494.

Conradus Leontorius, commonly called von Leonberg, of German nation, a monk of the monastery of Maulbronn, of the Cistercian order, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, excellently taught in secular matters, a philosopher, an orator, and a poet not to be rejected, skilled, as they say, in the three principal languages, subtle in talent and eloquent in speech, wrote some little works in verse and prose, by which he made his name known. Of these there is extant a volume: Letters to various persons: one book. Various orations. Many poems. And certain other things. He lives to this day among the Cistercians, and steadily continues in study under Maximilian, most renowned king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 1304, indiction 12.

Conradus Celtis Protucius, of German nation, born from Franconia in Germany, a man most learned in every respect, a distinguished philosopher, a fluent orator, an outstanding astronomer and cosmographer, a laureate poet, also not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, skilled in both languages, excellent in talent, eloquent in speech, wrote certain very fine little works, both in verse and in prose, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Of these he once read the following to me. To Maximilian, most renowned king of the Romans, on both rhetorical works of Marcus Tullius Cicero: An epitome, that is, an abridgment: one book. “Who in an assembly something.” On the Praises of Eloquence: one book. “The Morini celebrate with eternal [unclear].” On the Art of Versifying: one book. “Most illustrious prince, having received.” On Composing Letters: one book. “A letter or [unclear] is [unclear].” On the Situation of Nuremberg: one book. “When recently, to relax my mind.” A Sarmatian journey: one book. “To which he gave the name [unclear].” Poems: three books. “As often the proof of learned men.” Of loves which according to the four hidden [unclear] are inscribed: three books. “To write the things fated for our [unclear].” A panegyric to the duke of Bavaria: one book. “To attempt Italian lyres.” On the Life of Saint Sebald: one poem. “Offspring of royal stock.” The situation of Germany: one book. “About to write Germany.” Various orations: one book. He published many most elegant letters to various persons in verse and prose, and various epigrams; in cosmography, of which he is very knowledgeable, he wrote various things, which we trust will hereafter come to light. He is still living, being thirty-five years of age, and will write various things, under Maximilian, most illustrious king of the Romans, and the supreme pontiff Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1494.

Petrus Bonomus of Trieste, protonotary of the imperial court, a man most learned in the Latin language, in composing poems of every kind both very ready and very practiced, as one from whose storehouse the tuneful Muses pour forth, and for that reason of great name and most celebrated fame, wrote very many things in prose

Sebastianus Titio, otherwise Brant, of Strasbourg, German by nation, a distinguished professor of both laws, and excellently learned both in divine Scripture and in the other disciplines of secular literature, not moderately skilled in poetry, subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, outstanding in counsel and action, who by his learning and nightly studies wonderfully adorns Basel, the renowned city of Germany. He wrote, both in verse and in prose, certain little works of by no means contemptible reading, by which he made his name well known. Of these there are extant:

Besides these, with wonderful art and talent he compiled, in the common and vernacular language, a little book which he called The Ship of Narragonia. In it he so elegantly expressed the cause and root of all follies, censured the morals of men, and handed on certain salutary remedies to each person, that one would rightly call that work not the book of fools, but rather a divine satire. For I do not know whether anything more salutary for the uses of the present age, or more delightful, could be read. They say that he is striving greatly so that this same work may soon appear also in Latin, both in verse and in prose. He is still living at Basel, being 35 years of age, and printers make very great use of his work and industry in embellishing their books. For he writes various things under Maximilian, king of the Romans; since, being singularly diligent, he has composed several very charming poems about him and to him, even secret ones, as they say, in the year in which we write these things, 1493.

Jacobus Wimphelingus of Sélestat, German by nation, priest of the church of Speyer, a man most learned in divine Scripture and excellently taught in secular
